## Buddha Ratana
## Chapter 16
## The Arrival of the Two Wanderers, Upatissa and Kolita (the Future Chief Disciples), at the Buddha
(When the Exalted One arrived at the city of Rājagaha, King Suddhodana, having heard the news, began sending ministers with a thousand men each to invite the Exalted One to the royal capital, starting from around the full moon of Phusya (Pyatho). If this matter were written now, it would be difficult to interject the story of the two Chief Disciples, therefore...)
2:
(...I shall first present a brief account related to those two Chief Disciples.)
The time was about half a month after the Exalted One had arrived at Rājagaha, around the 1st waxing day of the month of Tabodwe. At that time, the great teacher Sañjaya the Wanderer (Sañjaya Paribbājaka) was residing in Rājagaha together with a retinue of two hundred and fifty wanderer disciples. During this period, Upatissa the Wanderer, the future Venerable Sāriputta, and Kolita the Wanderer, the future Venerable Mahā Moggallāna, were practicing the life of wanderers as disciples under the great teacher Sañjaya.*
Within two or three days of arriving at the teacher Sañjaya’s place, the two friends, Upatissa and Kolita, had reached the end of and mastered that teacher’s doctrine and practice. Finding no sight or realization of the Deathless Nibbāna in Sañjaya’s doctrine and practice, they made a pact: "Friend, this doctrine and practice of the teacher Sañjaya is empty. It has no essence. From now on, whoever among the two of us first attains and realizes the Deathless Nibbāna shall inform the one who has not yet attained or realized it."
When the 1st waxing day of Tabodwe arrived, about half a month after the Exalted One’s arrival in Rājagaha, the Venerable Assaji, one of the group of five monks (Pañcavaggī), having adjusted his robes in the morning and taking his bowl and double-robe, entered the city of Rājagaha for alms with a graceful deportment—in advancing, receding, looking ahead, looking aside,
* The detailed story of Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahā Moggallāna will be written upon reaching the chapter on the Saṅgha Ratana.
3:
bending, and stretching his limbs—with downcast eyes looking about a plow’s length ahead, and with a serene manner.
When Upatissa the Wanderer, the future Venerable Sāriputta, saw the Venerable Assaji entering Rājagaha for alms with such a serene deportment, the thought arose in Upatissa’s mind:
“This monk must surely be one of those who have reached the path and fruit of Arahantship in this world. It would be well if I were to approach this monk and ask: ‘Friend, under whom have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?’”
Then, Upatissa further thought:
“It is not yet the time to question this monk; he is still entering the city for alms. We two friends, who long for the Deathless Nibbāna, are seeking to personally realize that Nibbāna which we have inferred by reasoning: ‘If there is death, there must also be the Deathless Nibbāna.’ It would be well if I were to follow closely behind this monk, step by step.”
Thinking thus, he followed the Venerable Assaji closely without losing sight of him.
When Upatissa the Wanderer perceived that the Venerable Assaji had finished his alms-round and wished to sit down in a certain place,
4:
he spread out the small stool (pīṭha) that he carried as a wanderer’s utensil and offered it. After the Elder had finished his meal, Upatissa also offered water from his own water-jug. Having thus performed the duties toward a teacher, and after the Elder had finished his meal, he exchanged pleasant and polite greetings with him and asked:
“Friend, your faculties such as eyes, ears, and nose are very serene. Your complexion is pure, bright, and flawless. Friend, under whom have you gone forth? Who is your teacher? Whose Dhamma do you profess?”
Then the Venerable Assaji replied: “Friend, there is the Great Samana, a son of the Sakyans, who went forth from the Sakyan clan. I have gone forth under that Exalted One. That Exalted One is my teacher. I profess the Dhamma of that Exalted One.” When he said this, Upatissa the Wanderer asked again: “What is your teacher’s doctrine? What does he usually preach?” Then the Venerable Assaji thought: “These wanderers are those who hold views contrary to the Sāsana. I shall clearly show the depth and subtlety of the Sāsana to this Upatissa the Wanderer.” Wishing to make it clear that he himself was but a junior monk and could not yet explain extensively, he said: “Friend, I am but a junior monk; it has not been long since I went forth. I have only recently arrived in this Sāsana.
5:
(Therefore) I am not able to preach the Dhamma to you in detail. However, I can preach the essential meaning to you in brief.”
Then Upatissa the Wanderer, the future Venerable Sāriputta, thought: “I am a wise wanderer named Upatissa. Whether you preach a little or a lot according to your ability, it is my responsibility alone to expand and understand the Dhamma preached by the Venerable One through hundreds and thousands of methods.” He then said to the Venerable Assaji:
“Let it be, friend. Whether it be little or much, please preach it. (In doing so) please preach only the essential meaning to me. I wish to hear only the essential meaning. What use are many words, texts, syllables, and grammar to me?”
Thus addressed, the Venerable Assaji recited this verse to Upatissa the Wanderer:
Ye dhammā hetuppabhavā,
tesaṃ hetuṃ tathāgato āha.
tesañca yo nirodho,
evaṃ vādī mahāsamaṇo.
(Āvuso = Friend.) Ye dhammā = Those phenomena of the truth of suffering, namely the five aggregates. Hetuppabhavā = Have their origin and root cause in the truth of the origin, namely craving and greed.
6:
(Te ca = And those five aggregates of the truth of suffering.) Tesaṃ = Of those five aggregates of the truth of suffering. Hetuṃ ca = And their cause, the truth of the origin, namely craving and greed. Tesaṃ = Of those two truths of suffering and origin. Yo nirodho = That which is their cessation and the means to their cessation, namely the truth of cessation and the truth of the path. (Atthi = exists. Tañca = And those two truths of cessation and path.) Tathāgato = Our teacher, the Exalted One. Āha = Has analyzed and preached. Mahāsamaṇo = Our teacher, the Exalted One, who is the noble monk, the supreme of the three worlds. Evaṃvādī = Thus holds the pure doctrine of Vibhajja, which distinguishes and reveals the four noble truths.
Thus he preached the Dhamma discourse, which is full of the essential meaning of the four noble truths.
As soon as Upatissa the Wanderer heard the first half of the verse of this Dhamma discourse, he was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). He finished listening to the latter half of the verse after becoming a Stream-enterer. Then Upatissa the Wanderer, the future Venerable Sāriputta, recited this verse:
Es’eva dhammo yadi tāvad’eva,
paccabyatha padam asokaṃ.
adiṭṭhaṃ abbhatītaṃ,
bahukehi kappanahutehi.
(Bhante = Venerable Sir.) Tāvad’eva = Even by this much, reaching the first Fruit of Stream-entry. Pattabbaṃ = Should be attained by one’s own direct knowledge. Yadi hoti = If it be so, Dhammo = the Dhamma that we two friends have been searching for is:
7:
Es’eva = this very Dhamma. (Tumhe = You, Venerable Sirs.) Asokaṃ = The sorrowless state. Padaṃ = Nibbāna. Paccabyatha = Have clearly realized. Amhehi = By us. Idaṃ padaṃ = This Nibbāna. Adiṭṭhaṃ = Not having been clearly realized. Bahukehi kappanahutehi = For many hundreds of thousands of aeons. Abbhatītaṃ = Time has passed and been wasted in great loss.
Reciting this verse, he spoke of how he had suffered great loss for a long time. Then, before reaching the higher paths and fruits, Upatissa the Wanderer thought: “There must be further special reasons in this supramundane Dhamma.” He then asked the Venerable Assaji: “Venerable Sir, let it be for now. Do not preach the Dhamma discourse further. Where does our teacher, the Exalted One, reside at this time?” The Venerable Assaji replied: “Friend, the Exalted One resides at the Veluvana Monastery.” Upatissa then said: “Venerable Sir, if that is so, please go ahead. I have a friend remaining. We have made a pact with each other: ‘Whoever first realizes the Deathless shall tell the other.’ (Therefore) I shall fulfill that promise and then, bringing my friend, I will follow the path you have taken to the presence of the Exalted One.”
8:
Having prostrated at the Elder’s feet with the fivefold touching, he circumambulated the Venerable Assaji three times to the right, sent him on his way first, and then headed toward the wanderers’ monastery.
## Kolita the Wanderer Attains Stream-entry
At that time, Kolita the Wanderer saw Upatissa the Wanderer coming from afar and thought: “Today, my friend’s face is like no other day. Surely my friend must have attained and realized the Deathless Nibbāna.” He then asked Upatissa: “Friend, your faculties such as eyes, ears, and nose are very serene. Your complexion is pure, bright, and flawless. Friend, how is it? Have you attained the Deathless Nibbāna?” When Upatissa replied: “Yes, friend, I have attained the Deathless Nibbāna,” Kolita the Wanderer asked again: “Friend, in what manner did you attain the Deathless Nibbāna?” Then Upatissa the Wanderer recounted in detail the circumstances of his meeting with the Venerable Assaji and preached the same verse beginning with 'Ye dhammā hetuppabhavā' to Kolita the Wanderer. At the end of the verse, Kolita the Wanderer was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry and asked Upatissa: “Friend Upatissa, where does our teacher, the Exalted One, reside at this time?” Upatissa replied: “Friend Kolita, our teacher, the Venerable Assaji, told me that our teacher, the Exalted One, is currently residing at the Veluvana Monastery.”
9:
9
The wanderer Kolita (being quick-tempered and impulsive) said, "Friend, if that is so, let us go to the Exalted One. That Glorious Buddha is our master and great benefactor."
## Going to the Disciple Wanderers and the Teacher Sañjaya
Then, the wanderer Upatissa, the future Venerable Sāriputta, (being one who considers subordinates) said, "Friend, these two hundred and fifty wanderers live in this monastery depending on us and always looking up to us. Let us inform these two hundred and fifty wanderers as well; only then can they act according to their own wishes." Thus he spoke with patience and long-term consideration. Furthermore, as one who always respects and honors his teachers, he said, "Friend Kolita, let us also tell our teacher, the wanderer Sañjaya, about the Deathless Nibbāna, the Truth that we have attained and realized. If he is a wise man, he too will believe us and follow us to the Exalted One. Upon hearing the Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas, he will penetrate and realize the Path and Fruition." After saying this, the two friends first went to the disciple wanderers and said to those two hundred and fifty wanderers, "Friends, we are going to the Exalted One. That Glorious Buddha is our master and great benefactor."
The two hundred and fifty disciple wanderers also said, "Sirs, we live depending on you and always looking up to you..."
10:
...always looking up to you. If you two practice the holy life under the Blessed One, we all shall also practice the holy life under the Blessed One."

Then the two friends went to the teacher Sañjaya and invited him three times to go to the Blessed One together, but they did not succeed. Finally, Sañjaya asked, "My dears, in this world, are there more fools or more wise people?" When they answered, "Teacher, in this world, fools are many and the wise are very few," Sañjaya said, "My dears, if that is so, let the wise go to the wise Recluse Gotama. Let the fools come to me, the foolish one. You go; I cannot follow by any means." Having spoken these final, decisive words, the two friends took their two hundred and fifty disciple wanderers and went to the Veḷuvana Monastery where the Blessed One was residing.

As the two friends, Upatissa and Kolita, led the way with the two hundred and fifty disciple wanderers to the Veḷuvana Monastery, Sañjaya's assembly was split. The entire monastery of the wanderers became empty. Looking at his deserted monastery, Sañjaya was consumed by the inner fire of grief, and hot blood gushed from his mouth.
11:
At that time, the Blessed One was sitting gracefully in the midst of the assembly, preaching the Dhamma. He saw from afar the two friends, Upatissa and Kolita, coming toward the Veḷuvana Monastery together with the two hundred and fifty disciple wanderers. He then addressed the monks who were listening to the Dhamma in his presence:

"Monks, (look there) the two friends Kolita and Upatissa are coming to me. These two will be my pair of Chief Disciples, the left-hand and right-hand disciples."

Then the two friends, along with the two hundred and fifty disciple wanderers, approached the Blessed One and prostrated themselves, bowing their heads at the feet of the Blessed One.

## Becoming Ehi Bhikkhu Monks

Having respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One, they requested the going forth and full ordination, saying, "Exalted Buddha, may we receive the going forth in the presence of the Blessed One; may we receive the full ordination."

Then the Blessed One, in the same manner as before, called them with "Etha Bhikkhavo," saying, "Come, monks! Receive the going forth and full ordination you have requested. The Dhamma is well-expounded by me. Practice the holy life, which is the Sasana of the Threefold Training, to make an end of suffering."
12:
As soon as the Blessed One extended his golden hand and called "Ehi Bhikkhu," the two friends and the two hundred and fifty disciple wanderers were instantly adorned with miraculous requisites, each in its proper place. Like great elders of sixty years' standing, they respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One, having already become monks. Wonderfully, their lay appearance vanished and they were transformed into the appearance of monks. (The very act of the Blessed One calling "Etha Bhikkhavo" with his golden voice constituted the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination for the two friends and the two hundred and fifty disciple wanderers; there was no further need for a formal ordination ceremony in a Sima.)

## The 250 Disciple Monks Become Arahants

After they had become Ehi Bhikkhu monks, the Blessed One, observing the temperaments of the two hundred and fifty monks who were the followers of the two friends, preached a further Dhamma discourse suitable for them. (Except for the two Chief Disciples), the remaining two hundred and fifty disciple monks attained Arahantship in that very sitting.

For the two Chief Disciples, however, the work of the three higher paths was not yet complete. This is because among the three types of Sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa (Knowledge of the Perfections of a Disciple)—namely (1) Aggasāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa, (2) Mahāsāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa, and (3) Pakatisāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa—the Aggasāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa of these two noble ones was exceedingly great and vast.
13:
## Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Becomes an Arahant

Thereafter, on the seventh day after becoming a monk, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was striving and practicing the Dhamma of a recluse in a forest, having the small village of Kallavāḷaputta in the Magadha country as his alms-resort. While he was striving for seven days, walking to and fro, he became physically exhausted and sat nodding at the end of the walkway. While he was thus nodding, the Blessed One appeared and gave him a teaching to stir him. Having dispelled his drowsiness (thina-middha) and heard the meditation on elements (dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna) as instructed by the Blessed One, he completed the work of the three higher paths and reached the summit of Sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa.*

## Venerable Sāriputta Becomes an Arahant

Venerable Sāriputta, on the fifteenth day after becoming a monk (the full moon day of Tabodwe), was staying with the Blessed One at the Sūkarakhata Cave (Boar's Cave) on Gijjhakūṭa Hill near the city of Rājagaha. While the Blessed One was preaching the Dīghanakha Sutta (also known as the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta from the Majjhima Nikāya, Majjhima Paṇṇāsa, Paribbājaka Vagga) to his nephew, Dīghanakha the wanderer, the Elder followed the discourse with his own wisdom and contemplated the meditation on feelings (vedanā-kammaṭṭhāna). Like one enjoying a meal prepared for another, he attained Arahantship, reaching the summit of Sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa. He also penetrated and realized the sixteen types of knowledge.

* For details on this, one should refer to the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Sattaka Nipāta, Abyākata Vagga, Pacalayamāna Sutta, the Myanmar translation of the Piṭaka, and its commentary.
14:
(The nephew, Dīghanakha the wanderer, reached the fruit of Stream-entry and became established in the Three Refuges.)

[In this matter: A question may arise as to why Venerable Sāriputta, despite being the one of great wisdom, attained Arahantship later than Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. The brief answer is: Because Venerable Sāriputta's preparation for insight (vipassanā-parikamma) was much more extensive and grander than that of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, he attained Arahantship later. This is the brief answer. To make it clearer: When poor people wish to travel to another place, they can leave quickly because their belongings and ceremony are not grand or numerous. When universal monarchs wish to travel, they cannot leave quickly but only after a long time because their entourage and ceremony—such as the elephant corps, cavalry, chariot corps, and infantry—are so vast (as the proverb says, "When a king sets out, a boatload of beans is cooked"). In this matter, it should be understood according to this analogy.

To expand further for clarity: In this context, the collection of mental and physical phenomena (nāma-rūpa) and formations (saṅkhāra) that are the objects of insight for Bodhisattas, Paccekabuddha-aspirants, and Sāvaka-bodhi-aspirants is called 'Sammasanacāra' = meaning the range of the knowledge that contemplates and investigates them as impermanent, suffering, and non-self. It is also called 'Vipassanā-bhūmi' = meaning the ground where insight knowledge arises.

Among these three types of aspirants:
(1) Sammāsambuddha Bodhisattas (Buddhas-to-be) contemplate the mental and physical phenomena and formations existing within the continuums of beings throughout a hundred thousand crores of world systems, as well as external formations (inanimate things), by applying the three characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.
(2) Paccekabodhi-aspirants (Paccekabuddhas-to-be) contemplate the formations occurring within their own continuum...]
15:
15
Beings of Jambudīpa (alternatively, those of the Middle Country) contemplate and investigate the formations (saṅkhāra) arising within their own continuums, as well as external formations (bahiddha saṅkhāra) which are inanimate (anindriyabaddha), by applying the three characteristics: impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta).

(3) As for the future disciples of Enlightenment (Sāvaka-bodhi-laṅghyā)—namely, the future Chief Disciples, Great Disciples, and Ordinary Disciples—they contemplate and investigate the formations arising within their own continuums and those within the continuums of others. Without making distinctions between individuals, they treat them as one and the same due to their shared nature as external (bahiddha) phenomena, applying the three characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera contemplated and investigated by applying the three characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self, not to every single formation, but by selectively extracting and focusing on certain essential formations. The Venerable Sāriputta Thera, however, while applying the three characteristics to the same formations that serve as the objects of insight (vipassanā) for the aforementioned future disciples of Enlightenment, surpassed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna by extracting and contemplating every single formation, one by one, in its entirety.

Thus, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera investigated and contemplated only a portion of the collection of formations known as the disciples' range of contemplation (sammasana-cāra). Just as a person walking by prodding the ground with the tip of a staff touches only a small part of the earth (while the untouched part is greater), he attained the fruit of Arahantship after striving for a period of seven days. The Venerable Sāriputta Thera, setting aside the range of contemplation belonging to future Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, investigated and contemplated the entire collection of formations belonging to the disciples' range of contemplation without any omission. For a period of fifteen days,
16:
16
he strove and attained the fruit of Arahantship. Immediately upon reaching the fruit of Arahantship, he realized with bold clarity: "Except for the Exalted Buddhas and the Paccekabuddhas, there is no other disciple capable of reaching the Dhamma I have attained through wisdom to the same degree as I."

For example, when a first man desiring to cut a bamboo walking stick sees a large, tangled bamboo thicket, he might think, "If I spend time cutting and clearing the entanglements to select only the best from within, it will take a long time." Thus, he reaches his hand into the thicket, cuts only the stick within his reach at the base and tip, and goes his way. Although this man obtains a walking stick quickly, he cannot obtain one that is truly good, strong, and straight. Another, a second man desiring a walking stick, upon seeing the same tangled bamboo thicket, thinks, "If I only cut the stick within reach at the base and tip, I will not get a good, strong, and straight one." He then girds up his loins and, with a very sharp knife, cuts through the tangled thicket, selects, and cuts out only a truly good, strong, and straight walking stick before going his way. Although this second man obtains his walking stick later, he obtains only one that is truly good, strong, and straight.

In the same way as this analogy, the attainment of the path and fruit of Arahantship by these two Great Chief Disciples should be understood. The first man's cutting and obtaining the walking stick quickly is similar to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's dedicated practice and his attainment of the path and fruit of Arahantship. The second man's patient and careful cutting of the bamboo and his later acquisition of a truly good, strong, and straight stick is similar to the Venerable Sāriputta's patient striving for fifteen days and his attainment of the path of Arahantship, reaching the pinnacle of a disciple's perfection of wisdom (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa).

## The Distinction in the Practice of the Two Chief Disciples
The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's three lower paths were of the pleasant practice with slow intuition (sukha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā)—meaning the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) could be abandoned quickly and easily, but the insight wisdom required to reach the higher path was slow and deliberate. His path of Arahantship was of the painful practice with swift intuition (dukkha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā)—meaning the hindrances had to be abandoned with difficulty and hardship, but the insight wisdom required to reach the path of Arahantship was swift and sharp.

For the Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, his three lower paths (similar to Venerable Moggallāna's) were of the pleasant practice with slow intuition (sukha-paṭipadā dandhābhiññā). His path of Arahantship, however, was of the pleasant practice with swift intuition (sukha-paṭipadā khippābhiññā)—meaning the hindrances could be abandoned easily, and the insight wisdom required to reach the path of Arahantship was also swift and sharp.

This is the distinction between the practices of the two Great Theras. [From the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Vol. 2, page 345, Explanation of the Paṭipadā Vagga, Suttas 7-8].

## The Great Assembly of Disciples with Four Factors
## The Reason for Its Single Occurrence
The Blessed One finished preaching this Dīghanakha Sutta, also known as the "Vedanāpariggaha Sutta" (Majjhima Nikāya 2, 165), before sunset. He then descended from Gijjhakūṭa Hill and went to the Veḷuvana Monastery where:
(1) It was the full moon day of Tabodwe (Māgha);
(2) 1,250 (one thousand two hundred and fifty) monks (one thousand from the group of the three Kassapa brothers of Uruvelā and two hundred and fifty from the group of the two Great Chief Disciples) assembled according to their natural custom, without being invited by anyone;
18:
18
(3) All of those 1,250 (one thousand two hundred and fifty) monks were exclusively "Ehi Bhikkhu" monks (ordained by the Buddha's call);
(4) All of those monks were exclusively Arahants who had attained the six supernormal powers (chaḷabhiññā);

Having held this Assembly of Disciples (Sāvaka-sannipāta) endowed with these four factors, the Buddha conferred the rank of Chief Disciples upon the two Great Theras, Venerable Sāriputta and Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. On that very day, He recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha, which is an exhortation that no Buddha ever omits.

## Three Great Dhamma Assemblies
Just as there were three great occasions of Dhamma realization (Dhammābhisamaya) in the Chronicles of the Twenty-four Buddhas (presented in Volume 1), for our Inconceivable Supreme Buddha, the Pinnacle of the Three Worlds, there were also three great Dhamma assemblies that should be specially recorded. These three occasions are:
(1) As previously mentioned, after becoming the Buddha, when He traveled to the Migadāvana forest and preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, the Venerable Koṇḍañña Thera, along with eighteen crores of Brahmas, was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).
(This is the first great Dhamma assembly, known as the first Dhammābhisamaya, where humans, devas, and Brahmas were first made to realize the Four Noble Truths.)
(2) Later, on the auspicious day of the Great Blessing, in the midst of
19:
19
the assembly of devas and humans who had arrived from the ten thousand world systems, at the conclusion of the preaching of the Maṅgala Sutta, countless humans, devas, and Brahmas will realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation.
(This is the second great Dhamma assembly, known as the second Dhammābhisamaya, where humans, devas, and Brahmas were made to realize the Four Noble Truths for the second time.)
(3) Again, at a later time, when He preached the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 3, 324; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2, 324) to the Venerable Rāhula, thousands of devas and Brahmas, along with the Venerable Rāhula, will realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation.
(This is the third great Dhamma assembly, known as the third Dhammābhisamaya, where humans, devas, and Brahmas were made to realize the Four Noble Truths for the third time.)

## One Assembly of Disciples
For our Supreme Buddha, the Pinnacle of the Three Worlds, as mentioned previously (page 18), there was only one Great Assembly of Disciples endowed with the four factors.
At that very assembly, the Blessed One recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha for the first time.

## Concerning the Two Kinds of Pātimokkha
The summary of the Buddhas' exhortations (Ovāda) and the prescribed disciplinary rules (Sikkhāpada) are called "Pātimokkha" because they cause those who maintain, observe, and follow them to be liberated from the dangers of the woeful states (apāya) and so forth. This Pātimokkha is
20:
20
of two kinds: (1) Ovāda Pātimokkha and (2) Āṇā Pātimokkha.

Among these two, (1) the Ovāda Pātimokkha is recited and taught only by the Buddhas. The teaching of the Ovāda Pātimokkha, which only those Blessed Buddhas recite and teach, consists of the three verses beginning with "Khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā" (Enduring patience is the highest austerity). Every Buddha recites the Pātimokkha with these three verses of exhortation; there is no difference in the verses of the Dhamma teaching, only a difference in the time they are recited. The differences are as follows:

The Blessed Buddha Vipassī recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha once every seven years. The exhortation given once was sufficient for seven years. The Blessed Buddhas Sikhī and Vessabhū recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha once every six years. The Blessed Buddhas Kakusandha and Koṇāgamana recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha once every year. The Blessed Buddha Kassapa recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha once every six months. The exhortation given once by that Blessed Buddha Kassapa was sufficient and served as instruction for six months.*

Regarding this Ovāda Pātimokkha, I shall further cite the explanation from the Vinaya Commentary, Volume 1, in the opening of the Verañjakaṇḍa, pages 153-4: The Buddhas of the past recited only the Ovāda Pātimokkha. (And that Ovāda Pātimokkha was not recited once every fortnight). To elaborate further... the Blessed Buddha Vipassī...

* This is a passage from the Commentary on the Dhammapada, Volume 2, in the explanation of the Ānandattherapañha Vatthu.
21:
Every six years, on the day the six-year period was complete, the Buddha Vipassī would recite the Ovāda Pātimokkha. He alone performed this recitation. The disciple monks did not perform it in their respective monasteries. In the entire island of Jambudīpa, all the monks gathered together to perform the Saṅgha Uposatha only within the great monastery where the Buddha Vipassī resided, located in the great Khema Grove, a sanctuary for animals near the city of Bandhumatī.

During the time of the Buddha Vipassī, there were 84,000 monasteries across the island of Jambudīpa. In each monastery, ten to twenty thousand monks lived purely, unmixed with those of incompatible nature (visabhāga). Even more than that resided there. Devas who announce the Uposatha would go to the various monasteries where the monks resided and (once every year) would say: "O Venerable Ones who are free from suffering... one year has passed; two, three, four, five years have passed. This current year is the sixth year. On the coming full moon day, you must go to pay respects to and attend upon the Blessed One, and to perform the Uposatha. The time for your assembly has arrived."

Then, the monks possessing psychic powers traveled by their own psychic power to the Khema Migadāya monastery where the Buddha Vipassī resided. Those monks without psychic powers traveled by the power of the devas. The manner of their travel was as follows:
22:
Those monks without psychic powers, while residing in their respective monasteries near the Eastern Ocean, the Western Ocean, the Northern Ocean, and the Southern Ocean, would first fully perform their duties, such as cleaning the sleeping quarters and sitting places that traveling monks must do. Then, taking their bowls and robes, as soon as the thought "I shall go" arose in their minds, they would (by the power of the devas) find themselves already arrived at the Uposatha hall. There, they would respectfully pay homage to the Buddha Vipassī and remain seated.

The Buddha Vipassī, in the assembly of the complete monastic community, then recited and taught this Ovāda Pātimokkha:

(1) Khantī paramaṃ tapo titikkhā,
Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ vadanti buddhā.
Na hi pabbajito parūpaghātī,
Na samaṇo hoti paraṃ viheṭhayanto.

Titikkhā = Known as titikkhā. Khantī = The practice of patient endurance (the energy, or the mental state led by energy, that is able to endure the accusations and wrongs of others, cold, heat, etc., without a distressed face, is called adhivāsana-khantī). Paramaṃ = Is the highest. Tapo = Practice of austerity. Nibbānaṃ = Nibbāna, the escape from craving. Paramaṃ = Is the highest. Buddhā = The Buddhas. Vadanti = So they say. Parūpaghātī = One who habitually kills others. Pabbajito = Is a true renunciant. Na hoti = Is not. Paraṃ = Another. Viheṭhayanto = One who oppresses or harms. Samaṇo = A true ascetic who has calmed all defilements. Na hoti = Is not.
23:
(2) Sabbapāpassa akaraṇaṃ, kusalassa upasampadā.
Sacittapariyodapanaṃ, etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ.

Sabbapāpassa = Of all unwholesome states that are blameworthy. Akaraṇaṃ = The non-doing (or) not letting them arise. Kusalassa = Of wholesome states of the four planes (catubhūmika) that are blameless. Upasampadā = The fulfillment. Sacittapariyodapanaṃ = The purification of one's own mind by removing and cleansing the five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) which cause defilement. Etaṃ = These three principles. Buddhānaṃ = Of the various Buddhas. Sāsanaṃ = Are the teaching, advice, and instruction. (This means one must abandon all unwholesome states through the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara), fulfill the wholesome states of the four planes through the development of tranquility and insight (samatha-vipassanā bhāvanā), and finally purify one's mind through the Fruition of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). This is the teaching, advice, and instruction of every Buddha.)

(3) Anūpavādo anūpaghāto,
pātimokkhe ca saṃvaro.
mattaññutā ca bhattasmiṃ,
pantañca sayanāsanaṃ.
adhicitte ca āyogo,
etaṃ buddhāna sāsanaṃ.

Anūpavādo = Not insulting others oneself, nor causing others to insult (this teaches verbal virtue). Anūpaghāto = Not harming, oppressing, or killing others oneself, nor causing others to do so (this teaches physical virtue). Pātimokkhe = In the chief and noble virtue. Saṃvaro ca = Restraining and guarding against flaws...
24:
...restraining and guarding (this teaches both Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla and Indriya-saṃvara-sīla). Bhattasmiṃ = In the matter of almsfood. Mattaññutā ca = Knowing the proper measure in receiving and consuming (this teaches Ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla and Paccaya-sannissita-sīla). Pantañca sayanāsanaṃ = Dwelling and delighting in secluded forest monasteries far from people (this teaches suitable lodging, sappāya-senāsana). Adhicitte = In the noble training of the higher mind, the eight attainments (samāpatti) which are the basis for insight knowledge. Āyogo = Constant and diligent application. Etaṃ = This group of six principles. Buddhānaṃ = Of the various Buddhas. Sāsanaṃ = Are the teaching, advice, and instruction. (With this verse, the three trainings are taught in summary.)

In this same manner, other Buddhas such as the Buddha Sikhī also recited and taught the Ovāda Pātimokkha. As stated previously in the Dhammapada Commentary, there is no difference in the verses of the teaching; there is only a difference in the time of recitation.

Only these three verses constitute the Ovāda Pātimokkha verses of all Buddhas. Long-lived Buddhas recite these three verses of the Ovāda Pātimokkha until the end of their dispensation. Short-lived Buddhas, however, recite them only during the early period known as the Paṭhamabodhi. From the time those short-lived Buddhas prescribe the disciplinary rules (sikkhāpada), they no longer recite the Ovāda Pātimokkha. Instead, the disciple monks themselves recite the disciplinary rules called (2) Āṇā Pātimokkha once every fortnight (tapakkha). (This Āṇā Pātimokkha...

25
...Buddhas do not perform them). Therefore, our Inconceivable Supreme One of the Three Worlds, the Buddha, also recited the Ovāda Pātimokkha only during the first twenty years, known as the Pathama Bodhi. (From the first volume of the Vinaya Commentary, etc.)
## King Suddhodana Sending Ministers to Invite the Buddha to the Royal Capital
In terms of time, it was during the period after the full moon of Phusya (Pyatho) in the year 103 of the Great Era (Mahā Sakkarāj). While the Buddha (as described in the previous Chapter 15) was staying and delighting in the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha, providing the cool water of the Deathless Dhamma to humans, devas, and brahmas who approached Him, establishing some veneya beings in the Refuges and Precepts, establishing some in various Paths and Fruitions according to their past aspirations (abhinīhāra), and elevating noble sons of the Anga and Magadha regions to monkhood and the realization of Path and Fruition, thus holding great festivals of liberation daily, King Suddhodana heard the news: "My son, after practicing austerities (dukkara-cariyā) for six years, has attained supreme Buddhahood. Having preached the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, He now resides in the Veḷuvana Monastery of Rājagaha, surrounded by a host of monks, like the moon surrounded by stars in the middle of the sky, liberating veneya beings with the great and noble glory of the Buddhas." Upon hearing this, he summoned a minister to his presence and—
26:
"Dear minister, please go. Accompanied by a thousand attendants, go to the city of Rājagaha and, with the message I give you, say: 'O Blessed One of great glory, Your father King Suddhodana wishes to see You,' and invite my son, the Buddha, to come here."

Upon receiving this royal command, the minister replied, "Very well, your majesty." Taking the words of the father, King Suddhodana, to heart, he quickly traveled the distance of sixty yojanas (the distance between Kapilavatthu and Rājagaha is sixty yojanas) with his thousand attendants. He entered the Veḷuvana monastery just as the Blessed One was preaching Dhamma in the midst of the assembly.

The minister thought, "I will set aside the King's message for a moment and listen to the Dhamma first." Standing at the edge of the assembly, he listened to the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One. While still standing there, he and his thousand attendants attained the Fruition of Arahantship. He then requested, "O Blessed One of great glory, may we receive the novice and monk ordinations in the presence of the Lord Buddha."

The Blessed One then extended His golden hand and said, "Etha Bhikkhavo = Come, monks" (in the manner previously described). At that very moment, the minister and all thousand attendants found themselves instantly provided with miraculous (iddhimaya) bowls, robes, and requisites, each in its proper place.
27:
They were already fully robed and ordained, appearing like great elders of sixty years' standing (vassa) and eighty years of age, respectfully paying homage to the Blessed One. Their appearance as a minister and royal attendants miraculously vanished, and they were transformed into the appearance of monks.

(A special note: Since it is the nature of Noble Ones (Ariyas) who have attained the Fruition of Arahantship to be indifferent to worldly affairs, that minister did not deliver the King's message to the Blessed One but remained delighting only in the bliss of Arahantship.)

King Suddhodana thought, "The minister I sent should have returned by now, yet he has not returned, nor have I heard any news. What could be the reason?" He then summoned another minister and, giving the same instructions as before, sent him to invite his son, the Buddha. That minister also went to the Veḷuvana monastery in Rājagaha and, in the same manner as the first, listened to the Dhamma with his thousand attendants, became an Arahant, and received the Ehi Bhikkhu ordination. He, too, did not deliver the King's message but remained delighting only in the bliss of Arahantship.

In this manner, King Suddhodana sent nine ministers, each with a thousand attendants, on nine separate occasions. All nine, along with their respective thousand attendants, listened to the Dhamma, became Arahants, and were ordained as Ehi Bhikkhu monks. None of them delivered the King's message...

28
...they did not report the news to the Blessed One, nor did they send word back to the King, but lived delighting only in the bliss of Arahantship.
## Sending the Minister Kāḷudāyī, the Co-natal Friend
The royal father, King Suddhodana, not receiving anyone who would bring back news to him, thought and reflected: "These nine thousand and nine people (9 ministers and 9,000 men) have no intimate affection for me at all, which is why they do not even send word back. Who indeed will follow my command and act without delay as I have instructed?" While carefully searching among his host of ministers and soldiers, he saw the minister Kāḷudāyī. This minister Kāḷudāyī was a general-purpose minister who successfully carried out all the royal affairs of King Suddhodana. He was a trusted inner confidant in all palace matters, extremely intimate with the King, and a co-natal (born on the same day) of the Bodhisatta. He was also a dear childhood friend who had played in the dust with the Bodhisatta Prince.
Therefore, King Suddhodana asked the minister Kāḷudāyī, "Dear Kāḷudāyī, I wish to see my son, the Buddha. Although I have sent nine ministers, each with a thousand followers, to inform and invite my son, not a single person has sent back news. The danger to life is indeed difficult to know for certain. I wish to see my son, the Buddha, while I am still alive. Dear Kāḷudāyī, will you be able to strive and exert yourself so that I may see my son, the Buddha?"
29:
29
"I wish to see my son, the Buddha. Dear Kāḷudāyī, will you be able to strive and make efforts so that I may see my son, the Buddha?" When asked, the minister Kāḷudāyī replied, "Great King, if I may have the opportunity to become a monk, I shall strive and make efforts so that you may see your son, the Buddha."
Then the King said, "Dear Kāḷudāyī, whether by becoming a monk or without becoming a monk, just strive and make efforts so that I may see my son, the Buddha." Accepting this, saying "Very well, Great King," the minister Kāḷudāyī took the message from King Suddhodana and went to the region of Rājagaha with a retinue of a thousand men. Arriving while the Buddha was preaching, he stood at the edge of the assembly, heard the Dhamma, and together with his thousand followers, attained Arahantship and (as before) was established in the Ehi Bhikkhu monkhood.
## The Elder Kāḷudāyī Inviting the Buddha to the Royal Capital of Kapilavatthu with Sixty Verses
(After the Buddha became enlightened and spent the first rainy season (vassa) in the Isipatana Migadāya wood, He performed the Pavāraṇā and went to the Uruvelā forest. Staying there for three months, He disciplined and liberated the thousand hermit brothers, leading them to Arahantship. Surrounded by those thousand Arahant monks who were formerly hermits, He arrived at Rājagaha on the full moon day of Phusya (Pyatho). Staying in Rājagaha for two months, He preached and liberated the people of Anga and Magadha...)
30: 30 attained Arahantship and received monkhood. By this time, five months had passed since the Buddha departed from Vārāṇasī. The winter season (Hemanta) had ended, and the spring season (Vasanta) had begun, reaching the full moon day of Phagguna. This full moon day of Phagguna was the seventh or eighth day after the arrival of Venerable Kāḷudāyī.) At that time, on the full moon day of Phagguna, Venerable Kāḷudāyī reflected: "The winter season has passed; the spring season has arrived. The farmers have harvested their crops from the fields, and the roads have been cleared from all directions so that travelers may journey easily. The great earth is covered with lush green grass, and the forests have shed their old leaves, replaced them with new ones, and are beautifully fruiting and flowering. It is a good time to travel on every road, being neither too hot nor too cold. It is now the right time for the Buddha to visit and favor his relatives." Having thus reflected, he approached the Buddha and praised him with more than sixty verses, inviting him to journey to the royal city of Kapilavatthu. ## Chapter 17
## The Buddha Proceeding to the Royal Capital of Kapilavatthu Surrounded by Twenty Thousand Arahants
Surrounded by twenty thousand Arahant monks—ten thousand noble sons from the Anga and Magadha regions and ten thousand noble sons from Kapilavatthu—the Buddha departed from the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha (on the 1st waning day of Phagguna in the year 103 ME). He traveled at a pace of one yojana per day. Aiming to reach the royal capital of Kapilavatthu, which was sixty yojanas away from Rājagaha, in two months, He traveled by way of a journey called Aturita-desacārī (a journey that is not too fast).
## Along the Journey, the Buddha Sustaining Himself with Alms-food Offered from King Suddhodana's Golden Palace
While the Buddha was traveling on the Aturita-desacārī journey towards Kapilavatthu, the Elder Kāḷudāyī thought, "I shall go and inform King Suddhodana that the Buddha has departed from Rājagaha and is traveling to Kapilavatthu." Having so thought, he flew into the sky using his supernormal power (iddhividha-abhiññā) and, traveling through the air, descended at the golden palace of King Suddhodana. When King Suddhodana saw the Elder Kāḷudāyī, he was filled with great joy and respectfully invited him, saying, "Come, dear Kāḷudāyī, please sit here."

When the Elder Kāḷudāyī made a gesture as if to depart, King Suddhodana said, "Dear son, please eat right here on this royal throne." The Elder Kāḷudāyī replied, "Great King, I shall eat only when I reach the presence of the Blessed One." Then King Suddhodana asked, "Dear son, where is the Blessed One?" The Elder Kāḷudāyī replied, "Great King, the Blessed One, accompanied by twenty thousand Arahants, has set out on his journey to see you."

King Suddhodana, with a heart full of great joy, requested again, "Dear Kāḷudāyī, please eat the alms-food offered now right here in this golden palace, and until my son, the Buddha, reaches this city of Kapilavatthu, please bring and offer alms-food from this golden palace for my son, the Buddha." The Elder Kāḷudāyī accepted the King's request by remaining silent.

Furthermore, every day after finishing his own meal at the golden palace of Kapilavatthu, the Elder Kāḷudāyī would begin by saying, "Today the Blessed One has reached such a distance; today he has reached such a distance." By preaching Dhamma related to the virtues of the Blessed One, he caused the entire Sakyan clan to develop faith and devotion in the Buddha even before they had seen him.

For this reason, at a later time when the Blessed One was conferring Etadagga titles upon his disciples, he declared the Elder Kāḷudāyī to be the foremost, saying: "Etadaggaṃ bhikkhave mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ kulappasādakānaṃ yadidaṃ kāḷudāyī = Monks, among my monk disciples who inspire faith in their families, Kāḷudāyī is the best, the foremost." ## The Buddha Subduing the Pride of His Relatives by Performing the Twin Miracle of Water and Fire
When the Buddha arrived at Kapilavatthu, the Sakyan princes, led by King Suddhodana, held a meeting, thinking, "We shall now behold the Buddha, our noble relative." First (as step 1), while discussing the place for the Buddha to reside, they unanimously decided and confirmed: "The Nigrodha Sakyan's park is delightful. It is endowed with shade and spring water. It is neither too far from nor too near the city, possesses good access roads, is easy for those who wish to go there, and is quiet—thus fulfilling the five characteristics pleasing to the Buddhas. Therefore, that Nigrodha Sakyan's park is a suitable, appropriate, and excellent place for the Buddha to reside." After making this decision, they had all necessary repairs made in the park, and each taking perfumes and flowers...
79:
they went out to welcome the Blessed One on his journey—

(a) First, they sent and positioned young boys and girls (the children of the city's residents) who were fully adorned with ornaments.
(b) Following them, they sent princes and princesses, also fully adorned with ornaments.
(c) Behind those princes and princesses, they themselves followed, making offerings of perfumes, scented powders, and so on, and escorted the Blessed One to the Nigrodha Park.

Upon reaching the Nigrodha Park, the Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants, sat upon the noble Buddha-seat (Buddhāsana), the Dhamma-throne, which had been prepared in advance by the Sākiyan kings.

At that time, the Sākiyan kings, being stubborn and arrogant in their pride of birth, thought: "Prince Siddhattha is much younger than us. He is like our younger brother, nephew, son, or grandson." Thus, they said to the younger princes, "You boys, pay homage to him; as for us, we shall sit behind you." When the Sākiyan relatives thus sat behind the younger princes without paying homage to the Blessed One, the Blessed One, perceiving the intense pride in the hearts of the Sākiyan kings, thought: "These relatives of mine, full of pride, have grown old in vain without benefit, and thus they do not pay homage to me. These relatives of mine do not know at all what a Buddha is like, or what the power of the Buddhas is like."
80:
Thinking, "They do not know, 'Such is the nature of a Buddha; such is the power of the Buddhas.' Well then, I shall now demonstrate the strength and power of a Buddha by performing the Twin Miracle of water and fire. Having created a great jeweled walkway (Ratanacaṅkama) as wide as the ten thousand world systems in the open sky, I shall walk back and forth upon that jeweled walkway and, perceiving the dispositions of the beings who have gathered, I shall rain down the rain of the Dhamma-desanā." As soon as he made this resolution, the devas and brahmas from the ten thousand world systems shouted in acclaim and uttered "Sādhu."

Immediately after the Blessed One made this resolution, he entered the fourth jhāna based on the white kasiṇa (odāta-kasiṇa). Emerging from that attainment, he made the determination: "Let the light spread throughout the ten thousand world systems." Simultaneously with his determination, the ten thousand world systems were suffused with light. While many humans, devas, and brahmas were filled with joy and delight, he ascended into the sky by means of the fourth jhāna of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā)—

(1) Above and below, (2) front and back of the body, (3) both left and right eyes, (4) ears, (5) nose, (6) shoulders, (7) hands, (8) sides, (9) feet, (10) fingers and toes and the intervals between them,
81:
(11) From each and every hair, (12) from each and every pore—
In these twelve groups of locations, alternating jets of fire and streams of water, and alternating streams of water and jets of fire, were displayed. Each time they were beheld, the colors changed, causing wonder and praise. Without ceasing, as if sprinkling the dust of his feet repeatedly upon the heads of the assembly of Sakyan princes, he beautifully and magnificently displayed the Twin Miracle of fire and water in the midst of the great assembly of humans and devas.

## King Suddhodana
## The Third Act of Salutation

At that time, when the royal father, King Suddhodana, beheld that wonderful and extraordinary Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), he said: "O Glorious and Noble Son... On the day of your birth, when I brought you to pay respects to the hermit Kāḷadevala and joined my two hands toward the hermit, I saw your two feet fly up into the sky and rest upon the hermit's head; thus, I paid homage to you. That homage was my, your royal father's, first salutation. Later, on the day of the Royal Plowing Festival, when you were placed on a noble seat in the shade of a rose-apple tree, I saw that while the shadows of other trees moved according to the sun, the shade of the rose-apple tree where you sat remained still and continued to cover you; thus, I paid homage to your two feet. That homage was my, your royal father's, second salutation. Now, seeing this extraordinary Twin Miracle, which has never been seen before..."
82:
I pay homage to your feet with respect and devotion. This present homage is my third homage as your royal father." Having said this, he bowed and paid homage to the Blessed One with his hands raised in prayer.

When King Suddhodana paid homage, there was not a single Sākiyan king who could remain standing without paying homage to the Blessed One. All the Sākiyan kings paid homage to the Blessed One.

## Creating the Jeweled Walkway and Preaching the Dhamma

After the Blessed One had thus performed the Twin Miracle in the sky and subdued the pride of his relatives, he reflected on the mental states of the multitude. Wishing to preach a discourse suitable to their desires while walking on a walkway, he created a great jeweled walkway (Ratanacaṅkama) made entirely of jewels, extending across the ten thousand world systems from east to west. I shall briefly describe the appearance of that jeweled walkway—

Taking this world system as the center, the ten thousand Mount Sinerus located in the ten thousand world systems to the east and west were used as the foundation for the walkway, like a row of walkway pillars. He made those rows of Mount Sinerus (the walkway pillars) shine with a golden hue like great golden pillars, and above them, he created the broad and pure ground of the jeweled walkway. In creating it,

among the ten thousand world systems mentioned, he made the eastern edge of the easternmost world system the far end of the walkway, and the western edge of the westernmost world system the other end of the walkway.

The left and right edges of the ground of that jeweled walkway were golden in color, while the central part of the walkway ground was made of ruby. The beams, rafters, and cross-beams of that jeweled walkway were brilliantly fashioned from various kinds of jewels, and above them, it was covered and roofed with golden planks. The railings on the left and right sides of the walkway were made entirely of gold. On the surface of the jeweled walkway, rubies and pearls were spread like grains of sand. The jeweled walkway created in this manner shone brilliantly, illuminating the ten directions like the rising sun.

The Blessed One, with the incomparable glory of a Buddha, walked back and forth on the jeweled walkway he had thus created. At that time, many devas and brahmas from the ten thousand world systems gathered and made offerings by scattering celestial Mandārava flowers, Paduma lotuses, and Pāricchattaka flowers upon the jeweled walkway.

## The Arrival of Venerable Sāriputta and Five Hundred Arahants
After the Buddha had performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), He created a great jeweled walkway (ratana-caṅkama) and, while receiving the homage and offerings of devas and brahmas, He walked to and fro on that jeweled walkway. At that time, the Elder Sāriputta, the Right-hand Chief Disciple, was residing on the slopes of Mount Gijjhakūṭa in Rājagaha together with his retinue of five hundred disciple monks. Then, the Elder Sāriputta looked with his divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) and saw the Buddha walking on the jeweled walkway in the sky above the royal capital of Kapilavatthu. He thought, "I shall now approach the Great Buddha and request Him to preach the Buddhavaṃsa Dhamma, the lineage and practice of the Bodhisattas in all its details." Having so thought, he immediately assembled the five hundred Arahant elders living with him and consulted them, saying, "Friends, the Buddha is now performing the Twin Miracle of water and fire, along with the supernormal power of world-revelation (loka-vivaraṇa), which can inspire the whole world to bow in devotion. Let us also go to that miracle festival and pay homage to the Buddha. Friends, come, let us all go. After approaching and paying homage to the Buddha, let us ask and request about the past practices of the Buddhas and dispel our doubts."
(In this context: "kaṅkhaṃ vinodayissāma" = "let us dispel our doubts"—regarding this statement by the Elder Sāriputta, a question may arise: why did the Elder say this when Arahants, whose taints are exhausted, have no doubts whatsoever regarding any Dhamma? The answer is—)
86:
It is indeed true that Arahants do not have even a trace of doubt known as vicikicchā, as they have completely eradicated the sixteen types of doubt (kaṅkhā) even at the stage of the Path of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). The "doubt" (kaṅkhā) mentioned here by Venerable Sāriputta does not refer to the doubt of the mental factor vicikicchā. Rather, in this context, it refers to the lack of knowledge regarding the specific details (Buddhavamsa-paññatti) that define the succession of Buddhas who appeared within the four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, such as their respective aeons, names, lineages, and families. Furthermore, Venerable Sāriputta wished to ask the Buddha about the Buddhavamsa; however, the Buddhavamsa is the domain of the Buddhas alone, as only Buddhas can preach it in detail. It is not the domain of Paccekabuddhas or disciples. Therefore, because it was not within his own domain, the Elder spoke thus: "Let us ask the Buddha and dispel our doubts." (From the Buddhavamsa Commentary, page 65).

When Venerable Sāriputta spoke these words of consultation, the five hundred Arahant elders living with him, upon hearing his words, took their bowls and robes and quickly assembled near Venerable Sāriputta.

Then, Venerable Sāriputta, together with those five hundred Arahant elders, traveled through the air by the vehicle of meditative absorption (jhāna) and supernormal power (iddhividha-abhiññā). He approached and beheld the Buddha, who was still walking on the Gem Cloister in the sky above the city of Kapilavatthu. The five hundred Arahants who accompanied Venerable Sāriputta

At that time, great elders such as the Venerable Sāriputta, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, and the Venerable Mahākassapa also remained in the sky, paying homage to the Buddha with deep reverence. ## The Buddha Preaching His Own Virtues. Then, the Buddha, perceiving the flickering faith and devotion of the five hundred Arahants led by the Venerable Sāriputta, began to preach His virtues in detail, starting with: 'Cattāro te asankheyyā, koṭi yesaṃ na nāyati.'— 'Dear Sāriputta, there are four incalculable things (asankheyya) that cannot be counted. The beginning and end of these four incalculable things are unknowable. These four are: (1) The multitude of beings is without end or limit, (2) Space is without end or limit, (3) The universes (Cakkavāḷa) are without end or limit, (4) The Buddha's knowledge called the Golden Knowledge of Omniscience (Sabbannuta-ñāṇa) is without end or limit.' (At that moment, the minds of devas and humans were filled with great wonder at the Buddha's miraculous creation. To those devas, [it occurred]: 'There are even more wonderful things than this current miraculous creation...')

listen further to those exceedingly wonderful things of mine," He continued to expand the discourse as follows:)

"Dear Sāriputta, my wonderful attributes are not limited to this present miraculous creation. There are many other unprecedented and extraordinary wonders that are enough to make one's hair stand on end. (To mention those wonders briefly):—

After passing away from the life of King Vessantara (having fulfilled the Perfections, Sacrifices, and Conducts, and awaiting the time to become a Buddha), I became the celestial king named Santusita in the Tusita heaven. While I was enjoying celestial bliss for a duration of 576,000,000 (five hundred and seventy-six million) years by human reckoning, the devas and brahmas of the ten thousand world systems gathered before me and requested:

'O Peerless Bodhisatta, free from suffering! You have practiced and fulfilled the ten Perfections (pāramī) in detail as thirty, the three modes of Conduct (cariya), and the five Great Sacrifices (pariccāga). You did not fulfill them desiring the bliss of a Universal Monarch, the bliss of Sakka, the bliss of Māra, or the bliss of Brahma. Indeed, you fulfilled them desiring only Buddhahood to save the world of beings. O Peerless Bodhisatta! The time has now come for you to become the Buddha, as you have desired.'

'O Bodhisatta of intense effort! The time has come for you to become the Buddha for the sake of the world.'
89:
'Please be conceived in a mother's womb. Having rescued the world of beings, including devas, from the current of saṃsāra, may you realize the Deathless Nibbāna.'

Thus they requested me to become the Buddha.

Then, although requested by the devas and brahmas, I, the Bodhisatta, did not yet give my word or promise easily. Only after making the Five Great Observations (pañca-mahāvilokana), namely: (1) The proper time, (2) The proper continent, (3) The proper region, (4) The proper family, and (5) The lifespan of the mother; and having known that these five great factors were complete, did I give my promise to the devas and brahmas, saying: 'O assembly of devas and brahmas, the time has indeed come for me to become the Buddha (as you have said).' After remaining in that Tusita heaven until the end of my lifespan and passing away from there, I was conceived in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā in the noble family of the Unbroken Sakyan Lineage.

When I was thus conceived in the mother's womb without losing mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), the ten thousand world systems shook and trembled.

Without losing mindfulness and clear comprehension, like a Dhamma-preaching monk descending from the Dhamma-seat, or like a man descending a staircase with an upright posture, I was born from my mother's womb, stretching my hands and feet, without being smeared by any impurity (on Friday, the full moon day of Kason, in the year 68 of the Great Era). At that time also—"

"Dear Sāriputta, in the matter of taking conception, there is no one equal to the Bodhisatta. In the matter of being born from the mother's womb, there is no one equal to the Bodhisatta." (The Buddha said this because the Bodhisatta never loses mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) during these three occasions: when entering the mother's womb, when staying in the mother's womb for ten months, and when being born from the mother's womb.) (Regarding the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga-ñāṇa), the Arahattamagga of some disciples (sāvakas) yields only the fruit of Arahatship (arahatta-phala). For some disciples, the Arahattamagga yields the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), and for others, it yields the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa). The Arahattamagga-ñāṇa of Paccekabuddhas yields only the knowledge of Paccekabodhi. The Arahattamagga-ñāṇa of the Buddhas yields the fruit of being endowed with all the qualities and virtues of a Buddha. Upon attaining the Arahattamagga, all the qualities of a Buddha are fully realized. Therefore,) "In the matter of the Knowledge of the Path of Arahatship, I am the supreme. [In this context: In the matter of the Perfection of Giving (dāna-pāramī), the giving of external wealth and possessions is called dāna-pāramī. The giving of one's limbs (major or minor) is called dāna-upapāramī. The giving of one's own life is called dāna-paramattha-pāramī. In the same way, for the remaining nine perfections, the practice of virtue (sīla) without considering the loss of external wealth is sīla-pāramī. The practice of virtue without considering the loss of limbs is sīla-upapāramī. The practice of virtue without considering the loss of one's life is sīla-paramattha-pāramī. This is how they should be distinguished and remembered.

The lives in which the Bodhisatta fulfilled the perfections such as giving are indeed countless. Specifically:

He asked the brahmin to prepare a fire and, without regard for his life, jumped into the blazing flames to offer his own body. This act of giving by the Bodhisatta is called dāna-paramattha-pāramī.

The act of virtue of the Great Bodhisatta, who observed the precepts by sacrificing his life without any anger, is called the Ultimate Perfection of Virtue (Sīla-paramattha-pāramī).

(3) In the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka of the Cattālīsannipāta, when he was King Cūḷasutasoma, the Great Bodhisatta renounced the sovereignty of the capital Sudassana (at that time, the city of Vārāṇasī was known as Sudassana), which was already in his hands, without any regard for his life or safety, and went forth into the forest. This act is called the Ultimate Perfection of Renunciation (Nekkhamma-paramattha-pāramī).

(4) In the Sattubhasta Jātaka of the Sattakanipāta, when he was the wise Senaka, the Great Bodhisatta used his wisdom to accurately identify a venomous cobra inside a leather provision bag as if seeing it with his own eyes, thereby protecting the Brahmin owner of the bag from the danger of death. This wisdom of the Great Bodhisatta is called the Ultimate Perfection of Wisdom (Paññā-paramattha-pāramī).

(5) In the Mahājanaka Jātaka of the Mahānipāta, when he was Prince Janaka, the Great Bodhisatta swam across the great ocean with all his might without despair or wavering, even though others had perished in the sea. He remained like a log of wood, devoid of any ill will. This act of patience is called the Ultimate Perfection of Patience (Khanti-paramattha-pāramī).

(7) In the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka of the Asītinnipāta, when he was King Mahāsutasoma, the Great Bodhisatta gave his word to the man-eater Porisāda, saying, "I will surely return tomorrow morning." He kept his promise and returned without regard for his life, thereby saving one hundred and one kings...

...from the danger of death. This act of truthfulness in his auspicious speech is called the Ultimate Perfection of Truthfulness (Sacca-paramattha-pāramī).

(8) In the Mūgapakkha (Temiya) Jātaka of the Mahānipāta, when he was Prince Temiya, the Great Bodhisatta sacrificed his life to maintain his practice of pretending to be mute, deaf, and paralyzed until he could go forth into the forest. This act of loving-kindness is called the Ultimate Perfection of Loving-kindness (Mettā-paramattha-pāramī).

## (Chapter 17) Appendix

## Note regarding the Gotama Buddhavaṃsa

We have already written the chronicles of the twenty-four Buddhas, from the Blessed Dīpaṅkara to the Blessed Kassapa, arranging their names, clans, and lineages by combining the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi and its Commentary into a continuous narrative.

For the current Gotama Buddhavaṃsa, we have also striven to write as comprehensively as possible, using the Buddhavaṃsa Pāḷi and its Commentary as the primary source up to the chapter where the Buddhavaṃsa discourse was preached, while also extracting relevant facts from other Pāḷi texts and Commentaries.

Regarding this (Gotama Buddhavaṃsa), learned readers may wish to know the original words of the Gotama Buddhavaṃsa as preached by the Blessed One himself. Therefore, I shall present the 24 verses of the Gotama Buddhavaṃsa, preached by the Blessed One, in plain Burmese prose.

Upon the request of the Venerable Sāriputta, the Blessed One, while on the Jewel Walkway (Ratana-caṅkama) in the sky above the city of Kapilavatthu, preached the chronicles of the twenty-four Buddhas, including their names, clans, and lineages, starting from the Dīpaṅkara Buddhavaṃsa to the Kassapa Buddhavaṃsa, beginning with "Kappe ca satasahasse, caturo ca asaṅkhiye," like the flowing of a great celestial river. Then, regarding his own Gotama Buddhavaṃsa discourse:
101:
101
"Ahametarahi sambuddho,
Gotamo sakyavaḍḍhano.
Padhānaṃ padahitvāna,
patto sambodhimuttamaṃ—"

He preached these 24 verses. The prose translation of these 24 verses is as follows:

## The First Great Congregation

(1) Ahametarahi sambuddho,
Gotamo sakyavaḍḍhano.
Padhānaṃ padahitvāna,
patto sambodhimuttamaṃ.

Dear Sāriputta, I am now the Fully Enlightened One, Gotama, born of the Sakyan lineage. After six years of great exertion (padhāna), I have attained the supreme Omniscient Wisdom (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).

(2) Brahmunā yācito santo,
dhammacakkaṃ pavattayiṃ.
Aṭṭhārasannaṃ koṭīnaṃ,
paṭhamābhisamayo ahu.

Dear Sāriputta, after becoming the Buddha, in the eighth week, being requested by the Brahma Sahampati, I preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta in the Isipatana Deer Park near Vārāṇasī. naradevasamāgame.

## The Buddha's Service to Beings

(6) Virocamāno vimalo,
bhikkhusaṅghassa majjhago.
Dadāmi patthitaṃ sabbaṃ,
maṇīva sabbakāmado.

Dear Sāriputta, (just like the previous Buddhas), I shine with infinite Buddha-glory, free from the stains of defilements. Standing gracefully in the midst of the Saṅgha of monks, like the Cintāmaṇi jewel that can grant all wishes, I bestow all mundane and supramundane happiness desired and prayed for by humans, devas, and Brahmas.

(7) Phalamakaṅkhamānānaṃ,
bhavacchandajahasinaṃ.
Catusaccaṃ pakāsemi,
anukampāya pāṇinaṃ.

Dear Sāriputta, out of compassion and for the protection of humans, devas, and Brahmas who desire the four Fruits and wish to abandon the craving for existence, I have clearly preached the Four Noble Truths (so that they may attain the four Fruits and abandon craving for existence).

(This shows the Buddha's service to beings by helping them through the preaching of the Four Truths.)

(8) Dasavīsashassānaṃ,
dhammābhisamayo ahu.
Ekadvinnaṃ abhisamayo,
gaṇanato asaṅkhiyo.

Dear Sāriputta, (in my service to beings through the preaching of the Four Truths), in some Dhamma assemblies, ten thousand beings attained realization; in others, twenty thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths. The realization of the Four Noble Truths by individuals, such as one or two persons, is beyond counting.

(9) Vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ,
iddhaṃ phītaṃ suphullitaṃ.
Idha mayhaṃ sakyamunino,
sāsanaṃ suvisodhitaṃ.
105:
Dear Sāriputta, in this world, the Sāsana of I, the Buddha, who went forth from the Sākyan clan, shall be widespread (across the three realms of Brahmas, humans, and devas), clearly understood by many beings, and shall be exceedingly prosperous, flourishing, radiant, and pure.

(10) All those many hundreds of monks,
Who are taintless and free from lust,
With peaceful minds and concentrated,
Always surround me.

Dear Sāriputta, I am always surrounded by all these monks, numbering in the many hundreds, who have removed the taints (āsavas) and are free from lust, possessing peaceful hearts and a steady concentration like a lamp flame in a windless place.

(11) Those who now, at this time,
Abandon the human state,
Being learners (sekhas) who have not reached the goal,
Those monks are blamed by the wise.

Dear Sāriputta, in this present time of my dispensation, those monks who have not yet reached the fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala) but are still practicing the three trainings as learners (sekhas), and yet pass away from this human life—such monks are blamed by the wise.

(12) Praising the Noble Path,
Always delighting in the Dhamma,
Those mindful ones will awaken,
Having gone through the stream of Saṃsāra.
106:
Dear Sāriputta, those mindful persons who, day and night, always delight in the Dhamma and joyfully praise the Noble Eightfold Path, will cross the ocean of Saṃsāra in just a few lifetimes and, realizing the Four Noble Truths, will attain liberation.

## Birthplace and Lineage

(13) My city is Kapilavatthu,
King Suddhodana is my father.
The mother who gave birth to me
Is called Māyādevī.

Dear Sāriputta, my home city is named Kapilavatthu; my royal father is named Suddhodana; and my birth mother is called Māyādevī.

(14) For twenty-nine years,
I lived in the household life.
Ramma, Suramma, and Subhaka
Were my three supreme palaces.

Dear Sāriputta, for twenty-nine years I ruled and lived in the golden palace of Kapilavatthu. My residences were the three palaces: the nine-storied winter palace named Ramma, the five-storied summer palace named Suramma, and the seven-storied rainy season palace named Subhaka.
107:
(15) Forty thousand women,
Well-adorned, attended me.
The woman named Bhaddakaccānā was my wife,
And Rāhula was my son.

Dear Sāriputta, while I was ruling as king, there were forty thousand well-adorned ladies-in-waiting. My chief consort was named Bhaddakaccānā, and my son was named Rāhula.

(16) Having seen the four omens,
I departed on a horse-vehicle.
For six years I practiced
The difficult ascetic striving.

Dear Sāriputta, having seen the four great omens—an old man, a sick man, a dead man, and a monk—I departed for the forest riding the horse Kanthaka. In the Uruvelā forest, away from human society, I practiced for six years the great striving (padhāna) which is difficult for ordinary people to perform.

(17) In Bārāṇasī, at Isipatana,
The Wheel was set in motion by me.
I am Gotama the Fully Enlightened One,
The refuge of all living beings.

Dear Sāriputta, I preached the Discourse of Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion at the Isipatana Deer Park in Bārāṇasī. I am the Noble Buddha Gotama, the refuge of all living beings, known by my ancestral lineage name.

(18) Kolita and Upatissa
Are the two monks who are my chief disciples.
Ānanda is the name of my attendant,
Who remains in my presence.
Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā
Are my chief female disciples.

Dear Sāriputta, my pair of chief disciples are the monk Kolita (Venerable Moggallāna) and the monk Upatissa (Venerable Sāriputta). The attendant monk who has constantly served and looked after me in my presence (for over twenty years) is named Ānanda. The pair of noble female chief disciples are the Elder Nun Khemā and the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā.

(19) Citta and Hatthāḷavaka
Are the chief male lay supporters.
Nandamātā and Uttarā
Are the chief female lay supporters.

Dear Sāriputta, my noble male lay supporters (upāsakas) are the householder Citta (from Macchikāsaṇḍa in the Kosala country) and the householder Hatthāḷavaka (son of King Āḷavī of Āḷavī). My noble female lay supporters (upāsikās) are Nandamātā (an Anāgāmī from Veḷukaṇḍaka in the Dakkhiṇāgiri region of Rājagaha) and Khujjuttarā (a Sotāpanna who was a servant to Queen Sāmāvatī in Kosambī, who mastered the Tipitaka and attained the foremost rank in learning).
109:
(20) At the foot of the Assattha tree,
I attained supreme enlightenment.
My fathom-wide aura always
Extends sixteen cubits.

Dear Sāriputta, at the foot of the Bodhi tree (Assattha), which stands a hundred cubits high, I attained the noble Knowledge of the Path of Arahantship and Omniscience. My bodily radiance (extending eighty cubits all around) shines brilliantly at all times. I am sixteen cubits in height.

(21) The lifespan is short, a hundred years,
As it exists now at this time.
Remaining for that duration,
I cross over many people.

Dear Sāriputta, at this time, the human lifespan is short, only about a hundred years. I shall remain for four-fifths of the lifespan—eighty years (forty-five vassa)—and rescue the multitude of beings to be tamed from the ocean of Saṃsāra to the dry land of Nibbāna.

(22) Having set up the torch of Dhamma
For the enlightenment of later people,
I too, before long,
Together with the assembly of disciples,
Will attain Parinibbāna right here,
Like a fire when its fuel is exhausted.

Dear Sāriputta, I have also established the torch of Dhamma so that future generations may realize the Four Noble Truths.
110:
I have set up the torch of Dhamma, and before long, together with the assembly of my disciples, I shall enter Parinibbāna and reach the end of existence right here in this human realm at Kusinārā, just as a great flame is extinguished when its fuel is spent.

## Two Verses of Spiritual Urgency

(23) Those peerless powers,
And these Ten Powers,
And this body that bears the attributes,
Adorned with the thirty-two excellent marks;

(24) Having illuminated the ten directions
With the six-colored rays like the sun,
All these will disappear.
Are not all conditioned things empty?

Dear Sāriputta, those peerless powers of mine, these Ten Powers (Dasabala), this body which bears the supreme qualities such as the six unique knowledges and the ten powers of a Buddha, and is beautifully adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and these six-colored rays which illuminate the ten directions like the sun with its thousand rays—all of these will perish and disappear. Dear Sāriputta, are not all conditioned things (saṅkhāra), both animate and inanimate, empty of the essence of permanence, empty of the essence of happiness, and empty of the essence of self? (Therefore, develop insight by applying the three characteristics to conditioned things and strive diligently to reach Nibbāna.)
111:
This is the instruction and exhortation (anusāsanī) of the Buddhas for you, dear sons. Strive with diligence (appamāda) to fulfill this teaching of the Buddhas.

With this sequence of words, the Chronicle of Buddha Gotama according to the Buddhavamsa Pali and the Buddhavamsa Commentary is concluded. However, when Prime Minister U Nu requested the leading of the compilation of this Great Chronicle of Buddhas (see page 'Nya' of the Introduction):

(1) To lead the writing of the Great Chronicle of Buddhas; in doing so, to write in such a way that the true accounts of the Buddha are complete without missing even a needle's point; if it cannot be finished in one volume, let it be two, or four, or eight, etc.; focus primarily on the completeness of the accounts—

Because of this request, I shall not conclude this Great Chronicle of Buddhas here, but after the preaching of the Buddhavamsa, I shall continue to write the events and accounts of the Buddha under the title "The Great Chronicle of Buddhas: The Life of Gotama Buddha," expanding into new chapters as far as my ability and knowledge permit.
