## Chapter 18
## The Falling of the Pokkharavassa Rain (Lotus-leaf Rain)
## At the Assembly of Relatives

In this manner, while the Blessed One was walking upon the jeweled walkway in the air near the city of Kapilavatthu and preaching the Buddhavamsa, he caused the eighty thousand relatives to bow their heads and shed their pride in homage. Then, descending from the sky, he sat upon the noble Buddha-seat, the Dhamma-throne, which had been prepared.

As soon as the Blessed One sat upon the Buddha-seat, the relatives assembled in full. When all the relatives were seated with settled minds, the great Pokkharavassa rain* began to fall.

When that great Pokkharavassa rain fell, the stream of rainwater, which was red in color, flowed rapidly over the ground with a roaring sound. Only those who wished to be wet became wet; on the bodies of those who did not wish to be wet, not even a single drop of rain fell.

* Pokkharavassa rain is defined in the Gantha-pada as water the color of a lotus leaf. The great teachers say it is a great rain that falls after a cloud the size of a lotus leaf first appears in the middle of the sky and gradually becomes a thousand layers of rain clouds. (From the Vinaya Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā, Volume 3, page 245.)
113:
Seeing that miracle, all the relatives were filled with wonder and praised it, saying, "Oh, how wonderful, it is worthy of snapping one's fingers in praise! Oh, how extraordinary, such a thing has never happened before!" Hearing these words, the Blessed One said, "It is not only now that the Pokkharavassa rain falls at the assembly of my relatives; it has fallen before in the past." Having said this, he preached the noble Vessantara Jātaka, which is adorned with a thousand verses, regarding this event.

After hearing the noble discourse of the Vessantara Jātaka, all the relatives rose from their seats and departed. Not a single person invited him, saying, "Venerable Sir, please accept the alms-food we shall offer tomorrow."

His royal father, King Suddhodana, however, thought with confidence, "If my son, the Buddha, does not come to my palace, he has nowhere else to go. He will surely come only to the palace." Thus, he returned without specifically inviting the Blessed One. In the golden palace, he had gruel and other foods prepared for the twenty thousand Arahants led by the Buddha, and had the seats made ready.

## The Blessed One Entering Kapilavatthu for Alms
## Surrounded by Twenty Thousand Arahants

On the following day, the Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants, entered the city of Kapilavatthu for alms. Even as he entered for alms, not a single relative came out to meet him.
114:
No one invited Him. Not a single relative appeared to receive His alms-bowl.

As soon as the Buddha stood at the threshold of the city of Kapilavatthu, He reflected: "How did the Buddhas of the past collect alms in their fathers' royal cities? Did they skip houses to go only to the mansions of the wealthy and powerful, or did they go from house to house without distinction, following the sequence of dwellings?" Upon contemplating with His *pubbenivāsānussati-abhiññā* (knowledge of past lives), He saw that not a single Buddha had ever skipped houses to go only to the mansions of the wealthy; rather, every Buddha had collected alms from house to house without distinction. He then decided, "I, too, should now follow and uphold this lineage and tradition of the Buddhas of the past by collecting alms from house to house. By doing so, in the future, my disciples will also follow my example and fulfill the duty of a monk in collecting alms."

Having made this decision, He began His alms-round in sequence, starting from the very first house at the edge of the city gate.

[At this point, I shall briefly present the description of the Buddha's graceful entry into the royal city as explained in the Majjhima-paṇṇāsa Aṭṭhakathā, pages 16-17:

When the Buddha walks, the great earth shakes gently. The Buddha walks without treading upon or harming small creatures such as ants. He lifts His right foot first. Because the Buddha possesses the *supatiṭṭhitatā* mark—where the extremely soft soles of His feet are as even as golden sandals—He touches the ground with perfect evenness. No dust or impurities cling to His soles. When the Buddha travels, the earth, though insentient, causes low places to rise and high places to become level of its own accord. Large rocks, pebbles, stumps, and thorns move away from His path in advance. The Buddha walks with strides that are neither too long nor too short. When walking, His knees and ankles do not touch or rub against each other. He walks neither too fast nor too slow. Being one of great concentration (*samādhi*), He does not look up, nor does He look down, nor does He look around to the left or right; He looks only about a yoke's length (four cubits) ahead. He walks as gracefully as a Chaddanta elephant king adorned with all its trappings.]
115:
He walked without crushing, treading upon, or harming small creatures. He first lifted and set down his right foot. As the Blessed One walked, the very soft soles of his feet touched the ground evenly because he possessed the Mark of Level Feet (Supatiṭṭhita-lakkhaṇa), like a golden sandal. Dust and impurities did not adhere to his soles. When the Blessed One traveled, although the earth has no volition, low places rose up automatically and high places became level. Large stones, pebbles, stumps, and thorns moved away from the path of his journey beforehand. The Blessed One walked with strides that were neither too long nor too short. When he walked, he did so without his knees or ankles touching or rubbing against each other. He walked neither too fast nor too slow. Being one of great concentration (samādhi), he did not look up, nor did he look down. He did not look around to the front, back, left, or right; he looked only about four cubits (a yoke's length) ahead. He walked gracefully, like the Chaddanta elephant king adorned with all trappings.]

When the Blessed One went from house to house for alms within the royal city of Kapilavatthu, the people living in two-story and three-story buildings opened their lion-shaped windows and vied with one another to behold the Blessed One, saying, "Our Lord Prince Siddhattha is making his alms-round."

Princess Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula, also thought: "In the past, the Lord traveled within this very city of Kapilavatthu with great royal luxury and majesty, riding in golden palanquins and such; now, having shaved his hair and beard and wearing saffron-colored robes..."
116:
"...he is making his alms-round carrying a bowl. Is it graceful? Or is it perhaps not graceful?" Thinking thus, she opened the lion-shaped window and looked. She saw the Blessed One walking gracefully with incomparable Buddha-glory, illuminating the great and small streets of the city with his body-radiance that flickered and spread in various delightful ways, adorned with the thirty-two major marks, the eighty minor marks, and the aura of six-colored rays. (Pointing out the Buddha to her son, Prince Rāhula), she uttered praise for the virtues of the Blessed One's physical form (rūpa-kāya) from his forehead-band down to the soles of his feet using the ten Narasīha verses.

After praising the Buddha with these ten verses of the Narasīha (the physical glory of the Buddha), Queen Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula, approached King Suddhodana and informed him, "O Great King, your noble son, the Buddha, is now wandering for alms surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants."

## King Suddhodana Attains the Fruit of Stream-Entry

Upon hearing the words of Queen Yasodharā, King Suddhodana's heart was shaken with agitation. Holding his garment with his hand, he hurriedly left the golden palace and went quickly to the presence of the Blessed One. Standing before him, he said, "Venerable Sir, why do you put us to shame? Why do you wander for alms in this manner? Do you think that sufficient alms cannot be obtained from your father for these twenty thousand monks?"

The Blessed One replied, "O Great King, this practice of wandering for alms from house to house (sapadānacārika) is the lineage that has descended through the succession of Buddhas." King Suddhodana then said, "Noble Son, is our lineage not the Mahāsammata Khattiya lineage, which has descended unbroken from King Mahāsammata at the beginning of the aeon? In that Mahāsammata...
124:
...Khattiya lineage, there has never been even a single king who wandered for alms." Then the Blessed One said, "O Great King, that Mahāsammata Khattiya lineage is your lineage. My lineage, however, is the Buddha-lineage, beginning with Dīpaṅkara Buddha, Koṇḍañña Buddha, Maṅgala Buddha... up to Kassapa Buddha. These twenty-four Buddhas, my elder brothers, as well as thousands of other Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have always wandered for alms from house to house. They maintained their lives through the practice of wandering for alms from house to house." Having said this, while standing in the middle of the road, he spoke this verse:

Arise! Do not be heedless.
Practice the Dhamma well.
He who practices the Dhamma lives happily,
In this world and the next.

"O Great King, one who has become a monk should stand gracefully at the doors of the houses of lay devotees and should not be heedless regarding the alms received. He should practice the custom of wandering for alms, which is well-practiced and free from wrong livelihood (anesana). A monk who is thus habituated to the practice of alms-gathering lives happily in both body and mind in this life and in the life to come."

At the conclusion of this verse, King Suddhodana was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).
125:
## The Royal Father Attains the Fruit of Once-Returner and
## Step-mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī Attains the Fruit of Stream-Entry

After King Suddhodana, the royal father, attained the stage of a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), he personally took the alms-bowl from the Buddha's hand. Inviting the Buddha along with the twenty thousand Arahants to the golden palace, he offered them seats on the noble places prepared for them. Upon reaching the golden palace, the Buddha preached:

Dhammaṃ care sucaritaṃ,
na naṃ duccaritaṃ care.
Dhammacārī sukhaṃ seti,
asmiṃ loke paramhi ca.

"O Royal Father... one should practice the conduct of alms-gathering well, without mixing it with improper livelihood (anesana). One should not practice that alms-gathering conduct wrongly by frequenting improper places (agocara-ṭṭhāna) (such as the houses of maidens, eunuchs, taverns, courtesans, widows, or nuns). A monk who habitually practices the pure conduct of alms-gathering, free from improper livelihood, lives happily in this world and in the world hereafter."

Thus, He preached this second verse. At the end of this second verse, the royal father King Suddhodana was established in the Fruit of Once-returner (Sakadāgāmi-phala), and the step-mother Queen Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).
126:
Then, King Suddhodana served the twenty thousand Arahant elders, headed by the Buddha, with various kinds of excellent food and delicacies that had been prepared in advance.

## Teaching the Candakinnara Jātaka

When the meal was finished, all the ladies of the palace (except for Queen Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula) approached the Blessed One and paid him respectful homage.

As for Queen Yasodharā, although her attendants said, "O Lady, please leave your chamber and pay homage to your Lord," she replied, "Friends, if I have any special merit, the Lord himself will come to my presence. Only when he comes will I pay him homage." Thus, she remained in her own chamber with her dignity intact.

The Blessed One, having asked King Suddhodana to carry his bowl, went to the auspicious chamber of Queen Yasodharā together with the two Chief Disciples. (At that time, forty thousand dancing women and attendants were waiting upon Queen Yasodharā, among whom were one thousand and ninety princesses.) When Queen Yasodharā heard the news that the Blessed One was coming to her auspicious chamber...
127:
...she instructed the forty thousand attendants, "All forty thousand of you must wear robes dyed in bark-juice (saffron)." Those forty thousand women wore the dyed robes according to her instruction. (From the Commentary on the Candakinnara Jātaka).

When the Blessed One arrived at Queen Yasodharā's chamber, he said, "Do not say anything to hinder Princess Yasodharā as she pays homage to me as she wishes," and then sat down on the prepared seat.

Queen Yasodharā quickly approached the Blessed One, firmly grasped both his ankles with her hands, placed her head (forehead) upon his feet, and paid homage as much as she desired, turning her head from side to side. Then King Suddhodana said:

"O Blessed One, my noble son, from the moment my daughter heard the news that you were wearing robes dyed in bark-juice, she also wore dyed robes. When she heard that you eat only one meal a day, she also ate only one meal. When she heard that you had given up high and noble beds, my daughter slept only on a low pallet woven with cords."
128:
“Venerable Sir, even upon hearing the news that You had abstained from flowers, scents, and such, my daughter also abstained from the acts of wearing flowers and applying perfumes.

Venerable Sir, when You went forth into the forest, although other princes and relatives sent messages and news expressing their desire to support and care for her with great honor, my daughter did not look back at anyone even with a glance of household-based affection and craving (gehassita pema-taṇhā). In this way, my daughter is endowed with extraordinary virtues that are worthy of wonder and praise.”

Thus, he spoke words of praise, stating that she was endowed with love and devotion only for the Buddha. At that time, the Buddha said:

“Great King, it is not yet a matter of wonder that Princess Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula, protects herself now, while she is being looked after by you and while her wisdom has matured. In the past, when she had no protector or guardian (like you), while wandering at the foot of Mount Canda even before her perfections (pāramīs) had matured, she protected herself.”

Having said this, the Buddha related the past event, the Candakinnarī Jātaka (the second Jātaka of the Pakiṇṇaka Nipāta), and then—
129:
—rising from His seat, He returned to the Nigrodhārāma monastery accompanied by twenty thousand Arahants.

## The Ordination of Prince Nanda

(A few noteworthy points about Prince Nanda: Two or three days after Queen Mahāmāyā Devī gave birth to the Bodhisatta Prince Siddhattha, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, the younger sister of Māyā Devī and stepmother of the Bodhisatta, gave birth to Prince Nanda. After Nanda was born, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī handed her own son, Prince Nanda, to nurses, and she herself personally performed all the duties of caring for the Bodhisatta (her nephew) and nursed him with her own breast milk. Prince Nanda was only two or three days younger than the Bodhisatta. In terms of height, Prince Nanda was only four finger-breadths shorter than the Bodhisatta.)

On the third day after the Buddha arrived at the city of Kapilavatthu, King Suddhodana, the father, arranged for Prince Nanda to celebrate:

(1) Kesavissajjana Maṅgalā = The ceremony of loosening the childhood topknot to arrange the hair as a Crown Prince.
(2) Paṭṭabandha Maṅgalā = The ceremony of binding the golden diadem, inscribed with the title of Crown Prince, upon the forehead.
(3) Gharappavesana Maṅgalā = The ceremony of handing over the palace of the Crown Prince.
(4) Āvāha Maṅgalā = The marriage ceremony with his sister (cousin) Janapadakalyāṇī.
130:
(5) Chattussāpana Maṅgalā = The ceremony of raising the white umbrella of the Crown Prince.

These five auspicious ceremonies were being celebrated. At that time, the Buddha went to the golden palace and, wishing for Prince Nanda to become a monk, He had the Prince hold His alms-bowl. After delivering a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), the Buddha rose from His seat and returned to the monastery.

Even in the hall of the golden palace, although the Buddha was to take the bowl Himself, He did not take it from Prince Nanda’s hand because He wished to ordain him. Prince Nanda, out of extreme respect for his elder brother, the Buddha, did not dare to say, “Venerable Elder Brother, please take Your alms-bowl.” Thinking that the Buddha would take the bowl when He reached the head of the stairs, Prince Nanda followed, carrying the bowl. When they reached the head of the stairs, the Buddha still did not take the bowl.

Prince Nanda thought, “He will take the bowl when He reaches the foot of the stairs,” and continued to follow, carrying the bowl. When they reached the foot of the stairs, the Buddha still did not take the bowl. Prince Nanda thought, “He will take the bowl when He reaches the palace courtyard (the open ground outside the palace),” and continued to follow, clutching the bowl.
131:
He continued to follow. Even when they reached the palace courtyard, the Buddha did not take the bowl but continued walking as before. Prince Nanda followed unwillingly and wished to turn back, but out of extreme respect for his elder brother, he did not dare to say, “Please take the bowl, Venerable Sir.” He followed in the hope that the Buddha would take it, thinking, “He will take it when He reaches this spot; He will take it when He reaches that spot.”

At that time, the attendants of Janapadakalyāṇī saw this and went to her, saying, “My Lady, the Buddha has taken Prince Nanda away to separate him from you.” (At that moment, Janapadakalyāṇī was still washing her hair.) With water still dripping from her hair and having only half-combed it, she rushed and stood at the palace window and called out, “O Lord, please return quickly!” Janapadakalyāṇī’s words remained lodged in Prince Nanda’s heart as if they were placed crosswise.

The Buddha, without taking the bowl from Nanda’s hand, led him all the way to the monastery. Upon reaching the monastery, He asked, “Nanda, will you become a monk?” Out of great respect for his elder brother, Nanda did not dare to say, “I cannot become a monk.” Although he had no desire in his heart to ordain, he replied, “Very well, Venerable Brother, I will become a monk.”
132:
The Buddha then said, “If that is so, monks, ordain my brother Nanda.” Following the Buddha’s command, the monks ordained Prince Nanda.*

## The Ordination of Prince Rāhula as a Sāmaṇera

Then, on the seventh day, when the Buddha, accompanied by twenty thousand Arahants, came to His father’s palace for a meal, Princess Yasodharā, the mother of Rāhula, beautifully adorned the young Prince Rāhula (seven years old) and said: “Dear son, look at that Great Recluse who has a golden complexion and a straight body like the King of Brahmas, surrounded by twenty thousand noble monks. This noble one is your father. Before your father went forth and became a monk, he possessed four great pots of gold named Saṅkha, Ela, Uppala, and Puṇḍarīka. Since the time your father went forth to become a monk, your mother has not seen those four great pots of gold. Dear son, go to your father and say, ‘Father, I am a young prince. I must be anointed (muddhabhisikta) and become a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch) of the four islands. I desire the wealth and treasures befitting a king. Please give me the four great pots of gold that are your property.’ Ask for your inheritance, saying, ‘Indeed, it is natural for a son to own and receive his father’s inheritance.’” Having thus instructed him, she sent Prince Rāhula to the Buddha.

* The detailed account of Venerable Nanda becoming an Arahant will be presented when reaching the section on the Saṅgha Ratana.
133:
As soon as Prince Rāhula reached the presence of the Buddha, he felt the love for a father and, with a very joyful and happy mind, he said, “O Divine Father, Great Recluse, Your shadow is exceedingly cool and pleasant.” Apart from that, he spoke many other endearing words suitable for himself and remained near the Buddha. When the Buddha had finished His meal and delivered the discourse of appreciation (anumodanā), He rose from His seat, left the golden palace, and returned to the Nigrodhārāma monastery, accompanied by twenty thousand Arahants.

Prince Rāhula also followed closely behind the Buddha, asking for his inheritance, saying, “O Divine Father, Great Recluse, please give me my inheritance. O Divine Father, Great Recluse, please give me my inheritance.” The Buddha did not say to Prince Rāhula, “Dear son, go back.” The royal attendants also did not dare to stop Prince Rāhula, who was following the Buddha (as it was a son following his father). In this manner, Prince Rāhula reached the monastery together with the Buddha, still asking for his inheritance.
134:
Upon reaching the monastery, the Buddha thought: “This Prince Rāhula desires the inheritance of his father’s wealth. This worldly inheritance is included only within the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha) and leads only to great suffering. Come, I shall give Prince Rāhula the seven treasures of the Noble Ones (ariya-dhana)—Saddhā, Sīla, Hirī, Ottappa, Suta, Cāga, and Paññā—which I obtained by overcoming and defeating the fivefold army of Māra at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree. I shall make Prince Rāhula the owner of the supramundane (lokuttara) inheritance.” Having thus considered, He called the Venerable Sāriputta and said, “Dear Sāriputta, Prince Rāhula has come to me to ask for his inheritance; therefore, you should ordain Prince Rāhula as a sāmaṇera.”

(In this context, the seven treasures of the Noble Ones (Ariya-dhana) were taught by the Buddha in Aṅguttara Nikāya 2-398 as follows:
Saddhā-dhanaṃ sīla-dhanaṃ, hiri-ottappiyaṃ dhanaṃ.
Suta-dhanañca cāgo ca, paññā ve sattamaṃ dhanaṃ.

Linking the seven worldly treasures with the seven treasures of the Noble Ones, Venerable Mahā Raṭṭhasāra also composed in the Ko Khan Pyo:
“Hirī is silver, Ottappa is gold... Saddhā is emerald, Sīla is pearl, Cāga is ruby, and Buddhi (Paññā) is diamond—these seven shining treasures.” This should be specially noted.)
135:
When the Buddha gave this command, the Venerable Sāriputta acted as the preceptor (upajjhāya) for Prince Rāhula. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna acted as the teacher for the going forth (pabbajjācariya), performing the tasks of shaving the hair, giving the robes, and administering the refuges. The Venerable Mahākassapa acted as the instructing teacher (ovādācariya), providing guidance and instruction. Thus, they ordained him as a novice (sāmaṇera). Although these three great elders took their respective responsibilities, it is said that "In all matters of ordination, only the preceptor is the authority; the pabbajjācariya and ovādācariya are not. Whatever the pabbajjācariya and ovādācariya do is considered the work of the preceptor." Therefore, in the Pali Canon, it is stated: "Atha kho āyasmā Sāriputto Rāhulaṃ kumāraṃ pabbājesi = Then the Venerable Sāriputta gave the going forth to Prince Rāhula." This indicates that the entire process of ordination was conducted under the authority of the Venerable Sāriputta.

## At the Request of King Suddhodana
## The Laying Down of a Training Rule
When King Suddhodana heard the news that "Prince Rāhula has been ordained," he felt great distress and intense suffering in his heart. To explain further... after the birth of the Bodhisatta, the fortune-tellers predicted, "This prince will become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti)." Similarly, after the births of Prince Nanda and Prince Rāhula, on the days of their auspicious ceremonies, the fortune-tellers also predicted, "This prince will become a Universal Monarch."
136:
At that time, King Suddhodana was greatly encouraged, thinking, "I shall see the glory of my son Prince Siddhattha as a Universal Monarch." However, when Prince Siddhattha, the Bodhisatta, went forth into the forest and became a monk, his wish was not fulfilled, and he reached a state of great mental exhaustion and suffering.

Then again, he encouraged himself, thinking, "I shall see the glory of my younger son Prince Nanda as a Universal Monarch." But when the Buddha also ordained Prince Nanda, he reached a state of great mental exhaustion and suffering for the second time.

Having endured the mental suffering experienced twice in this way, he thought and resolved with his final hope, "Now, I shall fully behold the glory of my grandson Rāhula as a Universal Monarch." While he was holding onto this hope, the Buddha also ordained Prince Rāhula as a novice. Consequently, the thought arose in King Suddhodana's mind, "Now the lineage of the Sakyan kings has been severed. Where can the glory of a Universal Monarch be found?" and he felt even greater mental suffering than before. (At this time, King Suddhodana was only a Sakadāgāmī Noble One, and since the defilement of anger had not been eradicated at the root, he experienced intense mental suffering.)

Unable to bear that mental unhappiness, King Suddhodana approached the Buddha. After paying respects with great devotion and sitting in a suitable place free from the six faults, he addressed the Buddha: "O Blessed Son..."
137:
"I wish to ask a boon of the Blessed One," he began his request. Then the Buddha said, "O Great King of the Gotama lineage, the Buddhas are beyond boons."

(Note: The act of granting or giving boons is not the work of monks who live on alms. When someone says, "I ask for a boon," while one is an alms-receiving monk, it is not appropriate to easily say, "Ask for whatever boon you desire." This is not the custom of the Buddhas. Therefore, the Blessed One replied, "O Great King of the Gotama lineage, the Buddhas are beyond boons.")

Then King Suddhodana submitted, "O Noble Son, I shall ask for a boon that is allowable and blameless." Only then did the Buddha give permission, saying, "O Great King of the Gotama lineage, state the boon you wish to ask." Then King Suddhodana said:

"O Blessed Noble Son, when the Blessed One went forth into the forest and became a monk, I suffered immensely, beyond calculation. When Prince Nanda was ordained, I likewise suffered immensely, beyond calculation. When Rāhula (my grandson) was ordained, I suffered even more excessively."
138:
"O Blessed Noble Son, the love of parents and grandparents for their children and grandchildren cuts through the outer skin, the inner skin, the flesh, the sinews, and the bones, and remains fixed, striking the very marrow.

O Blessed Noble Son, I beg of you, may the Noble Ones not ordain a son or grandson without the permission of the parents."

Thus he made his request for a boon. Then the Buddha preached the Dhamma to King Suddhodana. After King Suddhodana had departed, the Buddha preached to the assembly of monks and, based on the request of King Suddhodana, laid down the training rule:

"Na bhikkhave ananuññāto mātāpitūhi putto pabbājetabbo. Yo pabbājeyya, āpatti dukkaṭassa = Monks, a son who is not permitted by his parents should not be ordained. Whoever should ordain [such a one], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

## King Suddhodana Hearing the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka
## and Attaining the Fruit of Anāgāmī
Then one day, the Buddha, surrounded by twenty thousand Arahants, went to the golden palace of King Suddhodana to partake of a meal. King Suddhodana (as an initial offering)...
139:
...offered rice gruel and hard food. During the interval before the main meal was served, while speaking words of joy, he said, "O Blessed Noble Son, while you were practicing the Great Striving (padhāna), deities came and stood in the sky, telling me, 'Your son Prince Siddhattha has died because he ate so little food.'" The Buddha asked, "Great King, when the deities spoke thus, did you believe them?" King Suddhodana replied, "O Blessed Noble Son, I did not believe them. I told the deities standing in the sky, 'It is impossible for my son to pass away without attaining Buddhahood at the foot of the Mahābodhi tree,' and I rejected the words of those deities."

Then the Buddha said, "Great King, (not to mention this life) in the past when you were the village headman of Mahādhammapāla, you did not believe the words of the world-renowned teacher (Disāpāmokkha) who showed you goat bones as evidence and said, 'Your son, the youth Dhammapāla, has died; these are the bones of your son Dhammapāla.' You refuted him, saying, 'In our Dhammapāla family, there is no such thing as dying at a young age.' Why would you believe it now in this final existence? You certainly would not believe it." Saying this...
140:
...at the request of the Great King, the Buddha preached the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka (the 9th Jātaka of the Dasaka Nipāta) in detail.

After the Buddha preached the Dhammapāla Jātaka to King Suddhodana, he continued to preach the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the discourse on the Four Noble Truths, King Suddhodana attained the Fruit of Anāgāmī (Non-returner).

## Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī Herself
## Weaving and Offering a Pair of Robes to the Buddha
On the day after the Buddha arrived at the city of Kapilavatthu, while he was walking for alms within the city, King Suddhodana, as mentioned before, spoke words of request and invited the Buddha and the twenty thousand Arahants to the golden palace.

Upon arriving at the golden palace, the foster-mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī beheld the glory of the Buddha's most beautiful physical body (rūpakāya) and thought, "How beautiful is the physical body of my son!" At that moment, a powerful feeling of joy (balava-somanassa) arose repeatedly in her mind. Then she continued to think:

"While he was a layman, until he reached the age of twenty-nine, I myself supervised all matters of his food, clothing, and living."
141:
"I even fed him with my own hands, even something as small as a banana. Now that he has become a Buddha, I shall personally supervise the weaving of cloth for robes and offer them to my son."

Then, she had a weaving shed built within the golden palace itself, had cotton brought from the market, and she herself performed tasks such as ginning and spinning the cotton. She invited expert weavers to the golden palace, entertained them with excellent food and snacks, and gave them wages and rewards to weave the cloth for the robes. Whenever she had the opportunity, she went to the weaving shed accompanied by her attendants and participated in the weaving herself.

When the fine cloth for the robes was finished, she gave great rewards and honors to the expert weavers. She then placed the pair of fine cloths in a perfume casket, scented them with fragrances, and said to King Suddhodana, "O Great King, I wish to personally take this pair of fine cloths for my son's robes and go to the monastery to offer them."

King Suddhodana had the road from the golden palace to the monastery cleared and prepared. Every road was swept, water pots were placed, and banners, streamers, and jasmine flowers were arranged...
142: After having the road prepared, a floral carpet was spread all along the way from the palace gate to the Nigrodhārāma monastery. The Great Foster Mother, Mahāpajāpati Gotamī, also dressed in full regalia and, surrounded by a retinue of nurses, personally carried on her head a scented casket containing a pair of fine cloths intended for robes. Approaching the Blessed One with great ceremony, she addressed him: "O Blessed One, my noble son... out of devotion to the Blessed One, I have personally spun, carded, and woven this new pair of fine cloths for robes. O Blessed One, out of compassion and consideration for me, please accept this pair of fine cloths that I have woven and now offer to you, Bhante." Thus she made her request and offering. (In this regard, the detailed story of the Foster Mother personally weaving and offering the robes should be noted from the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta, the 12th Sutta of the Vibhaṅga Vagga in the Uparipaṇṇāsa Pāḷi. A special point to note is that the Commentary on the Dakkhiṇāvibhaṅga Sutta explains that the intention to offer the robes to the Foster Mother arose during the Buddha's first visit to the city of Kapilavatthu. In that Pāḷi text, the Blessed One, in order to further increase her merit, urged her to offer that pair of cloths to the Saṅgha...)
143:
When the Buddha encouraged her, Venerable Ānanda spoke of the mutual gratitude between the Buddha and His step-mother, and requested the Buddha to accept the pair of fine cloth intended for robes, and so forth.

In this matter, there is a point to consider: Venerable Ānanda had not yet become a monk at the time the Buddha first visited the city of Kapilavatthu. He entered the monkhood only after the Buddha left Kapilavatthu and reached the Anupiya Mango Grove in the Malla country. Furthermore, in the Jātaka Commentary and other texts, it is only mentioned that the Buddha established His father, King Suddhodana, in the three lower Fruits and then proceeded to Rājagaha.

Therefore, it is very reasonable to conclude that: "When the Buddha first visited Kapilavatthu, the step-mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī had the intention to personally oversee the weaving of robes to offer Him; she then arranged and wove them, and when the Buddha visited Kapilavatthu for a second time, she offered the pair of fine cloth for robes with great ceremony."

## Here ends Chapter 18.
144: ## Chapter 19: The Ordination of One Thousand Sakyan Princes in the Presence of the Buddha. Thus, after the Buddha had established His father, King Suddhodana, in the three lower Fruitions (Sotāpatti-phala, Sakadāgāmi-phala, Anāgāmi-phala), He departed from the royal city of Kapilavatthu accompanied by twenty thousand Arahants and journeyed toward the city of Rājagaha. Along the way, He arrived at the mango grove named Anupiya in the Malla country and resided there. At that time, in the royal city of Kapilavatthu, the father King Suddhodana called a meeting of all the Sakyan princes and said in that great assembly: 'O Sakyan princes, if my noble son had remained to rule the kingdom, He would certainly have become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) ruling over the four islands, possessing the seven treasures. My grandson, Prince Rāhula, would also have followed that Cakkavatti King, my son, as the eldest son and heir (Parināyaka-ratana), surrounded by all the noble princes of the Khattiya lineage on earth. You Sakyan princes already know this well. Now, my noble son has become the Buddha, the Crown of the Three Worlds. For my son (as He has become Buddha from the royal lineage)...'
145: ...let only princes be His attendants. You Sakyan princes, give me one prince from each household. (I shall have those princes ordained as monks in the presence of my noble son, the Buddha).' When King Suddhodana had spoken these words, they replied, 'Very well, Great King,' and immediately one thousand (1,000) Sakyan princes went to the Anupiya mango grove where the Buddha was residing and were ordained as monks in the presence of the Buddha. ## The Ordination of the Six Sakyan Princes and Upāli the Barber. On the auspicious day of reading the marks after the birth of the Bodhisatta, eighty thousand Sakyan households had promised: 'Whether He becomes a Cakkavatti or a Buddha, He shall travel surrounded only by princes.' Among those Sakyan princes, when many had already ordained: (1) Prince Bhaddiya (who was the reigning king at that time), (2) Prince Anuruddha, (3) Prince Ānanda, (4) Prince Bhagu...
146:
(5) Prince Kimbila,
(6) Prince Devadatta—

Seeing that these six princes had not yet ordained, the Sakyan clansmen criticized them, saying, "We have sent our sons to become monks. These six Sakyan princes must not be our true kinsmen. How can they dare to remain without ordaining?"

Then, Mahānāma the Sakyan went to his younger brother, Prince Anuruddha, and consulted him, saying, "Dear brother Anuruddha... there is no one from our family who has become a monk yet. I would like you, my dear brother, to ordain. Or, if you do not wish to ordain, I myself shall do so." Prince Anuruddha was particularly delicate and lived in great luxury. He was someone who had never even heard the word "not have" (natthi) and did not understand its meaning.

## How Prince Anuruddha Did Not Understand the Word "Not Have"

To elaborate on this... One day, while those six Sakyan princes were playing a game of seed-tossing (gon-nyin) with the agreement that "the loser must provide cakes," Prince Anuruddha lost the game. According to the agreement, he sent a servant to his mother to get some cakes. His mother then prepared cakes and sent them to her son, Prince Anuruddha.

Those six princes ate the cakes joyfully and played the game again. Every time they played, Prince Anuruddha alone lost. Every time he lost, he sent a servant to his mother to get cakes.
147: his mother sent cakes three times. When the fourth time came, the mother sent back the message: "Puva natthi = There are no cakes." Because Prince Anuruddha had never heard the word "natthi" and did not understand it, he thought, "This 'natthi' must be the name of some special, extraordinary cake." He then said, "Bring me that 'natthi' cake," and sent the messenger back to his mother. When the messenger told Anuruddha's mother, "O mother... your son says to please send the 'natthi' cake," she thought, "My son has never heard the word 'natthi' and does not understand it. I must use this opportunity to make him understand the meaning of 'natthi'." She then took an empty golden bowl, covered it with another golden bowl, and sent it to her son. At that moment, the guardian deities of the city thought: "When this Sakyan prince Anuruddha was a poor man named Annabhāra, he offered his portion of rice to the Paccekabuddha named Upariṭṭha and made a wish: 'May I never even hear the word natthi (there is none); may I never even know the source of where food comes from.' If this Prince Anuruddha were to see an empty bowl, we would no longer be allowed to enter the assembly of deities, and our heads would split into seven pieces." Thinking thus, they miraculously filled that empty golden bowl with celestial cakes.
148: When the golden bowl filled with celestial cakes was placed in the marble game circle and opened, the fragrant aroma of the celestial cakes immediately permeated the entire city. As soon as a small piece of the cake was placed in his mouth, the divine essence spread through Prince Anuruddha's seven thousand taste nerves. Then Prince Anuruddha thought, "My mother has never fried and given me this 'natthi' cake for all this time; it seems she does not love me. From today onwards, I will not eat any other cakes; I will eat only 'natthi' cakes." Upon returning to the palace, he immediately asked his mother, "O mother... do you love me, your son, or not?" His mother replied, "Dear son Anuruddha... just as a person with only one eye loves and cherishes that eye to the utmost, or as one loves one's own heart, I love you, my dear son, beyond measure." Prince Anuruddha then asked again, "O mother... if you love and cherish your son so much, why have you not fried and given me this 'natthi' cake for all this time?" Hearing this strange question, the Queen Mother called the young messenger and asked, "My boy... was there something in the golden bowl?" The young messenger replied, "O mother... the entire golden bowl was full of cakes; I have never seen such cakes before." Then the Queen Mother thought, "My son must be a person of great merit who has performed extraordinary deeds in the past; the deities..."
149:
He thought to himself, "Surely, they must have sent the golden bowl filled with cakes."

Then, Prince Anuruddha said to his mother, the Queen, "O Mother, from this time onwards, I shall not eat any other cakes. For me, please fry and give me only 'no-more' cakes." From that time on, whenever Prince Anuruddha sent word saying, "I wish to eat cakes," the Queen-mother would simply cover an empty golden bowl with another golden bowl and send it to him. For as long as Prince Anuruddha remained in the household life before ordaining, the deities themselves provided the cakes for him. How could Prince Anuruddha, who did not even understand the word 'no-more' (n'atthi), understand what it meant to be a monk?

Therefore, Prince Anuruddha asked his elder brother, Prince Mahānāma, "O brother, what is this thing called 'becoming a monk' that you speak of? What kind of thing is it?" Prince Mahānāma replied, "Dear brother Anuruddha, one who becomes a monk must shave off his hair and beard, don robes dyed with vegetable dyes, and sleep on a wooden couch, or a bed woven with cane or bamboo strips, and must live by wandering for alms. This is what it means to be a monk." Prince Anuruddha then said, "O brother, I am a delicate person. I am not capable of becoming a monk."
150:
Then his elder brother, Prince Mahānāma, said, "Dear brother Anuruddha, if that is the case, you must learn to understand household duties and manage the estate. It is not possible for both of us brothers to remain without one of us becoming a monk." Prince Anuruddha then asked his elder brother, "O brother, what are these household duties?" How could the noble youth Anuruddha, who did not even understand the very origin of rice, understand household affairs?

## How Prince Anuruddha and others did not understand where rice comes from

To clarify this: one day, a discussion arose among the three princes—Prince Kimbila, Prince Bhaddiya, and Prince Anuruddha—as to "Where does rice come from?"

In that discussion, Prince Kimbila presented his view, saying, "Rice comes from the granary."

Then Prince Bhaddiya, dismissing Prince Kimbila's statement, said, "You do not know the exact origin of rice," and presented his view, saying, "Rice comes from the cooking pot."

* That prince (Kimbila) had only seen grain being taken out of the royal granary and had never seen a paddy field; thus, he spoke in that way.
† That prince (Bhaddiya) had only seen rice being cooked in a pot and had never seen grain being taken from the granary or the fields; thus, he spoke in that way.
151:
Then Prince Anuruddha, dismissing the statements of both princes, said, "Neither of you knows the exact origin of rice," and presented his view, saying, "Rice comes from the golden serving bowl adorned with the seven kinds of jewels."

In this way, all three princes were ignorant of the primary source of rice. Therefore, Prince Anuruddha (truly not understanding) honestly asked his elder brother, Prince Mahānāma, "O brother, what are these household duties?"

## Prince Anuruddha's Weariness of the Household Life

Then his elder brother, Prince Mahānāma, said, "Dear brother Anuruddha, come, I shall teach you about household duties:
(1) At the beginning of the rainy season, first, the field must be plowed.
(2) After plowing, the seeds must be sown.
(3) After sowing, (observing the time) the water must be let in.
(4) After letting the water in, observing the time, the water must be drained.

* This Prince Anuruddha had never seen grain being taken from the granary to be milled, nor had he seen rice being cooked or served. He had only seen the prepared rice placed before him in a golden bowl; thus, he assumed that "whenever one wishes to eat rice, it spontaneously appears in the golden bowl," and spoke accordingly.
152:
(5) After draining the water, the weeds must be cleared.
(6) After clearing the weeds repeatedly, when the paddy is ripe, it must be harvested.
(7) After harvesting, the reaped stalks must be transported by cart.
(8) After transporting by cart, when they reach the threshing floor, they must be stacked.
(9) After stacking, they must be threshed.
(10) After threshing, the straw must be removed.
(11) After removing the straw, the chaff must be separated.
(12) After separating the chaff, the grain must be winnowed.
(13) After winnowing, it must be transported into the granary.
(14) After transporting it into the granary, the same must be done the following year, and the same must be done in the years after that."

When he had taught him thus, Prince Anuruddha said, "O brother, if that is so, then household duties are never-ending. The end of household duties is not apparent.
153:
Indeed, it is not apparent! When will household duties ever end? When will the end of household duties be seen? When shall we be free from the burden of household duties and live in abundance, beauty, and joy, enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure?" he said in weariness.

Then his elder brother, Prince Mahānāma, said, "It is true, dear brother Anuruddha. Household duties are never-ending; their end is not seen. Even before household duties could be finished or ended, our parents and grandparents passed away." When he said this, Prince Anuruddha replied, "O brother, if that is the case, you yourself should remain, understanding and managing the household duties. I shall go forth from the household life into the homeless life of a monk," thus giving his word to ordain.

Thereafter, Prince Anuruddha went to his mother, the Queen, and requested, "O Mother, I wish to become a monk. Please grant me permission to ordain." When he said this, the Queen-mother said to her son, Prince Anuruddha, "Dear son Anuruddha, I love both of you brothers very much. Even when Death separates us, it will be against my will. How could I give permission for you two dear sons to become monks while you are still alive? (I cannot)." For a second time, Prince Anuruddha requested in the same manner,
154:
and for a second time, the Queen-mother replied that she could not grant permission. For a third time, Prince Anuruddha requested his mother, the Queen, "O Mother, I wish to become a monk. Please grant me permission to ordain."

At that time, the Sakyan prince named Bhaddiya was reigning over the Sakyans. (At that time, King Suddhodana was about ninety years old and was only in a position to give guidance and direction to the Sakyans). This Sakyan King Bhaddiya was a very close friend of Prince Anuruddha. Then, Prince Anuruddha's mother, the Queen, thought, "Now, the Sakyan King Bhaddiya, who is my son Anuruddha's friend, is currently ruling over the Sakyans. This Sakyan King Bhaddiya will by no means be able to become a monk." Having thought this, she said to her son, Prince Anuruddha, "Dear son Anuruddha, if your friend, the Sakyan King Bhaddiya, becomes a monk, then you, my son, may also become a monk."

Then Prince Anuruddha went to his friend, the Sakyan King Bhaddiya, and said, "O friend Bhaddiya, my becoming a monk depends on you." When he said this, King Bhaddiya said to Prince Anuruddha, "O friend Anuruddha, if your becoming a monk depends on me, then let that monkhood
155:
be without dependence. (Although he wanted to say quickly out of friendship, 'I will become a monk with you,' his greed and attachment to royal power pulled at his heart, so he could not speak fully and said only part of the sentence: 'I am with you...') You may become a monk happily as you wish." Prince Anuruddha said again, "O friend Bhaddiya, come, let us both become monks." Then the Sakyan King Bhaddiya said, "O friend Anuruddha, I am not capable of becoming a monk. I will do any other thing for you, my friend, except becoming a monk. (As for becoming a monk), you alone should do it."

Then Prince Anuruddha said to King Bhaddiya, "O friend, my mother told me, 'Dear son Anuruddha, if your friend, the Sakyan King Bhaddiya, becomes a monk, then you, my son, may also become a monk.' O friend Bhaddiya, you have already spoken words of yielding, saying, 'O friend Anuruddha, if your becoming a monk depends on me, then let that monkhood be without dependence. I am with you... You may become a monk happily as you wish.' O friend Bhaddiya, come, let us go. Let us both become monks," he said, urging him insistently so that he could not refuse.

(At that time, people were truthful in their speech and truthful in their promises. According to the truth...)
156:
Bhaddiya Sakyan said to Prince Anuruddha, "O friend Anuruddha, please wait for seven years. After seven years have passed, both of us friends will go forth as monks." Then Prince Anuruddha said, "O friend Bhaddiya, seven years is too long. I cannot wait for seven years." When he said this, Bhaddiya Sakyan said, "O friend Anuruddha, please wait for six years... (peyyāla) ...five years, four years, three years, two years, one year. After one year has passed, both of us friends will go forth as monks," thus gradually reducing the time. Prince Anuruddha insisted, "O friend Bhaddiya, one year is also too long. I cannot wait for one year."

Then Bhaddiya Sakyan reduced it further, saying, "O friend Anuruddha, please wait for seven months. After seven months have passed, both of us friends will go forth as monks." Prince Anuruddha again pressed him, "O friend Bhaddiya, seven months is too long. I cannot wait for seven months." Then Bhaddiya Sakyan said, "O friend Anuruddha, please wait for six months... (peyyāla) ...five months, four months, three months, two months, one month, fifteen days. After fifteen days have passed, both of us friends...
157: ...'we shall be ordained as monks.' As he kept reducing the time, Prince Anuruddha (without yielding) said again, 'Friend Bhaddiya, fifteen days is still too long; I cannot wait for fifteen days.' Then, the Sakyan King Bhaddiya (as a final proposal) said, 'O friend Anuruddha, let me hand over all state affairs to my sons, younger brothers, and elder brothers. Please wait for just seven days.' Prince Anuruddha, satisfied, replied, 'O friend Bhaddiya, seven days is not long; I will wait.' ## The Departure and Ordination of the Six Sakyan Princes along with Upāli (the Barber). Then, (1) Sakyan King Bhaddiya, (2) Prince Anuruddha, (3) Prince Ānanda, (4) Prince Bhagu, (5) Prince Kimbila, and (6) Prince Devadatta (= the royal brother-in-law Devadatta)—these six princes, making seven with Upāli the barber—enjoyed human pleasures for seven days like devas enjoying celestial bliss. Then, as if going out for a garden excursion, they left the royal city with a fourfold army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry. Upon reaching another country (= the border), they sent the army back by royal command and entered the other country (= the Malla country).
158:
Within that Malla territory, the six Sakyan princes took off their ornaments, wrapped them in their upper robes, and said to Upāli the barber, "Now, friend Upāli, you return. This much wealth will be sufficient for you to live on for the rest of your life." They gave the bundles of ornaments to Upāli the barber as a reward.

Upāli the barber rolled on the ground at the feet of the six princes and wept. Not daring to disobey the princes' command, he rose from his weeping, took the bundles of ornaments, and departed from the princes. When the Sakyan prince masters and the servant Upāli parted ways, the great forest roared with a terrifying sound as if it were wailing, and the great earth shook as if an earthquake had occurred.

After going a short distance, Upāli the barber stopped and thought, "The Sakyans are fierce. They might mistakenly think, 'This barber Upāli has done away with the six princes,' and they might even kill me. Even these six Sakyan princes can renounce such magnificent royal wealth and discard these priceless ornaments like spit to become monks. Why should a low-born person like me not be able to become a monk? (I certainly can)." Reflecting thus and gaining wisdom, he untied the bundles of ornaments he had brought, hung them on a tree, and said, "I have renounced and given away these items. Let whoever finds them take them as they wish."
159:
Having spoken thus and abandoned the items, he returned to the six princes. As soon as the six princes saw Upāli the barber from afar, they asked, "Friend Upāli, why have you returned?" Then Upāli the barber fully explained his thoughts and what he had done. The six princes then said, "Friend Upāli, it is very good that you did not return to the kingdom (according to the Sri Lankan version, it is good that you returned to us). The Sakyans are fierce; (if you had returned), they might have mistakenly thought, 'This barber has done away with the six princes,' and they might even kill you."

Then the six Sakyan princes took Upāli the barber with them and went to the Anupiya Mango Grove where the Blessed One was staying. They paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, sat in a suitable place, and said, "Venerable Sir, we Sakyans are arrogant and stubborn because of our birth. Venerable Sir, this Upāli the barber has been our servant for a long time. We wish for the Blessed One to ordain this Upāli the barber first,
160: ...(If Upāli is ordained first), we shall have to perform acts of homage, welcoming, salutation, and respect toward this monk Upāli. By doing so, our great and stubborn Sakyan pride as royal princes will be humbled.' Thus they requested. Then, the Buddha (as requested by the princes) had Upāli the barber ordained first, and only after that did He ordain the six Sakyan princes.* ## The Buddha's Journey to Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha for the Second Vassa. Then, the Buddha, surrounded by more than twenty thousand monks, departed from the Anupiya mango grove near the town of Anupiya in the Malla country and went to the Veḷuvana monastery in Rājagaha. There, He observed the second Vassa (rainy season retreat) together with the accompanying monks. ## About the Buddha's Vassa Residences. After attaining Buddhahood, during the period of the First Bodhi (the first part of His ministry), for twenty (20) years, the Buddha did not yet have a permanent residence for the Vassa retreat. Instead, He stayed in various places to benefit those who were ready to be liberated... *The details about the monk Upāli and the six Sakyan prince-monks will be written and described when reaching the chapter on the Saṅgha-ratana.
161:
(1) The Blessed One preached the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta in the Isipatana Migadāya (Deer Park) near the city of Vārāṇasī, providing the nectar of the Deathless Dhamma to eighteen crores of Brahmas, led by the Elder Koṇḍañña of the group of five. He spent the first Vassa in that Migadāya, depending on Vārāṇasī for alms.

(2) Next, the Blessed One spent the second Vassa at the Veḷuvana Monastery, depending on Rājagaha for alms.

(3-4) He also spent the third and fourth Vassa at that same Veḷuvana Monastery.

(5) Next, he spent the fifth Vassa at the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in the Mahāvana forest, depending on the city of Vesālī for alms.

(6) Next, he spent the sixth Vassa at the monastery on Makula Mountain.

(7) Next, he preached the Abhidhamma on the Paṇḍukambala Stone at the foot of the Parichattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and spent the seventh Vassa there.

(8) Next, he spent the eighth Vassa in the Bhesakaḷā Forest (also known as the forest ruled by the ogress Bhesakaḷā), a sanctuary for deer, depending on the city of Susumāragira in the Bhagga country for alms.
162:
(9) Next, he spent the ninth Vassa at the Ghositārāma Monastery, depending on the city of Kosambī for alms.

(10) Next, he spent the tenth Vassa in the Pārileyyaka forest, receiving the service and care of the Pārileyyaka elephant king.

(11) Next, he spent the eleventh Vassa at the Nāḷikārāma Monastery, depending on the Brahmin village named Nālā for alms.

(12) Next, he spent the twelfth Vassa near a Nimba tree (Naleru Nimba) ruled by the yakkha Naleru, depending on the city of Verañjā for alms.

(13) Next, he spent the thirteenth Vassa at the Cāliya Mountain Monastery, depending on the village of Jantu in the Cāliya region for alms.

(14) Next, he spent the fourteenth Vassa at the Jetavana Monastery, depending on the city of Sāvatthī in the Kosala country for alms.

(15) Next, he spent the fifteenth Vassa at the Nigrodhārāma Monastery, depending on the city of Kapilavatthu in the Sakyan country for alms.

(16) Next, he spent the sixteenth Vassa at the Aggāḷava Shrine Monastery, depending on the city of Āḷavī for alms.

(17) Next, he spent the seventeenth Vassa at the Veḷuvana Monastery, depending on the city of Rājagaha in the Magadha country for alms.

(18-19) Next, he spent the eighteenth and nineteenth Vassa consecutively at the Cāliya Mountain Monastery, depending on the village of Jantu in the Cāliya region for alms.
163:
163
(20) Thereafter, depending on the city of Rājagaha in the Magadha country for alms-resort, the Buddha spent His 20th Vassa (rainy season retreat) at the Veḷuvana Monastery.
(These were the locations where the Buddha spent His Vassas during the first period of His Enlightenment, which were not fixed to a single place.)
(21-44) Thereafter, from the 21st Vassa to the 44th Vassa, depending on the city of Sāvatthī in the Kosala country for alms-resort, He spent the Vassas by alternating between the Jetavana Monastery and the Pubbārāma Monastery.
(From the Buddhavamsa Commentary, page 4, etc.)
(45) Thereafter, when He was about to attain Parinibbāna, He spent His final 45th Vassa at the small village of Beluva near the city of Vesālī.
## Verse on the Sequence of Vassas
Regarding the locations where the Buddha spent His Vassas, the Mon-yway Jetavana Sayadaw composed a verse in the Samantacakkhudīpanī (Volume II), page 374, as follows:

The Friend of the Three Worlds, rising in glory, stayed for two full months and sixty days near the Bodhi tree at the site of victory, maintaining Himself in comfort, and then...
(1) The 1st Vassa, He relied on the forest of Bārāṇasī.
(2+3+4) For the subsequent 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Vassas, He resided at the beautiful Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) in the city of Rājagaha.
(5) The 5th Vassa, He stayed at the Mahāvana Monastery built by the Licchavī princes in the city of Vesālī.
(6) For the 6th, He was at Mount Makula.
(7) During the 7th Vassa, He reached Tāvatiṃsa.
(8) For the 8th Vassa, He was at Bhagga.
(9) When the 9th Vassa arrived, He relied on the golden abode of Ghositarāma in the city of Kosambī.
164:
164
(10) For the 10th Vassa, the Lord relied on the delightful Pāleyyaka forest, dense and undisturbed, accompanied by the noble elephant.
(11) The 11th Vassa was at the famous Brahmin village of Nālā.
(12) The 12th was spent at the place called Verañjā.
(13) For the 13th, He stayed at the beautiful Cāliya Mountain.
(14) During the 14th Vassa, He resided joyfully at the famous Jetavana on the outskirts of Sāvatthī.
(15) From the 15th Vassa, He stayed at the pleasant Nigrodhārāma monastery in the cool shade of Kapilavatthu.
(16) For the 16th Vassa, He dwelt happily in the peerless city of Āḷavī.
(17) During the 17th Vassa, He established a victory at the dark green Bamboo Grove in Rājagaha, a beautiful mansion comparable to a celestial abode.
(18+19) For the 18th and 19th Vassas, He reached and spent them at Cāliya Mountain.
(20) For the 20th Vassa, He returned again to Rājagaha.
For these twenty years of the first period of Enlightenment (Paṭhama-bodhi), the Great Sage did not have a fixed residence for the Vassa.
In the later period (21-44), He stayed for twenty-four years at Sāvatthī, moving between the two noble monasteries of Pubbārāma and Jetavana, which were not far apart.
(45) When He was about to depart for Nibbāna, He spent one Vassa relying on the village of Beluva. Thus, the number of locations is recorded as fifteen, spanning forty-five Vassas. At the age of eighty, the Supreme One, the pinnacle of glory, steered His golden raft to the Shore of Peace (Nibbāna) and entered the final rest, being the crown of the three worlds.
Furthermore, regarding this sequence of Vassas, Sayadaw U Budh wrote a 5-stanza poem of adoration; the Minister Caturangabala of Pinya wrote a 7-stanza poem of adoration; the Taungkhwin Thathanabaing Sayadaw wrote a verse of adoration in the Guḷhatthaviniccaya; and the Most Venerable Kyithe Laydat Sayadaw of Shwetaung also wrote a verse of adoration in the Jinatthapakāsanī. Interested scholars should extract and note them from those respective texts.
## Here ends Chapter 19.
165: ## Chapter 20: The Attainment of Special Dhamma by the Six Royal Monks. The Buddha (as mentioned before) observed the second Vassa at the Veḷuvana monastery in Rājagaha. During that second Vassa, the Venerable Bhaddiya* became a Tevijja Arahant, endowed with the three types of knowledge (Vijja): Knowledge of Past Lives (Pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa), Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu-ñāṇa), and Knowledge of the Destruction of Taints (Āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa). The Venerable Anuruddha, within the first Vassa after his ordination, attained the eight mundane meditative attainments (Samāpatti) and developed the supernormal power of the Divine Eye (Dibba-cakkhu), which enabled him to see a thousand (1,000) universes. One day, the Venerable Anuruddha went to the Venerable Sāriputta and (as stated in the Anguttara Nikāya, Tika Nipāta, Tatiya Paṇṇāsaka, 3-Kusināra Vagga, 8-Dutiya Anuruddha Sutta, page 285): (1) 'Friend Sāriputta, in this Dispensation of the Buddha, I can see a thousand (1,000) universes with the supernormal power of the Divine Eye. (2) My energy is strong and unwavering. My mindfulness is clear and established, never fading. My body is tranquil and unperturbed. My mind is concentrated and fixed on a single object.' *The details about this elder will be presented when reaching the chapter on the Thera-vamsa Saṅgha-ratana.
166:
166
(3) "Yet, despite this, my mind is not liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging (i.e., I have not yet become an Arahant)."
When he said this, the Great Elder Sāriputta replied: "Friend Anuruddha, (1) that you think 'I can see a thousand world systems' is your conceit (māna). (2) That you think 'My energy is aroused... my mind is concentrated' is your restlessness (uddhacca). (3) That you think 'Yet my mind is not liberated' is your remorse or worry (kukkucca). I urge and request you, Venerable Anuruddha, to abandon these three states of conceit, restlessness, and remorse, and instead direct and apply your mind only towards the Deathless Element, the Great Nibbāna." Having said this, he taught the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) to Venerable Anuruddha.
Venerable Anuruddha, having taken the meditation subject from Venerable Sāriputta and requested permission from the Blessed One, traveled to the Ceti country. While practicing the Dhamma of a recluse in the Bamboo Grove situated to the east of where the Blessed One was staying, he spent fifteen days (half a month) in walking meditation (without lying down). Due to the intensity of his exertion, his body became exhausted. While sitting under a bamboo thicket (as recorded in the Anguttara Nikāya, Aṭṭhaka Nipāta, 3-Gahapati Vagga, 10-Anuruddhamahāvitakka Sutta, page 62), he was reflecting on the eight Great Thoughts of a Great Man (Mahāpurisavitakka). When he became weary at the eighth thought, the Blessed One, perceiving this, went to that Bamboo Grove...
167:
167
The Buddha Himself went there, completed the eighth Great Thought for him, and taught the Mahāpurisavitakka Sutta along with the fourfold lineage of the Noble Ones (Ariyavaṃsa). Knowing that this very Bamboo Grove would be the supporting condition (upanissaya-paccaya) for Venerable Anuruddha to reach the Fruit of Arahantship, the Buddha instructed: "Dear Anuruddha, you should spend the coming Vassa right here in this Bamboo Grove." The Buddha then traveled instantly through the air by supernormal power (iddhividha-abhiññā) to the Bhesakaḷā Forest near the city of Susumāragira in the Bhagga country. Upon arrival, He taught the eight Great Thoughts of a Great Man again to the monks residing in that forest.
Venerable Anuruddha spent the next Vassa in that Eastern Bamboo Grove of the Ceti country as instructed by the Blessed One. By practicing and developing the Dhamma of a recluse, he attained the Fruit of Arahantship.
## Venerable Ānanda
The Noble Elder Ānanda attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and became a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna) after hearing and contemplating the Dhamma teaching of the Three Rounds (Tepariivaṭṭa Dhamma-desanā) from Venerable Puṇṇa Mantānīputta. This teaching used the simile of a face reflecting in a clear mirror or a bowl of water to explain how the conceit of 'I' arises based on the five aggregates, and the characteristics of impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anattā) of those five aggregates. (Saṃyutta Nikāya, 2, 86-87).
168:
168
## Venerable Bhagu and Venerable Kimbila
Venerable Bhagu and Venerable Kimbila later practiced Vipassanā meditation, attained the Fruit of Arahantship, and became Arahants.
## Devadatta
Devadatta developed the eight mundane meditative attainments and reached only the supernormal powers (iddhipāda) of a worldling (puthujjana). (This means he was only a worldling monk endowed with psychic powers, not an Ariya).
## The Teaching of the Ambalaṭṭhikā-Rāhulovāda Sutta
The Blessed One taught many Dhamma discourses to Venerable Rāhula. These include: (1) Sāmaṇerapañhā, (2) Rāhula Saṃyutta, (3) Abhiṇha-Rāhulovāda Sutta, (4) Mahā-Rāhulovāda Sutta, (5) Cūḷa-Rāhulovāda Sutta, and (6) the present Ambalaṭṭhikā-Rāhulovāda Sutta.
To elaborate: After the Blessed One had Rāhula ordained as a novice (sāmaṇera), He reflected: "Young children are prone to listen to and speak words that may or may not be logical or appropriate. Therefore, I shall give an exhortation to Rāhula who is still very young." He then called Rāhula and said: "Dear Rāhula, a novice should not speak words that are contrary to the Path and Fruit (i.e., words that do not support the attainment of Magga and Phala). Dear son, if you speak, you should only speak words related to the Dhamma of this nature."
169:
169
Having said this, He taught the discourse known as the "Sāmaṇerapañhā" (The Novice's Questions), which consists of a series of questions and answers from one to ten points, a teaching that all Buddhas do not abandon. (Khuddaka Nikāya, 1, 3).
Again, He reflected: "Young children enjoy telling untruths (musa). They might say they saw something when they did not, or say they did not see something when they did. Therefore, it is proper to give an exhortation to Rāhula, who is very young, not to tell lies." He then taught the Ambalaṭṭhikā-Rāhulovāda Sutta, using four similes of a water bowl, two similes of a great war elephant, and one simile of a mirror, all of which can be understood by sight. (Majjhima Nikāya, 2, 77).
He also taught the "Abhiṇha-Rāhulovāda Sutta," describing how craving (taṇhā) sinks into the four requisites, the abandonment of sensual desire (chandarāga) for the five cords of sensual pleasure, and the great benefit of associating with good friends (kalyāṇa-mitta). (Khuddaka Nikāya, 1, 328).
To show that one should not allow sensual desire and attachment to arise in the three realms of existence wherever one may be, He taught the collection of discourses known as the "Rāhula Saṃyutta." (Saṃyutta Nikāya, 1, 439).
To show that one should not indulge in "gehassita chandarāga" (sensual lust based on the five senses) by relying on the physical body with thoughts such as "I am beautiful, my appearance is pure and clear," He taught the "Mahā-Rāhulovāda Sutta." (Majjhima Nikāya, 3, 83).
170:
Shortly after Venerable Rāhula was ordained and before he had spent his first vassa (rains retreat), the Buddha preached the "Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta" to guide him toward the attainment of Arahantship. (Majjhima Nikāya 3, 324; Saṃyutta Nikāya 2, 324).

Among these various discourses, the exact time of the preaching of the "Abhiṇharāhulovāda Sutta" cannot be precisely determined. Indeed, it was preached as a constant and repeated instruction; therefore, it should be understood that the Buddha preached this sutta to Venerable Rāhula whenever the opportunity arose in various places where the Buddha resided.

The Rāhula Saṃyutta was preached during the period from when Venerable Rāhula was seven years old until the time he was newly ordained and had not yet spent his first vassa.

The Mahārāhulovāda Sutta was preached when Venerable Rāhula was an eighteen-year-old novice (sāmaṇera).

The Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta was preached when Venerable Rāhula was newly ordained and had not yet spent his first vassa.

The Sāmaṇerapañhā and this Ambalaṭṭhika Rāhulovāda Sutta were preached when Venerable Rāhula was a young novice of seven years.

Among these teachings, the Abhiṇharāhulovāda Sutta was preached for the purpose of constant instruction. The Rāhula Saṃyutta was preached to nurture the "embryo" of insight-wisdom (vipassanā-ñāṇa) in Venerable Rāhula. The Mahārāhulovāda Sutta was preached to abandon sensual desire related to the household life (gehassita chandatāga). The Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta was preached so that when the fifteen qualities that ripen liberation (vimuttiparipācanīya dhamma) had matured in Venerable Rāhula, who was newly ordained and had not yet spent his first vassa,
171:
he might attain the Fruit of Arahantship. The Sāmaṇerapañhā was preached to abandon unsuitable speech (speech that does not benefit the Path and Fruit). This Ambalaṭṭhika Rāhulovāda Sutta, which will now be presented, was preached to prevent the act of telling an intentional lie. (These are excerpts from the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, Vol. 3, pp. 88, 89).

In terms of time, this occurred when the Blessed One was spending his second vassa at the Veluvana Monastery in Rājagaha. At that time, the Venerable Rāhula (a young novice) was staying in a meditation pavilion named "Ambalaṭṭhikā," so called because it was built near a young mango tree on the outskirts of the Veluvana Monastery grounds, where he was dwelling in the practice of seclusion.

(Just as a thorn is not intentionally sharpened by anyone but is naturally sharp from the moment it begins to grow, in the same way, Venerable Rāhula, even as a young novice of seven years, dwelt practicing the two kinds of seclusion—physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) and mental seclusion (citta-viveka)—without being urged or prompted by anyone.)

Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) and went to the Ambalaṭṭhikā meditation pavilion where Venerable Rāhula was staying. Venerable Rāhula saw the Blessed One coming from afar and, having shaken out and prepared the seat that was already there for the Blessed One, he also set out water for washing the feet. The Blessed One sat on the seat prepared by Venerable Rāhula and washed his feet. (In this context, the washing of the feet was not because there was dust clinging to the Blessed One's feet,
172:
but rather it was solely to accept the service performed by his disciple). Venerable Rāhula, having paid homage to the Blessed One with deep respect, sat down at a place free from the six faults of sitting.

(1) Then the Blessed One, having left a small amount of water in the foot-washing vessel, asked Venerable Rāhula: "Rāhula, do you see this small amount of water left by me in this vessel?" When Rāhula replied, "I see it, Bhante," the Blessed One gave this instruction: "Rāhula, for those who feel no shame in telling an intentional lie, the noble recluseship (samañña) that leads to the cessation of defilements is as very little as this water in the vessel."

(2) Then the Blessed One poured out that small amount of water and asked: "Rāhula, do you see this small amount of water that has been poured out by me?" When Rāhula replied, "I see it, Bhante," the Blessed One gave the second instruction: "Rāhula, for those who feel no shame in telling an intentional lie, the noble recluseship that leads to the cessation of defilements is poured out just like this small amount of water."

(3) Then the Blessed One turned that vessel upside down and asked Venerable Rāhula: "Rāhula, do you see this vessel
173:
that has been turned upside down by me?" When Rāhula replied, "I see it, Bhante," the Blessed One gave the third instruction: "Rāhula, for those who feel no shame in telling an intentional lie, the noble recluseship that leads to the cessation of defilements is turned upside down just like this vessel."

(4) Then the Blessed One turned that vessel back up (note that at this time there was not a single drop of water in the vessel) and asked Venerable Rāhula: "Rāhula, do you see this empty, void vessel which does not have even a drop of water?" When Rāhula replied, "I see it, Bhante," the Blessed One gave the fourth instruction: "Rāhula, for those who feel no shame in telling an intentional lie, the noble recluseship that leads to the cessation of defilements is empty and void, without even a single drop, just like this vessel."

(5-6) Then the Blessed One continued to give this following exhortation to Venerable Rāhula: "Rāhula, for example, a king's great war elephant in a battlefield performs its task with its two front legs and its two back legs. (This means it crushes and kills the enemies
174:
by striking with its two front legs and kicking with its two back legs whenever they enter its range). It performs its task with the front part of its body and the back part of its body (meaning it uses its body to break down the enemy's defensive walls, which are built with planks and roofs but without peaks). It performs its task with its head (kumbha). (Performing with the head means it aims and thinks, 'I will crush this spot,' then draws back to gain momentum and stares intently; upon seeing such an intense stare from the great elephant, thousands of enemy soldiers become terrified and scatter). It performs its task with its two ears (meaning it uses its ears to deflect arrows shot by the enemy, making them fall to the ground). It performs its task with its two tusks (meaning it uses its tusks to gore the enemy's elephants, horses, and riders). It performs its task with its tail (meaning it uses small swords or iron maces attached to the end of its tail to cut and destroy the enemy forces). However, it protects its trunk by tucking it into its mouth.

While the great war elephant acts in this way, the mahout thinks: 'This great war elephant of the king performs its task in the battlefield with its front legs, its back legs, its front body, its back body, its head, its ears, and its
175:
tusks, and its tail, but it protects its trunk by tucking it into its mouth; this great war elephant of the king has not yet sacrificed its life.'

Rāhula, when the king's great war elephant in the battlefield performs its task with its front legs, its back legs (as mentioned before), its tail, and also performs its task with its trunk (by taking up an iron mace or a hardwood mace and striking and crushing everything within a radius of eighteen cubits), then the mahout thinks: 'This great war elephant of the king performs its task in the battlefield with its front legs, its back legs, its tail, and its trunk; this great war elephant of the king has now sacrificed its life. Now there is nothing that the king's great war elephant will not do.' In the same way, Rāhula, I say that for a person who feels no shame in telling an intentional lie, there is no evil that he will not dare to do.

Therefore, Rāhula, you should train yourself with great diligence in the Threefold Training, resolving: 'I will not tell a lie, even in jest.'" Thus did the Blessed One give this very profound word of exhortation.
176:
(7) Furthermore, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Rāhula: "Rāhula, what do you think? (You may speak as you see fit.) What is the purpose of a mirror?" When asked this, the Venerable Rāhula replied, "Venerable Sir, the purpose of a mirror is for reflecting upon and correcting blemishes such as moles or pimples on one's face." Then the Blessed One said, "In the same way, Rāhula, a bodily action should be performed only after reflecting with the eye of wisdom. A verbal action should be spoken only after reflecting with the eye of wisdom. A mental action should be thought only after reflecting with the eye of wisdom." Having thus laid down this brief summary, He taught in detail by analyzing the three stages of reflecting with the eye of wisdom before performing bodily, verbal, and mental actions.*

In brief: "When one intends to perform a bodily action, speak a verbal action, or think a mental action, one must reflect beforehand—before acting, speaking, or thinking: 'Will this bodily, verbal, or mental action that I am about to do lead to the suffering of myself, of others, or of both? Is it an unwholesome act that will increase and mature the state of suffering?' If, upon reflection, one realizes it is a bodily, verbal, or mental action that would cause suffering to oneself and others, and is an unwholesome act that would increase and mature...

* The details of this teaching should be studied in the Myanmar translation of the Piṭaka.
177:
...the state of suffering, then one must strive to avoid performing, speaking, or thinking such bodily, verbal, or mental actions. If, upon reflection, one realizes it is a bodily, verbal, or mental action that would not cause suffering to oneself and others, and is a wholesome act that would increase and mature the state of happiness, then one should perform, speak, or think such bodily, verbal, or mental actions.

While performing a bodily action, speaking a verbal action, or thinking a mental action, one should also (in the same manner) reflect: 'Is this bodily, verbal, or mental action that I am currently performing, speaking, or thinking leading to the suffering and distress of myself, of others, or of both? Is it an unwholesome act that increases and matures the state of suffering?' If, upon reflection, one realizes it is a bodily, verbal, or mental action that causes suffering and distress to oneself and others, and is an unwholesome act that increases and matures the state of suffering, then one must desist and stop (without continuing to perform, speak, or think it). If, upon reflection, one realizes it is a bodily, verbal, or mental action that does not cause suffering and distress to oneself and others, and is a wholesome act that increases and matures the state of happiness, then one should repeatedly perform, speak, and think such bodily, verbal, and mental actions with increased effort.

After having performed a bodily action, spoken a verbal action, or thought a mental action (in the same manner as before)...
178:
...one should reflect: 'Did this bodily, verbal, or mental action that I have performed or thought lead to the suffering and distress of myself, of others, or of both? Was it an unwholesome act that increases and matures the state of suffering?' If, upon reflection, one realizes it was a bodily or verbal action that caused suffering and distress to oneself and others, and was an unwholesome act that increases and matures the state of suffering, then one should openly, clearly, and without concealment disclose and confess such wrong bodily or verbal actions to the Blessed One or to wise companions in the holy life. After such disclosure, one must practice restraint and control to avoid committing such wrongs again in the future. If it was an unwholesome mental action, one should feel weary of it, be ashamed of it, and loathe it. After feeling weariness, shame, and loathing, one must practice restraint and control to avoid thinking such wrong mental actions again in the future.
