If, upon reflection, one realizes it was a bodily, verbal, or mental action that did not cause suffering and distress to oneself and others, and was a wholesome act that increases and matures the state of happiness, then one should dwell day and night with joy and gladness (pīti-pāmojja) associated with that wholesome deed, diligently developing the wholesome qualities of the Three Trainings.

In the three periods of time—past, future, and present—the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas,
179:
and Noble Disciples (Ariyasāvaka) have purified, will purify, and are currently purifying their bodily, verbal, and mental actions through this very method of repeated reflection.

Therefore, the Blessed One concluded His exhortation by saying, "Rāhula, you must train yourself thus: 'I will purify my bodily actions, verbal actions, and mental actions by means of repeated reflection (paccavekkhaṇā),' and you must diligently practice the Three Trainings."

[In this regard, there is a point to be examined: "At what point should bodily and verbal actions be purified and cleansed? At what point should mental actions be purified and cleansed?"

The answer is: Bodily and verbal actions performed in the morning should be purified and cleansed (without delay) while sitting in a quiet place for the day after the meal is finished. To elaborate: A monk sitting in a quiet place after his meal should reflect, "From dawn until sitting here now, have I committed any wrong bodily or verbal actions during this time that might have been displeasing to others?" If, upon reflection, he realizes there are bodily or verbal actions for which confession (desanā) is required, he should confess them. If there are bodily or verbal actions that should be made known, he should make them known to his companions in the holy life. If he realizes he has committed no wrong bodily or verbal actions, he should dwell in the joy and gladness (that arises from his own conduct).

Mental actions, however, should be purified and cleansed at the place where alms are sought. The method of purification is: "Today, in the place where I sought alms,
180:
did weak greed, strong greed, malicious hatred, or deluded ignorance arise within me toward objects such as visual forms?" If, upon reflection, he realizes they did arise, he should resolve in his mind, "I will not allow such acts of greed, hatred, and delusion to occur again." If they did not arise, he should dwell in the joy and gladness (arising from the awareness of their non-arising). This is the answer].

The preaching of the Ambalaṭṭhikā-Rāhulovāda Sutta is finished.
**********
## The Story of Anāthapiṇḍika
In the second year of the Blessed One's residence at Rājagaha, during the rainy season retreat, the Blessed One permitted the use of monastery requisites for the monks, following a request made by the merchant of Rājagaha through the monks.*

The merchant of Rājagaha and the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika of Sāvatthī were brothers-in-law (their wives were each other's sisters). Consequently, when goods produced in Rājagaha were cheap there but highly valuable in Sāvatthī, the merchant of Rājagaha would purchase those goods, load them onto five hundred carts, and transport them to Sāvatthī. One league (yojana) before reaching Sāvatthī, he would send word ahead to Anāthapiṇḍika about his arrival. Anāthapiṇḍika would then go out to welcome him,

* For the detailed account, see the Senāsanakkhandhaka in the Myanmar translation of the Vinaya Cūḷavagga.
181:
provide grand hospitality, and they would enter Sāvatthī together in a single carriage. If the merchant of Rājagaha could sell his goods quickly, he would do so. If not, he would leave them at his sister's house and return. Anāthapiṇḍika would do the same when visiting Rājagaha.

In that year, after the Blessed One had completed His second rainy season retreat in Rājagaha, Anāthapiṇḍika purchased goods produced in Sāvatthī, loaded them onto five hundred carts, and set out for Rājagaha. As on previous occasions, he sent a message ahead to the merchant of Rājagaha from one league away to announce his arrival.

The merchant of Rājagaha, however, was unable to attend to the message. He had gone to the forest monastery named Sītavana, where the Blessed One was staying, to listen to the Dhamma. After listening, he invited the Buddha and the community of monks for a meal the following day. He was busy managing the preparations in his house, such as digging pits for stoves and splitting firewood.

Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, "He will come to welcome me any moment now," continued his journey. Even when he reached the gate of the merchant's house, he found no one to welcome him. Upon entering the house, he did not receive much of a greeting, only: "Great Merchant, are the children well? On the journey..."
182:
"Did you arrive without fatigue and in comfort?" This was the only greeting Anāthapiṇḍika received from the Merchant of Rājagaha.

After offering only these two words of greeting to Anāthapiṇḍika, the Merchant of Rājagaha prioritized the arrangements for the next day's meal offering to the Buddha. He began directing his servants and workers, saying, "Friends, wake up early tomorrow morning. Boil the gruel, cook the rice, prepare the curries, and arrange the side dishes perfectly."

At that moment, a thought occurred to Anāthapiṇḍika: "In the past, whenever I arrived, this merchant would set aside all other matters and speak with me joyfully. Now, however, he is preoccupied with many tasks, instructing his servants and workers to boil gruel, cook rice, and prepare various dishes for tomorrow's meal. Could it be that he is preparing for a wedding ceremony to bring a bride for his son (āvāha), or a ceremony to send his daughter to her husband's home (vivāha)? Or is he preparing a great sacrifice, or has he invited King Bimbisāra along with his army for a meal tomorrow?"

After the Merchant of Rājagaha had finished making all the arrangements with his servants and workers, he approached Anāthapiṇḍika and engaged in pleasant conversation. Then, Anāthapiṇḍika asked:
183:
"Great Merchant, in the past, whenever I arrived, you would set aside all other matters and speak with me joyfully. Now, however, you are preoccupied with many tasks, instructing your servants and workers to boil gruel, cook rice, and prepare various dishes for tomorrow's meal. Is there a wedding ceremony to bring a bride for your son (āvāha), or a ceremony to send your daughter to her husband's home (vivāha)? Are you preparing a great sacrifice, or have you invited King Bimbisāra along with his army for a meal tomorrow?"

The Merchant of Rājagaha replied:

"Great Merchant, it is not a wedding for a son, nor a wedding for a daughter, nor have I invited King Bimbisāra with his army for a meal tomorrow. Indeed, I am preparing a great almsgiving. I have invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for tomorrow's meritorious deed."

Upon hearing the word "Buddha" uttered with such great enthusiasm from the mouth of the Merchant of Rājagaha,
184:
Anāthapiṇḍika experienced the five types of rapture: minor rapture (khuddikā pīti), momentary rapture (khaṇikā pīti), showering rapture (okkantikā pīti), uplifting rapture (ubbegā pīti), and pervading rapture (pharaṇā pīti). These five types of rapture overwhelmed him from his head down to his feet, and from his feet up to his head. They spread from his sides through his entire body, and from the center out to his sides. With his body completely permeated by these five types of rapture, he asked the Merchant of Rājagaha, "Great Merchant, did you say 'the Buddha'?" The Merchant of Rājagaha replied, "Great Merchant, I did say 'the Buddha'."

After asking and receiving the same answer three times, Anāthapiṇḍika said:

"Great Merchant, even the sound of the word 'Buddha, Buddha' is rare to hear in this world. Great Merchant, is it possible to go and see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, at this very moment?"

The Merchant of Rājagaha thought, "Buddhas are difficult to approach, like great venomous serpents. Moreover, the Buddha is currently residing in the Sītavana forest near the cemetery. At this hour (near sunset), Anāthapiṇḍika will not be able to go to that forest monastery." Reflecting thus, he replied:
185:
"Great Merchant, now is not the time to go and see the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One. You will be able to go and see the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, early tomorrow morning."

Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, "I will only be able to go and see the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, early tomorrow morning," fell asleep with mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, without thinking of anything else. To clarify further: having heard the rare sound of the word "Buddha," Anāthapiṇḍika lost interest in his caravan of goods and his servants for that day. Without even eating his evening meal, he went up to his seven-storied mansion and lay down on a noble, well-prepared, and decorated bed, falling asleep while reciting and meditating on the word "Buddha, Buddha."

After the first watch of the night had passed, Anāthapiṇḍika arose from his bed and repeatedly reflected on the virtues of the Buddha. At that time, intense devotion (balava-saddhā) toward the Buddha arose in him repeatedly. Light born of rapture appeared, and the darkness vanished. It was as if
186:
a thousand lamps had been lit, or as if the moon and sun had appeared. Anāthapiṇḍika exclaimed, "Oh, I must have been negligent! The sun has already risen!" He got up from his place, but seeing the moon still shining in the sky, he realized, "Only the first watch has passed; the middle watch and the last watch still remain." He then returned to his chamber and lay down again.

In this manner, he arose from his bed three times—at the end of the middle watch and again during the last watch. At the end of the final watch, just as dawn was about to break, he got up and walked along the balcony toward the main entrance. The main gates of the seven-storied mansion opened automatically. Anāthapiṇḍika descended from the mansion and walked along the main road of the city.

When Anāthapiṇḍika reached the gate named Sivaka, the (Ariya) guardian deities of the city thought, "This Anāthapiṇḍika has set out with the intention of serving and attending to the Buddha. If he sees the Buddha for the first time, he will be established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala) and become the foremost lay supporter of the Triple Gem. He will build an incomparable monastery (saṅghārāma) and keep its doors open for all the Noble Ones (Ariyas) coming from the four directions. For such a person,
187:
it is not proper to keep the gate closed." Thinking thus, they opened the city gate in advance.

However, as Anāthapiṇḍika stepped out of the city, the light vanished and darkness returned. Fear, trembling, and horripilation (hair-standing-on-end) arose in him. Consequently, Anāthapiṇḍika wished to turn back from that spot. (The city of Rājagaha was very populous and diverse. Eighteen crores of people lived there—nine crores inside the city and nine crores outside. Because the city gates were closed at night, people could not take the bodies of those who died at untimely hours outside for cremation. Instead, they would stand on the watchtowers of the city wall and throw the corpses outside the gates. Thus, as soon as Anāthapiṇḍika stepped outside the city, he stepped on a freshly discarded corpse and his foot struck another. Flies flew up with a buzzing sound. The stench of the corpses entered his nostrils. Because of this, the clear faith (pasāda-saddhā) that had been arising in him toward the Buddha weakened. The light born of rapture emanating from his body vanished, and darkness returned. Fear, trembling, and horripilation arose, and he wished to turn back.)
188:
Then the yakkha Sivaka, remaining invisible, thought, "I shall encourage the merchant to continue forward." In a voice as sweet as the sound of golden bells, he said:

"A hundred thousand elephants, a hundred thousand horses,
A hundred thousand chariots drawn by mules,
A hundred thousand maidens adorned with jeweled earrings—
These are not worth even a sixteenth part
Of a single step taken toward the Buddha."

(O Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, whose glory shines bright!) A hundred thousand elephants of noble breed and great value; a hundred thousand horses of noble breed and great value; a hundred thousand chariots drawn by Sindh horses of noble breed and great value; a hundred thousand maidens of noble birth and great value, adorned with various jeweled earrings—all these are not worth a sixteenth part of the merit of a single step (or the volition behind a single step) taken by a man of courage who travels to the monastery with the intention: "I shall see the Buddha, I shall listen to the Dhamma, and I shall serve the Saṅgha."
189:
one sixteenth of a sixteenth part. (Or) one part out of two hundred and fifty-six parts. Nāgghanti = they are not worth.

“Go forward, O Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika! Go forward, O Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika! For you, Great Merchant, going forward is indeed praiseworthy and noble; retreating is neither praiseworthy nor noble.”

Thus spoke the yakkha.

At that moment, the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika reflected, “I thought I was alone, but I have followers and companions. Why should I be afraid?” and he became courageous again. Then, a powerful faith (devotion to the Buddha) arose within the merchant. Consequently, the darkness vanished and light appeared, and his fear, trembling, and hair-standing-on-end subsided.

Thereafter, as the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika continued his journey forward, he again saw various types of corpses along the frightening cemetery path. He heard the terrifying sounds of domestic dogs, wild dogs, and so on. Therefore, fear entered him again, and for a second time, just as before, the light vanished and darkness arrived. When this happened, the yakkha Sīvaka spoke words of encouragement as before, and the darkness vanished and light appeared. As he continued his journey, for the third time—
190:
—just as before, the light vanished. He repeatedly cultivated faith and devotion toward the Buddha to overcome and transcend all the dangers he encountered, and thus he proceeded.

By traveling in this manner, the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika eventually reached the Sītavana grove. At that time, the Buddha was walking back and forth on the open-air ambulatory path (caṅkama) during the early dawn as it was about to become light.

While walking, the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika thought, “In this world, great heretical teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa say, ‘We are Buddhas. We are Buddhas.’ How shall I truly know for certain that the Blessed One is indeed the Buddha?” Then, a further thought occurred to the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika: “Many people know my name as ‘Anāthapiṇḍika,’ which arose from the virtue of giving food to those who are helpless. But no one other than myself knows the name given to me by my parents (Sudatta). If he is truly the Buddha, the Blessed One will call me by the name given by my parents (Sudatta).”

The Blessed One saw the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika coming from afar, descended from the ambulatory path, and sat on the prepared seat. When Anāthapiṇḍika approached (as the Buddha already knew his thought)—
191:
—“Ehi Sudatta = Come, dear Sudatta,” the Buddha called out. Then, the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika thought, “The Blessed One calls me by the original name given by my parents,” and with a heart full of joy and upliftment, he approached the Blessed One. He bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One in homage and inquired, “Exalted Buddha, has the Lord, the Master of Glory, slept in comfort?”

Then the Blessed One addressed the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika:

Sabbadā ve sukhaṃ seti,
Brāhmaṇo parinibbūto.
Yo na limpati kāmesu,
Sītibhūto nirūpadhi.

(Gahapati = Disciple Anāthapiṇḍika). Yo = That Arahant. Kāmesu = in the objects of sensual pleasure. Na limpati = is not smeared by the mire of defilements. Sītibhūto = having become cool, being free from the heat of defilements. Nirūpadhi = is free from the three kinds of acquisitions (upadhi): defilements (kilesa), volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra), and sensual pleasures (kāmaguṇa). Brāhmaṇo = one who has put away evil. Parinibbūto = one who has attained the extinction of defilements (kilesa-parinibbāna) and ended the heat of suffering. So = that Arahant. Sabbadā = at all times, day and night. Ve-ekantena = indeed, in truth. Sukhaṃ = in both body and mind, happily. Seti = sleeps and dwells.
192:
Sabbā āsattiyo chetvā,
Vineyya hadaye daraṃ.
Upasanto sukhaṃ seti,
Santiṃ pappuyya cetasā.

(Gahapati = Disciple Anāthapiṇḍika). So = That Arahant. Sabbā = all. Āsattiyo = cravings (taṇhā) that cling to and pursue the five sense objects. Chetvā = having completely cut them off with the four paths of knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). Hadaye = in the heart. Daraṃ = all the heat of defilements. Vineyya = having removed. Santiṃ = Nibbāna, the state where all defilements are extinguished. Cetasā = with the noble mind of the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala-samāpatti). Pappuyya = having reached repeatedly and reflectively. Upasanto = having become peaceful, with all the heat of defilements cooled. Sukhaṃ = in both body and mind, happily. Seti = sleeps and dwells.

After declaring that he himself dwells happily in all four postures, the Blessed One preached to the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika the sequence of the Dhamma (Anupubbīkathā), which is the noble path to reaching the Path and Fruit (as previously mentioned): (1) Discourse on Giving (Dānakathā), (2) Discourse on Virtue (Sīlakathā), (3) Discourse on Heaven (Saggakathā), (4) Discourse on the Path (Maggakathā), the danger of sensual pleasures (kāmānaṃ ādīnava), and the benefits of renunciation (nekkhamma āniśaṃsa). When the Buddha knew that the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika’s mind was ready, soft, free from hindrances (nīvaraṇa), uplifted and joyful, and clear, he preached the Four Noble Truths—
193:
—the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma teaching. Upon hearing this, the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala).

Then the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika said, “Excellent, Exalted Buddha! Excellent, Exalted Buddha! Exalted Buddha, it is as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what had been hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms. In the same way, the Blessed One has explained the Dhamma in many ways. Exalted Buddha, I go to the Blessed One, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha for refuge. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka) who has taken refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.” Having thus taken the supramundane refuge, he requested, “Exalted Buddha, may the Lord Buddha together with the community of monks graciously accept a meal from me tomorrow for the sake of merit.”

The Blessed One accepted the invitation of the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika by remaining silent. Then, the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, knowing that the Blessed One had accepted—
194: 194. He rose from his seat, paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, and after circumambulating Him to the right, returned to his lodging at the house of the Great Merchant of Rājagaha. ## The Great Merchant of Rājagaha, the Guild of Merchants, and King Bimbisāra Offering Assistance. As soon as the Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for a meal, the news spread instantly. When the Great Merchant of Rājagaha heard the news that "The Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika has invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for a meal tomorrow for the sake of merit," he said to Anāthapiṇḍika: "O Great Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, I have heard that you have invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for a meal tomorrow for the sake of merit. You are a guest here in this place. Let me provide you with the necessary provisions and assistance. With the provisions I provide, please serve the meal to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha." Then, Anāthapiṇḍika replied: "O Great Merchant, it is alright. I have my own provisions to give. I shall serve the meal to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with the provisions I already have." The householders who were members of the Guild of Merchants living in Rājagaha also heard the news and, like the Great Merchant of Rājagaha, spoke words of invitation, wishing to provide assistance with provisions. On that occasion as well, he replied in the same manner as before.
195: 195. King Bimbisāra also heard the news and, like the Great Merchant of Rājagaha, spoke words of invitation, wishing to provide assistance with provisions. On that occasion, Anāthapiṇḍika replied: "Great King, it is alright. I have my own provisions to give. I shall serve and attend to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with the provisions I already have." When the next morning arrived, Anāthapiṇḍika served the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with excellent food and delicacies at the house of his brother-in-law, the Great Merchant of Rājagaha. After the meal, he sat in a suitable place free from the six faults and addressed the Buddha: "Exalted Buddha, may the Blessed One together with the assembly of monks consent to reside in Sāvatthī for the rainy season retreat for the benefit of us disciples." The Buddha then said to Anāthapiṇḍika: "Householder Anāthapiṇḍika, the Tathāgatas delight in secluded places." Anāthapiṇḍika replied: "Exalted Buddha, I understand. O Blessed One who speaks well, I understand." Then, the Buddha, after delivering a Dhamma discourse to Anāthapiṇḍika, returned to the monastery. ## Constructing a Rest House at Every League Between Rājagaha and Sāvatthī. At that time, Anāthapiṇḍika was a man with many friends and associates...
196:
When people respectfully listen to what is said, it is then that success is achieved. Thus, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika quickly completed his business affairs in the city of Rājagaha and returned to the city of Sāvatthī.

Along the way, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika addressed the people living there: "Friends, prepare parks for resting, build monasteries, and establish regular offerings. The Blessed One has appeared in the world! At my invitation, that Blessed One will travel along this very path where you live."

Thus he exhorted and encouraged them. Then, those people, who were friends of the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika along the way, if they were wealthy themselves, did not take the merchant's help but built parks and monasteries and established regular offerings with their own wealth. For those who had little wealth or were entirely unable to afford it, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika himself provided financial assistance. Those people also built parks and monasteries and established regular offerings with that money.

In this way, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika provided assistance in the form of one hundred thousand coins and timber and bamboo buildings worth another hundred thousand. Along the forty-five yojana journey between Rājagaha and Sāvatthī, he built a residence at every yojana and finally arrived at the city of Sāvatthī.
197: 197. ## Anāthapiṇḍika Searching for and Purchasing the Site for Jetavana Monastery. Then, Anāthapiṇḍika reached Sāvatthī and searched for a place, considering: "Where should the Blessed One reside? It must be a place not too far from the town, not too near to the town, well-provided with access roads, easy for everyone to come and go as they wish, and secluded from the five sensory objects—the sounds of the city, the village, and people." While searching, he saw the garden of Prince Jeta which was endowed with these four attributes. He went to Prince Jeta and made an offer to buy it: "Prince, I wish you to give me your garden (at a fixed price) for the purpose of building a monastery." Prince Jeta replied: "Merchant, I cannot give my garden even if it were covered with gold coins to its very edge." (Note: If Prince Jeta had simply said "I cannot give my garden," it would not be considered a valuation. However, because he said "even if it were covered with gold coins to its very edge," it is considered that he not only set a price for his garden but even stated a price higher than its value.) Then, Anāthapiṇḍika took the meaning of Prince Jeta's words and asserted: "Prince, you have already made a contract (to sell) the Jetavana garden." Prince Jeta denied it, saying: "Merchant, I have not spoken any words (to offer to sell) my garden at all."
198:
In this way, Anāthapiṇḍika claimed, "The Prince has already spoken and contracted to sell his own garden," and Prince Jeta claimed, "I have not spoken at all about an offer to sell my own garden." As they disputed with each other, they went to the court of law to receive a judgment from the ministers who were judges. The ministers who were judges then gave their decision: "Prince, since you spoke a valuation, even if excessive, by saying 'even if it were covered with coins edge to edge,' you have spoken and contracted to sell the garden you own." (This is a very subtle worldly matter; it can only be understood and accepted by those who can contemplate with great wisdom.)

When he won the case at the court of law, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika had gold coins brought out by carts and had them spread over the ground of Prince Jeta's garden, edge to edge. For the areas of ponds and trees within the garden where spreading was not possible, he measured the circumference of those ponds and trees and gave the equivalent amount of gold coins by spreading them edge to edge in another place. In this way, the wealth of the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, amounting to one hundred and eighty million (18 crores) gold coins which he had stored for emergencies, was spent just on the purchase of the monastery site.

With those coins that the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika had first brought out by carts...
199:
...while he was having the site of Jetavana Monastery covered with coins edge to edge, a large portion of the monastery ground was covered, and only a small plot of land at the gateway lacked coins. Then the merchant gave an order to his men, saying, "Friends, go and bring out more gold coins; we shall cover the ground at this monastery gateway."

## Prince Jeta Donating the Gateway Pavilion

The face of the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, who was renouncing and donating such a vast amount of wealth, became increasingly radiant. Seeing this, Prince Jeta thought to himself, "The fact that this great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika is donating and renouncing such a vast amount of gold coins with an increasingly radiant countenance means this must surely be a noble merit." Prince Jeta then made a request to the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, saying, "That is enough, great merchant. Do not cover that spot. Please give this small space to me. This small space shall be my donation."

Then the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika thought, "This Prince Jeta is a famous and well-known person. In this Dispensation of the Buddha, where such famous and well-known people are righteously guided, their faith and devotion are of great benefit." Having thought thus, he gave that spot to Prince Jeta.
200:
Then, Prince Jeta built and donated a great seven-story gateway pavilion on that plot of land.

## Anāthapiṇḍika Building the Great Jetavana Monastery

Then, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika spent another one hundred and eighty million (18 crores) gold coins. In Prince Jeta's garden, he removed the trees that should be removed and kept the trees that should be kept to make the monastery beautiful and cool. He created and built the monastery complex completely, with each structure in its proper place, including the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭī) for the Buddha to reside, peripheral dwellings, magnificent gateway pavilions, large circular halls for the Saṅgha to assemble, fire rooms, storehouses (kappiyakuṭī), latrines (vaccakuṭī), covered walkways (caṅkama), buildings for those walkways, wells, sheds over the wells, bathrooms, saunas (jantāghara), buildings to cover those saunas, square ponds, and pavilions—everything needed for day and night use. The area of the Jetavana Monastery site was approximately eight min-pai.

Twenty-four inches is called a ye-than-taung. After that, if it is twenty inches plus eight, it is correctly called a sin-taing-taung. Finally, if it is thirty-two inches, in the human realm, it is a le-pwe-taung. Seven cubits make one ta. Truly, in this way...
201:
...twenty ta is called one kyo. If there are four such kyo in a square, with a perimeter of eighty ta, it is one le-tapa. (This is an ancient verse on measurements to be noted if desired.)

## The Site of Jetavana Monastery

This site of Jetavana Monastery was not only a monastery site during the time of this Buddha; it was also the monastery site of previous Buddhas, the elder brothers, such as Kassapa Buddha. To make it clear:

(1) During the time of Vipassī Buddha, a great merchant named Punabbhasumitta purchased it by spreading gold bricks edge to edge and built and donated a great Saṅgha monastery one yojana wide.

(2) During the time of Sikhī Buddha, a great merchant named Sirivaḍḍha (according to the Jātaka Commentary) purchased it by spreading gold plowshares (according to the Vinaya Commentary, gold staffs) edge to edge and built and donated a great Saṅgha monastery three gāvutas wide on that very spot.

(3) During the time of Vessabhū Buddha, a great merchant named Sotthija purchased it by spreading gold blocks cast in the shape of elephant feet (according to the Jātaka Commentary) or gold plowshares (according to the Vinaya Commentary) edge to edge and built and donated a great Saṅgha monastery half a yojana...
202:
...(two gāvutas) wide on that very spot.

(4) During the time of Kakusandha Buddha, a great merchant named Accuta purchased it by spreading gold bricks (according to the Jātaka Commentary) or gold blocks cast in the shape of elephant feet (according to the Vinaya Commentary) edge to edge and built and donated a great Saṅgha monastery one gāvuta wide on that very spot.

(5) During the time of Koṇāgamana Buddha, a great merchant named Ugga purchased it by spreading gold tortoises (according to the Jātaka Commentary) or gold bricks (according to the Vinaya Commentary) edge to edge and built and donated a great Saṅgha monastery half a gāvuta wide on that very spot.

(6) During the time of Kassapa Buddha, a great merchant named Sumangala purchased it by spreading gold ingots (according to the Jātaka Commentary) or gold tortoises (according to the Vinaya Commentary) edge to edge and built and donated a great Saṅgha monastery (according to the Jātaka Commentary) sixteen pai or (according to the Vinaya Commentary) twenty usabhas wide on that very spot.

(7) During the time of our Gotama Buddha, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, whose original name was Sudatta, purchased it by spreading coins edge to edge and on that very spot...
203:
He constructed and donated the great Saṅgha monastery (Jetavana Monastery), which spanned an area of approximately eight pe.

## A Matter for Reflection
Considering deeply the area of the monasteries of these seven Buddhas and the prices paid for the monastery sites, one should think, "In this way, worldly attainments and wealth indeed diminish and decline over time." It is truly fitting and appropriate to become weary of various worldly attainments (mundane wealth), to be free from attachment, and to strive diligently for liberation.

## The Blessed One's Journey to the City of Sāvatthī
In this manner, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, having sacrificed eighteen crores of gold coins for the delightful garden site, spent another eighteen crores to plan and construct the magnificent Jetavana Monastery. He then dispatched a messenger to the presence of the Blessed One to formally invite Him to come. Upon hearing the invitation from the messenger, the Blessed One (considering that He would reside in Sāvatthī for a long time and that it would become a victorious ground for the Sāsana where many humans, devas, and brahmās would attain the Dhamma) set out, surrounded by a great assembly of noble monks.
204:
Departing from the Veḷuvana Monastery in the city of Rājagaha, the Blessed One traveled towards Sāvatthī, staying for one night at each of the rest houses (residences) that the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika had pre-arranged and constructed at every league (yojana) along the way.

When the Blessed One departed from Rājagaha and arrived at the city of Vesālī, while residing in the gabled hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in the Mahāvana forest, He laid down a training rule (Sikkhāpada) regarding the assignment of construction management (Navakamma) through a formal act of the Saṅgha (Ñattidutiya-kammavācā) to any monk capable of supervising and managing the various construction works donated by lay supporters.*

Later, as the Blessed One departed from Vesālī and continued His journey towards Sāvatthī, the disciples of the Chabbaggī monks went ahead of the Saṅgha led by the Buddha. They claimed the best lodgings and sleeping places, saying, "These rooms and beds shall be for our preceptors (Upajjhāya); these rooms and beds shall be for our teachers (Ācariya)."

Whenever the Blessed One traveled with His assembly of disciples, the Venerable Sāriputta, despite being the Right-hand Chief Disciple and having the privilege to stay close to the Buddha, did not do so for his own comfort.

* For details, see the Senāsanakkhandhaka of the Vinaya Cūḷavagga in the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka.
205:
The Venerable Sāriputta used to follow at the rear of the procession to personally manage, support, and assist the sick (gilāna) and elderly monks so they could travel comfortably. Consequently, because he was assisting the sick and elderly, the Venerable Sāriputta arrived at the resting place last, after the disciples of the Chabbaggī monks had already taken the rooms and beds. Finding no place for himself, the great Elder had to spend the entire night at the foot of a tree. Regarding this incident, the Blessed One reflected with great spiritual urgency (Dhamma-saṃvega): "If even now, while I am still alive, the monks live without mutual respect and deference, what will they do when I have entered Parinibbāna?" At dawn, He called for an assembly of monks and asked, "Monks, is it true that the Chabbaggī monks went ahead, took the best places, and prevented the senior Elders from getting lodgings?" When the monks confirmed it was true, He rebuked the Chabbaggī monks, gave a Dhamma discourse, and then asked the monks: "Monks, which monk deserves the best seat, the first water, and the first alms-food?"

Some monks replied, "A monk ordained from a royal family deserves the best seat, the first water, and the first alms-food." Some said, "A monk ordained from a brahmin family deserves them."
206:
Some monks replied, "A monk ordained from a merchant or householder family deserves the best seat, the first water, and the first alms-food." Some suggested a monk who is an expert in the Vinaya (Vinayadhara), some a Dhamma preacher (Dhammakathika), some a monk who has attained the first jhāna, (etc.), the second jhāna, the third jhāna, or the fourth jhāna. Others suggested a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna), (etc.), a Once-returner (Sakadāgāmī), a Non-returner (Anāgāmī), an Arahant who is a dry-insight practitioner (Sukkhavipassaka), an Arahant with the three knowledges (Tevijja), or an Arahant with the six higher powers (Chaḷabhiñña). When the monks had answered according to their own preferences, the Blessed One said:

"Monks, in my Sāsana, when it comes to matters like the best seat, being of royal birth is not the measure. Being of brahmin birth, merchant or householder birth, being a Vinaya expert, a Sutta bearer, an Abhidhamma bearer, or having attained the first jhāna etc., or being a Sotāpanna etc., is also not the measure. Monks, in truth, in this Sāsana of mine, one must practice salutation, rising to greet, salutation with joined palms, and showing respect according to seniority of ordination (Vassa). Only according to seniority are the best seat, the first water, and the first alms-food to be received. In these matters, seniority in age and training is the measure. Therefore, a monk who is a senior (venerable) is the one worthy and deserving of the best seat, the first water, and the first alms-food. Monks, at this time—"
207:
—Sāriputta is my Right-hand Chief Disciple. He is my eldest legitimate son (orasa) who can turn the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka) that I have preached. He is the one worthy of receiving the place immediately next to me. Yet, this Sāriputta, having not received a place for this entire past night, had to spend his time walking and sitting only at the foot of a tree. Monks, if even now while I am alive you do not show respect and deference in this way, what will you do in the future when I have entered Parinibbāna?"

Then, to give further instruction to those monks, the Blessed One said: "Monks, in the past, even animals thought, 'It is not proper for us to live without mutual respect and deference. Let us investigate who among us is the eldest, and then we shall show him respect, honor, and salutation.' After careful investigation, they identified the eldest and practiced the noble conduct of respecting the elderly (Vuḍḍhāpacāyana), which is the path to the celestial realms, and they reached the deva world." He then related the story of the past (Ekakanipāta, 4-Kulāvaka Vagga, 7-Tittira Jātaka).
208:
The Blessed One recited this verse:

Ye vuḍḍhamapacāyanti,
Narā dhammassa kovidā.
Diṭṭhe dhamme ca pāsaṃsā,
Samparāye ca suggati.

(Those people who are skilled and wise in the Dhamma of respecting the elderly; who honor those who are great in age and virtue among the three types of greatness—birth, virtue, and age; they are worthy of praise in this very life, and in the life hereafter, they attain a happy destination in the human or celestial realms.)

After preaching this Tittira Jātaka, He said:

"Monks, even those three animals—the monkey, the elephant, and the partridge—lived with mutual respect and deference and shared a common livelihood. You, monks, who have gone forth out of faith in this Sāsana where the Dhamma is well-taught, if you live without mutual respect, without deference, and without a common livelihood, would such living be beautiful? (= It would certainly not be beautiful). Monks, such disrespectful and irreverent living does not lead to the faith of those not yet faithful, (etc.)—"
209:
After rebuking the Chabbaggī monks in this manner and preaching extensively on the benefits of mutual respect and deference, the Blessed One said:

"Monks, I allow salutation, rising to greet, salutation with joined palms, showing respect, the best seat, the superior seat, the first water, and the first alms-food to be given according to seniority (Vassa). Monks, one must not obstruct the use of communal (Saṅghika) lodgings and beds according to seniority. For a monk who obstructs, there is an offence of wrong-doing (Dukkhaṭa)."

## Ten Types of Persons Not to be Saluted
After the Blessed One had laid down these two training rules—the allowance (anuññāta) and the prohibition (paṭikkhitta)—He continued:

"Dasa yime bhikkhave avandiyā— Monks, these ten types of persons are not to be saluted:
(1) One who was ordained earlier should not salute one who was ordained later.
(2) A monk should not salute one who is not a monk.
(3) A monk should not salute a monk of a different communion (nānāsaṃvāsa) who speaks contrary to the Dhamma (adhammavādī), even if he is senior."
210:
(4) A monk should not pay homage to a woman.
(5) A monk should not pay homage to a eunuch (paṇḍaka).
(6) A regular monk should not pay homage to a monk undergoing probation (parivāsa).
(7) A regular monk should not pay homage to a monk undergoing the penalty of being sent back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassanā). (This refers to a monk who, while undergoing probation, or while being worthy of penance after probation, or while undergoing penance, or while being worthy of rehabilitation after penance, commits another Saṅghādisesa offense and is thus sent back to the beginning of his original probation.)
(8) A regular monk should not pay homage to a monk worthy of penance (mānatta). (This refers to a monk who has completed probation and is eligible for penance.)
(9) A regular monk should not pay homage to a monk undergoing penance (mānatta).
(10) A regular monk should not pay homage to a monk worthy of rehabilitation (abbhāna). (This refers to a monk who has completed penance and is eligible for rehabilitation.)
Having taught these ten types of persons to whom homage should not be paid, the Buddha continued:
## Three Types of Persons to be Paid Homage To
Monks, these three types of persons should be paid homage to:
211: 211. (1) A monk who was ordained later must pay homage to a monk who was ordained earlier. (2) A monk must pay homage to a senior monk of the same communion (saṃvāsa) if that senior is a speaker of Dhamma (dhammavādī). (3) O Monks, in this world of beings including devas and brahmas, homage must be paid to the Blessed One, who is the Worthy One (Arahaṃ) and the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha). O Monks, these three types of persons are to be paid homage. Thus, He preached the three types of persons to whom monks should and may pay homage. ## Re-prescribing Not to Prevent Senior Elders from Seats in Pavilions etc. Dedicated to the Saṅgha. When the Buddha, surrounded by many monks, was traveling in stages toward Sāvatthī, the people living along the way prepared pavilions, floor coverings, and meeting places for the Saṅgha. The disciples of the Chabbaggiya monks took the seats beforehand as they had done before. Consequently, the Ven. Sāriputta, arriving late as before, did not get a seat and had to spend the whole night at the foot of a tree. Regarding this matter, the Buddha investigated the facts, rebuked the Chabbaggiya monks, and then—
212:
“Monks, one should not obstruct [seniority] even in a place intended for the Saṅgha. Whoever does so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
Thus, He prescribed the training rule.
(Note: Regarding the story of the Chabbaggiya monks, the Vajirabuddhi-ṭīkā states that the Chabbaggiya monks appeared only after the twentieth year of the Blessed One's ministry. Since there is a teaching (M. i. 175) stating, “The monks have satisfied my mind...” meaning that during the first twenty years (Paṭhamabodhi), the monks lived well and satisfied the Buddha's heart, it should be understood that this event occurred during a journey to Sāvatthī at a later time, and is brought here to illustrate the offense.)
## Permission for the Property of Laypeople
At that time, in the village refectory, people laid out high and luxurious seats (uccāsayana-mahāsayana), such as very high seats, thrones, long-haired rugs, variegated woolen coverings, white woolen rugs, embroidered woolen coverings, cotton-stuffed quilts, coverings with animal figures, double-fringed rugs, single-fringed rugs, silk coverings embroidered with gold, silk coverings, large woolen rugs, elephant rugs, horse rugs, chariot rugs, antelope skin rugs, skins of the Kadali deer, and excellent red canopies with red cushions at both ends. The monks, having doubts that these were not allowable, did not dare to sit on them.
213: 213. When this matter was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha prescribed the rule: "Anujānāmi bhikkhave ṭhapetvā tīṇi āsandiṃ pallaṅkaṃ tūlikaṃ—Monks, I allow the use of high and large beds and seats (uccāsayana mahāsayana) belonging to laypeople for sitting, except for these three: a high-legged couch, a throne, and a cotton-stuffed mattress. However, I do not allow them for sleeping." In that same village refectory, lay donors provided couches and stools stuffed with cotton and covered with cloth. The monks, being doubtful, did not dare to sit. Regarding this: "Anujānāmi bhikkhave gihivikataṃ abhinisīdituṃ, na tveva abhinipajjituṃ = Monks, I allow sitting on couches and stools stuffed with cotton belonging to laypeople, but I do not allow sleeping on them." Thus He prescribed the rule. ## Anāthapiṇḍika Inviting the Buddha to Jetavana Monastery with Great Ceremony. As mentioned before, the Buddha, surrounded by a large assembly of monks, traveled from Rājagaha toward Sāvatthī and eventually arrived within the region of Sāvatthī.
214:
The great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, having prepared a grand ceremony for the dedication of the monastery, made arrangements to invite the Blessed One to Jetavana Monastery. Those arrangements were as follows:
## Princess Sumanā
King Pasenadi of Kosala had a daughter named Sumanā. Ninety-one aeons ago, during the time of Vipassī Buddha, when the citizens had the opportunity to serve the Buddha, she was a merchant's daughter (Saddhāsumanā) with sharp wisdom. She was the first among the people to offer pure milk-rice to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha and made a wish: “Blessed One, in the round of rebirths, may I never have to earn a living with great longing and hardship. Like this garland of jasmine (sumanā) flowers I offer today, may I be a woman loved and cherished by all in every life, and may my name be Sumanā.” Due to the fulfillment of that wish, she did not fall into the lower realms for ninety-one aeons, but wandered only through the human and celestial worlds. In every life, at the time of her birth, a rain of jasmine flowers fell, deep enough to reach her knees; thus, she was always named “Sumanā.” (The detailed story may be found in the Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 3, p. 13 onwards.)
In this present age, she became the daughter of King Pasenadi Kosala, born to his chief queen. At the time of her birth, a rain of jasmine flowers fell, deep enough to reach her knees,
215:
so the King named her Sumanā. There were five hundred maidens born on the same day as Princess Sumanā. King Pasenadi Kosala raised Princess Sumanā and her five hundred companions in comfort. As part of her royal retinue, he provided five hundred chariots; whenever Princess Sumanā went on a journey, the five hundred companions would follow, each in her own chariot.
In the whole of Jambudīpa, there were only three women who received such a retinue of five hundred companions, each riding in their own chariot provided by their fathers: (1) Princess Cundī, daughter of King Bimbisāra; (2) Visākhā, daughter of the merchant Dhanañjaya (who later became the great donor of Pubbārāma Monastery); and (3) Princess Sumanā, daughter of King Pasenadi Kosala mentioned here.
When Princess Sumanā was seven years old, the Blessed One arrived at Sāvatthī to accept the donation of Jetavana Monastery. The merchant Anāthapiṇḍika went to King Pasenadi Kosala and said, “Great King, the Blessed One’s arrival in our city of Sāvatthī is a great blessing for us and for Your Majesty as well. Therefore, I wish for Your Majesty to send Princess Sumanā, along with her five hundred maidens, carrying full water pots, perfumes, and flowers, to welcome and invite the Blessed One.” King Pasenadi Kosala agreed, saying, “Very well, householder,”
216:
and he made arrangements as requested by Anāthapiṇḍika.
Princess Sumanā, following her father’s instructions, went with her retinue to welcome the Blessed One. She paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, honored Him with perfumes and flowers, and stood in a suitable place. The Blessed One taught the Dhamma to Princess Sumanā. Princess Sumanā, along with her five hundred companions, was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Furthermore, five hundred other maidens, five hundred women, and five hundred laymen also attained the Fruit of Stream-entry during that same teaching.
Thus, on the day the Blessed One arrived at Jetavana Monastery, two thousand Noble Ones (Ariyas) who were Stream-enterers were established along the way. (From Aṅ. A. iii. 13-15).
## The Retinue of Anāthapiṇḍika
Anāthapiṇḍika did not only request King Kosala to send Princess Sumanā to welcome the Blessed One; he also had his own son dressed in full finery and sent him, along with five hundred other youths (sons of merchants) who were also fully dressed and adorned, to welcome the Blessed One. Anāthapiṇḍika’s son, following his father’s arrangements, went with his retinue of five hundred youths, carrying five-colored
217:
Each holding five hundred banners shining with various clothes, they took their places in front of the Blessed One and led the procession. 

Following these youths, the daughters of the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, Cūḷasubhaddā and Mahāsubhaddā, along with five hundred merchant daughters as their retinue, followed and invited the Buddha while carrying full water pots on their heads.

Following these merchant daughters, the great merchant's wife (Puññalakkhaṇādevī), fully adorned with ornaments, along with five hundred merchant wives, followed and invited the Buddha while holding gold and silver bowls filled with scented water and other offerings.

Following everyone else, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika himself, dressed in brand-new merchant's attire, along with five hundred merchants also dressed in brand-new merchant's attire, welcomed and invited the Blessed One on his journey.

The Blessed One, placing this assembly of lay devotees in front and surrounded by a great multitude of monks, entered the Jetavana Monastery. He made the various parts of the forest shine with a golden hue, like molten gold or the color of yellow orpiment, through his own bodily radiance, and with the infinite grace and incomparable glory of a Buddha.
218:
## Dedicating the Jetavana Monastery 
## to the Saṅgha of the Four Directions

Then, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika respectfully invited the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for a meal the following morning. When the next morning arrived, he prepared exquisite hard and soft foods in his home and sent word to the Blessed One of the time, saying, "O Blessed One, it is time for the meal; the food is ready."

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One, surrounded by the assembly of monks, went to the house of the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika and sat on the prepared seat. Then, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika personally served the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha with exquisite hard and soft foods with his own hands (sāhatthika). After the meal, he sat in a suitable place and addressed the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, how should I manage the donation of this Jetavana Monastery?" (meaning, "How should I perform the water-pouring ceremony for the donation?")

Then the Blessed One said to the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, "In that case, Anāthapiṇḍika, dedicate this Jetavana Monastery to the Saṅgha of the four directions, those who have come, those who are present, and those yet to come." Following the Blessed One's instruction, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika dedicated the Jetavana Monastery to the Saṅgha of the four directions, present and future (āgatanāgata catuddisā saṅghika), by performing the water-pouring ceremony.
219:
## 5 Verses of Appreciation for the Monastery

After the Blessed One accepted the Jetavana Monastery, wishing to deliver a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā) for the monastery, he spoke these five verses:

(1) Sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanti,
tato vāḷamigāni ca.
Sarīsape ca makase,
sisire cāpi vuṭṭhiyo.

(The monastery we donate) wards off the cold caused by internal disturbances and external seasonal changes. It wards off the heat caused by forest fires and such. Furthermore, it wards off the dangers of wild beasts such as lions, leopards, and tigers. It wards off crawling creatures like snakes, scorpions, and lice. It wards off gadflies, mosquitoes, and flies that bite and disturb concentration. It wards off the extreme cold that occurs during the Sisira season (the two months from the day after the full moon of Phussa to the full moon of Phagguna) and during periods of continuous rain for seven days. It also wards off the heavy rains that fall at various times.
220:
It wards off the rains. 

(2) Tato vātātapo ghoro,
sañjāto paṭihanyati.
Leṇatthañca sukhatthañca,
jhāyituñca vipassituṃ.
Vihāradānaṃ saṅghassa,
aggaṃ buddhena vaṇṇitaṃ.

Furthermore, (by this monastery), the various fierce and terrifying winds and the intense heat of the sun that arise according to the seasons are warded off. (These words describe the great benefits of the donated monastery for the monks). For the purpose of dwelling in seclusion without the mind wandering to various objects; for the purpose of living happily and free from danger; for the purpose of repeatedly entering and developing the jhāna of meditating on an object (ārammaṇūpanijjhāna); and for the purpose of practicing insight meditation (vipassanā). (These four points indicate the benefits of the monastery that the donors should keep in mind). The gift of a monastery to the Saṅgha is praised as supreme by the Buddhas.
221:
(3)
Tasmā hi paṇḍito poso,
sampassaṃ atthamattano.
Vihāre kāraye ramme,
vāsayettha bahussute.

Therefore, a wise man of good family, clearly perceiving his own welfare—the three types of prosperity: human, celestial, and Nibbāna—should have pleasant monasteries built that are comfortable and delightful to dwell in. In these monasteries he has built, he should have learned ones (bahussuta), who are virtuous and known as residents, dwell there. (This means that in the monastery he has built and donated, he should appoint a senior monk who possesses the five qualities of a resident monk: being well-versed in the ten subjects, the two Vibhaṅgas, the Kammavācā, the Khandhakas, and being able to clearly teach mind and matter).

(4)
Tesaṃ annañca pānañca, vatthasenāsanāni ca.
Dadeyya ujubhūtesu, vippasannena cetasā.

To those learned resident monks who are upright and pure in their intentions, one should give food, drink, clothing, and lodgings with a mind that is clear and confident in the virtues of the Triple Gem and the law of Kamma and its results.
222:
One should give with pure faith. (This verse indicates the support through the four requisites from the donor's side).

(5)
Te tassa dhammaṃ desenti, sabbadukkhāpanūdanaṃ.
Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāya, parinibbātināsavo.

Those learned resident monks, out of compassion and loving-kindness, preach the Dhamma that dispels all the suffering of the round of rebirths to the donor who serves them with the four requisites. (This indicates the reciprocal support through the Dhamma from the monks' side). That donor, who gives the monastery with clear faith, by understanding and practicing that Dhamma preached by the resident monks in this wonderful Dispensation of the Buddha, becomes an Arahant (one free from the four taints) and attains Nibbāna, ending the cycle of suffering.

After the Blessed One preached the discourse of appreciation to the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika with these verses on the benefits of a monastery (Vihārānisaṃsa), he returned to stay at the Jetavana Monastery.

## The Great Nine-Month Dedication Ceremony

From the second day onwards, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika began the great celebration of the monastery's dedication. The dedication ceremony of the Pubbārāma Monastery by the great female lay devotee Visākhā took four months to complete. However, the dedication ceremony of the Jetavana Monastery by the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika took nine months to complete. During the monastery dedication
223:
festival, he spent and donated eighteen koṭis (180 million) in gold coins.

Thus, for the Jetavana Monastery alone, he spent eighteen koṭis for the land, eighteen koṭis for the construction of the monastery, and eighteen koṭis for the dedication ceremony—totaling fifty-four koṭis of gold coins (540 million) donated to the Dispensation.

End of the story of Anāthapiṇḍika.

**********

## Leading Prince Nanda to Arahantship 
## by Exchanging His Focus with Celestial Nymphs

While the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery after accepting it, the Venerable Nanda (the Buddha's half-brother) was dissatisfied with the holy life in the Dispensation. He said to his fellow monks: "Friends, I am not finding delight or joy in the Dispensation, yet I am practicing the holy life of the three trainings. I am no longer able to continue carrying out and practicing this holy life; I shall give up the monk's training and return to the lay life."

The Blessed One, hearing this news, had the Venerable Nanda summoned before him and asked: "Friends, I am not finding delight or joy in the Dispensation, yet I am practicing the holy life of the three trainings..."
224:
"Is it true, Nanda, that you have told many fellow monks: 'I am living the holy life (brahmacariya) of the Sāsana, but I am no longer able to endure and practice this holy life; I shall give up the training and return to the lower life of a layman'?" When asked thus, the Venerable Nanda answered truthfully and without concealment, "It is true, Venerable Brother."

Then the Blessed One asked again, "Dear Nanda, why is it that you are dissatisfied and find no pleasure in the Sāsana, the holy life of the Threefold Training? Why are you unable to continue practicing this holy life? Why do you wish to give up the training and return to the lower life of a layman?"

The Venerable Nanda replied, "Exalted Brother, when I was leaving the palace carrying your alms-bowl, my sister, the Sakyan princess Janapadakalyāṇī, with her hair only half-combed, looked out from the window and called after me, 'O Prince, please return quickly!' Venerable Brother, because I am constantly thinking of the words spoken by my fiancée, the Sakyan princess Janapadakalyāṇī, I am dissatisfied and find no pleasure in the Sāsana, the holy life of the Threefold Training. I am no longer able to continue practicing this holy life. I shall give up the training..."
225:
"...and return to the lower life of a layman; I shall leave the monkhood, Exalted Brother."

Thus he spoke with honesty and uprightness. Then the Blessed One, taking the Venerable Nanda by the arm, used his psychic power to transport him to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, as if one were to stretch out or draw back an arm. On the way, the Buddha showed him an old female monkey, whose ears, nose, and tail were mutilated and whose body was scorched, sitting on a burnt stump in a field that had been cleared by fire. After showing this, he proceeded to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Upon reaching Tāvatiṃsa, five hundred nymphs with feet as red as the blood of a dove, who had come to attend upon Sakka, the king of gods, stood there after paying homage to the Blessed One. The Blessed One pointed them out to the Venerable Nanda and asked:

"Dear Nanda, what do you think of this? Between your fiancée, the Sakyan princess Janapadakalyāṇī, and these five hundred nymphs with feet as red as the blood of a dove, who is more beautiful, more fair to behold, and more pleasing?"

(Note: These five hundred nymphs possessed soft, red feet like those of a dove because of their past merit of offering foot-massage oil to the Saṅgha during the time of Kassapa Buddha.)
226:
(Note: One might ask why the Blessed One showed the nymphs to the Venerable Nanda, whose mind was already drenched with the rain of lust, thereby potentially increasing his defilements. The answer is that the Blessed One showed them so that Nanda's defilements could be easily removed. To illustrate: a skilled physician, wishing to cure a patient suffering from an excess of phlegm, bile, and wind, first administers oil or other treatments to ripen and increase those humors, and then easily removes them with emetics and purgatives. Similarly, the Blessed One, the incomparable Physician in disciplining those to be tamed, showed the nymphs to the patient Nanda, who was afflicted by the disease of lust, to ripen and increase that lust more than before. This was done so that he could then completely remove and expel the defilements without remainder using the emetics and purgatives of the Noble Path.)

When the Blessed One asked this, the Venerable Nanda replied:

"Exalted Brother, just as the old female monkey with mutilated ears, nose, and tail, and a scorched body—whom you showed me on the way—cannot be counted as beautiful, so too, the Sakyan princess Janapadakalyāṇī, when compared to these five hundred nymphs, cannot be counted as beautiful at all. Indeed, these five hundred nymphs are far more beautiful, fair to behold, and pleasing, Exalted Brother."
227:
The Blessed One then said:

"Delight, Nanda, in the holy life of the Sāsana, the Threefold Training. Delight, Nanda, in the holy life of the Sāsana, the Threefold Training. If you delight in this holy life, I guarantee that you will obtain the five hundred nymphs with feet as red as the blood of a dove."

When the Blessed One gave this guarantee, the Venerable Nanda joyfully replied:

"Exalted Brother, if you guarantee that I shall obtain the five hundred nymphs with feet as red as the blood of a dove, I shall indeed delight and find pleasure in practicing the holy life of the Sāsana, the Threefold Training, under your guidance."

(Note: One might ask why the Blessed One gave a guarantee for the unholy life of enjoying five hundred nymphs when his true intention was for Nanda to practice the holy life. The answer is that Nanda's lust was intensely focused on the Sakyan princess Janapadakalyāṇī. By shifting that intense lust to a new object—the five hundred nymphs—it would become easier to eventually abandon it. Therefore, the Blessed One..."
228:
"...gave the guarantee for the unholy life.")

Then the Blessed One, taking the Venerable Nanda, vanished from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and reappeared at the Jetavana monastery. Upon arriving at Jetavana, the Venerable Nanda performed his duties for the Blessed One and went to his place of daytime retreat. The Blessed One then informed the monks who came to attend and listen to the Dhamma about this matter. (Using a worldly analogy: just as a skilled man might use a small wooden peg to knock out a larger peg that is stuck in a plank or post and cannot be easily removed, and then discard the new peg by hand; similarly, the Blessed One wished to use the new object of the five hundred nymphs to knock out Nanda's lust for Janapadakalyāṇī, which was deeply ingrained through habit, and then lead him to the path of the holy life to discard that new attachment as well.) He then instructed the monks:

"Monks, go and mock the monk Nanda by calling him a 'hireling' and a 'laborer'."

Following the Blessed One's instruction, many monks spread the news: "It is said that the monk Nanda, the son of the Blessed One's aunt Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and the Buddha's own brother, is living the holy life because he wants to obtain five hundred nymphs. It is said the Blessed One has guaranteed that he will get five hundred nymphs with feet as red as the blood of a dove."
229:
Then the Venerable Nanda's companion monks went to him and mocked him with words of reproach, saying: "So, the Venerable Nanda is a 'hireling'! So, the Venerable Nanda is a 'laborer'! It is said he is practicing the holy life because he wants to obtain five hundred nymphs, and that the Blessed One has guaranteed he will get five hundred nymphs with feet as red as the blood of a dove!"

The Venerable Nanda was deeply distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by his companions' words calling him a "hireling" and a "laborer." Consequently, he went into solitary seclusion and, with diligent, unremitting effort and a mind directed towards Nibbāna, he practiced the ascetic life of a monk. Before long, he attained the destruction of the taints (āsavas) and reached the state of Arahantship. Having attained Arahantship, he became one of the eighty Great Disciples (Asītimahāsāvaka).
230:
Then, at midnight, a certain Brahma who had destroyed the taints approached the Blessed One, stood in a suitable place, and joyfully informed him that the Venerable Nanda had become an Arahant. Immediately after the Brahma's report, the Blessed One's own Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) also confirmed: "The monk Nanda has realized the Fruit of Arahantship."

## The Venerable Nanda Approaches the Buddha

As previously mentioned, because the Venerable Nanda had been mocked by his companion monks, he felt a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), thinking: "Having gone forth in this well-proclaimed Dhamma-Vinaya, I have made the Blessed One a guarantor for the sake of obtaining nymphs. I have committed a burdensome act." Developing shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa), he practiced tirelessly and attained the Fruit of Arahantship. He then thought: "It would be well if I were to release the Blessed One from that guarantee." When the night had passed and dawn arrived, he approached the Blessed One and said:

"Exalted Brother, you previously gave a guarantee for me to obtain five hundred nymphs with feet as red as the blood of a dove. Exalted Brother, I now release you..."
231:
“I (your younger brother) am released from that promise and guarantee.”

At that time, the Blessed One also addressed the Venerable Nanda, his younger brother:

“Dear Nanda, I too, having discerned your mind with my own mind, have known that ‘The monk Nanda has attained Arahantship.’ A Great Brahma also came to me and reported that you, dear brother, have become an Arahant. Dear Nanda, at the very moment (the very thought-moment) your mind was liberated from the taints (āsavas), in the moment immediately following that, I was released from that guarantee and promise.”

Having said this, the Blessed One, with a heart full of great joy and appreciation, uttered this inspired verse (Udāna):

He who has crossed the mire,
And crushed the thorn of sensual lust,
Who has reached the destruction of delusion,
That monk does not tremble in pleasure or pain.

*Yassa* = For which Noble One. *Paṅko* = the mire of wrong views, (or) the mire of Saṃsāra. *Nittiṇṇo* = has been crossed over to the other shore, which is Nibbāna, by treading upon the bridge of the Noble Path. *Kāmakaṇṭako* = the thorn of sensual defilements that pierces and disturbs beings like a physical thorn. *Maddito* = has been crushed and destroyed into fine powder by the weapon-like staff of wisdom.
232:
He has crushed it. *Yo* = Which Noble One. *Mohakkhayaṃ* = to the end of delusion, which is the Fruition of Arahantship and Nibbāna. *Anuppatto* = has reached by following the four stages of Path-knowledge. *Sa bhikkhu* = That Noble Arahant who has shattered and destroyed the dense mass of the darkness of ignorance. *Sukhadukkhesu* = because of these two, pleasure and pain, (or) because of the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma), both pleasant and unpleasant. *Na vedhati* = he does not waver or tremble.

Thus, the Blessed One uttered this inspired verse.

One day, the monks asked Venerable Nanda: “Friend Nanda, in previous days you said you did not delight in the Dispensation (Sāsana). How is your mind now?” Venerable Nanda replied: “Friends, I no longer have any desire to return to the lay life.”

When they heard this statement, the monks spoke disparagingly, saying: “Venerable Nanda is speaking what is not true. He is claiming Arahantship. In past days he said, ‘I do not delight in the Sāsana,’ and only now he says, ‘I have no desire at all to return to the lay life.’” They then went to the Blessed One and reported the matter.

At that time, the Blessed One said: “Monks, in past days, the body of the monk Nanda was like an ill-thatched
233:
house. But now, it is like a well-thatched house. Indeed, from the time this monk Nanda saw the celestial nymphs, he practiced and exerted himself until he reached the summit of the monk’s duty. Now he has reached the summit of the monk’s duty (Arahantship).” He then spoke these verses:

(1) Just as rain penetrates
An ill-thatched house,
So does lust penetrate
An undeveloped mind.

*Bhikkhave* = O monks. *Ducchannaṃ* = ill-thatched. *Agāraṃ* = a house. *Vuṭṭhi* = rain. *Yathā samativijjhati* = just as it penetrates and overwhelms the interior. *Evaṃ* = in the same way. *Abhāvitaṃ* = not developed through the two types of meditation, Tranquility (Samatha) and Insight (Vipassanā). *Cittaṃ* = the mind. *Rāgo* = the defilement of lust, (or) the rain of defilements starting from lust, hatred, delusion, and pride. *Samativijjhati* = penetrates and overwhelms the interior.

(2) Just as rain does not penetrate
A well-thatched house,
So lust does not penetrate
A well-developed mind.

*Bhikkhave* = O monks. *Succhannaṃ* = well-thatched. *Agāraṃ* = a house. *Vuṭṭhi* = rain. *Yathā na samativijjhati* = just as it cannot penetrate and overwhelm the interior. *Evaṃ* = in the same way. *Subhāvitaṃ* = through the two types of meditation, Tranquility and Insight,
234:
well-developed. *Cittaṃ* = the mind. *Rāgo* = the defilement of lust, (or) the rain of defilements starting from lust, hatred, delusion, and pride. *Na samativijjhati* = is not able to penetrate or overwhelm the interior at all.

The Buddha preached these two verses of Dhamma. At the conclusion of the verses, many monks attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth. Thus, this Dhamma teaching was highly beneficial to the multitude of people.

## Preaching the Kappaṭa Jātaka

Later, the monks were discussing in the Dhamma Hall: “Friends, the Buddhas are truly worthy of great praise and admiration. Even though Venerable Nanda was dissatisfied and did not delight in the Sāsana because of the Sakyan princess Janapadakalyāṇī, the Blessed One tamed him by using celestial nymphs as bait.” While they were speaking about the Buddha’s marvelous qualities, the Blessed One arrived at the Dhamma Hall and asked: “Monks, what is the subject of your discussion as you sit gathered here now?” The monks replied: “We are gathered here discussing this matter (regarding how the Buddha tamed Venerable Nanda).”

Then the Blessed One said: “Monks, not only now, but in the past too, I tamed this monk Nanda
235:
by luring him with a female.” Being requested by the monks, he related the Kappaṭa Jātaka of the past:

Monks, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a merchant named Kappaṭa who lived in that city. This merchant Kappaṭa had a donkey (mule) that could carry a load weighing one kumbha. That donkey could travel as far as seven leagues (yojanas) in a single day.

On one occasion, the merchant Kappaṭa went to the city of Takkasilā along with other donkey-caravan merchants. Before he could successfully sell his goods, he released his donkey to graze freely for food. While the merchant Kappaṭa’s donkey was wandering and grazing on the tender grass by the side of a moat, he saw a female donkey and approached her. Then, the female donkey and the male donkey exchanged words of affection as follows:

Female Donkey: “Sir, where have you come from?”
Male Donkey: “I have come from Bārāṇasī.”
Female Donkey: “On what business have you come?”
Male Donkey: “I have come on the business of trade.”
Female Donkey: “Sir, how heavy a load do you carry?”
Male Donkey: “I carry a load weighing one kumbha.”
236:
Female Donkey: “Sir, while carrying such a heavy load, how many leagues do you travel?”
Male Donkey: “I travel up to seven leagues a day.”
Female Donkey: “Sir, in the various places you reach, do you have any attendant to provide you with care, such as massaging your legs and feet?”
Male Donkey: “I have none.”
Female Donkey: “If that is so, sir, you must be experiencing great suffering.” (She spoke this teasingly).

(Although animals do not have anyone to massage their feet, she spoke such words to bind him with the fetters of sensual desire).

Because of those (teasing and graceful) words of the female donkey, the male donkey became despondent and could no longer find joy in his work. When the merchant Kappaṭa had finished selling his goods, he came to the donkey and said: “Dear son, come, let us go.” The donkey refused, saying: “You go ahead; I cannot follow.”

Then, although the merchant Kappaṭa repeatedly pleaded with him to follow, the donkey did not wish to go. The merchant thought: “I must take this donkey after threatening him,” and he recited this verse:
237:
(1) I will make a goad for you,
With sixteen-inch iron spikes.
I will cut your body to pieces,
Know this, O donkey!

*Gadrabha* = O wretched donkey of low mind. *Te* = To you, wretched donkey. *Ahaṃ* = I. *Soḷasaṅgulikaṇṭakaṃ* / *Soḷasaṅgulikaṇṭakena* = with a cane fitted with iron spikes sixteen inches long. *Patodaṃ* = the act of prodding and beating. *Karissāmi* = I shall do. *Te* = Your, wretched donkey's. *Kāyaṃ* = body. *Sañchindissāmi* = I shall cut so that it is pierced and torn. *Evaṃ* = Thus. (*Tvaṃ* = You, wretched donkey). *Jānāhi* = Mark this well.

Hearing these words, the donkey replied: “If that is so, I too shall know what I must do to you,” and he said:

(2) You will make a goad for me,
With sixteen-inch iron spikes.
Planting myself on my front legs,
And kicking up from behind,
I will knock out your teeth,
Know this, O Kappaṭa!

*Kappaṭa* = O merchant named Kappaṭa. (*Tvaṃ* = You). *Me* = To me. *Soḷasaṅgulikaṇṭakaṃ* / *Soḷasaṅgulikaṇṭakena* = with a cane fitted with iron spikes sixteen inches long. *Patodaṃ* = the act of prodding and beating. *Karissasi* = If you should
238:
do. (*Evaṃ* = If you do thus). *Ahaṃ* = I. *Purato* = with my two front legs. *Patiṭṭhitvāna* = standing firmly and steadily on the ground. *Pacchato* = with my two hind legs. *Uddharitvāna* = jumping and kicking with all my might. *Te* = Your. *Dantaṃ* = all your teeth. *Pātayissāmi* = I shall break so that they fall to the ground. *Evaṃ* = Thus. (*Tvaṃ* = You, merchant Kappaṭa). *Jānāhi* = Mark this well.

Upon hearing the donkey’s bold words of retaliation, the merchant Kappaṭa reflected: “For what reason does this donkey speak like this?” As he looked here and there, he saw the young female donkey and thought: “This young female donkey must have coached this male donkey to speak thus. Therefore, I should lure this male donkey by saying, ‘Dear son, I will bring you a young female donkey of such a nature for you,’ and take him with me.” Having so planned, he said:

(3) A four-footed, conch-faced,
Woman, beautiful in every limb,
I will bring as a wife for you,
Know this, O donkey!

*Gadrabha* = My dear son, Master Donkey. *Te* = For you. *Catuppadiṃ* = having four feet. *Saṅkhamukhiṃ* = having a face as pure and white as a conch shell. *Sabbaṅgasobhiṇiṃ* = beautiful and graceful in all parts of the body. *Nāriṃ bhariyaṃ* = a young female donkey as a wife.
239: I will bring [her] = When I reach Bārāṇasī, I will quickly search and bring her to you. Thus = In this way. (You = my eldest son, the donkey). Know = Know this for certain. He recited this (enticing) verse. Hearing this, the male donkey was very pleased and joyful, and said: (4) A four-footed one with a face like a conch, a female beautiful in every limb. You will bring me a wife; know this, Kappaṭa. Kappaṭa, I will go further, fourteen yojanas. Kappaṭa = My benefactor, Master Kappaṭa. For me = For my sake. Four-footed = Having four legs, of the same species. Conch-faced = Having a face as pure as a conch shell. Beautiful in every limb = Beautiful and graceful in all parts of the body. A female wife = A young female donkey wife. You will bring = When you reach Bārāṇasī, you will quickly search and bring her to you. Thus = If this is indeed true. Kappaṭa = My benefactor, Master Kappaṭa. I = I, your eldest son, the wise donkey. Further = More than before, doubling the effort. Fourteen yojanas = A long distance of fourteen yojanas. I will go = I will travel to reach there in a single day. Thus = In this way. (You = You, my benefactor, Master Kappaṭa). Know = Know this for certain.
240: He recited this (verse expressing his encouragement). Then, the merchant Kappaṭa called the male donkey, saying, "Dear son, if that is so, come," and went to his place in Bārāṇasī. After two or three days had passed, the donkey spoke up, saying, "My benefactor, Master Kappaṭa, did you not tell me, 'I will bring and give you a young female donkey wife for your sake'?" Then the merchant Kappaṭa said: "Yes, what I said is true; I do not break my word. I will search for and bring a young female donkey wife for you. However, as for provisions, I can only provide for one of you (I cannot provide for your young female wife). Whether the provisions I give for you are enough for your wife as well, or not enough, you yourself must consider and understand. Specifically, I want to say... because of the joyful union of you two, children will be born. Whether the provisions I give for you are enough for those many children as well, or not enough, (it is not my responsibility). You yourself must think and consider this matter of provisions, dear son." Thus he gave this word of advice and instruction. While the merchant Kappaṭa was giving this advice...
241: ...his attachment and longing for the young female donkey were severed. The Buddha, having brought forth this noble Dhamma teaching of the Kappaṭa Jātaka, said: "Monks, at that time, the Sākyan princess Janapadakalyāṇī was the young female donkey. At that time, the monk Nanda was the male donkey. At that time, I myself was the merchant Kappaṭa. Thus, in the past also, I have tamed this monk Nanda by enticing him with a woman and instructing him to be wise," and thus he concluded the Jātaka. The Kappaṭa Jātaka ends. ********** Note: Regarding the time when the Buddha spent the second, third, and fourth Vassa (rainy season retreats) in the city of Rājagaha, in the "Old Vassa Chronology" (Pubba-vassūpanāyika-vatthu): (1) The story of the Brahmin friend of Venerable Sāriputta (Sāriputtattherassa Sahāyaka-brāhmaṇa-vatthu) found on page 422 of the first volume of the Dhammapada Commentary; (2) The story of the pig-slaughterer named Cunda (Cunda-sūkarika-vatthu) found on page 80 of the first volume of the Dhammapada Commentary; (3) The story of Venerable Mahā-Kassapa (Mahākassapatthera-vatthu) found on page 383 of the first volume of the Dhammapada Commentary— Having presented these three stories, it is written: "In this way, from the second Vassa to the fourth Vassa, at the Veḷuvana Monastery in the city of Rājagaha,
242:
Having written, "By virtue of the promise given to King Bimbisāra, he preached such teachings to many devas and humans, bestowing upon them the Dhamma of the Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna," the section on the second, third, and fourth Vassa (Rainy Season) retreats is concluded.

One should look up and note the three stories mentioned in that "Old Chronicle of the Vassa Stories" in the Burmese translation of the Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā.

The great teacher Saya Lin, who first compiled this Mahā Buddhavaṃsa, set forth the following table of contents for this chapter on the Vassa retreat in Rājagaha:

(1)
(a) The story of the wealthy merchant Jotika,
(b) The story of the wealthy merchant Jaṭila,
(c) The story of the wealthy merchant Meṇḍaka,
(d) The story of the wealthy merchant Kākavaliya,
(e) The story of the wealthy merchant Puṇṇa; regarding these five wealthy merchants, and—
(2) The story of Sumana the florist,
(3) The story of the thousand ascetics led by the ascetic Aggidatta,
(4) The story of the Elder Jambuka—
