He left instructions to write about these. Among them, the stories of the five wealthy merchants mentioned in (1) will be described upon reaching the chapter on the Sangha Ratana. Here, I shall write about the accounts of (2), (3), and (4) in order (as the 21st Chapter).

## Here ends Chapter 20.
243:
## Chapter 21
## The Story of Sumana the Florist of Rājagaha

While the Buddha was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha, he preached this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Taṃ ca kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu," concerning the florist named Sumana.

In that city of Rājagaha, the florist named Sumana would present eight measures (eight salays) of jasmine flowers to King Bimbisāra early every morning, receiving eight pieces of silver (kahāpaṇas) daily.

One day, as Sumana the florist was entering the city carrying the jasmine flowers, the Buddha, surrounded by a great assembly of monks and emitting the six-colored rays, entered the city of Rājagaha for alms with the great majesty and grace of a Buddha.

(Special note: Sometimes the Buddha covers his six-colored rays with his robes and travels incognito like an ordinary monk, such as when he went alone to meet the robber Angulimāla from a distance of thirty yojanas. Sometimes he travels emitting the six-colored rays, such as when he entered the city of Kapilavatthu for alms. On this day when he was to meet Sumana the florist, he also entered Rājagaha for alms, emitting the six-colored rays from his body with the great majesty and grace of a Buddha.)
244: The florist Sumana, seeing the Buddha's body which was like a jeweled portal, and observing the collection of splendor beautiful with the thirty-two major marks, the eighty minor marks, and the six-colored rays, felt a heart overflowing with faith and devotion. He thought, "What kind of extraordinary (adhikāra) meritorious deed should I perform for the Buddha?" Seeing no other object of offering, he thought, "I will worship the Buddha with these jasmine flowers in my hand." Then he thought again, "These jasmine flowers are flowers that must be offered regularly to the King. If the King does not receive these jasmine flowers which are his regular offering, he might bind me with some kind of fetter, prison, or bond; or he might kill me; or he might banish me from the country. What should I do?" Then, in the stream of the florist Sumana's mind: "If the King wishes to kill me, let him kill me; if he wishes to bind me, let him bind me; if he wishes to banish me from the country, let him banish me. Indeed, if the King gives me a reward, it would only be wealth enough to sustain my life in this existence. But worshipping the Buddha will certainly be able to lead to my welfare and happiness for many millions of aeons." Having had such a brilliant thought, he made the decision to sacrifice his life for the Buddha.
245: The florist Sumana, thinking, "I will perform the offering of these jasmine flowers before my heart, overflowing with faith and devotion, wavers," was greatly delighted and encouraged, and he worshipped the Buddha with the jasmine flowers he had brought. The manner of worship was: (1) First, he threw two handfuls of jasmine flowers above the Buddha as an offering. Those jasmine flowers remained above the Buddha's head like a canopy or ceiling. (2) When he threw another two handfuls of jasmine flowers, those jasmine flowers descended and remained on the right side of the Buddha in the form of a flower curtain (a floral fabric). (3) When he threw another two handfuls of jasmine flowers, those jasmine flowers descended and remained behind the Buddha in the form of a flower curtain (a floral fabric). (4) When he threw another two handfuls of jasmine flowers, those jasmine flowers descended and remained on the left side of the Buddha in the form of a flower curtain (a floral fabric). In this way, the eight measures of jasmine flowers became eight handfuls and surrounded the Buddha in four places—the left side, the right side, the back, and above—remaining as a flower canopy and flower curtains. In front, there remained an open space like a doorway just enough to enter and walk. The stems of the jasmine flowers were all arranged neatly facing inward.
246:
Remaining in place, the petals were arranged facing only outwards. Thus, the Blessed One proceeded as if surrounded by a silver garment. Although jasmine flowers are naturally insentient, by relying on the sentient Blessed One, they acted like sentient objects, neither separating nor falling down, but following along with the Blessed One. Wherever the Blessed One stood, the jasmine flowers also stood. From the Blessed One's body, rays of light radiated and flickered like thousands of streaks of lightning. Among the rays that radiated continuously from the five places—the front, back, left, right, and above the head—not even a single ray shot straight ahead; instead, all the rays circled the Blessed One three times to the right and, becoming the size of a young palmyra tree (as if a great searchlight were shining), they raced ahead of the Blessed One. Consequently, the entire city of Rājagaha was in a state of great excitement and commotion. Among the population of 180 million—90 million inside the city and 90 million outside—there was no one, man or woman, who did not come out carrying alms-food to offer.

The multitude of people, shouting bold roars like the king of lions and tossing up thousands of head-cloths and garments, marched together in a mass ahead of the Blessed One. The Blessed One, in order to make the virtues of Sumana the florist manifest, traveled for three gāvutas.
247:
He traveled along the main ceremonial route within the vast city of Rājagaha. Because of this, the entire body of Sumana the florist was suffused with the five kinds of joy (pīti).

Sumana the florist followed and circled with the Blessed One for a short while, and like one diving into a stream of liquid vermilion, he entered within the rays of the Blessed One. After offering praise and paying respectful homage to the Blessed One, he returned to his home carrying the empty basket, which contained not a single flower.

When he arrived home, his wife asked him, "Where are the flowers?" Sumana the florist replied, "My dear, I have honored the Blessed One with the flowers." Then the wife asked again, "Lord, if that is so, what will you do now for the flowers to be presented to the King?" Sumana the florist replied, "Let the King kill me if he wishes, or let him banish me from the country; I have sacrificed my life to honor the Blessed One with the flowers. All the jasmine flowers I brought, which were about eight measures (kuṭumba), became only eight handfuls in size. Such a wondrous offering has occurred!" (He then related in detail all that he had seen). "The population of 180 million is following the Blessed One, shouting thousands of 'Sādhu' cries. This sound of the multitude shouting 'Sādhu' that you hear now is from the place where the Blessed One, whom I honored with flowers, is traveling."
248:
He spoke thus to his wife in a delightful and satisfying manner.

At that time, because Sumana the florist's wife was extremely foolish, she was unable to develop faith and devotion in such a wondrous and extraordinary miracle. Instead, she abused and scolded her husband, Sumana, saying, "Kings are very harsh; if they become angry even once, they can cause great harm by cutting off hands, feet, and so on. Because of what you have done, harm may come to me as well." Muttering thus, she took her children and went to the King's palace. When the King summoned her and asked, "What has happened?", the florist's wife said, "Great King, my husband (Sumana) offered the flowers that were to be presented to you to the Blessed One and returned home empty-handed. When I asked him, 'Where are the flowers?', he told me what had happened. I scolded and abused him in various ways, saying, 'Kings are very harsh; if they become angry even once, they can cause great harm by cutting off hands, feet, and so on. Because of what you have done, harm may come to me as well.' Having scolded him, I have abandoned him and come to this golden palace. Whether the deed he did is good or bad, it is his deed alone. Noble King, please be informed beforehand that I have abandoned (= divorced) that husband."
249:
Since King Bimbisāra had reached the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) from the very first time he saw the Blessed One at the Palmyra Grove near Rājagaha, he was a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) with unwavering faith and devotion in the Triple Gem. He thought, "Oh, this woman is exceedingly foolish. She is unable to develop faith in such a wondrous and noble quality." Although he was not angry, he pretended to be angry and asked, "Lady, did you say that your husband Sumana offered the flowers intended for me to the Blessed One?" The florist's wife replied, "It is true, Great King."

The King said, "Lady, you have done well to abandon your husband Sumana. Now consider the royal punishment that should be meted out to Master Sumana, who offered the flowers intended for me to the Blessed One." Having spoken these words of artifice, he dismissed the woman and then quickly went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and followed behind the Blessed One.

The Blessed One, knowing the King's heart was overflowing with devotion, traveled through the city along the main ceremonial route and arrived at the gate of the King's palace. King Bimbisāra took the alms-bowl from the Blessed One's hand and desired the Blessed One to enter the golden palace. However, the Blessed One indicated his intention to stay in the palace courtyard.
250:
The King, perceiving this intention, urged his men, saying, "Friends, build a pavilion quickly!" and in that very moment, he had a jeweled pavilion (ratanamandapa) completed.

The Blessed One, together with the assembly of monks, sat upon the seats prepared within the jeweled pavilion.

(In this matter, one might ask: Why did the Blessed One not enter the golden palace? The answer is: The thought arose in the Blessed One's mind, "If I enter and sit inside the palace, the 180 million people will not have the opportunity to behold me. The virtue of Sumana the florist will also not become famous. If I sit in the palace courtyard, the people will have the opportunity to behold me, and the virtue of Sumana the florist will become clearly manifest." (This is why he did not enter the golden palace). Indeed, only the Buddhas can make the virtues of the virtuous manifest; other people tend to be envious when the virtues of the virtuous are praised).

As soon as the Blessed One sat upon the prepared seat within the jeweled pavilion, the four great flower canopies went and stood at the four corners of the assembly as if they were living things. The multitude of people stood well-surrounding the Blessed One on all sides. King Bimbisāra served the assembly of monks headed by the Buddha with excellent alms-food and hard and soft delicacies. When the Blessed One had finished his meal, he gave a discourse of appreciation (anumodanā).
251:
After delivering the discourse, the Blessed One returned to the Veḷuvana Monastery, surrounded by the four flower canopies on the left, right, back, and above, and accompanied by the multitude of people who were shouting bold roars like the king of lions, just as before.

King Bimbisāra, having accompanied the Blessed One and returned, summoned Sumana the florist and asked, "How did you offer the flowers you brought for me to the Blessed One?" Sumana the florist replied, "Great King, I offered them sacrificing my life, thinking, 'Let the King kill me if he wishes, or let him banish me from the country.'" Then King Bimbisāra said, "You are truly a great man," and being greatly pleased, he had eight elephants, eight horses, eight male slaves, eight female slaves, eight sets of ornaments, eight thousand coins, eight well-adorned women, and eight great village boons brought from the palace. Thus, he performed the "Gift of Eights" (Sabbaṭṭhaka), giving eight of each kind.

## The Blessed One's Declaration of Prophecy

Then, the Venerable Ānanda thought, "Since early this morning, thousands of bold lion-like roars and thousands of tossings of head-cloths and garments have occurred wonderfully and extraordinarily. What will be the benefit to be enjoyed by Sumana the florist?" Having thought thus, he approached the Blessed One.
252:
He asked and reported that matter. Then the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda:

“Dear Ānanda, do not think that this florist Sumana has performed only a small merit. Indeed, this florist Sumana has performed the offering of flowers to me by sacrificing his own life with a clear and devoted heart. Because he has gladdened his mind in me:

Kappānaṃ satasahassaṃ,
Duggatiṃ na gamissati.
Ṭhatvā devammanussesu,
Phalaṃ etassa kammuno.
Pacchā paccekasambuddho,
Sumano nāma bhavissati.

For a hundred thousand aeons, he will not go to the states of misery (duggati). Wandering and remaining only in the realms of devas and humans, and enjoying the fruits of this merit of offering jasmine flowers, he will later become a Paccekabuddha named Sumana.”

Thus, the Buddha gave the prophecy.

(It is particularly noteworthy that when the Blessed One arrived at the Veluvana Monastery and entered the Gandhakūṭī chamber, those jasmine flowers fell and remained in heaps at the doorway.)

In the evening of that day, the monks gathered in the Dhamma-sabhā (the hall for discussing the Dhamma) and spoke words of praise: “Friends, the merit of the florist Sumana is indeed wonderful and worthy of applause! While the Buddha is still living—”
253:
“—because he made an offering of jasmine flowers by sacrificing his life to the living Buddha, he received the immediate fruit (diṭṭhadhamma) in this very moment, obtaining from the King the gift known as Sabbaṭṭhaka, which consists of eight of each kind of animate and inanimate property.”

The Blessed One came out from the Gandhakūṭī chamber, proceeded to the Dhamma-sabhā, and sat upon the designated Buddha seat on the Dhamma throne. He asked, “Monks, what was the subject of your conversation as you sat gathered here before my arrival?” When the monks replied, “We were gathered here discussing such and such a matter,” the Blessed One said, “It is true, monks. An act should be done such that one does not have to repent afterwards, and which brings only joy every time it is recollected. Such an act is indeed worth doing.” Then, connecting the preceding and following words in sequence, he preached the Dhamma by reciting this verse:

Tañca kammaṃ kataṃ sādhu,
Yaṃ katvā nānutappati.
Yassa patīto sumano,
Vipākaṃ paṭisevati.

“That deed is well done which, after being performed, one does not repent; and the fruit of which one experiences with a delighted and happy mind. Such a deed is faultless and excellent.”

Thus, he preached this Dhamma verse.
254: 254. At the end of the discourse, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Dhamma and attained liberation. The story of Sumana the florist ends. ********** ## The Disciplining of the Ascetic Aggidatta, Former Chaplain of King Kosala, and One Thousand Ascetics. The Buddha preached this Dhamma discourse beginning with "Bahuṃ ve saraṇaṃ yanti" while residing at Jetavana Monastery, concerning the ascetic named Aggidatta (the former chaplain of King Kosala) who lived near a sand dune. (Note: Aggidatta's residence was between the three regions of Aṅga, Magadha, and Kuru. Because it was close to Rājagaha, it is likely that the teacher U Lin placed this story of Aggidatta in the section where the Buddha spent the Vassa in Rājagaha.) The brahmin Aggidatta was the chaplain of King Mahākosala, the father of King Pasenadi of Kosala. When King Mahākosala passed away, his son King Pasenadi respected and honored Aggidatta, saying, "This teacher was my father's chaplain." He kept him in the same position of chaplain and, whenever Aggidatta came to pay him a visit, the King would go out to welcome him respectfully. He would say, "Teacher, please sit here," and offer him an equal seat. One day, the teacher Aggidatta thought: "This King Pasenadi of Kosala shows me great respect, however..."
255:
“—it is not possible to always keep the minds of kings under one's influence. Indeed, royal happiness is only possible for a chaplain of the same age. As for me, I have become elderly; it is only appropriate for me to become an ascetic.” Having thought thus, he asked the King for permission to renounce. He had a proclamation made throughout the city of Sāvatthī and, within seven days, gave away all his wealth in charity and became an ascetic outside the Buddha's dispensation.

Following the example of the teacher Aggidatta, ten thousand men also became ascetics. The great hermit Aggidatta lived together with those ten thousand disciple-hermits between the three kingdoms of Aṅga, Magadha, and Kuru. He gave this instruction: “Disciples, if any hermit thinks of sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka), malicious thoughts (byāpāda-vitakka), or harmful thoughts (vihiṃsā-vitakka), he must carry a bag of sand from the river and pile it here.” The ten thousand disciples agreed, and whenever such thoughts arose in their minds, they followed the teacher's advice, carrying a bag of sand and piling it in the place designated by the teacher as a form of penance. As they did this repeatedly, a great mound of sand eventually formed.

A dragon king (nāga) named Ahichatta took possession of and lived upon that great sand mound. People living in the three great kingdoms of Aṅga, Magadha, and Kuru brought many offerings every month and gave them as gifts to those hermits. At that time, the great hermit Aggidatta told those people: “Disciples, —”
256:
“—go to the mountains for refuge; go to the forests for refuge; go to the parks and gardens for refuge; go to the trees for refuge. If you seek refuge in these mountains, forests, gardens, and trees, you will be liberated from all suffering.” He gave this advice and instruction. He also instructed his ten thousand disciple-hermits with this same teaching.

The Bodhisatta (Prince Siddhattha) also renounced the world, practiced austerities (dukkara-cariyā), and attained Buddhahood. While the Blessed One was dwelling in the Jetavana Monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī—during the time when the hermit Aggidatta was popular for giving such erroneous instructions to his disciples—the Buddha surveyed the world at dawn to see which beings (devas, humans, or Brahmas) were ready for liberation. He saw the hermit Aggidatta together with his ten thousand disciples entering the net of his golden knowledge. Recognizing that “all these hermits possess the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of past merit to attain the fruit of Arahatship,” he spoke to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna in the evening: “Dear Moggallāna, why do you look on with indifference at the hermit Aggidatta, who is leading the masses down a path that is not the way to Nibbāna? Dear son, go. Give instruction and advice to those hermits.”

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said, “Exalted Buddha, those hermits are —”
257:
“—very many in number. They will not accept the instruction of me alone. If you, Blessed One, also come, they will accept the instruction.” When he reported this, the Buddha said, “Dear Moggallāna, I will also come. You go ahead first and instruct them.”

As the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was going ahead according to the Buddha's command, he thought, “These hermits are many and possess great strength. If I give any word of instruction in the place where all those hermits are gathered, they might all rise up in a mass and become unruly.” Thus, by his psychic power, he caused a great rain with very large raindrops to fall. When the large raindrops fell, the hermits rose one by one and entered their respective leaf-huts.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna stood at the door of the hermit Aggidatta's hut and called out, “O Aggidatta!” As soon as the hermit Aggidatta heard the voice of the Venerable Moggallāna, he thought, “There is no one in this world who can call me by the name Aggidatta. Who is it that calls me by the name Aggidatta?” Being very arrogant and harsh, he asked back, “Who is this person who just called me by my name?” The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied, “It is I, Brahmin Aggidatta.” Aggidatta asked again, “What do you wish to say? —”
258:
“—What is it you want to say?” Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna spoke in a pleasant and gentle voice, “Brahmin Aggidatta, I would like you to tell me of a place for me to stay for just this one night.” Aggidatta replied curtly, “There is no place for you to stay here (no vacancy). Each hermit has only one leaf-hut.”

Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said, “O Aggidatta, it is the nature of humans to visit humans; it is the nature of cattle to visit cattle; it is the nature of monks to visit monks. Do not act like this. Give me just one place for this one night.” Aggidatta then asked, “Are you a monk?” “Yes, I am a monk,” Moggallāna replied. Aggidatta asked further, “If you are a monk, where are your hermit's requisites? What are your monk's utensils and requisites?” Then the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied profoundly, “O Brahmin, I do have the monk's requisites. However, thinking that ‘it is burdensome to carry those requisites separately while wandering,’ I carry those requisites only within myself as I wander.” The hermit Aggidatta, [hearing about] carrying the monk's requisites—
259:
259
Thinking, "Is it proper for him to wander about?", he became angry with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.

Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, knowing the ascetic's thoughts, said, "O Aggidatta, do not be angry with us. I only wish for you to point out a place for me to stay."

Aggidatta the ascetic replied curtly, "There is no place for you here."

Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna pointed to a large sand mound and asked patiently, "Who lives on that large sand mound?"

Aggidatta the ascetic replied briefly, "A king of dragons (nāga) lives there."

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna spoke again, "Give that sand mound to me."

Aggidatta the ascetic, wanting to avoid responsibility, said, "I am not able to give it to you; I dare not say 'stay there.' The nature of that dragon king is extremely fierce and terrifying."

"Let it be so. You just give that place to me," the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna insisted.

Aggidatta the ascetic then said, "If that is the case, you yourself must consider whether it is suitable to stay or not."

As the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna approached the large sand mound, the dragon king Ahichatta saw him coming and thought, "This monk is coming straight toward my place on the sand mound. He seems not to know that I am here. I shall kill this monk by emitting smoke." He then emitted clouds of smoke.

Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna thought, "This dragon king seems to think that only he can emit smoke, and others cannot."
260:
260
Reflecting thus, he himself also emitted clouds of smoke. The smoke billowing from the bodies of both the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and the dragon king Ahichatta spread and rose in a dense mass as far as the Brahma realm. Both types of smoke did not harm the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, but they did harm the dragon king Ahichatta.

Unable to endure the force of the smoke, the dragon king Ahichatta became intensely angry and emitted blazing flames. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna also entered the fire-element absorption (tejo-kasiṇa-jhāna)—the fourth fine-material sphere functional jhāna having the fire-element as its object—and, competing with the dragon king, emitted blazing flames. The flames spread and rose as far as the Brahma realm. Both types of flames did not harm the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, but they did harm the dragon king Ahichatta. At that time, the entire body of the dragon king Ahichatta appeared as if it were burning with roaring fire.

The head ascetic Aggidatta and the entire group of disciple ascetics, seeing only the roaring fire, thought wrongly, "The dragon king has caused the monk to burn with roaring fire. Because the monk did not listen to our words, he has met with a terrible destruction. How good!"

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, having disciplined the dragon king Ahichatta and made him free from pride, sat upon the large sand mound. The dragon king Ahichatta then coiled himself around the sand mound and, having created a large hood the size of a gabled pavilion chamber, held it over the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's body as a canopy.
261:
261
Early in the morning, the ascetics thought, "Let us go and investigate whether the monk is dead or alive." When they went to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and saw him sitting gracefully upon the sand mound, they raised their joined palms in respect and praised him in various ways, asking, "O monk, did the dragon king not harm you?"

When the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied, "Do you not see him standing there, spreading his hood over me like a white parasol?", the ascetics said, "O friends, it is truly worthy of wonder and applause! The monk has subdued and disciplined such a powerful dragon king." They then stood surrounding the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.

At that moment, the Blessed One arrived. Seeing the Blessed One, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna rose from his seat and paid respectful homage. Then, when the ascetics asked the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, "Is this great monk superior to you?", the Elder replied, "This Noble Monk is my Teacher, endowed with the six glories. I am but a disciple of this Blessed One."

The Blessed One sat upon the large sand mound. The group of ascetics, raising their joined palms, spoke words of praise to the Blessed One, thinking, "The subduing of this dragon king is merely the psychic power of the disciple. What might the psychic power of this Blessed One, the Teacher of such a powerful monk, be like?"

The Blessed One called the head ascetic Aggidatta to listen to the Dhamma and asked, "Aggidatta, when you give instructions and advice to your disciples and supporting lay devotees, what do you say to them?"
262:
262
Then, the head ascetic Aggidatta replied truthfully, "Blessed One, I give this instruction and advice to my disciple ascetics and supporting lay devotees: 'Disciples, you should go to that mountain as a refuge; go to that forest, that park, or that tree as a refuge. Indeed, one who goes to such a mountain, forest, park, or tree as a refuge can be liberated from all suffering.'"

When he had reported this, the Blessed One said:

"Aggidatta, one who goes to such a mountain, forest, park, or tree as a refuge cannot be liberated from all suffering. In truth, only by going to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha as a refuge can one be liberated from all the suffering of the round of rebirths."

Having said this, He preached these five verses:
263:
263
(1) Bahuṃ ve saraṇaṃ yanti,
pabbatāni vanāni ca.
ārāmarukkhacetyāni,
manussā bhayatajjitā.

(Aggidatta!) Driven by fear, men go for refuge to many places: to mountains (such as Isigili, Vepulla, Vebhāra, etc.), to forests (such as Mahāvana, Gosiṅga Sāla forest, etc.), to parks and gardens (such as Veḷuvana, Jīvaka's Mango Grove, etc.), and to tree-shrines (such as the Udena shrine tree, the Gotama shrine tree, etc.).

(2) Netaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ,
netaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ.
netaṃ saraṇamāgamma,
sabbadukkhā pamuccati.

(Aggidatta!) This refuge (in mountains, forests, parks, and trees) is not secure. This refuge is not supreme. By depending on such a refuge, one is not released from all suffering.
264:
264
(3) Yo ca buddhañca dhammañca,
saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato.
cattāri ariyasaccāni,
sammapaññāya passati.

(4) Dukkhaṃ dukkhasamuppādaṃ,
dukkhassa ca atikkamaṃ.
ariyaṃ caṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ,
dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ.

(Aggidatta!) But he who—whether a layperson or a monk belonging to the Noble Fold—has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, perceives with right wisdom the Four Noble Truths through the supramundane path-consciousness. These are: Dukkha (the Truth of Suffering, which is the round of rebirth in the three planes); Dukkha-samuppāda (the Truth of the Origin of Suffering, which is unwholesome craving); Dukkhassa-atikkama (the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, which is Nibbāna, the transcendence of suffering); and the Ariya-aṭṭhaṅgika-magga (the Noble Eightfold Path, such as Right View, Right Intention, etc., which is the Truth of the Path leading to Nibbāna, the cessation of suffering).

(5) Etaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ.
etaṃ saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccati.
265:
265
(Aggidatta!) Indeed, this taking of refuge with abundant faith in the Triple Gem of the Noble Lineage is a secure refuge. This taking of refuge with abundant faith in the Triple Gem of the Noble Lineage is the supreme refuge. By depending on this refuge, one can be liberated from all the suffering of the round of rebirths.

At the conclusion of the teaching, all those ascetics attained Arahantship together with the four analytical knowledges. Having paid homage to the Blessed One, they requested for monkhood. The Blessed One extended His golden hand from within His robes and granted the "Ehi Bhikkhu" ordination, saying, "Etha bhikkhavo (Come, monks); caratha brahmacariyaṃ (lead the holy life, which is the practice of the three trainings)."

At that very moment, all the teachers and disciple ascetics were instantly endowed with the eight requisites, appearing like senior elders of sixty years of vassa (eighty years of age), and they stood paying respectful homage to the Blessed One.

The day those ascetics became Arahants and were ordained as Ehi Bhikkhu monks was a day when many people from the countries of Aṅga, Magadha, and Kuru...
266: It was the day when people brought offerings and came together to the ascetic's grove. When all those people arrived with their offerings and saw that the ascetics had become monks, they wondered, 'Is our teacher, the great ascetic Aggidatta, superior, or is the Great Shaman Gotama superior?' Then they thought, 'Since the Great Shaman Gotama has come to our teacher Aggidatta, our teacher Aggidatta must be the superior one.' The Buddha, knowing the intentions and thoughts of those people, said, 'Aggidatta, my son, you yourself must cut off the doubts of your followers.' Aggidatta replied, 'Exalted Buddha, I too desire to dispel the doubts of the followers.' After saying this, he used his psychic powers to fly into the air seven times and descend repeatedly. He then paid homage to the Buddha and declared, 'Satthā me bhante bhagavā, sāvakohamasmi—Venerable Sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am the disciple of the Buddha.' Thus, he clearly showed that he was a disciple of the Buddha. The story of Aggidatta the ascetic ends. *This story is found in the Dhammapada Commentary, Volume 2, 14-Buddhavagga, starting from page 156.
267:
## The Story of the Monk Jambuka

While the Buddha was staying at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha, he preached this Dhamma teaching beginning with "Māse māse kusaggena," concerning the naked ascetic named Jambuka.

## The Past Evil Deed of Jambuka

In the past, during the time of Kassapa Buddha, a householder living in a forest village built a monastery for a monk. He constantly supported the resident monk (āvāsika) of that monastery with the four requisites: robes, alms-food, lodging, and medicine. The resident monk would go to the householder's home daily for his meal.

Then one day, a great Arahant Elder arrived at the door of the householder's home while on his alms round. The householder, upon seeing the Arahant and being greatly inspired by his posture, invited him inside. He respectfully offered him excellent food and said, "Venerable Sir, please have this cloth made into a robe and wear it." After offering the excellent robe-cloth, he further said, "Venerable Sir, your hair has grown long. I will bring a barber to shave your hair. I will also bring a couch (bed) for you to rest upon."
268: The resident monk (kūlūpaka āvāsika) who always took his meals at the householder's home saw this honor and offering given to the Arahant. Jealousy over gains (lābhamacchariya) and jealousy over the family (kulamacchariya) arose in him, and he became displeased. He thought, 'This householder gives such honor to this monk whom he has just met, but he does not give such honor to me, who always eats at his house.' Feeling angry, he returned to the monastery. The visiting Arahant monk also went to the monastery with the resident monk and had the cloth offered by the householder sewn and dyed into a robe. The householder then brought a barber to the monastery, had the Arahant's hair shaved, and had a couch (bed) he had brought prepared cleanly. He said, 'Venerable Sir, please rest on this couch,' and after inviting both monks for the next day's meal, he returned home. The resident monk could not endure the honor shown by the householder to the visiting Arahant. Overwhelmed by intense jealousy over the family and gains, he went to the Arahant's resting place in the evening and addressed him—
269: (1) Friend visitor, it would be better for you to eat excrement than to eat alms-food at my supporter's house. (2) It would be better for you to have your hair plucked out with a palmyra nut than to have it shaved by the barber brought by my supporter. (3) It would be better for you to go about naked than to wear the robe offered by my supporter. (4) It would be better for you to sleep on the ground than to rest on the couch brought by my supporter. Thus, he insulted him in four ways. The great Arahant monk thought, 'Let not this foolish man be ruined because of me.' Considering this, he did not accept the meal invited by the householder and left early for a place of his choosing. The resident monk performed his minor and major duties in the monastery early. When it was time for alms, he thought, 'Even now, that lazy visiting monk is still sleeping. He might wake up if I ring the bell loudly.' He then lightly struck the bell with his fingernail and entered the village for alms.
270: The householder, having prepared grand offerings, looked toward the path where the two monks would come. Seeing only the resident monk arriving alone, he asked, 'Venerable Sir, where is the great visiting monk?' Then the jealous resident monk told the householder, 'Lay disciple, do not speak of him. Your teacher has been sleeping in his room since you left yesterday. I woke up early to sweep the monastery, pour water into the drinking and washing pots, and rang the bell for alms-time, but he knew nothing of it. (He is such a heavy sleeper.)' The householder thought, 'It is impossible for my master, who is endowed with such inspiring posture, to sleep until this time. Seeing the honor I paid to that noble one, this resident monk must have surely said something offensive.' Being a wise man, he did not show his anger. He respectfully served the resident monk, washed his bowl carefully, filled it with excellent food, and said, 'Venerable Sir, if you see my master, please offer this food to him,' and handed over the bowl.
271:
The resident monk, possessed by stinginess (macchariya), took the bowl filled with food and thought, "If this lazy visiting monk gets to eat such good food, he will become attached to this monastery and stay here." With this wrong thought, he threw away the food offered by the lay devotee on the way. He then went to the place where the Arahant Elder was staying, but could no longer find him.

At that time, because he had committed such a grave evil deed (obstructing the gains of an Arahant), even the monastic practice he had observed for twenty thousand years could not protect him (as the power of the unwholesome karma was so great). Thus, when his lifespan ended, he passed away and was reborn in the great Avīci hell. After suffering great misery in hell for the long interval between the times of Kassapa Buddha and our Gotama Buddha, he was reborn in a wealthy family in Rājagaha during the time our Buddha appeared in the world.

## The Present Suffering of Jambuka

His parents named the boy "Jambuka." From the time he could walk, he had no desire to sleep on a bed or eat food; he would only eat his own excrement. His parents thought, "He does this only because he is young...
272:
...and does not know better," and they tried to feed and care for him. However, even as he grew older, he did not want to wear clothes and wandered around naked. He slept only on the ground and ate only his own excrement.

## The Parents Sending Him to the Monastery of the Naked Ascetics

Then, Jambuka's parents thought, "This person is not fit for a respectable family like ours. He is utterly shameless and is only suited for the naked ascetics (Titthiyas)." Having considered this, they took Jambuka to the naked ascetics and said, "Please initiate this youth."

The naked ascetics then initiated him. The manner of his initiation was as follows:

They placed Jambuka in a pit as deep as his neck. They laid planks over his shoulders (so he could not struggle or escape) and sat on those planks while plucking out his hair with the shells of palm nuts. (This was the manner of initiation among the naked ascetics). After the initiation, Jambuka's parents invited the naked ascetics for a meal the next day and returned home.

The next day, when the naked ascetics said to Jambuka, "Come, let us enter the village," Jambuka refused, saying, "You go ahead; I shall remain here in this monastery." Although they called him repeatedly, he refused to go, so they left him behind and went into the city.
273: They went away. Jambuka, knowing that the naked ascetics had left, opened the cover of the latrine pit (vacca-kuṭī), descended into it, and ate the excrement with great relish. (Unaware of this), the senior naked ascetics sent food from the city to Jambuka. Jambuka did not want the food sent by the seniors. Even though the naked ascetics repeatedly urged him to eat, he said, "I do not want this food. I have already obtained my portion of nourishment." When asked where he got it, he replied, "I obtained it right here in this monastery." In this way, on the second, third, and fourth days, although the naked ascetics invited him in various ways to accompany them into the city, he refused, saying, "I will remain right here in this monastery garden," and did not wish to follow them into the city or village. Then the naked ascetics thought, "This Jambuka does not want to enter the city or village every day, nor does he want to eat the food we send. He says, 'I have already obtained my nourishment in this monastery garden.' What is he doing? We shall investigate this Jambuka." Having planned this, when they went for alms in the city, they left one or two naked ascetics behind to spy on Jambuka. Those assigned to spy pretended to follow later but stayed behind to watch in secret. Jambuka, thinking the naked ascetics had gone for alms...
274:
Just as on previous days, he descended into the latrine pit and ate excrement.

## Expulsion from the Monastery of the Naked Ascetics

The naked ascetics who were spying on him saw his behavior clearly and reported it to the others. Upon hearing this, the naked ascetics said, "Oh, Jambuka's conduct is very grave. If the disciples of the Monk Gotama find out about this, they will spread the word that 'the naked ascetics wander about eating excrement,' and our reputation will be ruined. This Jambuka is not fit for us." Having agreed, they expelled Jambuka from their presence.

After being expelled by the naked ascetics, he found a large stone slab near the place where the citizens of Rājagaha went to defecate. Near that stone slab was a large stone drain for foul water. Using the stone slab as a screen, the citizens would defecate nearby. Jambuka went to that stone slab; at night he ate the excrement left by people, and during the day, when people came to defecate, he would stand with one hand leaning on an edge of the stone slab, one leg raised and placed upon the other knee, facing the wind with his mouth wide open.

The people who came to defecate saw Jambuka, approached him, and paid respect, asking, "Venerable Sir, why do you keep your mouth open...
275: 275. When they asked, "How do you survive?" Jambuka boasted, "I eat only air. I have no other food besides air." When the people asked again, "Venerable sir, if that is so, why do you stand on one leg with the other placed on your knee?" he boasted again, "I am one of fierce and intense practice. If I were to step with both feet, the earth would not be able to bear my virtue and would tremble violently. Therefore, I stand on one leg. Indeed, because of this reason of earth-trembling, I spend my time standing day and night; I do not sit, nor do I sleep." (People generally respect and believe only what is spoken; those who reflect and consider whether it is true or not are very few.) Therefore, saying, "Oh, how wonderful! Such persons of fierce and intense practice exist in the world. We have never seen such persons of intense practice before," they spoke words of praise. Most people from the regions of Aṅga and Magadha were stirred and flocked to Jambuka, making great offerings and honors every month. ## Boasting Continually and Suffering the Rounds of Misery for 55 Years. When the people made offerings, Jambuka would say, "I eat only air; I eat no food other than air. Truly, if I were to eat food other than air, my practice would be ruined." He would then take the food offered by those people...
276: Jambuka did not desire any good food and only refused it. People repeatedly pleaded, "Venerable Sir, do not let us be ruined; if a person of such intense practice as you partakes, it will lead to our long-term welfare and happiness." For Jambuka, he liked no food other than excrement. However, because people pleaded so insistently, he would take a bit of ghee or molasses brought by them with the tip of a blade of grass, place it on the tip of his tongue, and say, "Go now, this much is enough for your welfare and happiness," and send them away. Thus, for fifty-five years, Jambuka spent his time (following the four types of karmic debt for insulting an Arahant): (1) Unable to wear clothes, (2) Eating only excrement, (3) Plucking his hair with a palmyra nut shell, (4) Sleeping only on the ground. (Note): How frightening is the karmic debt of harsh and impolite speech! ## Jambuka the Naked Ascetic's Attainment of Liberation. Every morning at dawn, the Buddha surveys the world to see which beings are ready for liberation...
277: Therefore, one day at dawn, when the Buddha surveyed the world of beings ready for liberation with his golden eye of omniscience, Jambuka the naked ascetic appeared within the net of the Buddha's omniscience. As the Buddha further reflected, "What will happen?", he saw Jambuka's past merit which would enable him to attain the Fruit of Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa). He clearly understood, "I shall preach a verse of Dhamma, making this Jambuka the primary listener. At the end of the verse, eighty-four thousand beings will realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation. Depending on this noble son Jambuka, many people will attain happiness." The next day, after wandering for alms in the city of Rājagaha and returning from his alms round, he said to the Venerable Ānanda, "Friend Ānanda, I shall go to Jambuka the naked ascetic." When the Venerable Ānanda asked, "Exalted Buddha, will you be going alone?", the Buddha replied, "Yes, friend Ānanda, I shall go alone." That evening, the Buddha went alone to Jambuka. At that time, the assembly of righteous devas (Sammā-deva) thought, "The Buddha is going to Jambuka the naked ascetic this evening. That Jambuka lives on a stone slab that is unsightly, foul-smelling, and disgusting with old excrement, urine, and tooth-sticks. It is only proper that rain should fall."
278: Thinking thus, by their divine power, they caused a heavy rain to fall at that very moment. The large stone slab became clean, pure, and free from filth. After that, the assembly of righteous devas caused a rain of five-colored flowers to fall upon that stone slab. In the evening, when the Buddha reached Jambuka the naked ascetic, he called out, "Jambuka!" Jambuka the naked ascetic thought, "Who is this low person who calls me so harshly by my name, Jambuka?" and in anger, he asked back, "Who is this person who just called me?" The Buddha replied, "I am a noble monk." Jambuka then asked, "O monk, what is your business?" When the Buddha said, "I would like you to give me a place to stay for this one night," Jambuka spoke dismissively, "O monk, there is no place for you here." Then the Buddha said, "Jambuka, do not do this. I would like a place for one night. It is natural for monks to seek out monks, for humans to seek out humans, and for animals to seek out animals." When Jambuka asked again, "What? Are you a monk?", the Buddha replied, "Yes, I am a noble monk."
279: Then Jambuka asked again, "If you are a noble monk, where is your water-vessel? Where is your fire-drill? Where is your sacrificial thread?" The Buddha replied, "I have the water-vessel, the fire-drill, and the sacrificial thread that you ask about. Considering that it is very burdensome to carry those objects and wander about, I carry them only within myself." Hearing this, Jambuka became very angry with the Buddha, saying, "You wander about seeking food (as a monk) without carrying those monastic requisites like the water-vessel." Then the Buddha spoke to him gently and kindly, "Let it be, Jambuka. Do not be angry with me. I only wish for you to tell me of a place to stay." However, Jambuka spoke curtly, "O monk, there is no place for you to stay here." Not far from Jambuka's location, there was a mountain valley. The Buddha pointed to that valley and asked, "Jambuka, who lives in that valley?" Jambuka replied, "O monk, there is not a single person living in that valley." The Buddha then said, "Jambuka, if that is so, I would like you to give me that valley as a place to stay." Jambuka replied, "O monk, you alone should know your own place (meaning, stay in that valley if you wish)."
280:
“(You alone should consider and know whether it is appropriate to stay or not),” he replied, giving permission only in a way that avoided taking responsibility.

The Blessed One spread his sitting mat in the valley and sat down. During the first watch of the night, the Four Great Kings came to visit the Blessed One, illuminating the four directions with a single mass of light. Jambuka the naked ascetic saw that light and wondered, “What kind of light is that?” During the middle watch, when Sakka, the King of Devas, came to visit, Jambuka wondered in the same manner. During the last watch, Mahābrahmā—who is capable of illuminating one world system with one finger, two world systems with two fingers, and ten world systems with ten fingers—came to visit, making the entire forest glow with a single radiance. Jambuka saw that light as well and wondered in the same way, “What kind of light is that?”

When early morning arrived, Jambuka approached the Blessed One, and after exchanging pleasantries, he stood in a suitable place and asked the Blessed One, “O Great Recluse, who were those who came to you during the first watch, each illuminating the four directions?” The Blessed One replied, “Jambuka, those were the Four Great Kings.”
281:
“Why did they come?” Jambuka asked again. “They came to attend to and serve me,” the Blessed One replied. Jambuka the naked ascetic continued, “O Great Recluse, how is it? Are you superior to the Four Great Kings?” The Blessed One replied, “Yes, Jambuka. I am the King of Dhamma, superior even to the Four Great Kings.”

Again, Jambuka asked, “O Great Recluse, who was the one who came during the middle watch?” The Blessed One replied, “That was Sakka, the King of Devas, Jambuka.” “For what reason did he come?” Jambuka asked again. “He came to attend to and serve me,” the Blessed One replied. Jambuka continued, “O Great Recluse, how is it? Are you superior even to Sakka, the King of Devas?” The Blessed One replied, “Yes, Jambuka. I am superior even to Sakka. That Sakka is like a novice (sāmaṇera) who is a dedicated attendant (kappiyakāraka) to me.”

Again, Jambuka asked, “O Great Recluse, who was the one who came during the last watch, illuminating the entire forest with his radiance?” The Blessed One replied, “Jambuka, the one who came during the final watch is the Mahābrahmā, whom brahmins and others invoke when they sneeze or stumble, saying, ‘Namo Mahābrahmuno’ (Homage to the Great Brahma).”
282:
Jambuka asked again, “O Great Recluse, how is it? Are you superior even to Mahābrahmā?” The Blessed One replied, “Yes, Jambuka. I am the King of Brahmās, superior even to the Great Brahmā.”

Then Jambuka the naked ascetic said:

“O Great Recluse, you are indeed worthy of praise with a snap of the fingers. Not a single one of those beings has ever come to visit me, though I have practiced and lived in this place for fifty-five years. Indeed, for these fifty-five years, I have lived only on air and remained standing. In all that time, those Devas, Sakka, and Brahmā have never come to visit me.”

As he spoke such boastful words, the Blessed One said to Jambuka:

“O Jambuka, you who deceive the foolish people of this world who lack wisdom, do you wish to deceive me as well? Have you not been eating only excrement for these fifty-five years? Have you not been sleeping only on the ground? Have you not been wandering about naked? Have you not been plucking out your hair with a palmyra nut shell?”
283:
“Have you not been plucking out your hair (with great pain)? Despite this, you deceive the people, saying, ‘I live only on air and stand on one leg. I neither sit nor lie down.’ And now you wish to deceive even me.

O Jambuka, in the past as well, relying on a vile and evil wrong view, you ate excrement for such a long time, you slept only on the ground, you wandered about naked, and you suffered the pain of plucking your hair with a palmyra nut shell. Yet even now, you still hold onto that same vile and evil wrong view.”

Thus the Buddha spoke clearly. Then Jambuka asked the Blessed One, “O Great Recluse, what evil deed did I commit in the past?” The Blessed One then preached in detail the evil unwholesome kamma that Jambuka had committed in his previous life. While the Blessed One was preaching about his past unwholesome kamma, intense spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arose in Jambuka’s mind, and the two qualities of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa) also arose. Because of this shame and fear, he crouched down, trying his best to cover his body.

Then the Blessed One threw a bathing cloth to Jambuka. Jambuka took the cloth given by the Blessed One,
284:
Wearing that bathing cloth, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat in a place free from the six faults. The Blessed One then preached the progressive discourse, such as the discourse on giving (dāna) and virtue (sīla), and then taught the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the teaching, Jambuka attained Arahantship along with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa). He paid homage to the Blessed One with great respect, rose from his seat, and requested both the novice and higher ordination.

(With this, the past unwholesome kamma of Jambuka was completely exhausted. To elaborate: this Jambuka had insulted a Great Arahant Elder during the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha with the four kinds of insults mentioned earlier. Consequently, he suffered in the Avīci hell until the earth rose by one yojana and three gāvutas. As a remaining result of that unwholesome kamma, he reached such a state of inhuman degradation—eating excrement, sleeping on the ground, being naked, and painfully plucking hair with a palmyra shell—for fifty-five years. Since the great evil result had been fully paid, Jambuka’s unwholesome kamma was exhausted.

However, that unwholesome kamma could not destroy the merit of the monkhood practice that Jambuka had fulfilled for twenty thousand years. Therefore—)

When Jambuka requested ordination, the Blessed One extended his right hand and gave the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' (Come, Monk) ordination, saying: “Ehi bhikkhu, cara brahmacariyaṃ sammā dukkhassa antakiriyāya—Come, monk; (receive the ordination you desire); practice the noble life of the three trainings to make an end of all suffering.”
285:
At the very moment the Blessed One said “Ehi Bhikkhu,” Jambuka’s lay appearance vanished. He appeared as a senior monk, complete with the eight requisites and looking as if he had been ordained for sixty years.

That day (when Jambuka became an Arahant and an Ehi Bhikkhu monk) was the day when the people of Anga and Magadha were coming to offer gifts to Jambuka. Thus, when the people from both great regions arrived with their offerings and saw the Blessed One, they thought, “How is it? Is our lord Jambuka superior, or is the Recluse Gotama superior?” They then mistakenly thought, “If the Recluse Gotama were superior, this Jambuka would have gone to him. But now, because our lord Jambuka is superior, the Recluse Gotama has come to him.”

The Blessed One, knowing the mistaken thoughts of the crowd, said, “Dear son Jambuka, clear the doubts of your supporters yourself.” Venerable Jambuka replied, “Exalted Blessed One, I too desire to dispel the doubts of the assembly.” After saying this, he entered the fourth jhāna, rose from his seat, and flew into the air to the height of one palm tree. Then he said, “Exalted Blessed One,
286:
“The Blessed One is my teacher; I am a disciple of the Buddha,” he declared. He then descended to the ground, paid homage with great respect, and flew up again to the height of two palm trees, then three, and in this manner, up to the height of seven palm trees. After descending to the ground each time, he made it clear to the people that he was a disciple of the Blessed One.

Seeing this, the people were amazed and thought, “Oh, the Buddhas are indeed worthy of praise with a snap of the fingers! They are endowed with incomparable virtues!” The Blessed One, wishing to converse with the people, said:

“Lay devotees, for fifty-five years, this Jambuka lived here boasting of his austerity, placing the offerings you brought on the tip of his tongue with a blade of kusa grass. Even if this Jambuka had continued such austerity without eating for a hundred years, and even if there were a blameless intention in not eating due to scrupulousness (kukkucca) regarding what is allowable or not for an Ariya—that hundred years of austerity would not be worth even one two-hundred-and-fifty-sixth (1/256) part of that blameless intention.”
287:
Having spoken thus, and wishing to preach the Dhamma by connecting the two statements, he uttered the following verse:

## Verse of Dhamma
Māse māse kusaggena, bālo bhuñjeyya bhojanaṃ.
Na so saṅkhātadhammānaṃ, kalaṃ agghati soḷasiṃ.

Bālo = A foolish heretic ascetic who does not know the Four Noble Truths. Māse māse = Month after month (or, once every month). Kusaggena = With the tip of a thin and coarse blade of kusa grass. Bhojanaṃ = Food. Bhuñjeyya = Even if he were to consume it for a hundred long years, thinking, "I shall practice austere conduct." So = That foolish heretic ascetic who does not know the Four Noble Truths. Saṅkhātadhammānaṃ = Of the Noble Ones (Ariyas) who have realized the Four Noble Truths. Soḷasiṃ kalaṃ = A sixteenth part (or, even one part out of two hundred and fifty-six parts). Na agghati = Is not worth.

(In this verse, the teaching is presented in terms of persons (puggalādhiṭṭhāna). The meaning in terms of Dhamma (dhammādhiṭṭhāna) is as follows: (1) There is the volition (cetanā) that arises in a foolish heretic ascetic from practicing such austere conduct for a hundred long years. (2) There is also a single wholesome volition of the Noble Ones who have realized the Four Noble Truths, which arises from abstaining from food because of scruples (kukkucca) as to whether the time or the food is allowable or not.
288:
Among these two types of volition, (1) the many volitions of that foolish heretic ascetic that arise over a hundred years cannot equal even one part out of two hundred and fifty-six parts of (2) the single volition of a Noble monk that arises from abstaining from food due to scruples regarding the time and the food; only that one part is truly valuable.

To clarify further: when Noble Ones who have realized the Four Noble Truths refrain from eating due to doubt and scruples regarding the time and the food, the fruit of that single blameless volition is divided into sixteen parts, and each of those is again divided into sixteen (totaling 256 parts). Even one such part is far more beneficial and noble than the (wrongful) austere practice of that foolish heretic ascetic for a hundred long years. This is the intended meaning.

At the conclusion of the teaching, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation.

The story of Jambuka Thera ends.

## Chapter 22
## The Founding of the City of Vesālī
In the distant past, a conception took place in the womb of the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī. Having realized this, the Queen informed the King. The King provided the Queen with protection for the fetus. With the protection given by the King, the Queen looked after the fetus comfortably and without hardship. When the pregnancy reached full term, she entered the maternity chamber.

It is the natural way for noble women of great merit to give birth at the break of dawn when the night is nearly over.

The Queen, being one of those noble women of great merit, gave birth at the break of dawn to a lump of flesh as red as a piece of lac or a Bandhujīvaka flower. At that time, the Queen thought, "Other queens give birth to sons who resemble golden statues. I, the Chief Queen, have given birth to a lump of flesh. This will bring disgrace upon me in the presence of the King." Fearing the spread of such a disgraceful reputation, she placed the lump of flesh in a casket, covered it with another casket, sealed it with the royal seal, and cast it adrift on the current of the Ganges River.

Remarkably, as soon as it was discarded by human hands, the deities (devas) arranged for its protection. Furthermore,
290:
On a gold plate, they wrote with pure cinnabar: "These are the children born of the Chief Queen of the King of Bārāṇasī," and they fastened that gold plate to the casket.

Under the protection arranged by the devas, the casket floated along the current of the Ganges without being harmed by waves or other dangers.

At that time, an ascetic lived near the banks of the Ganges, depending on a cowherd village for his alms-resort. When that ascetic went down to the Ganges early in the morning, he saw the casket floating by and, thinking it was a discarded object (paṃsukūla), he retrieved it. Later, seeing the gold plate (gold leaf) fastened to the casket and the royal seal, he opened the cover and saw the lump of flesh. Upon seeing it, the ascetic thought, "This lump of flesh must be a fetus; because it is a fetus, it has no foul smell or decay whatsoever." After reflecting thus, he took the lump of flesh to his hermitage and placed it in a clean spot.

After half a month (15 days) had passed, the single original lump of flesh miraculously became two lumps of flesh. Seeing this wonder, the ascetic kept them even better than before. Then, after another half month (15 days) had passed, five small protrusions (the five branches) for the two arms, two legs, and the head miraculously appeared on each lump of flesh. Seeing this wonder again, the ascetic kept them even better than before. Then, after another half month (15 days) had passed, one lump of flesh became a male child resembling a golden statue,
291:
and the other lump of flesh became a female child resembling a golden statue.

A strong parental love for the boy and the girl arose in the ascetic. Consequently, milk began to flow from both of the ascetic's thumbs. From that time onwards (due to the merit of the children), he also received milk-rice mixed with cow's milk from the alms-village (the cowherd village). The ascetic ate the meal himself and poured the milk into the mouths of the children. Whatever entered the stomachs of those children could be seen from the outside, like an object placed inside a crystal vessel. Because of having such delicate and thin skin, the boy and the girl received the name "Licchavī."

(The meaning is: Ni = thin and delicate + Chavi = those who have skin = Nicchavi, meaning those with thin and delicate skin; the letter 'n' was changed to 'l', and thus they were called Licchavī. This is the origin of the name Licchavī.)

Because the ascetic had to feed and clean the children, he entered the village for alms very late in the day. He also had to leave the alms-village in great haste when it was very late. Realizing his preoccupation, the cowherds said, "Venerable sir, raising children is a great hindrance (palibodha) for ascetics and monks, preventing them from practicing the Dhamma. Therefore, please give the children to us. We ourselves will feed
292:
and clean them. May you, venerable sir, only practice and perform your duties as a monk." When they requested thus, the ascetic agreed, saying, "Very well, lay devotees (dāyakas)."

On the second day (the next day), the cowherds leveled the road, scattered flowers, erected banners and flags, and then, playing various musical instruments, they gathered at the ascetic's hermitage. The ascetic said, "Lay devotees, these children are persons of great merit. Raise them with care and diligence until they reach maturity. When they reach maturity, marry them to each other. Please the King of Bārāṇasī with the five products of the cow (gorasa)—namely, milk, curd, butter, buttermilk, and ghee—and request a portion of land from the King to found a city. In that new city, consecrate the youth as king by pouring the water of royal consecration (rājābhiseka)." After giving these full instructions, he handed the two children over to the cowherds. The cowherds said, "Very well, venerable ascetic," and took the two children to the cowherd village and raised them according to the ascetic's instructions.

When the two children reached maturity, they played together with other children. In situations where disputes arose, they would hit and kick the other cowherd children with their hands and feet. When those other cowherd children cried, their parents asked, "Why are you crying?"
293:
When asked, they replied, "These two children raised by the ascetic, who have no mother or father, hit and kick us severely with their hands and feet." Then, even the parents who were feeding and cleaning those two children raised by the ascetic said, "These two children harass and oppress the other children; they cause trouble. These two siblings should not be supported; these two siblings should be shunned (vajjitabbā)." From that time on, that region, which was three hundred yojanas in extent, came to be known as the "Vajjī" region.

(Based on the words "Vajjetabbā ime" = "These two should be shunned," spoken by the parents of the other children as well as the foster parents (posāvanika) who were feeding and cleaning the two children raised by the ascetic, the region became known as the "Vajjī" country. It is said to be three hundred yojanas in extent.)

Thereafter, the cowherds, following the ascetic's instructions, pleased the King with the five products of the cow and obtained that land. After founding a new city in that place, they consecrated the youth, who had reached sixteen years of age, with the water of consecration and made him king. After making him king, they performed the marriage ceremony with that same maiden and made a covenant: "No maidens from other foreign countries shall be brought to be crowned as queen, and no maiden from this country of ours shall be given to any foreigner."
294: Through the union and intimate relations of the consecrated King and Queen, a daughter and a son were born for the first time. In this manner, sixteen pairs of sons and daughters were born. When these children reached maturity, they also married in the same way as their parents. Just as before, each pair gave birth to sixteen pairs of sons and daughters, resulting in a great increase and prosperity of princes and princesses. Subsequently, as the number of these princes and princesses grew and flourished, the space within the city became insufficient for their parks, gardens, residences, palaces, and retinues. Therefore, centered on the original capital, the city walls were expanded by one gāvuta in each of the four directions. Later, as their numbers increased again, the children, retinues, and ceremonial buildings once more exceeded the city's capacity. For a second time, the city walls were expanded by one gāvuta in each of the four directions. When they increased yet again, the city walls were expanded for a third time by one gāvuta in each of the four directions. Thus, because the city flourished so much that the children, retinues, and ceremonial buildings could not be contained, and the city walls were expanded three times by one gāvuta in each direction, becoming increasingly vast, the city became famous throughout Jambudīpa by the name 'Vesālī'.
295: This is the explanation of why they are called Licchavī kings, why it is called the Vajjī country, and why it is called the city of Vesālī. (From Khuddakapāṭha Commentary, page 133, and Sāratthadီpanī-ṭīkā, Vol. 2, page 169). The account of the founding of Vesālī ends. ********** ## The Buddha Quelling the Three Great Dangers in Vesālī with the Ratana Sutta. This aforementioned city of Vesālī, like Rājagaha and Sāvatthī, reached a state of great prosperity and abundance when the Buddha appeared. Indeed, when the Buddha appeared in Vesālī, there were 7,707 crowned kings. Similarly, there were 7,707 crown princes, 7,707 generals, and 7,707 treasurers and other officials. There were 7,707 long palaces where these kings resided, as many courtrooms, as many gabled halls, and as many parks and ponds. It was densely populated and food was abundant. Later, due to the decline of the Aparihāniya Dhamma (principles of non-decline), rain became scarce, crops failed leaving only stalks, and the great danger of famine (dubbikkhantarakappa) occurred. (This is the first danger.)
296: When the calamity of famine struck, the poor were the first to die in large numbers. Those corpses were discarded haphazardly outside the city. Because of the repulsive stench of those corpses, non-human beings (amanussa) entered the city and began to possess and oppress the people. (This is the second calamity.) When the combined calamities of famine and non-human beings struck, even more people died than before. As more people perished due to these two calamities, like 'a centipede stinging where a snake has already bitten,' hearts became terrified and minds became uneasy. Consequently, the pestilence known as the plague (ahivātaro-ga) struck, and living beings died in even greater numbers than before. (This is the third calamity.) Thus, being oppressed and afflicted by these three great evils—the calamity of famine, the calamity of oppression by non-human beings, and the calamity of the plague—the citizens of Vesālī approached the King and addressed him: 'O Great King, three great calamities have arisen in this city of Vesālī. From now back through seven generations of kings, such terrible calamities have never occurred. We believe that these three great calamities have arisen now because Your Majesty does not observe the Dhamma.'
297: Thus they petitioned. The King gathered all the people at the court and said, 'O people, examine my failure to observe the Dhamma.' When the people examined the entire sequence of the King's daily activities, they could not find even the slightest fault in him. Subsequently, finding no fault in the King, they deliberated and consulted one another, saying, 'By what means shall these three great calamities currently afflicting our country be pacified?' Among those people, some (disciples of the heretics) suggested, 'If the six great heretical teachers (Titthiya) enter our city of Vesālī, the three great calamities will surely be pacified.' However, many others (who had faith in the Triple Gem) said: 'O friends, it is said that the Buddha has appeared in the world. That Buddha is said to preach the Dhamma for the benefit of all beings. His power and majesty are said to be very great. If that Blessed Buddha himself were to arrive and enter our city of Vesālī, all calamities would surely be pacified.' Upon this proposal, all the people were delighted and agreed, but some expressed doubt, saying, 'Where is that Blessed Buddha residing now? Even if we invite him, might he not come?' Then, some wise and far-sighted people said:
298: 'Those known as Buddhas have compassion for and protect the world of beings. Why would he not come? However, there is a special consideration: that Buddha is currently residing in the city of Rājagaha. King Bimbisāra (a stream-enterer and lay supporter) is currently attending to the Buddha with the four requisites so that nothing is lacking. It may be that King Bimbisāra will not give permission for the Buddha to come.' All agreed with this statement and unanimously decided: 'If that is the case, we shall inform King Bimbisāra of Rājagaha of the situation to obtain his permission, and then we shall invite the Buddha to our city of Vesālī.' They gave instructions, saying, 'Inform King Bimbisāra to obtain his permission and then invite the Buddha,' and they dispatched two Licchavī kings along with a large army and many gifts to King Bimbisāra. Those two Licchavī kings went to Rājagaha, presented the gifts to King Bimbisāra, informed him of the entire situation, and said, 'O Great King, we wish to invite the Buddha to our city of Vesālī.' When they said this, King Bimbisāra,
299: ...without accepting responsibility, saying, "I want you yourselves to find out whether the Buddha wishes to come or not." Those two Licchavī princes went to the presence of the Buddha, prostrated, and said, "Exalted Buddha, three great dangers are prevailing in our city of Vesālī. If the Buddha would compassionately come, it would bring happiness and welfare to the people of Vesālī." When the Buddha reflected, he realized, "If I preach the Ratana Sutta in Vesālī, that protection and warding will spread to a hundred thousand million universes. At the end of the preaching of the Ratana Sutta, 84,000 beings will realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation." Thus, he accepted the invitation of the two Licchavī princes. ## King Bimbisāra Organizing the Ceremony. When King Bimbisāra heard the news that the Buddha had accepted the invitation to go to Vesālī, he ordered a proclamation throughout the city, "O people, the Buddha has accepted the invitation to go to Vesālī." Then he approached the Buddha and asked, "Exalted Buddha, have you accepted the invitation to go to Vesālī?"
300: 'Yes, I have accepted, Great King,' the Buddha replied. Then King Bimbisāra petitioned, 'Exalted Buddha, if that is so, please wait until the road for the journey has been prepared.' Then King Bimbisāra had the ground leveled for the five-yojana distance between Rājagaha and the Ganges River. He had a rest house built at every yojana and then informed the Buddha of the time for the journey. The Buddha set out on the journey accompanied by five hundred monks. King Bimbisāra had the five-yojana road strewn knee-deep with flowers of five colors. He had banners, flags, full water pots, and live plantain trees set up. He had two white umbrellas held over the Buddha (on the left and right) and one white umbrella held over each monk. Accompanied by his own retinue and making offerings of flowers and perfumes, he had the Buddha rest at each rest house to recover from the fatigue of the journey. Providing great alms, he escorted the Buddha comfortably over the five-day journey to the banks of the Ganges River. While the royal ceremonial boat was being decorated with all kinds of ornaments on the bank of the Ganges, word was sent to the kings of Vesālī: 'The Buddha is coming. Please prepare and decorate the road, and let all the Licchavī kings come to welcome the Buddha.'

They leveled the ground for a distance of three yojanas between the city of Vesālī and the Ganges River. They prepared four white umbrellas for the Blessed One and two white umbrellas for each monk. When the raft departed, King Bimbisāra accompanied the Blessed One, wading into the water up to his neck. He supplicated, "O Blessed One, I shall remain waiting here on the bank of the Ganges until the Blessed One returns," and then released the raft and returned to the shore.

In the heavens above, the devas and brahmās performed offerings up to the Akanittha Brahma realm. Below, in the Ganges, the Naga kings such as Kambala and Assatara performed their offerings.

## The Falling of the Pokkharavassa Rain
At the very moment the raft carrying the Blessed One reached the bank of the Ganges on the side of Vesālī, thunder roared in the four directions, lightning flashed, and dark, heavy rain clouds gathered until the sky was completely dark. Then, as soon as the Blessed One placed his first right foot on the bank of the Ganges, a great Pokkharavassa rain fell. Only those who wished to be wet were drenched; for those who did not wish to be wet, not a single drop touched them. Throughout the city of Vesālī, the floodwaters flowed steadily, reaching the knees in some places, the thighs in others, the waist in some, and the neck in others. This flood of rainwater naturally swept away the decaying corpses that had been discarded in various places and carried them into the current of the Ganges. Consequently, the entire ground of the city of Vesālī became clean and pure.

The Licchavī kings invited the Blessed One to stay for one night each in the rest houses they had prepared at every yojana along the three-yojana journey between the Ganges and Vesālī. As soon as the Blessed One arrived at Vesālī, Sakka, the king of devas, descended to Vesālī where the Blessed One was, accompanied by a host of devas. As soon as the Venerable Ānanda began reciting the first verse, "Yaṃ kiñci vittaṃ," the yakkhas, spirits, and ghosts who had not fled earlier but were clinging to rubbish heaps, walls, and other places, fled through the four city gates. ## Preaching the Ratana Sutta
The people of Vesālī, including the kings, perfumed and smeared the central assembly hall with various scents, hung canopies, and decorated it with various ornaments. In the Ratana Sutta Pali that Buddhist devotees see today in the Great Paritta, the passages from "Paṇidhānato paṭṭhāya" to "Parittaṃ taṃ bhaṇāma he" are the introductory prose (cūṇṇiya) and two verses composed by ancient teachers. The fifteen verses from the verse "Yānīdha bhūtāni samāgatāni" to the verse "Khīṇaṃ purāṇaṃ nava natthi sambhavaṃ" are the verses spoken by the Buddha. The final three verses beginning with "Yānīdha bhūtāni samāgatāni" are the verses recited by Sakka, the king of devas, at that Dhamma assembly.

At the conclusion of the preaching of the Ratana Sutta on the first day, the people of Vesālī and the Licchavī kings became free from suffering and attained happiness.
