## About the Procedure of Reciting Paritta
Paritta refers to the noble words of the Buddha that protect against various dangers and hazards from all around. It means the Suttas, which are the Buddha's words, that protect and guard so that existing dangers are calmed and future dangers do not arise.

[Pari = samantato bhayaṃ tāyati = rakkhatīti parittaṃ. Pari = samantato = from all around. Bhayaṃ = various dangers and hazards. Tāyati = rakkhati = protects and guards so that they are calmed and do not occur. Iti = therefore. Parittaṃ = it is called Paritta. (The Burmese word 'Parit' is derived from the Pali word 'Paritta'.)]

The Suttas preached by the Buddha, such as the Maṅgala Sutta and Ratana Sutta, are given the special name "Paritta" because, when they are recited, they possess the special quality of protecting both the reciter and the listener by preventing future dangers from arising, calming existing dangers, and bringing about benefits, happiness, and auspiciousness.

In reciting these Parittas, the attainment of the aforementioned benefits and powers depends on: (a) The person reciting the Paritta...
308:
3 or 4 factors; (b) 3 or 4 factors of the person listening to the Paritta; only when these factors on both sides—3 or 4 each—are fulfilled can the results be fully achieved.

## (a) Factors of the Person Reciting the Paritta
There are 3 (or alternatively 4) factors for the person reciting the Paritta. Among them:
(1) Being able to recite the Pāḷi text of the Paritta with correct pronunciation and articulation.
(2) Knowing the precise and correct meaning of the Pāḷi text of the Paritta.
(3) Reciting the Paritta with a pure mind, preceded by loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā), without regard for gain, offerings, or honor.
These are the 3 factors of the person reciting the Paritta.

Alternatively, the factors of the person reciting the Paritta may be stated as:
(1) Being able to recite the Pāḷi text of the Paritta with correct pronunciation and articulation.
(2) Knowing the precise and correct meaning of the Pāḷi text of the Paritta.
(3) Having no mind that regards gain, offerings, or honor.
(4) Reciting the Paritta with a pure mind, preceded by loving-kindness (mettā) and compassion (karuṇā).
In this way, it should be said that there are 4 factors.
309:
309
Mnemonic verse for brief memorization:
A. (1) Pure in sound, (2) clear in meaning, (3) with heartfelt loving-kindness.
B. For the reciter, these are the three factors; remember the words of the texts.
C. (4) Adding 'without regard for gain,' note these as the four factors.

Only when reciting with the 3 or 4 factors mentioned above will the power and majesty of the Paritta be exceedingly great, and those who listen can reach happiness, with dangers being extinguished and vanishing in their very presence. It should be understood that if one is not endowed with the 3 or 4 factors previously described, the desired benefits cannot be accomplished.

[The source of these statements is: 'Suggahitāti atthañca vyañjanañca parisodhetvā suṭṭhu uggahitā. Samattā pariyāputāti padavyañjanāni ahāpetvā paripuṇṇaṃ uggahitā, atthampi pāḷimpi visaṃvādetvā sabbaso vā pana appaguṇaṃ katvā bhaṇantassa hi parittaṃ tejavantaṃ na hoti, sabbaso paguṇaṃ katvā bhaṇantasseva tejavantaṃ hoti. Lābahetu uggahetvā bhaṇantassāpi atthaṃ na sādheti, nissaraṇapakkhe ṭhatvā mettaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā bhaṇantasseva atthāya hotīti dasseti.' (Dī.A. 3, 149, 150)]

'Suggahitā' means that both the meaning and the phonetics of the Pāḷi text have been repeatedly purified and well-learned. 'Samattā pariyāputā' means that the words and syllables have been fully learned without omission. Indeed, the Paritta of one who recites by distorting the meaning or the Pāḷi, or by reciting without thorough study and mastery, cannot have power and majesty. Only the Paritta of one who recites with thorough study and mastery in every aspect can have power and majesty. The Paritta of one who learns and recites for the sake of gain also cannot accomplish the desired benefit. Only the Paritta of one who recites while standing on the side of liberation from the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa), making loving-kindness the precursor,
310:
310
is for the sake of benefit; this meaning is shown by the words 'suggahitā samattā pariyāputā.' (This is the Burmese translation of the Commentary).

Note: The person reciting the Paritta should well-learn the Pāḷi text of the Paritta along with its Commentary from a teacher, ensuring correct pronunciation and articulation. After studying the method of recitation, only when reciting with a clear distinction of both grammar and meaning, without any distortion or omission of words and syllables, will the Paritta possess power and majesty, and the desired benefits, such as the cessation of dangers, will surely be accomplished.

If, during recitation, there are distortions or omissions of words and syllables, ignorance of grammar and meaning, or regard for gain, offerings, and honor, the power and majesty of the Paritta will be meager, and it will not be able to accomplish the desired benefits like the cessation of dangers.

In truth, it should be understood that only when reciting the Paritta with a mind aspiring for liberation from the round of rebirths, preceded by loving-kindness and compassion, and without regard for gain, offerings, and honor, will the power and majesty be great and able to accomplish the desired benefits like the cessation of dangers. Therefore, the person reciting the Paritta should recite with a great wholesome mind (mahākusala citta) dominated by loving-kindness and compassion, standing only on the disposition of aspiring for liberation from the round of rebirths without regard for gain, with correct pronunciation and a good understanding of grammar and meaning.

## Explanation of the Failure (Vipatti) and Success (Sampatti) of the Reciter
The failure (vipatti) of the person reciting the Paritta is of two kinds:
(1) Payoga-vipatti (Failure in effort),
(2) Ajjhāsaya-vipatti (Failure in intention).
Among these two:
311:
311
(1) Payoga-vipatti refers to the failure or distortion of effort. Not knowing the meaning of the Paritta Pāḷi and being unable to recite the words and syllables correctly and precisely are called the failure of effort (payoga-vipatti).
(2) Ajjhāsaya-vipatti refers to the failure or distortion of intention. Reciting while desiring, craving, or regarding gain, offerings, and honor is called the failure of intention (ajjhāsaya-vipatti).

The success (sampatti) of the person reciting the Paritta is of two kinds:
(1) Payoga-sampatti (Success in effort),
(2) Ajjhāsaya-sampatti (Success in intention).
Among these two:
(1) Payoga-sampatti refers to the fulfillment of effort. Knowing the meaning of the Paritta Pāḷi and being able to recite the words and syllables correctly and precisely are called the success of effort (payoga-sampatti).
(2) Ajjhāsaya-sampatti refers to the fulfillment of intention. Reciting with a great wholesome mind (mahākusala citta) dominated by loving-kindness and compassion, standing on the side of liberation from the round of rebirths without desiring or regarding gain, offerings, and honor, is called the success of intention (ajjhāsaya-sampatti).

[These vipatti and sampatti are extracted and presented from the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta Ṭīkā.]

Note: The person reciting the Paritta should abandon the two failures (vipatti) mentioned above and recite the Paritta in accordance with the two successes (sampatti). Only by reciting in such a way can the power,
312:
312
benefits, and efficacy of the Paritta be surely obtained by those who listen. This should be so understood.

Mnemonic verse for brief memorization:
(1) If grammar and meaning are flawed and omitted, payoga is failed.
(2) If the disposition of mind is flawed, craving gain, ajjhāsaya is failed.
(3) If grammar, meaning, and oral recitation are perfect, payoga is successful.
(4) If there is no regard for gain and it is infused with mettā, ajjhāsaya is successful.
(5) These are the factors of the Paritta reciter; let the wise understand them.

The section on the factors of the person reciting the Paritta is finished.
**********

## (b) Factors of the Person Listening to the Paritta
There are 3 (or alternatively 4) factors for the person listening to the Paritta. Among them:
(1) Absence of the obstruction of kamma (kammantarāya), namely the five heinous crimes (pañcānantariya kamma).
(2) Absence of the obstruction of defilement (kilesantarāya), namely fixed wrong view (niyata micchādiṭṭhi).
(3) Being endowed with faith (saddhā) that unshakably believes in the virtues and benefits of the Paritta Pāḷi.
These are the 3 factors of the person listening to the Paritta.

Alternatively, the factors of the person listening to the Paritta are:
(1) Absence of the obstruction of kamma, namely the five heinous crimes.
313:
313
(2) Absence of the obstruction of defilement, namely fixed wrong view.
(3) Being endowed with faith (saddhā) that unshakably believes in the virtues and benefits of the Paritta Pāḷi.
(4) Listening to the Paritta Pāḷi respectfully.
In this way, it should be said that there are 4 factors. Therefore, in the Milindapañha Pāḷi (Meṇḍakapañha section), page 155, Maccupāsamutti-pañha section:
'Tīhi mahārāja kāraṇehi parittaṃ na rakkhati kammāvaraṇena kilesāvaraṇena asaddahanatāya' = "O Great King, because of these three reasons, the Paritta does not protect: (1) because of the obstruction of kamma (kammantarāya), namely the five heinous crimes; (2) because of the obstruction of defilement (kilesantarāya), namely fixed wrong view; and (3) because of lack of faith in the Paritta Dhamma." Thus did the Venerable Nāgasena preach. Based on this Pāḷi, it should be understood that the Paritta can protect those who are free from these three causes mentioned in that Pāḷi so that they are free from danger.

Mnemonic verse for brief memorization:
(1) Absence of the five ānantariya kammas is one factor.
(2) Absence of niyata diṭṭhi kilesa is one factor.
(3) Being endowed with faith (saddhā) is one factor.
(4) Listening with respect is one factor.
(5) If endowed with these four, listen and be free from danger.
314:
314
## Explanation of the Failure (Vipatti) and Success (Sampatti) of the Person Listening to the Paritta
The failure (vipatti) of the person listening to the Paritta is of two kinds:
(1) Payoga-vipatti,
(2) Ajjhāsaya-vipatti.
Among them:
(1) Payoga-vipatti is the failure of effort itself. Not listening to the Paritta Pāḷi respectfully with hands raised in anjali, and not listening with a good, steady, and calm mind without letting the mind wander to objects other than the Paritta, are called the failure of effort (payoga-vipatti).
(2) Ajjhāsaya-vipatti is the failure or distortion of intention. Not believing in the virtues, power, and majesty of the Paritta, and listening only out of regard for the person who invited one to the Paritta recitation, are called the failure of intention (ajjhāsaya-vipatti).

The success (sampatti) of the person listening to the Paritta is of two kinds:
(1) Payoga-sampatti,
(2) Ajjhāsaya-sampatti.
Among them:
(1) Payoga-sampatti is the fulfillment of effort itself. Listening to the Paritta Pāḷi respectfully with hands raised in anjali, and listening with a good, steady, and calm mind without letting the mind wander to objects other than the Paritta, are called the success of effort (payoga-sampatti).
315:
315
(2) Ajjhāsaya-sampatti is the fulfillment of intention. Believing in the virtues, power, and majesty of the Paritta, and listening with a good wholesome right desire (kusala sammā-chanda) rather than merely out of regard for the person who invited one to the Paritta recitation, is called the success of intention (ajjhāsaya-sampatti).

Persons listening to the Paritta Dhamma should abandon the two failures (vipatti) mentioned above and listen in accordance with the two successes (sampatti). Only by listening in such a way should it be understood that the benefits and efficacy of the Paritta, such as freedom from danger, will surely be obtained.

Just as the occurrence of the two failures and two successes can be found in the person reciting the Paritta, so too can the occurrence of the two failures and two successes be found in the person listening to the Paritta.

The section on the procedure for reciting Paritta is finished.

## Parittas with Exceptional and Sharp Power and Majesty
(1) The power of the Ratana Sutta Paritta spreads throughout ten billion world-systems and causes the audience of five hundred and eighty-eight thousand devas, humans, and brahmās who listen to the Dhamma to attain the Knowledge of the Path, the Knowledge of the Fruit, and Nibbāna. Therefore, this Ratana Sutta Paritta is a Paritta with exceedingly sharp, exceptional, and great power and majesty.
(2) The power of the Maṅgala Sutta Paritta spreads throughout ten billion world-systems and causes an innumerable multitude of devas, humans, and brahmās who listen to the Dhamma to attain the Knowledge of the Path, the Knowledge of the Fruit, and Nibbāna.
316:
Therefore, this Maṅgala Sutta Paritta is also a Paritta of exceedingly sharp, extraordinary, and great power.

(3) The Metta Sutta Paritta spreads its authority throughout a hundred thousand crores of universes and enabled five hundred forest-dwelling monks to exhaust their taints and reach the state of Arahantship. If one perfectly practices the sixteen duties contained within the Metta Sutta, one can certainly attain the noble Path and Fruition. Therefore, this Metta Sutta Paritta is also a Paritta of exceedingly sharp, extraordinary, and great power.

(4) The Khandha Sutta Paritta spreads its authority throughout a hundred thousand crores of universes and can always dispel and prevent all kinds of poisons, dangers, and calamities. Since it contains the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, as well as the practice of loving-kindness (metta), it is exceptionally noble. Therefore, this Khandha Sutta Paritta is also a Paritta of exceedingly sharp, extraordinary, and great power.

(5) The Dhajagga Sutta Paritta spreads its authority throughout a hundred thousand crores of universes and can provide escape from dangers and calamities. By focusing on and cultivating the qualities of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha contained within the Dhajagga Sutta, one can achieve mental growth, be reborn in the celestial realms for thirty thousand aeons, become the King of Devas (Sakka) eighty times, become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) a thousand times, become a regional or independent king countless times, be wealthy and prosperous in every life without losing one's possessions, and for a hundred thousand aeons...
317:
...avoid falling into the four woeful planes, reach the Fruition of Arahantship in the final existence, and be free from terror, fear, trembling, and horripilation. Therefore, this Dhajagga Sutta Paritta is also a Paritta of exceedingly sharp, extraordinary, and great power.

(6) The Bojjhaṅga Sutta Paritta spreads its authority throughout a hundred thousand crores of universes and can cure dangers and illnesses. If one fully develops and cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) contained within the Bojjhaṅga Sutta, one can attain the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna in this very life. Therefore, this Bojjhaṅga Sutta Paritta is also a Paritta of exceedingly sharp, extraordinary, and great power.

(7) Regarding the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta Paritta, the four Great Kings themselves assembled in the celestial city named Āṭānāṭa, paid homage by reflecting on the virtues of the seven Buddhas, and recited this Āṭānāṭiya Sutta Paritta. They then issued a royal decree: "We shall punish such and such unruly spirits who do not obey the Dhamma-wheel of the Blessed One and our own authority." Afterward, they approached the Blessed One with a large army of guardian deities and offered this protective discourse of the four Great Kings. The Blessed One himself then taught this great protective Paritta to the monks. Its power and authority are immense and potent. Therefore, the Commentary describes the procedure for reciting it as follows:
318:
The procedure for reciting the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta is as follows:

For a patient possessed by malevolent spirits (bhūta or peta), the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta should not be recited initially. Instead, the Metta Sutta, Dhajagga Sutta, and Ratana Sutta should be recited for seven days. If the patient is freed from the possession by these recitations, it is well and good; there is no need to recite the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta.

Only if they are not freed after seven days of reciting the Metta, Dhajagga, and Ratana Suttas should the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta be recited. The monk who is to recite the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta must not eat cakes made of flour or meat and fish. He must not reside in a cemetery. The reason is that if he eats flour-cakes, meat, or fish, or stays in a cemetery, malevolent spirits will have the opportunity to enter (possess) that monk himself. The place where the Paritta is to be recited should be smeared with turmeric, and clean seats should be prepared.

The people who escort the monk from the monastery to the house must surround him with weapons such as bows, arrows, swords, and spears. Upon reaching the house, the monk should not recite the Paritta in an open space. He should sit with doors and windows closed, surrounded by people holding weapons, and recite the Paritta with a mind preceded by loving-kindness (metta). The procedure is:

First, the sick person should be established in the precepts (sīla). To the patient thus established in virtue, the Paritta protection should be given...
319:
...(the Paritta should be recited). If this method still fails to free the person possessed by malevolent spirits, the patient should be taken to the monastery and laid down on the courtyard of a stupa (cetiya). After performing offerings such as decorating the stupa's site, lighting lamps, and sweeping the courtyard, one should first recite auspicious Dhamma verses and prose (cuṇṇiya) starting with "Divā tapati ādicco" (The sun shines by day). An announcement should be made that the entire Saṅgha has assembled.

In the forest near the monastery, there will be a chief tree (the lord of the forest). One should go to that tree and invite the deity, saying, "The Saṅgha of monks desires the presence of you, the Great Tree Deity (Rukkha-deva)." (The deity cannot fail to come to the place where all the monks are assembled).

Then, one should ask the spirit possessing the patient, "What is your name?" When the name is given, address the spirit by that name (for example, if the possessing spirit is named Naradeva):

"Friend Naradeva, we share with you the merit (puñña) of offering flowers and scents, the merit of honoring the Buddha's seat, and the merit of offering alms-food. The Saṅgha of monks has recited auspicious Dhamma words as a gift of Dhamma to you. Out of respect for the Saṅgha...
320:
please release this patient."

Thus, a request should be made for the release. If the spirit still does not release the patient, one should inform the righteous deities (Sammā-deva), saying, "O Great Sammā-deva Kings, be aware. This malevolent spirit does not follow our words of loving-kindness. Therefore, we must now exercise the noble authority of the Blessed One." After making this declaration, the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta Paritta should be recited.

What has been described above is the procedure for laypeople. If the person possessed by a malevolent spirit is a monk, the area should be cleaned and purified, the Saṅgha should be invited to assemble, the merit from offerings such as flowers and scents should be shared, and the Āṭānāṭiya Paritta should be recited as before. This is the procedure for both monk and lay patients.

As stated, the Commentary on the Āṭānāṭiya Sutta describes the preparatory procedures in great detail. Therefore, this Āṭānāṭiya Sutta Paritta is also a Paritta of exceedingly sharp, extraordinary, and great power.

Similarly, the remaining Sutta Parittas each possess exceedingly sharp, extraordinary, and great power. To summarize here, the words of the Piṭaka and the Five Nikāyas taught by the Blessed One spread their authority throughout a hundred thousand crores of universes...
321:
...and can increase both worldly and supramundane benefits. They can dispel and prevent dangers and calamities, and since they can assist in reaching the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna, they are the most noble of all speech. Therefore, one should believe and note without doubt that the words of the Piṭaka and the Five Nikāyas taught by the Blessed One possess exceedingly sharp, extraordinary, and great power.

Yaṃ buddho bhāsate vācaṃ,
khemaṃ nibbānapattiyā.
Dukkhassantakiriyāya,
sā ve vācānamuttamā.

Buddho = the Blessed One, the Lord of the World known as the Omniscient Buddha; nibbānapattiyā = for the sake of reaching Nibbāna; dukkhassa = of the suffering of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa-dukkha); antakiriyāya = for the sake of making an end, a final closure; khemaṃ = which is secure and free from harm; vācaṃ = that word known as the Five Nikāyas and the Piṭaka; bhāsate = speaks out of compassion. Sā vācā = those words of the Buddha, the three Piṭakas and five Nikāyas; ve = indeed; uttamā = are the most noble, being faultless and worthy of praise, among all speech. (From the Sagāthāvagga Saṃyutta Pāḷi, page 191).

## Preaching the Story of the Bodhisatta Saṅkha Brahmin

After the Blessed One had resided in the city of Vesālī for half a month (fifteen days), he informed the Licchavī princes, saying, "We shall now depart."
322:
Then, the Licchavī princes escorted the Blessed One to the banks of the Ganges River with a ceremony of honor and offerings that was twice as great as that of King Bimbisāra, completing the three-day journey.

At that time, the Nāga kings living in the Ganges River thought, "Human beings are making great offerings to the Blessed One. Why should we not do the same? We certainly shall." After consulting together, they created golden boats, silver boats, and ruby boats. In those boats, they prepared golden thrones, silver thrones, and ruby thrones. They covered the entire surface of the Ganges with five-colored lotuses and then entreated the Blessed One, saying, "O Blessed One of great glory, please show us compassion and honor us."

The Blessed One accepted the invitation of the Nāga kings and boarded the jeweled boat created by them. The five hundred monks also boarded five hundred jeweled boats respectively. The Nāga kings then escorted the Blessed One along with the Saṅgha of monks to the Nāga realm. In the celestial mansion of that Nāga realm, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to the assembly of Nāgas throughout the three watches of the night. The next day, the Nāga kings offered a great alms-giving of celestial food and delicacies to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. After preaching the sermon of appreciation (Anumodanā), the Blessed One departed from the Nāga realm.

The earth-dwelling deities (Bhumma-deva) thought, "Humans and Nāgas are making great offerings to the Blessed One."
323:
323
“Why should we not do it? We shall certainly do it,” they deliberated, and then they made offerings by raising and planting exceedingly beautiful umbrellas over the forests, trees, mountains, and so forth. In this manner, a great and special honor was established reaching up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm. King Bimbisāra also made offerings that were twice as great as those performed by the Licchavī princes when the Buddha returned. Following the previously mentioned method, he escorted the Buddha on a five-day journey until they reached the Veḷuvana Monastery in the city of Rājagaha.
(In this regard, it should be noted: from Rājagaha to the Ganges River is 5 yojanas; the surface of the Ganges River is 1 yojana; from the Ganges River to the city of Vesālī is 3 yojanas—totaling a distance of 9 yojanas).
When the Buddha arrived at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha, in the afternoon, the monks gathered in the assembly hall. In the intervals between their discussions on meditation subjects, they said:
“Friends, the majesty of the Blessed One, who is possessed of great glory, is indeed wonderful! For the sake of the Buddha, the ground spanning eight yojanas—five yojanas on this side of the Ganges and three yojanas on the other side—was leveled in both low and high places, spread with white sand, and covered with flowers. Within the Ganges River, the water surface for the extent of one yojana was covered with five-colored lotuses. Up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm, exceedingly beautiful divine white umbrellas and Brahma white umbrellas were raised and planted.”
324:
324
Thus, words of praise concerning the greatness of the Buddha’s power and majesty arose. (This means that in the intervals between their meditation talks, the monks were speaking of the Buddha’s virtues as described above).
The Buddha, knowing this matter, emerged from the Gandhakuṭī and, through a psychic power appropriate for that moment, sat upon the Buddha-seat prepared within the assembly hall. He then asked, “Bhikkhus, with what talk are you sitting here gathered now that I have arrived?” When the monks reported the entire matter, the Buddha said:
“Bhikkhus, this special honor is not due to the Buddha-power of my current life, nor is it due to the power of Nagas, Devas, or Brahmas. In truth, it has arisen due to the power of a small act of merit and generosity performed in the distant past.”
Thus, he spoke these words as a hint. The monks then requested, “Exalted One, we do not know of that small act of merit and generosity. Exalted One, we entreat you. May the Blessed One preach that matter to us so that we may know it clearly and distinctly.” Upon their request, the Buddha preached the story of the past as follows:
325:
325
Bhikkhus, in the past, there was a Brahmin named Saṅkha in the city of Takkasilā. That Brahmin Saṅkha had a son, a young man named Susīma, who was sixteen years of age. One day, the son Susīma approached his father, paid him respectful homage, and stood there. When the father Saṅkha asked, “Dear Susīma, what is the matter?” the young Susīma replied, “O father, I wish to go to the city of Bārāṇasī to study the arts and sciences.” Then the father Saṅkha said, “Dear Susīma, if that is so, there is a great teacher (Pāmokkha) Brahmin of such-and-such a name in Bārāṇasī who is my friend. Go to that great teacher and study the arts.” He then gave the young Susīma one thousand coins.
Susīma took the thousand coins, paid respectful homage to his parents, and set out on his journey. In due course, he reached Bārāṇasī. Following the proper conduct for one attending upon a teacher, he approached the great teacher Brahmin, paid respectful homage, and introduced himself as the son of the Brahmin Saṅkha from Takkasilā. The great teacher accepted him, saying, “He is indeed the son of my friend,” and performed all the duties of hospitality for the guest.
After Susīma had recovered from the fatigue of his journey, he placed the thousand coins he had brought at the feet of the teacher and requested permission to study the arts. The teacher gave him permission and
326:
326
began teaching him the arts. Being a person of great merit (pāramī), Susīma learned quickly and extensively. He retained everything he learned without loss, like lion’s oil kept in a golden vessel. He mastered in just two or three months the arts that others took twelve years to learn.
When the young Susīma recited the Vedas, he could see only the beginning and the middle, but not the end. He then approached the great teacher and said, “O teacher, I see only the beginning and the middle of the knowledge in these Vedas, but I do not see the end.” The great teacher replied, “Dear son, I too, like you, see only the beginning and the middle, but I do not see the end.” When Susīma asked again, “Teacher, if that is so, who knows the end of this knowledge?” the teacher replied, “Dear Susīma, the Paccekabuddhas residing in the Isipatana Migadāya forest would know the end of this knowledge; I think they would know it.” When Susīma asked for permission, saying, “Teacher, if that is so, let me approach those Paccekabuddhas and ask them,” the teacher granted permission, saying, “Dear Susīma, ask them as you wish and as you find comfort.”
Susīma, the man of merit, went to the Isipatana Migadāya forest, approached the Paccekabuddhas, and asked, “Do the venerable ones know the beginning, the middle, and the end?”
327:
327
When he asked this, the Paccekabuddhas replied, “Yes, we know, lay disciple Susīma.” Susīma then requested, “Please teach me that knowledge which enables one to know the end.” The Paccekabuddhas said, “Lay disciple Susīma, if that is so, you must ordain. One who is not a monk cannot learn that knowledge.” Susīma, the man of merit, replied, “Very well, venerable ones. If you wish me to ordain, please ordain me. Not only will I ordain, but you may do with me as you wish; just please teach me so that I may know the end.” The Paccekabuddhas then ordained Susīma. However, they were unable to engage him in the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) in detail (for Paccekabuddhas, unlike Omniscient Buddhas, are not capable of instructing others on how to practice Vipassanā meditation). Therefore, they only taught and instructed him in the minor rules of conduct (Abhisamācārika Sīla), such as, “You must wear the inner robe evenly all around; you must wear the outer robe evenly all around,” and so forth.
As the newly ordained monk Susīma thoroughly practiced the Abhisamācārika Sīla as instructed by the Paccekabuddhas, because he was endowed with the supporting conditions (upanissaya) of past merits to mature the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha (Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa), he attained the four Path Knowledges called Paccekabodhi in a short time (i.e., he became a Paccekabuddha). He became famous throughout the city of Bārāṇasī as Susīma Paccekabuddha,
328:
328
and being endowed with a retinue of disciples, he reached the pinnacle of gain, offerings, and fame. Because that Susīma Paccekabuddha had performed unwholesome kamma in the past that causes a short life, he attained Parinibbāna shortly thereafter. The citizens, along with the other Paccekabuddhas, performed the cremation of Susīma Paccekabuddha’s physical remains, collected the relics, and built a stupa (cetiya) near the gate of Bārāṇasī to enshrine the relics for worship.
At that time, the father, the great Brahmin Saṅkha, thought, “It has been a long time since my son Susīma left, and I have heard no news of him.” Desiring to see his son, he left Takkasilā and in due course reached Bārāṇasī. Seeing a large crowd gathered (near the stupa of Susīma Paccekabuddha), he thought, “Surely someone among these many people will know the news of what happened to my son.” He approached the gathering and asked, “Sirs, there is a young man named Susīma who came to this city of Bārāṇasī (to study). Do you know the news of what happened to that young man Susīma?” Many people replied:
“Yes, we know, teacher Brahmin. (The young man Susīma) became a master of the three Vedas under the great teacher Brahmin in this city of Bārāṇasī, and after ordaining under the Paccekabuddhas, he attained Paccekabodhi-ñāṇa.”
329:
329
...having attained [Paccekabuddhahood] and become a Paccekabuddha, he has entered the Parinibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-parinibbāna) and passed away. (Pointing to the cetiya) This cetiya is the shrine where the relics of that Venerable Susīma Paccekabuddha are enshrined."

So they spoke.

When the father, the Brahmin Sankha, heard these words, he struck the ground with his hands and wept and lamented bitterly. After weeping and lamenting to his heart's content, he went to the courtyard of the cetiya, cleared away the grass, and using his upper robe, he brought white sand and scattered it over the courtyard of the cetiya. To prevent dust from rising, he sprinkled water from a pitcher all around the ground. Then, he offered and worshipped the cetiya with whatever wild flowers he could find. He made a banner out of his own upper robe and hoisted it, and having fastened and offered his umbrella above the cetiya, he departed.

After the Blessed One had thus preached the past story in detail, wishing to connect that past event with the present story, he preached the Dhamma as follows to the monks:

"Monks, the thought might occur to you, 'Was the Brahmin Sankha at that time someone else?' This matter should not be viewed thus. I myself was the Brahmin Sankha at that time. (1) The Bodhisatta cleared and removed the grass in the courtyard of the cetiya of Susīma Paccekabuddha.
330:
330
As a result of that meritorious deed of the Bodhisatta clearing the grass in the courtyard of the cetiya, now the multitude of people have cleared the road of stumps and thorns, making it smooth and clean for a distance of eight yojanas—five yojanas on this side of the Ganges and three yojanas on the other side.

(2) The Bodhisatta spread white sand all over the courtyard of the cetiya of that Susīma Paccekabuddha. As a result of that meritorious deed, the multitude of people have spread white sand along the aforementioned eight-yojana road.

(3) The Bodhisatta made offerings with various wild flowers at the cetiya of that Susīma Paccekabuddha. As a result of that meritorious deed of mine, over the nine-yojana journey, both on land and in water, the multitude of humans and devas have scattered and spread flower-beds of various kinds of flowers.

(4) The Bodhisatta poured and sprinkled water from a pitcher onto the ground (to prevent dust from rising) in the courtyard of the cetiya of that Susīma Paccekabuddha. As a result of that meritorious deed, now, as soon as I set foot in the region of Vesālī, the Pokkharavassa rain (rain that falls momentarily from clouds as large as lotus leaves) fell abundantly.

(5) The Bodhisatta offered a banner at the cetiya of that Susīma Paccekabuddha.
331:
331
He also fastened and offered an umbrella. As a result of those deeds I performed, now banners have been hoisted and offered even up to the Akanittha Brahma realm. White umbrellas of humans, white umbrellas of devas, and white umbrellas of Brahmas have been hoisted and held by humans, devas, and Brahmas in successive levels.

Monks, thus this extraordinary honor and worship is not due to the Buddha-power of the Buddha, nor is it due to the power of Nagas, Devas, or Brahmas. In truth, it has arisen due to the power of the meritorious deed of a small gift given (as mentioned, when the Bodhisatta was the Brahmin Sankha)."

Having thus preached the Dhamma, at the conclusion, he recited this verse:

Matta-sukha-pariccāgā,
passé ce vipulaṃ sukhaṃ.
Caje matta-sukhaṃ dhīro,
sampassaṃ vipulaṃ sukhaṃ.

Bhikkhave = O monks, my dear sons. Matta-sukha-pariccāgā = because of renouncing a small measure of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) with a generous and willing heart. Vipulaṃ sukhaṃ = the vast and great happiness of Nibbāna. Ce passé = if one clearly sees with the eye of wisdom that one will surely attain it. Vipulaṃ sukhaṃ = the vast and great happiness of Nibbāna. Sampassaṃ = seeing clearly
332:
332
with the eye of wisdom. Dhīro = the wise man. Matta-sukhaṃ = a small measure of pleasant feeling. Caje = should renounce with a generous and willing heart.

At the conclusion of the teaching, many beings attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and so forth.

The story of the Bodhisatta as the Brahmin Sankha is finished.
**********
## The Story of Uggasena, the Son of a Treasurer and an Acrobat
During the time of the Blessed One, a large troupe of five hundred performers, in the sixth month or after a year, went to the city of Rājagaha and held a festival for seven days in the presence of the King, receiving many rewards of gold and silver. In between the various acts of the performance, the rewards given by the spectators who were greatly pleased were beyond measure and very numerous. When the festival was held, the townspeople stood on couches, high couches, and even higher couches (couches arranged in tiers) to watch the festival.

At that time, a certain female acrobat, the daughter of a master acrobat, climbed a bamboo pole and performed tumbles on top of it. Then, at the very top of the bamboo pole in the air, she walked back and forth gracefully, dancing and singing with a sweet voice.
333:
333
## Uggasena, the Son of a Treasurer
At that time, a treasurer's son named Uggasena was standing on a viewing platform with a friend. He watched the young female acrobat intently and with amazement. He became deeply infatuated and enamored with her movements—the way she placed her hands and feet, the way she lifted, bent, and stretched them. Returning home, he thought and said, "If I get this female acrobat, I shall live; if I do not get her, I shall die right here on this couch." He then fasted and lay down on his couch.

When his parents asked, "Dear son, what illness do you have?", he spoke openly, "O dear mother and father, my benefactors, if I get the young female acrobat I saw at the festival in the palace courtyard, I shall live; if not, I shall die right here on this couch." Although his parents tried to persuade him, saying, "Dear son, do not do this; we will bring and marry you to another maiden suitable to our family, lineage, and wealth (instead of that acrobat)," Uggasena the treasurer's son did not change his words. He spoke as before and remained lying on his bed.

Then, Uggasena's father pleaded with and admonished his son many times in private, but being unable to persuade him, he sent for Uggasena's friend. Giving him a thousand pieces of silver (kahāpaṇas), he said, "Accept these thousand pieces of silver and tell the master acrobat that I wish him to give his daughter to my son Uggasena."
334: ...after giving instructions, they sent him to the master acrobat. The master acrobat replied, "I cannot accept money and give my daughter. If the merchant's son Uggasena cannot live without my daughter, then let him follow us wherever we go. Only if he can follow us will I give my daughter to him in marriage." ## The Merchant's Son Uggasena Following the Acrobat Girl. When the parents told this to their son Uggasena, he said, "O parents, I will follow and travel with those acrobats." Although his parents and relatives pleaded with him repeatedly, he did not listen, left home, and went to the master acrobat. The master acrobat gave his daughter in marriage to Uggasena as promised and traveled through villages and towns performing acrobatics together with Uggasena. The acrobat girl soon gave birth to a son through her union with Uggasena. While playing with the son, she sang mockingly: "Son of a cart-guard (sleep now), son of a fool who carries the prize-money, son of one who knows not a bit of skill (sleep now)."
335:
335
It is true—Uggasena had to find grass for the oxen and guard the circle of carts at the places where the acrobats halted their wagons. He also had to carry and look after the rewards and wealth obtained at the performance sites. Referring to these facts, the acrobat girl sang and spoke those mocking and jesting words while playing with the child.

Uggasena, realizing that she was singing mockingly at him, asked her directly, "Are you singing like this referring to me?" The acrobat girl replied, "Yes, I am singing like this referring to you." When Uggasena said (words he could hardly bear), "If that is the case, I will leave you and run back to my parents," the acrobat girl said, "Whether you go or stay, what does it matter to me?" and she sang that same song again and again (knowing Uggasena disliked it). (That acrobat girl, relying on her own beauty and the ease with which she earned wealth, spoke thus, not caring for Uggasena in the least.)

## Uggasena Becomes an Acrobat
When Uggasena reflected and thought, "On what does this acrobat girl's pride depend?", he realized, "This acrobat girl's pride depends on her skill in acrobatics." He thought, "Let it be; I too will learn the art of acrobatics," and he approached his father-in-law, the master acrobat.
336: After learning the acrobatics known by the master, he performed in villages and towns and eventually returned to Rājagaha. He had it proclaimed throughout the city, "Seven days from today, the merchant's son Uggasena will perform wonderful acrobatics for the citizens." The townspeople arranged high couches, and even higher couches, and gathered on the seventh day. Uggasena climbed a bamboo pole sixty cubits high and stood at the top to perform. ## The Acrobat Uggasena Appearing in the Buddha's Net of Knowledge. On the day Uggasena was to perform, the Buddha, while surveying the world at dawn, saw the merchant's son Uggasena enter his golden net of omniscience like a fish. He reflected, "What will happen?" and saw: "Tomorrow morning, Uggasena will stand on top of a sixty-cubit bamboo pole to perform. A great crowd will gather to watch the acrobat Uggasena. In that assembly, I will preach a verse of four lines. Upon hearing that verse, 84,000..."
337:
beings will realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation. Uggasena, the banker's son, will also be established in the fruit of Arahantship."

Having clearly perceived this, the Buddha, noting the appropriate time for alms-round the next morning (the day of Uggasena's performance), entered the city of Rājagaha for alms, surrounded by a company of monks. Before the Buddha entered the city, Uggasena signaled the spectators with his finger to raise a resounding shout of praise. He then stood on top of the bamboo pole, performed seven somersaults in the air, and landed back on the pole.

At that moment, the Buddha entered the city and performed a psychic feat so that the audience would not look at Uggasena, but instead, every single person would look only at the Buddha. While standing on the pole, Uggasena looked at the crowd and saw that they were only gazing at and paying homage to the Buddha. He became dejected, thinking, "I only perform this acrobatics once a year. When the Buddha enters the city, the spectators do not look at me but only at him. Alas, my strenuous performance of acrobatics is in vain and fruitless."

The Buddha, knowing Uggasena's thoughts, called Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and said:
338:
"Go, dear Moggallāna, and tell the banker's son: 'The Buddha wishes you to continue your acrobatics.'" Venerable Moggallāna went and stood at the foot of the bamboo pole, calling out to Uggasena with this encouraging verse:

"Come, look, Uggasena the acrobat,
Possessed of great strength.
Perform your feat for the assembly,
And make the great crowd rejoice."

(Meaning: O acrobat named Uggasena, who possesses great strength, I urge you. Look! For the sake of the gathered assembly, perform the acrobatics you have mastered with a happy heart. Make the great multitude of people rejoice and shout praises in great wonder.)

When Uggasena heard the words of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, he was greatly delighted and thought, "The Buddha must wish to see my acrobatics." Standing atop the pole, he replied with this verse:

"Come, look, O Moggallāna of great wisdom,
Possessed of great psychic power.
I shall perform my feat for the assembly,
And I shall make the great crowd rejoice."
339:
(Meaning: O Venerable Moggallāna, who possesses great wisdom and supreme psychic power, I address these words of invitation to you. Please look! I, Uggasena, shall perform the acrobatics for the gathered assembly with a happy heart. I shall make the great multitude of people rejoice and shout praises in great wonder, O Venerable Sir.)

After reciting this verse, while standing on top of the bamboo pole, he leaped into the air, performed fourteen somersaults, and landed back on the pole.

## The Buddha Preaches the Dhamma

Then the Buddha said to him, "Dear Uggasena, a wise person should abandon attachment and craving for the five aggregates of the past, the five aggregates of the future, and the five aggregates of the present, and strive to be liberated from the suffering of birth, aging, and death."

He then spoke this verse:

"Let go of the past, let go of the future,
Let go of the middle, having reached the further shore of existence.
With a mind liberated in every way,
You shall not again undergo birth and aging."
340:
(Meaning: Dear Uggasena, let go of and abandon craving and attachment for the five aggregates of mind and matter that occurred in the past. Let go of and abandon craving and attachment for the five aggregates that will occur in the future. Let go of and abandon craving and attachment for the five aggregates of the present. If one thus abandons craving for the aggregates of the three periods, one becomes a 'pāragū'—one who has reached the further shore through the five types of mastery: mastery of higher knowledge, mastery of full understanding, mastery of abandonment, mastery of development, and mastery of realization—thereby reaching the end of the three realms of existence: the sensual, the fine-material, and the immaterial. Having a mind liberated from all conditioned things, you shall never again encounter the perils of rebirth, aging, sickness, and death.)

When the Buddha finished preaching this verse, eighty-four thousand beings realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation. Uggasena, while still standing on top of the bamboo pole, attained Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā). Having become an Arahant possessed of analytical insights, he descended from the pole and approached the Buddha.
341:
He paid homage to the Buddha with the five-point prostration and requested ordination. The Buddha then stretched out his right hand and said, "Ehi Bhikkhu" (Come, monk). At that very moment, Uggasena's appearance as an acrobat vanished; he appeared wearing the eight requisites, looking like a senior elder of sixty years of rains (eighty years of age), and became a fully ordained monk.

## The Monks Ask Whether He Was Afraid

Later, fellow monks asked Venerable Uggasena, "Friend Uggasena, were you not afraid when you descended from the top of that sixty-cubit bamboo pole?" When Uggasena replied, "Friends, I did not have even the slightest fear," the monks reported this to the Buddha, saying, "Exalted Buddha, Venerable Uggasena says he is not afraid at all. He is making a false claim to have attained Arahantship."

The Buddha said, "Monks, monks like my son Uggasena, who have abandoned and cut the ten fetters and have exhausted the taints (āsavas) to become Arahants, have no fear or trembling whatsoever." Confirming this, he spoke this verse from the Brāhmaṇavagga of the Dhammapada:

"He who has cut all fetters and does not tremble,
Who has transcended attachments and is unbound—
Him I call a Brahmin."
342:
(Meaning: O monks, that monk who has exhausted the taints and become an Arahant, having completely cut the long ropes of the ten fetters with the sword of the Path of Arahantship, truly does not tremble with fear born of greed. He has transcended the seven attachments—lust, hatred, delusion, pride, wrong view, defilements, and misconduct. He is free from the four bonds (yogas). Such an Arahant, who has cast away and abandoned all evil, I call a glorious Brahmin.)

At the conclusion of the teaching, many people attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti) and so forth.

## The Story of Uggasena's Past Karma

Later, one day, the monks were discussing in the Dhamma Hall: "Friends, what was the cause for Venerable Uggasena, who is endowed with past merits that led to Arahantship, to wander with acrobats because of an acrobat girl? And what was the powerful supporting cause (upanissaya) for his attainment of Arahantship?" The Buddha arrived at the Dhamma Hall and asked, "Monks, what are you discussing now?"
343:
"With what talk were you gathered here?" the Buddha asked. When the monks replied that they were gathered with such and such talk, He said, "Monks, this Uggasena has performed both the cause for wandering and dancing with acrobats and the cause for attaining the fruit of Arahantship." He spoke these words in brief and then, to explain the matter in detail, He related the story of the past as follows.

Long ago, when the golden stupa of the Blessed Kassapa Buddha was being built, the young men and women living in Bārāṇasī loaded various kinds of food onto small carts and went to the site of the stupa, saying, "We will perform service with our own hands; we will worship with our labor." On the way, they saw a thera entering for alms.

At that time, a young woman, seeing the thera on his alms round, felt a heart full of faith and said to her husband, "Lord, the thera is on his alms round. There is much food in our cart. Go and take the thera's bowl; let us offer alms." That noble young man went and took the thera's bowl, filled it with food, and offered it back into the thera's hands. Then both husband and wife made a wish: "Venerable Sir, by this merit, may we both realize the same truth that you have realized..."
344:
The thera on his alms round was no ordinary monk; he was an Arahant whose taints were exhausted. Therefore, looking with his knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa) to see whether their wish would be fulfilled, he saw that their aspiration would be realized and smiled. Seeing the Arahant thera smile, the woman said to her husband, "O Lord, our alms-recipient venerable one is smiling; he must be a dancer." The husband agreed, saying, "Yes, dear. It must be as you say; he must be a dancer," and they went their way. This was the past kamma of the couple, Uggasena and his wife.

After living out their lifespan in that existence, they passed away and were reborn in the celestial realm. When they passed away from the celestial realm, in this final existence (pacchima-bhava), the woman became the daughter of a master acrobat, a young female dancer. The husband, in this final existence, became Uggasena, the son of a treasurer in the city of Rājagaha. Because Uggasena had mistakenly agreed with his wife, saying, "Yes, dear. It must be as you say; he must be a dancer," he had to wander and perform with dancers in this life despite being a treasurer's son. However, by virtue of the merit of offering alms with a faithful heart to the Arahant whose taints were exhausted, he attained Arahantship.
345:
## The Acrobat Girl Also Becomes an Arahant Theri

When the treasurer's son Uggasena, the acrobat, became an Arahant and was ordained as an 'Ehi Bhikkhu', his wife, the acrobat girl, thought, "If my husband, the treasurer's son Uggasena the acrobat, has such wisdom, my own wisdom must be of the same nature as his." Prompted by her past merits, she had this good thought and ordained as a nun among the bhikkhunīs. After ordaining, she practiced the Dhamma with great effort and, with the exhaustion of the taints (āsavas), attained the state of an Arahant Theri.

The story of Uggasena's past karma ends here.

**********

## The Sakyan Princes of Kapilavatthu and the Koliyan Princes
## The Conflict over the Rohiṇī River

The Sakyan princes of Kapilavatthu and the Koliyan princes of Koliya dammed the Rohiṇī River, which flowed between the two kingdoms, with a single embankment. They shared the water harmoniously, taking turns to irrigate their fields.

At that time, in the month of Nayon, the water level was low, and the crops began to wither. The farmers of both kingdoms held a meeting. At that meeting, the farmers of Koliya said:

"Friends, if we divide this small amount of water within this dam between both sides..."
346:
it will not be enough for you, nor will it be enough for us. Our crops, however, will ripen and succeed with just one more watering. Therefore, please give this small amount of water to us."

The farmers of Kapilavatthu replied:

"Friends, when you have filled your granaries with grain and live at ease, we will not be able to wander to your doorsteps with gold, silver, and coins, carrying empty baskets and bags, unable to buy anything. Our crops will also ripen and succeed with just one more watering. Therefore, do not take this small amount of water; give it to us."

Then, both sides became stubborn, saying, "We will not give it under any circumstances," and "We too will not give it under any circumstances." As they quarreled, one farmer struck a farmer from the other side. The one who was struck hit back at the other farmer. In this way, starting from the farmers striking one another, the quarrel escalated (like a small spark burning down a palace) into insults directed at the royal lineages of the princes. The escalation was as follows:
347:
"You people rely on the Sakyan princes of Kapilavatthu and speak so boldly. Those Sakyan princes you rely on are like domestic dogs and wild dogs, for they cohabit with their own sisters. What can the elephants, horses, and weapons of those Sakyan princes do to us?"

When the Koliyan farmers spoke such insults, the Sakyan farmers of Kapilavatthu retorted:

"You people are now boasting while holding onto those little lepers. Those Koliyan princes you rely on are people who, having been exiled, had no refuge and lived like animals in the hollows of Kola trees. What can the elephants, horses, and weapons of those Koliyan princes do to us?"

Refusing to back down, they exchanged hostile words. The farmers of both sides returned to their respective cities and reported the matter to the ministers in charge of agriculture. When the news reached the ears of the kings, the Sakyan princes boasted, "We shall show the power and strength of those of us who cohabit with our sisters," and they marched out of the city with their armies. The Koliyan princes also boasted, "We shall show the power and strength of those of us who live in the hollows of Kola trees," and they marched out of the city with a great army.
348:
At that time, the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana monastery in Sāvatthī. On that day, when the kings of the two nations were about to march out with their armies in the evening, the Blessed One surveyed the world of beings at dawn. Seeing the impending war between the two nations, He reflected, "If I go, will this conflict be settled or not?" He then understood: "I shall go to the place where the two nations are preparing for war and, to settle the conflict, I must preach these three Jātakas: the Phandana Jātaka, the Dubbhaya Jātaka, and the Laṭukika Jātaka. Then the conflict will be settled. After that, to show the benefits of unity, I must preach these two Jātakas: the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka and the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, followed by the Attadaṇḍa Sutta. After hearing the Dhamma, the kings of both nations will each offer two hundred and fifty princes to be ordained by me. I shall ordain those five hundred princes, and then there will be the great assembly of the Mahāsamaya."

Having made this decision, He performed His morning duties early, went for alms in Sāvatthī, and upon returning, He departed from the Gandhakuṭī in the evening without informing anyone. Taking His bowl and robes, He went alone and sat cross-legged in the air above the space between the two armies.
349:
To instill a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in the kings of the two nations, He emitted blue rays from His hair, causing a great darkness to fall even in broad daylight, and remained sitting there.

Then, while the kings of both nations were terrified, He revealed Himself clearly and emitted the six-colored Buddha-rays.

## The Kings of Both Nations Discard Their Weapons

As soon as the Sakyan princes of Kapilavatthu saw the Blessed One, they thought, "The Blessed One, our noble kinsman, has arrived. Has the Blessed One clearly seen that we are engaged in conflict?" They consulted and decided, "It is entirely improper and unworthy for us to cast weapons at another's body in the presence of the Blessed One while He has arrived. If the Koliyan princes wish to kill us, let them kill; if they wish to capture us, let them capture." They then discarded their weapons and sat down, paying respectful homage to the Blessed One.

The Koliyan princes also thought in the same manner, discarded their weapons, and sat down, paying respectful homage to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One descended from the sky and sat with matchless Buddha-glory upon the Buddha-seat prepared on a pleasant sandy bank.

## The Dhamma Discourse for Settling the Enmity

Although He already knew, the Blessed One asked, "O great kings, why have you [come] to this place?"
350:
"Why have you come?" When the Buddha asked this, the kings of the two nations replied, "Great Blessed One, we have not come to look at the river, nor have we come to play in the water. Indeed, we have come to wage a great war on this sandbank."

Again, the Buddha asked, "O Great Kings, what is the cause of your quarrel?" The kings of the two nations replied, "Great Blessed One, our quarrel is because of the water of the Rohiṇī dam."

Then the Buddha asked, "O Great Kings, how much is the water of the Rohiṇī dam worth?" The kings of the two nations replied, "Great Blessed One, the water of the Rohiṇī dam is of very little value." Taking it a step further, the Buddha asked, "O Great Kings, how much is the earth worth?" The kings of the two nations replied, "It is of immeasurable value, Blessed One."

Then the Buddha asked directly, "O Great Kings, how much are the nobles of the Khattiya lineage worth?" When the kings of the two nations replied in unison, "Great Blessed One, the nobles of the Khattiya lineage are of immeasurable value," the Buddha said:
351:
"O Great Kings, why do you wish to destroy the priceless Khattiyas for the sake of the water of the Rohiṇī dam, which is of so little value? Indeed, there is no pleasure in quarreling. O Great Kings, because of a quarrel, a grudge formed between a tree deity and a bear has followed throughout this entire Bhadda-kappa."

Having said this, He preached the Phandana Jātaka (from the Terasa Nipāta). The summary of the Phandana Jātaka is as follows:

## Preaching the Phandana Jātaka

O Great Kings, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, there was a carpenter village outside the city. In that village, a Brahmin carpenter made a living by bringing timber from the forest and making and selling chariots.

At that time, there was a large Phandana tree in the Himavanta region. A bear, after searching for and eating food in the forest, came and slept comfortably under that large Phandana tree. One day, when a strong wind blew, a dry branch of the Phandana tree broke off and fell onto the bear's back. The bear, feeling a slight pain in its back, jumped up in alarm and ran away. When it turned back to investigate the path it had come and saw no enemy, it thought:

"There is no enemy like a lion, leopard, or tiger chasing and catching me. Indeed, the tree deity living in this Phandana tree
352:
must be displeased and unhappy that I am sleeping under this Phandana tree. Let it be; I will consider and take my revenge." Thus, forming a grudge where none was due, the bear gored the Phandana tree with its tusks, scratched it with its claws, and struck it, saying, "I do not eat the leaves of your tree, nor do I break your branches. You are jealous of the other animals living under this Phandana tree, and you are jealous of me. What is my fault? Wait just two or three days; (after two or three days) I will have your tree deity's Phandana tree uprooted, roots and all, and have it cut into pieces."

After threatening and rebuking the tree deity in this way, the bear stayed near the Phandana tree, searching and waiting for a man who could destroy the tree.

At that time, the Brahmin carpenter, wanting to find wood for making chariots, took two or three companions and went to that forest area in a small cart. Leaving the cart in one place and holding a billhook and an axe, he arrived near the Phandana tree while searching for trees suitable for making chariots.

When the bear saw the Brahmin carpenter, it thought, "Today I should look at my enemy's back," and went to stand at the base of the Phandana tree. As the carpenter was looking here and there and passing near the Phandana tree, the bear thought, "I will speak to the Brahmin carpenter before he passes by," and said:
353:
(1) Kuṭhārihattho puriso,
vanaṃ ogayha tiṭṭhasi.
Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi,
kiṃ dāruṃ chetumicchasi.

O man, holding an axe, you stand within this forest. O friend, answer me truly as I ask you: what wood do you wish to cut?

Thus, it recited this first (questioning) verse.

When the Brahmin carpenter heard the bear's words, he thought, "O friends, how wonderful! I have never seen or heard a beast speak human language before. This bear, who speaks human language so exceptionally, must know which wood is good for making chariots. I will ask that bear."

(2) Isso vanāni carasi,
samāni visamāni ca.
Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi,
kiṃ dāruṃ nemiyā daḷhaṃ.

O King of Bears, you are one who roams through these forests, over level and uneven ground. O friend King of Bears, answer me truly as I ask you: what wood is the strongest for making a chariot rim?

Thus, he recited this second (questioning) verse. Hearing those words, the bear thought, "Now the desire of my heart
354:
will reach its peak and be successfully accomplished."

(3) Neva sālo na khadiro,
nāssakaṇṇo kuto dhavo.
Rukkho ca phandano nāma,
taṃ dāruṃ nemiyā daḷhaṃ.

O friend Brahmin, Sāla wood is not strong for making a chariot rim; Khadira wood is the same; Assakaṇṇa wood is the same; and what need is there to speak of Dhava wood (it is also not strong). Indeed, there is a kind of tree called Phandana. That Phandana wood is the strongest for making a chariot rim.

Thus, it recited the third verse. Hearing those words, the Brahmin carpenter was delighted and thought, "I have entered the forest on a very auspicious day. Even a bear, though an animal, tells me which wood is good for making a chariot. Oh, how good!" Then, wishing to ask about the Phandana tree, he said:

(4) Kīdisānissa pattāni,
khandho vā pana kīdiso.
Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi,
yathā jānemu phandanaṃ.

O friend bear, what are the branches and leaves of the Phandana tree like? Furthermore, what is the trunk of the Phandana tree like? O friend bear, I want you to answer me so that I may know the Phandana tree well.

Thus, he recited this fourth verse and asked. Then the bear, wishing to answer the Brahmin, said:
355:
(5) Yassa sākhā palambanti,
namanti na ca bhañjare.
So rukkho phandano nāma,
yassa mūle ahaṃ ṭhito.

(6) Arānaṃ cakkanābhīnaṃ,
īsānemirathassa ca.
Sabbassa te kammaniyo,
ayaṃ hessati phandano.

O friend Brahmin, the branches of that tree hang down and bend. They do not break easily (they are resilient). I am standing at the base of that very tree; that tree is indeed the Phandana. This Phandana tree will be very good for you to make spokes, hubs, axles, rims, and all other parts of the chariot.

After reciting these two verses, the bear, with a joyful heart, went to roam in a suitable place.

The Brahmin carpenter also prepared to cut the tree. Then the deity guarding the Phandana tree thought, "Even though I did not drop anything on that bear, this bear has formed a grudge where none was due and has planned for the destruction of my abode. If my abode is destroyed, I too will be destroyed. I will also destroy this bear by a ruse."

Having thought thus, the Phandana tree deity transformed into the likeness of a workman, approached the Brahmin carpenter, and asked, "O man, you have found a beautiful large Phandana tree. After cutting this large Phandana tree, what will you make?" The Brahmin carpenter replied, "I will make chariot rims."

"Who told you that it is good to make a chariot with this Phandana wood?" When the Phandana tree deity asked this, the Brahmin carpenter said, "A bear told me."

Then the Phandana tree deity said, "O man, it is good; that bear has told you what is good. The chariot you will build with this Phandana wood will be as beautiful and excellent as that bear said. I wish to give you a piece of advice: if you skin the bear's neck and wrap the circumference of the chariot rim with it, about four inches wide, as if wrapping it with an iron plate, the chariot rim will be even stronger. You will also obtain much wealth."

When the Brahmin carpenter asked, "O friend, where can I get bear skin?" the Phandana tree deity said:
356:
...devised a plan: "If my abode is destroyed, I too will be destroyed. I will destroy this bear through a stratagem." Having thought this, the deity of the Kakudha tree transformed into the likeness of a workman, approached the brahmin carpenter, and asked, "O man, you have obtained a beautiful Kakudha tree. What will you make after cutting down this great Kakudha tree?" "I will make the rim of a chariot wheel," the brahmin carpenter replied.

"Who told you that it is good to make a chariot from this Kakudha wood?" the tree deity asked. The brahmin carpenter said, "A bear told me." Then the tree deity said, "O man, it is well. That bear has told you something good. The chariot you will build with this Kakudha wood will be as beautiful and excellent as that bear said. I would like to give you a piece of advice: if you skin the bear's neck and wrap it around the rim of the chariot wheel, about four finger-breadths (four inches) wide, as if wrapping it with an iron plate, the rim will be much stronger. You will also obtain much wealth."

"O friend, where can I get bear skin?" the brahmin carpenter asked. The tree deity said:

"O man, are you a child? This great Kakudha tree, being inanimate, will stay right here in this forest and will not run away elsewhere. You..."
357:
should go to the bear who told you about the Phandana tree and lure him by asking, 'O Lord Bear, from which part should I cut the Phandana tree you pointed out?' Then, kill that bear, who will stretch out his long snout and point without any fear or hesitation, saying, 'Cut here, cut here,' with a very sharp axe. After he has reached the end of his life, skin him, eat the fat meat, and then cut this Phandana tree."

Thus, the deity incited the act of enmity. The Buddha, wishing to make this matter clear, preached these three verses:

(7) Iti phandanarukkhopi,
tāvade ajjhabhāsatha.
Mayhampi vacanaṃ atthi,
Bhāradvāja suṇohi me.

(8) Issassa upakkhandhamhā,
ukkacca caturaṅgulaṃ.
Tena nemiṃ pasāresi,
evaṃ daḷhataraṃ siyā.

(9) Iti phandanarukkhopi,
veraṃ appesi tāvade.
Jātānañca ajātānaṃ,
issānaṃ dukkhamāvahi.

(7) O Kings, thus the Phandana tree deity also spoke at that moment: "O Brahmin of the Bhāradvāja clan, I too have a word (for you); listen to me."
358:
I have a word of advice to give; please listen to my words.
(8) Cut a piece of skin about four fingers wide from the shoulder (nape) of a bear, and wrap it around the rim of the chariot wheel. By doing so, the rim of the chariot wheel will become much stronger.
(9) O kings, thus the Phandana tree deity incited enmity at that moment. He brought suffering upon all bears, both present and future. (These verses are Abhisambuddha gāthā, spoken by the Blessed One).
The brahmin carpenter, hearing the deity's advice, exclaimed, "Oh, today is a truly auspicious day for me!" After saying this, he killed the bear, cut down the Phandana tree, and returned to his home. To illustrate this and provide instruction, the Buddha spoke these Abhisambuddha gāthā:
(10) Thus the Phandana [deity] [hated] the bear,
And the bear [hated] the Phandana.
Through mutual dispute,
They caused each other's destruction.
O kings, thus the Phandana tree deity and the bear, by quarreling with each other, brought about each other's death.
359:
(11) Even so, wherever disputes arise among men,
They dance like peacocks,
Just as the bear and the Phandana deity did.
O kings, even so, in whatever place disputes and quarrels arise among men, in that place people dance like peacocks, just as the bear and the Phandana tree deity did. (Meaning: Just as peacocks reveal their hidden parts when they dance, so do people reveal their secrets and faults when they quarrel; this is called dancing like a peacock).
(12) I tell you this for your welfare, all you who are gathered here:
Live in harmony, do not dispute,
Do not be like the bear and the Phandana deity.
O kings, I wish to speak these words of advice for your welfare; may it be auspicious for you. All you kings gathered here at this Rohiṇī river, may you blend together in loving-kindness like the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers. Do not quarrel or dispute; do not be like those who resemble the bear and the Phandana tree deity.
360:
(13) Train yourselves in unity alone;
This is praised by the Buddhas.
One who delights in unity, standing in the Dhamma,
Does not fall away from the security from bondage.
O kings, strive only to practice unity. Indeed, this unity is praised by all the Buddhas. One who delights in unity and stands in the ten-fold wholesome Dhamma does not fall away or lose the bliss of Nibbāna, which is the end of the four yokes (yogakkhama).
The Sakyan kings of both sides, having heard the Dhamma taught by the Buddha, were reconciled with one another.
After delivering this discourse, the Buddha identified the birth: "At that time, the deity who witnessed the quarrel between the Phandana deity and the bear and who ruled over that forest was I, the Buddha."
End of Phandana Jātaka.
**********
## The Teaching of the Dubbuha Jātaka
Then the Buddha said, "O noble kings, one should not believe another's words without reflection. Indeed, because they believed the words of a single rabbit (who cried 'The earth is collapsing! The earth is collapsing!'), the four-footed animals in the three-thousand-league wide Himavanta forest almost plunged into the great ocean...
361:
...and suffered greatly. Therefore, one should not believe another's words without reflection." Thus he told the Dubbuha Jātaka* from the Catukka Nipāta.
## The Teaching of the Laṭukika Jātaka
Then the Buddha said, "O noble kings, sometimes even a weak person can find a vulnerability in a strong person. Sometimes a strong person also finds a vulnerability in a weak person. Indeed, even a tiny mother quail once killed a great tusker." Thus he told the Laṭukika Jātaka (from the Pañcaka Nipāta) as follows:
O kings, in the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as an elephant. When he reached maturity, he was inspiring and possessed a massive body. He was the leader of a herd of eighty thousand elephants and lived in the Himavanta region.
*The Dubbuha Jātaka is the story where a young rabbit, resting under a palmyra leaf beneath a wood-apple tree, heard a wood-apple fall on the leaf and cried "The earth is collapsing! The earth is collapsing!" The four-footed animals of the Himavanta believed him and fled toward the ocean. The Bodhisatta, as a lion king, investigated and saved them. The full story can be found in the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā.
362:
At that time, a mother quail laid her eggs in the path of the elephants. When the chicks had just hatched and were not yet strong enough to fly, the Bodhisatta elephant king, accompanied by eighty thousand elephants, arrived at that spot while searching for food.
Seeing the Bodhisatta elephant king, the mother quail thought, "If I do not plead, this elephant king will crush my young. I will now ask him for righteous protection for my children." She folded her wings (like hands in prayer), stood directly in front of the Bodhisatta, and recited this verse of plea:
(1) I salute you, O elephant, sixty years of age,
The famous leader of the forest herd.
With my wings, I pay you homage;
Do not kill my weak little children.
Thus she pleaded with this verse. The Bodhisatta said, "Mother quail, do not be anxious or lose heart. I will protect your children from harm." After giving her these words of encouragement, he stood over the chicks...
363:
...covering them with his body. After the eighty thousand elephants had passed by, the Bodhisatta elephant king called the mother quail and said, "Mother quail, behind us comes a rogue elephant who wanders alone. He will not listen to our words. When he arrives, you must also plead with him for the lives of your children." Then he departed.
When the rogue elephant arrived, the mother quail went to meet him as the Bodhisatta had instructed. Folding her wings in homage, she recited this verse of plea:
(2) I salute you, O elephant who wanders alone,
Frequenting the forest and the mountain slopes.
With my wings, I pay you homage;
Do not kill my weak little children.
Thus she pleaded as before. Hearing her words, the rogue elephant said:
364:
(3) I will kill your children, O quail!
What can you do to me, you who are so weak?
Even a hundred thousand like you,
I could crush with my left foot.
"Hey, quail! (Why did you leave your children in my path? Since you have insolently left them in my way), I will crush and kill your children. What kind of revenge can you take against me? You are a weakling. Even a hundred thousand quails like you, I could crush to pieces with my left foot."
Having said this, the rogue elephant crushed the quail's young into pieces with his foot, let them be washed away in the stream of his urine, and trumpeted loudly as he walked away.
The mother quail, perched on a branch, thought, "O foolish elephant, trumpet now while you have the upper hand. Within two or three days, you shall see my work. You do not know that the power of wisdom is greater than physical strength. Just wait; I will let you know within two or three days." Threatening the rogue elephant, she said:
(4) Not in all things is physical strength sufficient;
For the strength of a fool leads only to his destruction.
I will bring ruin upon you, O elephant king,
You who killed my weak little children.
365:
O elephant king, not every task is to be accomplished by physical strength alone. Indeed, the strength of a fool is only for his own destruction. You, elephant king, have crushed and killed my weak little children. O elephant king, I will bring about your ruin (within two or three days).
After making this vow, the mother quail served and befriended a crow for a few days. The crow, being pleased, asked, "Friend quail, what important task can I perform for you?" The mother quail replied, "O noble crow, I have no other task. I only ask that you peck out and destroy both eyes of that rogue elephant who wanders alone."
When the crow agreed, the mother quail went to a bluebottle fly and served and befriended her in the same way. When the fly asked, "What important task can I perform for you?", the mother quail said, "When my friend the crow has destroyed the eyes of the rogue elephant, I desire that you, noble fly, lay your eggs (or maggots) in his blinded eyes."
366:
The black fly also agreed, saying, "Very well." Then the little female quail went to a frog and, having served and befriended him as before, the frog asked, "What important matter must I perform for you?" The little female quail replied, "With the help of my friends, the crow and the black fly, that rogue lone elephant has had both his eyes destroyed. When he searches for water because he is very thirsty, I would like you, friend frog, to first make a sound from the mountain top. Hearing that sound, when the rogue elephant climbs the mountain top, I would like you, friend frog, to descend from the mountain top and make a sound from within the precipice. This is the extent of the help I wish to receive from you, friend." Hearing the little female quail's request for help, the frog agreed, saying, "Very well."

Then one day, the crow pecked and destroyed both eyes of the rogue elephant with his beak (according to the little female quail's wish). In those destroyed and wounded eyes, the black fly laid fly eggs (otherwise, living maggots). As the rogue lone elephant was bitten by the maggots, he suffered great pain and, being severely oppressed by thirst, he wandered here and there, groping about in search of drinking water.

At that time, the frog made a sound from the mountain top. Hearing the frog's croaking, the rogue lone elephant, thinking and relying on the idea that "there must be water in the place where this frog croaks,"
367:
climbed the mountain top. When the rogue elephant reached the mountain top, the frog descended from the mountain top and, staying within the precipice, made the sound again. The rogue lone elephant, thinking and relying on the idea that "there must be water in the place where this frog croaks," went towards the precipice and, sliding down from the mountain, fell headlong to the foot of the mountain and reached the end of his life.

The little female quail, knowing well that her enemy, the rogue elephant, was dead, was filled with joy, thinking, "I have indeed seen the back of my enemy!" She walked to and fro on his back to her heart's content and then departed to her desired destination.

The Blessed One said to the kings of the two nations, "O kings, one should not engage in hostility with anyone. As has been told, even a great elephant of immense strength was brought to the end of his life by the four—the crow, the black fly, the frog, and the quail—acting together in unity." Having said this, He preached this Abhisambuddha Gāthā:

(5) Behold the crow, the quail,
The frog, and the black fly.
These have slain the elephant;
Behold the result of hostility among the hostile.
Therefore, one should not create enmity,
Even with one who is disliked.
368:
Rājāno = O kings of the noble Sakyan lineage. Kākañca = the crow. Laṭukikañca = the little female quail. Maṇḍūkañca = the frog. Nīlamakkhikañca = the black fly. Passa-passatha = behold them. Ete = these four. (Ekato hutvā = being united as one.) Nāgam = the great elephant of firm strength. Aghātesuṃ = have caused to fall and enter the realm of death. Verīnaṃ = of those who desire malice. Verassa = of the act of hostility and resentment. Gatiṃ = the course of the result. Passa-passatha = behold. Tasmā hi = for that very reason. Kenaci = with anyone. Appiyenapi = even with one who is not loved or liked. Veraṃ = hostility and resentment. Na kayirātha = one should not create.

Having preached this Abhisambuddha Gāthā, the Blessed One identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the rogue lone elephant became Devadatta; at that time, the virtuous elephant king, the leader of the herd, became I, the Buddha."

The Laṭukika Jātaka is finished.
**********
## Preaching the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka
Thus, the Blessed One, having preached these three Jātakas—the Phandana Jātaka, the Dubdubha Jātaka, and the Laṭukika Jātaka—to settle the dispute of His relatives, preached two more Jātakas to show the benefits of unity. The manner of preaching was as follows:
369:
O noble kings, you are close relatives; it is only proper for relatives to be united and harmonious. Indeed, if there is unity among relatives, enemies cannot find an opening. Let alone human beings who possess consciousness, even for trees which lack consciousness, it is only proper when they achieve unity. To elaborate: in the past, a great storm blew through a large Sal forest in the Himalayan region. However, because the large and small trees, shrubs, and creepers of that great Sal forest stood intertwined with one another, the storm could not topple even a single tree, but merely passed over the tops of the trees.
