But a large tree growing alone in an open plain, though it was complete with branches and a thick trunk, was uprooted and fell headlong to the ground because it was not at all entwined or bound with other large or small trees, shrubs, and creepers. For this reason, O kings, it is only proper and fitting that you also have unity and harmony.

Having said this, being requested by the kings, He brought forth the details of the past story.

O kings, in the long past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in the city of Bārāṇasī, the first Vessavaṇa, the king of devas, passed away. Sakka, the king of devas, appointed another deva to the position of Vessavaṇa. During this change of Vessavaṇa, the new Vessavaṇa
370:
issued a new decree: "Among the large and small trees, shrubs, and creepers, take up your celestial abodes in whatever place you please."

At that time, the Bodhisatta was a tree-spirit king in a Sal forest in the Himalayan region. The Bodhisatta tree-spirit king advised his relative devas, "Friends, when you take up your abodes, do not take them in trees standing in the open plain. Instead, take up abodes in the trees that surround the abode I have taken in this Sal forest."

Among those devas, the wise ones who followed the Bodhisatta's words took up abodes in the trees surrounding the Bodhisatta's abode. But the foolish devas thought and consulted among themselves, "What benefit is there for us in abodes situated in the deep, remote forest far from humans? We shall only take up abodes in trees standing near villages, market towns, and royal city gates on the paths of men. Indeed, devas who dwell depending on villages and market towns reach the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame." Thus, they took up abodes in trees growing in open plains along the paths of men.

Then one day, a great storm with rain blew and fell heavily. Because the force of the wind was so intense, even the large forest trees growing in the open plains, though their roots were very firm, had their branches broken and fell, and were toppled along with their roots. When the storm reached the Sal forest (where the Bodhisatta ruled), where the trees stood connected to one another,
371:
even though the great storm blew from here and there, it was unable to topple even a single tree.

The devas whose abodes were destroyed became helpless and, taking their young sons and daughters by the hand, went to the Himalayas and told their forest-dwelling friend devas about their helpless state. The forest-dwelling friend devas told the Bodhisatta tree-spirit king about how those devas whose abodes were destroyed had arrived in such a helpless condition.

The Bodhisatta said, "Those who do not listen to the words of the wise and go to live in places that cannot provide benefit are always of this nature (meaning, they naturally encounter such suffering)," and wishing to preach the Dhamma, he uttered this verse:

Many kinsmen are good,
Even trees born in the forest.
The wind carries away a lone,
Even a giant lord of the forest.

Ñātayo = O good devas, the assembly of relatives. Sambahulā = many relatives, from four up to a hundred thousand, who live together depending on one another. Araññajā = growing throughout the forest. Rukkhā api = even trees that stand well, supporting one another. Sādhu = are excellent and beautiful as they cannot be oppressed by enemies.
372:
Vāto = the storm wind that blows with great force. Ekaṭṭhaṃ = standing alone in an open plain. Vanappatiṃ = a giant forest tree. Brihantampi = though it is very large with many branches and leaves. Vahati = it topples and overthrows it, leaving not even the roots.

After the Bodhisatta preached this matter, at the end of his life, he passed away according to his kamma.

The Blessed One also brought forth this Dhamma teaching, saying, "O kings, in this way, relatives should first achieve unity. Having achieved unity, live only in a state of friendship, harmonizing with one another in joy and loving-kindness." Then, connecting the sequence of the story, He identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the assembly of forest-dwelling devas became my current followers; at that time, the wise tree-spirit king was I, the Teacher of the three worlds."

The Rukkhadhamma Jātaka is finished.
**********
## Preaching the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka (or Sammodamāna Jātaka)
Thereafter, the Blessed One said, "O kings, quarreling among relatives is not at all proper. Indeed, let alone humans, even animals in the past, when they were united, overcame their enemies and reached happiness, but when they quarreled, they came to great ruin."
373:
373
At the request of the gathered kings, the Buddha related the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka (Sammodamāna Jātaka), an event of the past.

O Kings, in the long-distant past, while King Brahmadatta was reigning in the city of Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born as a quail and lived in a forest, surrounded by many thousands of quails.

At that time, a fowler used to go to the place where those quails lived and fed. He would mimic the call of a quail, and when the quails gathered together at that sound, he would cast a net over the flock. He would then trample and beat the edges of the net to frighten them, and when the quails were huddled together in the middle of the net, he would pack them into his basket, take them home, sell them, and make a living from the proceeds.

One day, the Bodhisatta said to the quails of his flock:

“O quails, this fowler has repeatedly brought destruction upon our kinsfolk. I have thought of a clever stratagem so that this fowler will no longer be able to catch us. From now on, the moment the fowler casts his net over us, let each quail put its head through a single mesh of the net. Then, all together in unison, lift the net and fly away with it to whatever place you desire, and drop it onto a thorn bush. After that, we shall
374:
374
escape from under the net and fly away to our respective places.”

Thus he gave them this advice. All the quails of the flock agreed, saying, “Very well.” On the following day, when the net was cast over the flock, all the quails, following the method told by the Bodhisatta, lifted the net in unison, dropped it onto a thorn bush, and they themselves escaped from under the net and flew away to their respective places.

By the time the fowler had disentangled the net from the thorn bush, the day was spent. He returned home empty-handed. From the next day onwards, the quails did the same. The fowler spent his time until sunset disentangling his net and returned home empty-handed without catching a single bird. Then the fowler’s wife became angry and rebuked him, saying, “Day after day you return empty-handed. It seems you must have another household to support elsewhere besides me.”

The fowler replied, “O lady, I have no other household to support but yours. However, those quails are now living and moving about in unity. The moment I cast the net, they lift it up in unison, drop it on a thorn bush, and escape elsewhere. But truly, those quails will not be able to remain in harmony forever. Lady, do not be
375:
375
overly anxious. One day, those quails will fall into a quarrel. At that time, I shall bring them all back and return to make your face beam with joy.” Thus he comforted his wife and recited this verse to her:

Sammodamānā gacchanti,
zālamādāya pakkhino.
Yadā te vivadissanti,
tadā ehinti me vasaṃ.

Bhaddē = O lady. Pakkhino = the quails. Sammodamānā = being in harmony of body and mind (or because they are united). Zālaṃ = the net cast by me. Ādāya = carrying away. Gacchanti = they go to a place of safety after dropping it on a thorn bush. Te = those quails. Yadā = on some day unexpectedly. Vivadissanti = shall quarrel with differing views, one saying this and another that. Tadā = on that day of discord and dispute. Te = those quails. Me = my. Vasaṃ = power/will. Ehinti = shall come under.

Reciting this verse, he reassured his wife.

## The Destruction of the Quails Due to Disunity

Then, after two or three days had passed (just as the fowler had calculated), as one quail was alighting on the feeding ground, it inadvertently stepped on the head of another quail. The quail whose head was stepped on became angry and shouted,
376:
376
“Who is this? Which bird stepped on my head?” Although the quail that stepped on it apologized, saying, “Friend, I did it inadvertently, please do not be angry,” the quail whose head was stepped on remained angry. As the two quails argued back and forth, they began to quarrel, saying things like, “Do you think you alone are the one who can lift the net?” and so on.

When those quails began to quarrel with one another, the Bodhisatta, the king of the quails, thought:

“There can be no happiness in a place where there is quarreling. Now these birds will no longer lift the net in unison. Then the quails will come to great destruction. The fowler will find his opportunity. It is no longer suitable for me to stay in this place.”

Having considered the matter truthfully, he took his own following of quails and moved to another place. Only the quails ruled by the foolish quail, who was the future Devadatta, remained there.

After two or three days, the fowler went to that forest, mimicked the quail’s cry, and when the quails led by the future Devadatta gathered together, he cast the net over them. Then, at the moment they should have lifted the net, one quail said to another,
377:
377
“As you were lifting the net, the feathers on your head fell off! (If you are so brave), lift it now!” Thus he spoke provocatively. The other quail retorted to the first, “As you were lifting the net, the feathers on both your wings fell off from exhaustion! (If you are so brave), you lift it now!”

While all those quails were thus quarreling, saying, “If you are brave, you lift it! If you are brave, you lift it!”, the fowler gathered the net, rounded up all the quails, filled his basket, and returned home, making his wife joyful and happy.

The Blessed One, having related this Dhamma teaching, said, “O Kings, in the manner described, quarreling among kinsfolk is in no way suitable; quarreling is indeed the root cause of destruction.” He then connected the past and present stories: “At that time, the foolish leader of the quails was Devadatta, and the wise leader of the quails was I, the Buddha.”

Thus ends the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, also known as the Sammodamāna Jātaka, from the Ekaka Nipāta.
**********
## Preaching the Attadaṇḍa Sutta

In this manner, the Blessed One preached these five Jātakas to the kings of the two nations, and
378: At the end, he preached the Attadaṇḍa Sutta* (from the Sutta Nipāta). ## The Kings of Two Kingdoms Offering 250 Princes Each to the Buddha for Ordination. Then the kings of the two kingdoms, being united and having faith and devotion, thought, "If the Buddha had not come, we would surely have killed each other and caused rivers of blood to flow. Because of the Buddha, we have received our lives. Furthermore, if the Buddha had remained in the lay life, he would have become a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) ruling over the four continents and two thousand islands. He would have had a thousand sons endowed with wisdom and strength and traveled surrounded by a royal retinue. This noble relative of ours gave up that sovereignty, went forth into the forest, and attained Buddhahood. Now that he is a Buddha, let him travel and live surrounded by royal monks." After consulting together, the kings of the two kingdoms each offered 250 princes to the Buddha. The Buddha ordained those five hundred princes as Ehi Bhikkhu monks and took them to the Mahāvana forest near Kapilavatthu. *If one wishes to know the Attadaṇḍa Sutta in detail, one should refer to the Sutta Nipāta translation. It is not written here at length for fear of being too long.
379:
From the next day, the Buddha, accompanied by those five hundred prince-monks, wandered for alms sometimes in the kingdom of Kapilavatthu and sometimes in the kingdom of Koliya. The people of both kingdoms performed great acts of worship and offerings.

## The Five Hundred Monks' Dissatisfaction in the Dispensation

Those five hundred princes did not ordain out of their own desire, but only because they did not wish to disregard or reject the words of their parents and relatives. Therefore, before many days had passed, the state of dissatisfaction and boredom with the Dispensation (anabhirati) clearly arose within those five hundred prince-monks.

As the saying goes, "fanning the flames," their former wives also sent letters and messages, saying, "O lords, do not be happy in the Dispensation; from the day you left, the household wealth has been declining and deteriorating day by day." Thus, like the saying "already weak and then entangled in a morning glory patch," those five hundred prince-monks became even more dissatisfied and unhappy in the Dispensation than before.

## The Buddha Preaching the Kunāla Jātaka to the Five Hundred Monks and Establishing Them in Stream-entry

The Buddha contemplated his disciple monks six times a day—three times at night and three times during the day—protecting them just as a jungle fowl protects its egg, or as a yak protects its tail-hair...
380:
...just as a mother protects her beloved son, or as a man with only one eye protects that eye with great care. (From Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā, Vol. 3, p. 354). Thus, when the Buddha reflected on whether those five hundred monks were satisfied or dissatisfied with the Dispensation, he clearly saw that they were dissatisfied. He then considered, "These monks, though living with a Buddha like me, are weary. What kind of Dhamma discourse would be suitable for them?" Upon investigation, he saw the noble Kunāla Jātaka discourse. Then, the thought arose in the Buddha's mind:

"I shall take these monks to the Himālaya. By means of the Kunāla Jātaka discourse, I will reveal the faults of women and remove their dissatisfaction with the Dispensation, and then grant them the vision of the Path of Stream-entry."

The Buddha went for alms in the city of Kapilavatthu in the morning, and after returning from the alms round in the afternoon, he asked those five hundred monks, "Monks, have you ever seen the delightful Himālaya region before?" When the monks replied, "We have not seen it, Bhante," he asked again, "Dear sons, do you wish to go on a journey to the Himālaya?" The monks replied, "Glorious Buddha, we are those without psychic powers. How shall we be able to go?"
381:
"Dear sons, if someone with psychic powers were to take you, would you go?" When he asked this, the monks consented, saying, "Āma bhante—Yes, Bhante, we would go."

The Buddha, taking all five hundred monks by his psychic power, flew into the sky and headed towards the Himālaya. While remaining in the sky, he showed them various mountains in the delightful Himālaya region, such as the Golden Mountain, Silver Mountain, Ruby Mountain, Cinnabar Mountain, Collyrium Mountain, the mountain named Sānu, and the Crystal Mountain. He also showed them the five great rivers and the seven great lakes. The Himālaya mountain is very vast, being five hundred leagues high and three thousand leagues wide. He showed only a portion of the delights of the Himālaya through his psychic power. He also showed a portion of the four-footed animals living in the Himālaya, such as lions, tigers, and elephants. In that Himālaya, he showed delightful parks and gardens, various flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees, various kinds of birds, various kinds of water flowers and land flowers, the golden plateau on the eastern side of the Himālaya, and the cinnabar plateau on the western side.

From the moment they saw these delights, the lustful desire (chandarāga) for their former wives was abandoned by those five hundred monks. Then, the Buddha took those five hundred monks and descended from the sky to the western side of the Himālaya.
382:
On the Manosilā plateau, which is sixty leagues wide, beneath a great Sal tree (which would last for an entire aeon) that was seven leagues high and wide, the Buddha sat gracefully on the Manosilā surface, which was three leagues wide. Surrounded by the five hundred monks, he emitted the six-colored rays, making the surface of the ocean tremble, appearing like the sun rising with brilliant radiance. He then gave permission and invited the monks, saying, "Monks, ask about anything in this Himālaya region that you have never seen before."

At that moment, two young female Karavīka birds flew through the sky, carrying a stick by its ends in their beaks, with their master, the Karavīka King, sitting in the middle. They were surrounded by eight young female Karavīka birds in each of the six directions: left, right, front, back, above, and below. Seeing that extraordinary flock of birds they had never seen before, the monks asked the Buddha, "Glorious Buddha, what are the names of those birds?" The Buddha replied:

"Monks, this lineage of birds is my own ancestral lineage from the past; it is a tradition I have left behind. In the very beginning, they attended to and served me in this same manner. At that time, this flock of birds was even more numerous than now. Three thousand five hundred young female birds attended to and served me. Gradually decreasing, they have now become only this many, just enough to keep the lineage from disappearing."
383:
When the monks asked, "In such a great forest, in what manner did those three thousand five hundred female birds attend to and serve you, Bhante?", the Buddha said, "Monks, if that is so, listen," and after causing mindfulness to arise in the monks, he preached the Kunāla Jātaka* of the Asīti Nipāta, adorned with three hundred verses.

## The Monks Becoming Stream-enterers
At the conclusion of the discourse, all five hundred Sakyan princes who were monks were established in the Fruition of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). Notably, as soon as those five hundred monks attained the Path, they also achieved and reached psychic powers and Jhanas, such as diving into the earth and flying through the sky.

In this matter: Worldlings (puthujjana) can only attain mundane Jhanas, attainments (samāpatti), and higher knowledges (abhiññā) by developing and practicing Samatha meditation subjects such as Kasinas.

As for Noble Ones (ariya), some Noble Ones attain mundane Jhanas, attainments, and higher knowledges by practicing Samatha meditation only after they have attained the Noble Path and Fruition. Some have already attained mundane Jhanas, attainments, and higher knowledges while still worldlings; after becoming Noble Ones, they do not need to practice Samatha meditation anew but can easily enter those mundane attainments they had already achieved as worldlings.

Some Noble Ones, who did not attain mundane Jhanas, attainments, and higher knowledges while they were worldlings,

* This Kunāla Jātaka should be studied in detail from the 550 Jātaka stories.
384:
attain and reach mundane Jhanas, attainments, and higher knowledges simultaneously with their arrival at the Supramundane Noble Path and Fruition, and they are able to easily enter and enjoy them at any time they wish. Such Jhanas and higher knowledges are called "Maggasiddhi-jhāna" and "Maggasiddhi-abhiññā."

Now, these five hundred Sakyan monks, in accordance with their special past merits, were those who attained Maggasiddhi-jhāna and Maggasiddhi-abhiññā. Therefore, they no longer had to specially practice Samatha meditation to gain mundane Jhanas and higher knowledges, but "could enter and enjoy those mundane Jhanas and higher knowledges at any time they wished." (Maggasiddhi-jhāna = Jhana accomplished and obtained through the Noble Path. Maggasiddhi-abhiññā = Higher knowledge accomplished and obtained through the Noble Path.)

The Buddha, thinking, "Let this much, the knowledge of the Path and Fruition of Stream-entry, be enough for these five hundred monks for now," returned to the Mahāvana forest through the sky. Those five hundred monks, who had gone there by the Buddha's psychic power, returned by their own psychic power, surrounding the Buddha as they flew through the sky and descended into the Mahāvana forest.

## The Five Hundred Monks Becoming Arahants and
## The Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya)
The Buddha sat on the prepared Buddhāsana (Buddha's seat) in the Mahāvana forest and called those five hundred monks:

"Come, dear monks, sit down. I shall preach the meditation Dhamma to you so that you may abandon the defilements that are to be abandoned and destroyed by the three higher Paths."
385:
Having said this, he preached the meditation Dhamma to those monks for the attainment of the higher Paths and Fruitions. The five hundred monks reflected:

"The Buddha, knowing well our dissatisfaction with the Dispensation, took us to Lake Kunāla and not only completely removed our dissatisfaction but also enabled us to reach the Fruition of Stream-entry at that lake. Now, in this Mahāvana forest, he preaches the meditation Dhamma for the three higher Paths. It is not proper for us to spend time carelessly, thinking 'We are Stream-enterers.' We should only be satisfied when we are equal to the noble persons (ājānīya) who have gone before us."

Having reflected thus, they paid homage with faith and devotion to the lotus-like feet of the Buddha. They rose from their seats, shook out their sitting cloths (nisīdana), and went respectively to the valleys, ravines, and the feet of trees to practice the Dhamma of a recluse.

When those five hundred monks had gone, the Buddha reflected:

"These five hundred monks are naturally those who do not let go of the meditation Dhamma. (These five hundred monks, having become Stream-enterers, are those who have already obtained the excellent method and means of the practice that leads to the Path and Fruition.) For a monk who has obtained the excellent method and means of the practice leading to the Path and Fruition, there is no reason at all for difficulty or exhaustion in attaining the higher Paths and Fruitions. Each and every one of those five hundred monks who have gone will develop insight (vipassanā) and respectively reach the Fruition of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala). Thinking, 'We shall report the qualities of Arahantship we have attained,' they will come before me in the evening. When those five hundred monks arrive, the Devas and Brahmas living in the ten thousand world systems will assemble in this single world system. (Then) there will be a Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya). It is proper for me to stay in a secluded place in advance."

Reflecting thus, he rose from that place, had a Buddha's seat prepared in a secluded spot, and stayed there, entering the Attainment of Fruition (phalasamāpatti).
386:
...they are those who have already obtained the excellent method of practice). For a monk who has obtained the excellent method of practice leading to the Paths and Fruits, there is no reason at all for difficulty or exhaustion in attaining the higher Paths and Fruits. All those five hundred monks, as they go, will develop insight (vipassanā) and each will reach the Fruit of Arahantship. Then, thinking, 'We will report the virtues of the Fruit of Arahantship we have attained,' they will come to my presence in the evening. When those five hundred monks arrive, the devas and Brahmas living in the ten thousand world systems will gather in this single world system. Then there will be a Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya). It is appropriate for me to go and stay in a secluded place beforehand."

Reflecting thus, He rose from that place, prepared a seat in a secluded spot, and stayed there, entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti).

## The Five Hundred Monks Become Arahants

Among those five hundred monks, the first thera (who took the meditation subject and left) attained the Fruit of Arahantship along with the four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) through his practice. Then the second thera likewise attained the Fruit of Arahantship. Then the third thera likewise attained the Fruit of Arahantship. In this way, all five hundred monks, like lotus flowers in a lotus pond...
387: Just as flowers bloom one after another, they realized the Four Noble Truths and attained the Fruition of Arahantship in succession. The Elder who first reached Arahantship thought, "I shall inform the Blessed One," and so he broke his cross-legged posture, shook out his sitting cloth, rose from his seat, and approached the Blessed One. In the same manner, the second Elder approached, and the third Elder approached as well. Thus, the five hundred Arahants came before the Blessed One in a line, according to their seniority, just as monks enter a refectory in order. The first Elder to arrive paid homage to the Blessed One, spread his sitting cloth, and sat in a suitable place. Desiring to report the extraordinary attainment of Arahantship he had achieved to the Blessed One, he turned his head and looked back at the path he had come to see if there were any other monks. He then saw the second Elder, and then another, and in this way, he saw the entire line of five hundred monks. Thus, all five hundred monks arrived before the Blessed One and sat in suitable places. While observing one another, they realized, "This monk is hesitant to speak out of modesty toward that monk; that monk is hesitant to report to the Blessed One out of modesty toward this monk."
388:
## Two Characteristics of Arahants

(1) In the hearts of the Noble Arahants, there always arises a thought desiring the welfare of beings: "If only all people, including devas and Brahmas, could quickly realize and attain the special Dhamma of the Fruit of Arahantship that I have attained, how good it would be!"

(2) However, they do not wish to tell others about their own attainment of Arahantship (as it might seem like boasting), just like a man who has found a pot of gold.

(These are the two characteristics of Arahants.)

**********

## Preaching the Mahāsamaya Suttas

The day those five hundred Arahants gathered was the full moon day of Nayon, in the evening. Thus, as soon as those five hundred Arahants sat down together, the full moon—free from the five impurities of mist, haze, clouds, Rāhu (Asurinda), and smoke—rose from the peak of Mount Yugandhara in the eastern world-element. It appeared like a large silver mirror held up in the east to clearly show the delightful state of the world adorned by the appearance of the Buddha, or like a silver wheel being turned while held by its rim, shining brightly as it rose from the center of the eastern world-element. At such an auspicious time, the Blessed One was residing in the Great Mahāvana Forest near Kapilavatthu in the Sakyan country, surrounded by five hundred Arahants.
389: ## The Gathering of Devas and Brahmas At that time, the devas living around the Mahāvana forest became stirred and, raising their voices loudly, said, "Friends, come, let us go! To see the Buddha is a great blessing. To hear the Dhamma is a great blessing. To behold the Sangha of monks is a great blessing. Come, let us go! Come, let us go!" Having arrived, they paid homage to the Blessed One and the five hundred monks who had just attained Arahantship at that moment, and stood in suitable places. In the same way, hearing the tumultuous shouting and urging of those devas, the call spread further and further—to the distance of a call, half a gāvuta, one gāvuta, half a yojana, one yojana, and so on. With this universe as the center, the hosts of devas and brahmas living in the ten thousand surrounding world-systems gathered in this universe. Only the Asaññasatta brahmas, the Arupa brahmas, and those brahmas currently absorbed in meditative attainments were unable to come. At that time, this entire universe was filled with the gathered devas and brahmas up to the Brahma realms, just like a needle case packed with needles without any space in between. If a great stone the size of the seven-storied Lohapāsāda palace on the island of Sri Lanka were dropped from the Brahma realm, it would take four months by human reckoning to reach the ground. In a place so vast, high, and distant (from the human world to the Brahma realm), from below looking up,
390:
390
The devas and brahmas were so densely packed that there was no space for flowers or incense thrown into the air to rise, nor was there any gap for mustard seeds thrown from above to fall to the ground. 

In particular, just as when a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) and his assembly of kings gather, the place where the Universal Monarch resides does not feel cramped or narrow, and all the powerful kings who arrive find a place to stay near the Universal Monarch while those who arrive later find it very crowded and narrow in the further areas; likewise, the place where the Buddha, who is like a Universal Monarch, resides is neither cramped nor narrow. All the powerful and majestic (mahesakkha) devas and brahmas who arrive find a place to stay in the vicinity of the Buddha. Indeed, in the areas near the Buddha, even in a space as small as the tip of a yak-tail hair, ten, twenty, and further back, thirty, forty, fifty, or sixty devas and brahmas, having created subtle and even subtler forms, stood there.

## Four Great Suddhāvāsa Brahmas
## Arriving Late

When the Buddha, along with five hundred Arahants and the assembly of devas and brahmas from the ten thousand world-systems, had gathered (as previously mentioned), four great (Arahant) brahmas from the Suddhāvāsa realms entered into meditative attainment (samāpatti). Having emerged from that attainment at the determined time, they looked upon the Brahma realm (and when it was afternoon, a time quiet from humans...
391: Seeing the Brahma realm entirely empty of brahmas, they reflected, "Where have the brahmas gone?" and they realized the great Mahāsamaya assembly was taking place. They thought: "This assembly is very large. We have been left behind, and it will be difficult for those who are late to find a place. Therefore, when we go, let us not go empty-handed, but let each of us compose a verse (gāthā) to take with us. With these gift-verses, we shall make our arrival known at the great Mahāsamaya assembly and also praise the virtues of the Blessed One." After consulting together, while still in the Brahma realm, those four Arahant Brahmas each composed a verse. Then: (1) One Brahma descended to the eastern edge of the universe. (2) Another to the southern edge. (3) Another to the western edge. (4) And another to the northern edge. Then, (1) the Brahma who descended to the eastern edge of the universe entered into a meditative absorption using the blue kasina (nīla-kasiṇa) as an object, emitting shimmering blue-dark rays. As if covering the gathered devas and brahmas from the ten thousand world-systems with a robe of emerald, he made his arrival known. (There is always a path called the Buddha-vīthi where no one is allowed to block the way in front of the Buddhas. By this path,
392: all devas and humans who arrive approach and behold the Blessed One). By that very Buddha-vīthi path, the first Brahma approached, paid respectful homage to the Blessed One, and stood there. He then recited the verse he had composed: "Mahāsamayo pavanasmiṃ, devakāyā samāgatā. Āgatamha imaṃ dhammasamayaṃ, dakkhitāye aparājitasanghaṃ." (Venerable Blessed One), in this forest known as Mahāvana, (today) a great assembly of devas and brahmas has occurred. The hosts of devas from the ten thousand world-systems have gathered together to see the Sangha of Arahants, who cannot be conquered by any enemy and who have today conquered the three Maras. (We also) have come to this Dhamma-assembly of devas and brahmas to listen to the Dhamma and to see the unconquered Sangha of Arahants with clear faith. Having recited this verse (and because there was no room to stay near the Buddha), he departed and stood at the eastern edge of the universe.
393: After that, (2) the Brahma who had descended to the southern edge of the universe also entered into a meditative absorption using the yellow kasina (pīta-kasiṇa) as an object, emitting shimmering golden rays. As if covering the gathered devas and brahmas from the ten thousand world-systems with a robe of gold, he made his arrival known. Then, in the same manner as the first Brahma, he recited: "Tatra bhikkhavo samādahaṃsu, cittamattano ujukamakaṃsu. Sārathīva nettāni gahetvā, indriyāni rakkhanti paṇḍitā." (Venerable Blessed One), in that place where the devas and brahmas have assembled, the five hundred monks have established their minds firmly with supramundane absorption (appana-samādhi). they have made their minds straight, free from the three types of crookedness—the crookedness of a bull's horn, the crookedness of a moon's crescent, and the crookedness of a plowshare. Just as a charioteer driving a carriage harnessed with well-trained Sindh horses holds the reins gently and remains at ease, so too, the five hundred Arahant Elders, endowed with the wisdom of the Path, guard their six faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—which ought to be restrained, by means of mindfulness.
394:
With protection, they are able to guard against the entry of the enemies of defilements. (Bhagavā = The Blessed One. Mayaṃ = We. Ete = These five hundred Arahants. Daṭṭhuṃ = To see/pay homage. Idha = To this Mahāvana forest. Āgatā = Have come. Amha = We are.)

Having recited and offered the verse he had composed, he stood at the edge of the Southern universe as before.

Then, (3) the Great Brahma who descended to the edge of the Western universe entered into a meditative absorption (jhāna) with the red kasiṇa (lohitakasiṇa) as the object. He emitted shimmering red rays, making his arrival known to the assembly of devas and brahmas who had gathered from the ten thousand universes, as if covering them with a red woolen blanket. Then, in the same manner as the previous Brahmas:

Chettvā khilaṃ chettvā palighaṃ,
Indakhīlaṃ ūhacca maneja.
Te caranti suddhā vimalā,
Cakkhumatā sudantā susunāgā.

(Bhante = Venerable Blessed One). Ye susunāgā = Those young Arahants. Cakkhumatā = By the Buddha who is endowed with the five eyes: the Buddha-eye, the Dhamma-eye, the All-seeing eye, the physical eye, and the divine eye. (Damitā = Having been tamed). Sudantā = They are exceedingly well-tamed through the Dhamma, without their six sense faculties being disturbed. Te susunāgā = Those young Arahants. Khilaṃ = The spikes of lust, hatred, and delusion. Chettvā = Having cut and removed them with the sword of the fourfold Path knowledge (Magga-ñāṇa).
395:
Having cut and removed them with the sword of the fourfold Path knowledge. Palighaṃ = The cross-bar of lust, hatred, and delusion. Chettvā = Having cut and removed them with the sword of the fourfold Path knowledge. Indakhīlaṃ = The pillar of lust, hatred, and delusion that stands firmly at the gate of the city of self-identity (sakkāya). Ūhacca = Having uprooted and removed them without leaving any root by the fourfold Path knowledge. Aneja = Being free from the trembling of craving and greed. Suddhā = Being pure and clean from the danger of defilements. Vimalā = Being free from the stains of defilements. Caranti = They are able to wander and dwell in the four directions without any obstruction of defilements. (Tesaṃ = Those young Arahants. Dassanāya = To see/pay homage. Mayaṃ = We. Āgatā = Have come. Amha = We are.)

Having recited and offered the verse he had composed, he stood at the edge of the Western universe as before.

Then, (4) the Great Brahma who descended to the edge of the Northern universe entered into a meditative absorption (jhāna) with the white kasiṇa (odhātakasiṇa) as the object. He emitted shimmering white rays, making his arrival known to the assembly of devas and brahmas who had gathered from the ten thousand universes, as if covering them with a jasmine-flower blanket. Then, in the same manner as the previous Brahmas:

Ye keci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse,
Na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ.
Pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ,
Devakāyaṃ paripūressanti.
396:
(Bhante = Venerable Blessed One). Ye keci = Whosoever. Buddhaṃ = To the Buddha. Saraṇaṃ = As a refuge. Gatāse = Have approached and taken refuge with faith and devotion through the supramundane refuge. Te = Those people. Apāyabhūmiṃ = To the four woeful states: hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the realm of asuras. Na gamissanti = They will certainly not go. Mānusaṃ dehaṃ = This physical body called the human life. Pahāya = Having abandoned. Devakāyaṃ = The host of devas (the celestial realm). Paripūressanti = They will certainly and surely fill.

Having recited and offered the verse he had composed, he stood at the edge of the Northern universe as before.

At that time, when the Blessed One reflected and looked, he saw the devas and brahmas assembled from the surface of the earth to the edge of the universe, and upwards to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm. He thought: "This assembly of devas and brahmas is very large. These five hundred monks will not know that this is such a vast assembly of devas and brahmas. I shall inform those five hundred monks right now." Then he addressed them, saying: "Yebhuyyena bhikkhave dasasu lokadhātūsu devatā sannipatitā honti..." which means: "Monks, the devas and brahmas dwelling in the ten thousand universes (ten thousand-fold world system) have assembled to see the assembly of monks together with the Fully Enlightened Buddha, who has come well, just like the Buddhas of the past."
397:
"Monks, just as there is now this great assembly of devas and brahmas for me, so too there were assemblies of devas and brahmas of this same extent for the Buddhas who arose in the past (not exceeding this)."

"Monks, just as there is now this great assembly of devas and brahmas for me, so too there will be assemblies of devas and brahmas of this same extent for the Buddhas who will arise in the future (neither more nor less than this)," he declared.

(In this regard, it should be specifically noted that since there is no other Buddha arising at the very same moment as the current Buddha, the Buddha did not preach the 'present' category as a separate comparison, but instead used himself as the example for the present to show the comparison with the Buddhas of the past and the future.)

## The Thoughts of the Devas and Brahmas and the Buddha

At that Great Assembly (Mahāsamaya), the devas and brahmas thought, "In this great assembly of so many devas and brahmas, the Buddha will likely only announce the names and lineages of the powerful devas and brahmas. How could he possibly announce the names and lineages of the devas and brahmas of little power? (He will not do so)." Then, the Buddha, reflecting on what these devas and brahmas were thinking, knew their thoughts just like a person who reaches his hand into his mouth and grasps his heart, or like one who catches a thief together with the stolen goods...
398:
knowing the state of mind of those devas and brahmas, he thought and decided:

"I shall fully proclaim the names, types, and lineages of all devas and brahmas, both powerful and not, who have arrived from the ten thousand universes."

Buddhas are indeed very great and noble supreme persons. Among the six sense objects that are seen, heard, smelled, tasted, touched, and known by the world of beings including devas, there is not a single object that does not appear in the knowledge of the Buddhas. Thus, the Blessed One, who is the possessor of wisdom that penetrates all objects without any obstruction or hindrance, divided the devas and brahmas who had assembled to fill the universes into two groups (through his knowledge): (1) those who are ready for liberation (veneyya) and (2) those who are not. Having set aside those not ready for liberation, he took only those ready for liberation into his knowledge. Among these ready for liberation, he further categorized them into six groups based on their temperaments (carita): "This many devas and brahmas are of lustful temperament; this many are of hateful temperament; this many are of deluded temperament; this many are of speculative temperament; this many are of faithful temperament; and this many are of wise temperament."
399:
After that, he reflected and considered the Dhamma teaching that would be suitable for those six groups of devas and brahmas. He decided with his knowledge the discourses he should preach: "For the devas and brahmas of lustful temperament, the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta should be preached. For those of hateful temperament, the Kalahavivāda Sutta should be preached. For those of deluded temperament, the Mahāvyūha Sutta should be preached. For those of speculative temperament, the Cūḷavyūha Sutta should be preached. For those of faithful temperament, the Tuvaṭṭaka-paṭipadā (Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta) should be preached. For those of wise temperament, the Purābheda Sutta should be preached."

Furthermore, regarding the assembly of devas and brahmas categorized into six groups, he reflected on the four ways of delivering a discourse (suttanikkhepa):
(1) Attajjhāsaya-suttanikkhepa = Preaching according to the Blessed One's own inclination.
(2) Parajjhāsaya-suttanikkhepa = Preaching according to the inclination of the listeners.
(3) Atthuppattika-suttanikkhepa = Preaching based on a particular event that has arisen.
(4) Pucchāvasika-suttanikkhepa = Preaching in connection with the questions and problems of others.

Among these four, he reflected again: "Will this assembly of devas and brahmas understand if I preach by the Attajjhāsaya method? Or will they understand by the Parajjhāsaya method? Or will they understand by the Atthuppattika method?"
400:
"Or will they understand if I preach by the Pucchāvasika method?"

Then he realized: "This assembly of devas and brahmas will only realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation if I preach by the Pucchāvasika method." He then reflected: "Is there anyone who can ask questions that harmonize with the temperaments and inclinations of these devas and brahmas?" He saw that among those five hundred monks, not even one was capable. Then he reflected whether the eighty Great Disciples or the two Chief Disciples could ask. He saw that even those Great and Chief Disciples were not capable. Then he reflected: "If there were a Paccekabuddha, would that Paccekabuddha be able to ask?"

Knowing that "a Paccekabuddha is also not capable," he reflected whether someone like Sakka, the King of Devas, or Suyama, the King of Devas, would be able to ask. Indeed, if any one of them like Sakka or Suyama were capable of asking, the Blessed One would have had them ask and then he would have answered. However, not even one among Sakka, Suyama, and others was capable of asking.

At that time, this thought arose in the mind of the Blessed One: "Only a Buddha like myself is capable of asking questions that harmonize with the inclinations and temperaments of these devas and brahmas. In any world system, there is no one besides a Buddha like myself..."
401:
“Does another Buddha exist?” Thus, the Buddha spread His infinite golden knowledge throughout the infinite world systems and looked; however, He did not see any other Buddha besides Himself (as none existed).

(It is not surprising that He did not see any other Buddha equal to Himself now that He had attained Buddhahood; even at the moment of His birth as Prince Siddhattha, His final existence, the Great Being did not see any human or celestial being equal to Himself. That is why, at the moment of His birth, He uttered the bold words beginning with “Aggohamasmi lokassa” (I am the foremost in the world). For the Great Bodhisatta, who had no equal even at birth, how could He possibly see another Buddha equal to Himself now that He had attained Buddhahood? Indeed, He could not.)

## Creating the Created Image

Thus, the Buddha, seeing no other Buddha equal to Himself, thought and decided: “If I myself ask the questions and I myself answer them, this assembly of devas and brahmas will not be able to realize the Dhamma with penetrative insight. However, if another Buddha asks and I answer, it will be a cause for wonder, and the assembly of devas and brahmas will be able to realize the Dhamma. Therefore, I shall create a created image (nimmitarūpa) of a Buddha.” Having so decided, He entered the fourth rūpāvacara jhāna (functional), which is the basis for supernormal powers (abhiññā). Emerging from that jhāna, He made a formal resolve (adhiṭṭhāna) with the consciousness of the great functional (mahākiriyā) associated with knowledge: “Let there be another created Buddha-image, identical to me in every way—in the manner of holding the bowl and robes, in the manner of looking straight ahead, looking aside, bending, and stretching.”
402:
After performing the preliminary preparations with the javana process of the resolve, He created another Buddha-image through the consciousness of the fourth rūpāvacara jhāna (functional) of supernormal power, appearing as if the full moon were emerging by breaking through the summit of Mount Yugandhara in the east.

## The Various Thoughts of Devas and Brahmas

When the assembly of devas and brahmas saw that created Buddha-image, they said, “O friends, another moon has appeared besides the first one!” Later, as the created Buddha-image left the lunar mansion and gradually drew closer, they said, “Friends, it is not the lunar mansion; the sun has risen!” Again, as it drew closer than before, they said, “Friends, it is not the sun; it is a great celestial mansion!” As it drew closer still, they said, “Friends, it is not a celestial mansion; it is a deva!” As it drew closer than before, they said, “Friends, it is not a deva; it is a Great Brahma!” Finally, as it drew very close, they said, “O friends, it is not a Great Brahma; another Buddha has arrived!”

Among those devas and brahmas, the worldlings (puthujjana) thought, “Friends, if there is such a vast gathering of devas and brahmas filling the entire universe for one Buddha, it is beyond estimation how great it will be for two Buddhas!” The Noble Ones (ariya) among the devas and brahmas, however, thought, “Two Buddhas do not appear simultaneously in a single world system; surely the Blessed One has created another created Buddha-image similar to Himself.”
403:
Thereafter, while the assembly of devas and brahmas was watching, the created Buddha approached the Blessed One and, without prostrating, sat down upon a seat created to be equal to the Blessed One’s, facing Him directly.

The thirty-two marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) were manifest on the Blessed One’s body, and the thirty-two marks of a Great Man were also manifest on the created Buddha’s body. The six-colored rays (chabbaṇṇaraṃsī) emanated and radiated from the Blessed One’s body, and the six-colored rays also emanated and radiated from the created Buddha’s body. The rays from the Blessed One’s body struck and rested upon the created Buddha’s body, and the rays from the created Buddha’s body struck and rested upon the Blessed One’s body. Those six-colored rays radiated from the bodies of these two Buddhas—the natural Buddha and the created Buddha—reached up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm, then descended back to touch the crowns of the devas and brahmas, and finally rested at the edge of the universe. Thus, the entire universe was as beautiful as a pagoda house covered with curved rafters made of pure gold.

The devas and brahmas residing in the ten thousand world systems gathered in this single world system and entered within the chamber of the rays of the two Buddhas.
404:
While remaining seated, the created Buddha praised the Blessed One’s abandonment of defilements at the Bodhi-throne and asked a question by reciting the verse beginning with:

“Pucchāmi muniṃ pahūtapaññaṃ,
tiṇṇaṃ pāraṅgataṃ parinibbutaṃ ṭhitattaṃ—”
(I ask the Sage of broad wisdom, who has crossed over, reached the far shore, attained Nibbāna, and is firm in Himself—)

The natural Buddha thought and considered: “Before answering the questions asked by the created Buddha (that is, before preaching the Samma-paribbājanīya Sutta, etc.), I shall first announce the names and lineages of all the devas and brahmas who have assembled, without distinction between the high and the low, so that their hearts may become firm and gentle.” Having so considered, He preached the Mahāsamaya Sutta beginning with “Ācikkhissāmi bhikkhave devakāyānaṃ nāmāni” (O monks, I shall announce the names of the celestial hosts).

(The detailed Pali and meaning of this Mahāsamaya Sutta have already been extracted and written from the Sutta Mahāvā Pali by various scholars, so they are not included in this text. If desired, one should study them from those various Mahāsamaya Sutta translations. In particular, the Pali translation and commentary titled “Mahāsamaya Suttas: Pali Translation and Exposition,” written by the Venerable Nandiya, the presiding monk of Mahā-visutārāma Monastery in Pakokku, provides a detailed explanation of the Mahāsamaya Sutta along with the six suttas, such as the Samma-paribbājanīya Sutta, preached at the end of that sutta according to the six temperaments; one should study from that work.)
405:
## The Liberation of Many Devas and Brahmas

At the conclusion of the Mahāsamaya Sutta discourse, one hundred thousand crores of devas and brahmas attained the Fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala); the number of those who became Noble Ones such as Stream-enterers (sotāpanna) was so vast it could not be delimited. (This is the explanation found in the Sutta Mahāvā Commentary, pages 287, 288).

## Explanation by Sayadaw U Budh

If one considers the Mahāsamaya Sutta as a whole, it can be seen that it primarily announces the names, types, and lineages of the devas and brahmas. Therefore, a question or objection may arise:

“Without the preaching of ultimate truths (paramattha), how could these devas and brahmas realize the Four Noble Truths and attain liberation (becoming Noble Ones such as Stream-enterers) merely by the announcement of their names and lineages?”

The answer is: (1) Knowing that those devas and brahmas (by hearing the Mahāsamaya Sutta) possessed ready minds, gentle minds, minds free from hindrances, uplifted minds, and clear minds, the Blessed One preached the Sāmukkaṃsika Dhamma-desanā, the discourse on the Four Noble Truths. By hearing that discourse on the Four Truths, the devas and brahmas became Noble Ones. (2) Alternatively, because the hearing of the Mahāsamaya Sutta caused a causal sequence of states in the continuums of those devas and brahmas—namely, joy (pīti), tranquility (passaddhi), happiness (sukha), concentration (samādhi), knowledge of things as they are (yathābhūta-ñāṇa), disenchantment (nibbidā-ñāṇa), dispassion (virāga-ñāṇa), the knowledge of liberation (vimuccana-ñāṇa) which is Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), the knowledge of liberation (vimutta-ñāṇa) which is Fruit-knowledge (phala-ñāṇa), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana) called reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa)—
406:
Because these sequences of Dhamma occurred as a chain of cause and effect, those devas and brahmas became Ariyas (Noble Ones).

Therefore, Sayadaw U Budh, in his introductory explanation (nissaya-amvun) of the Mahāsamaya Sutta, wrote:

Nāmakkhānemha yajjevaṃ,
Dhammābhisamo kathaṃ.
Kallādiṃ saccadīpena,
Nesaṃ pītādito vā—

Regarding the source for such writing and clarification, he stated:

"Based on the method in the Pali text: 'Kallacittaṃ muducittaṃ vinīvaraṇacittaṃ udaggacittaṃ pasannacittaṃ, atha yā buddhānaṃ sāmukkaṃsikā dhammadesanā, taṃ pakāsesi dukkhaṃ samudayaṃ nirodhaṃ maggaṃ'—and since it is a characteristic of 'citta-kalla' (readiness of mind) in the Commentary (devatānaṃ cittakallatājananatthaṃ), it is said 'Kallādiṃ saccadīpena'."

## The Devas' Devotion and Reverence for the Mahāsamaya Sutta

The devas have great devotion and reverence for this Mahāsamaya Sutta. Therefore, a noble person who recites or preaches this Dhamma, which is a source of worldly and supramundane happiness and associated with auspicious blessings, should prioritize the recitation of this Mahāsamaya Sutta in new places such as new houses, new monasteries, or new villages. (Commentary)

(In this regard, if one considers the reason why the devas have such devotion and reverence for the Mahāsamaya Sutta...)
407:
In this great assembly (Mahāsamaya), the Blessed One acted as the Chairman (Sabhāpati). This assembly included devas and brahmas ranging from the Bhummaso devas, whose power and majesty are small, to Hārita Brahma, whose power and majesty are greatest. This Mahāsamaya Sutta is like the opening greeting speech of the Blessed One, who was the Chairman of the assembly.

In an assembly consisting of three types of people—those of high status, middle status, and low status—if the Chairman delivers an opening greeting speech to satisfy and please all three types, he must speak starting from the group of people with low status and proceed in order; only then will all three types be satisfied and pleased. If he were to start with those of high status, saying, “Such and such distinguished gentlemen have also attended this assembly,” those of low status might feel discouraged and dissatisfied from the very beginning.

Similarly, in this Mahāsamaya assembly where the three types of devas and brahmas—those of great power, middle power, and small power—had gathered, if the Blessed One, as the Chairman, had delivered this Mahāsamaya Sutta (which is like a greeting speech) starting with the most powerful Hārita Brahma, saying, “The Great Hārita Brahma has also come to this Mahāsamaya assembly surrounded by his host of brahmas,” the Bhummaso devas of small power might have felt discouraged and dissatisfied from the start.

Now, however, because He delivered the greeting speech starting from the Bhummaso devas of small power, all three types of devas and brahmas attained satisfaction and pleasure. Through this Mahāsamaya Sutta discourse, the Blessed One...
408:
It should be understood that He gave the following instruction to those who act as chairpersons of various meetings: "When delivering a welcoming speech, one should start from those with lesser prestige and gradually ascend to those with greater prestige, placing them last; only then will everyone in the meeting be satisfied and pleased."

According to the aforementioned analysis and reflection, the powerful and high-ranking (mahesakkha) deities and Brahmas were satisfied and pleased, feeling great devotion, as they were featured in the latter part of this Mahāsamaya Sutta, which was the primary part for them. The less powerful (appesakkha) deities were also satisfied and pleased, feeling great devotion, as they were featured at the very beginning of the assembly.

Based on the reasons mentioned, the deities, wishing to listen to this Mahāsamaya Sutta, remained attentive and moved about, frequenting the four directions. The following story serves as evidence of the deities' devotion and reverence for this Mahāsamaya Sutta:

In the great monastery of the Koṭipabbata peak, there was a grotto called Nāgaleṇa (Dragon Cave) shaded by ironwood (gaṅgaw) trees. A certain deva-daughter resided in a large ironwood tree near the entrance of that cave. One day, a young monk residing in that cave recited this Mahāsamaya Sutta. The deva-daughter listened respectfully, and when the sutta ended, she uttered a loud cry of appreciation (Sādhu). At that time, the young monk and the deva-daughter questioned and answered each other as follows:
409:
(Question) Who is it that utters 'Sādhu' now?
(Answer) Venerable Sir, I am a deva-daughter.
(Question) Why do you utter 'Sādhu'?
(Answer) Venerable Sir, I heard the Mahāsamaya Sutta once on the day the Blessed One preached it while sitting in the Mahāvana forest, and I have only heard it again today. You, Venerable Sir, have learned this Dhamma well, without omitting or distorting even a single syllable from what was preached by the Blessed One. (That is why I utter 'Sādhu', Venerable Sir).
(Question) Did you, deva-daughter, personally hear it when the Blessed One was preaching?
(Answer) I heard it personally, Venerable Sir.
(Question) It is said that there was a great assembly of deities and Brahmas when the Blessed One preached the Mahāsamaya Sutta. In what place did you stand and listen, deva-daughter?
(Answer) Venerable Sir, I was a deva-daughter living in the great Mahāvana forest near the city of Kapilavatthu. However, when the powerful deities and Brahmas arrived, I could not find a place in Jambudīpa. I came to this island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka) and, while striving to listen to the Dhamma standing at the port of Jambukola, powerful deities arrived there as well. I had to gradually retreat and give way, eventually reaching the area behind Mahāgāma in the Rohaṇa region.
410:
I had to descend into the sea up to my neck and listen while standing in that spot, Venerable Sir.
(Question) O deva-daughter, could you see the Blessed One who was staying in the Mahāvana forest, which is very far from where you stood?
(Answer) Venerable Sir, how can you say that? (O, I could certainly see Him, Venerable Sir! Why do you ask so?) While the Blessed One was preaching the Dhamma in the Mahāvana forest, it seemed as if He was constantly looking at me. I was both afraid and ashamed, feeling as if I had to hide among the waves, Venerable Sir.
(Question) O deva-daughter, it is said that on that day (when the Mahāsamaya Sutta was preached), one hundred thousand crores of deities and Brahmas attained the Fruit of Arahantship. Did you also attain the Fruit of Arahantship at that time?
(Answer) I did not attain the Fruit of Arahantship, Venerable Sir.
(Question) If so, I suppose you attained the Fruit of Anāgāmī (Non-Returner).
(Answer) I did not attain it, Venerable Sir.
(Question) If so, I suppose you attained the Fruit of Sakadāgāmī (Once-Returner).
(Answer) I did not attain it, Venerable Sir.
411:
(Question) O deva-daughter, it is said that the number of deities and Brahmas who attained the three lower Paths (after listening to the Mahāsamaya Sutta) is beyond counting. I suppose you became a Sotāpanna (Stream-enterer).
(Answer) (Because the deva-daughter was one who had attained the Fruit of Sotāpatti on that day, she replied evasively out of modesty:) "Venerable Sir, you are asking what should not be asked."

Then the young monk said to the deva-daughter, "O deva-daughter, can you show your form to us?" The deva-daughter replied, "Venerable Sir, I cannot show my whole body, but I will show a single joint of a finger." Saying this, she pointed her finger through the keyhole into the cave. At that moment, the entire cave was illuminated as if a thousand moons and a thousand suns had risen. (In this instance, although the deva-daughter was capable of showing her whole body, she skillfully replied, "Venerable Sir, I cannot show my whole body," because she wished to prevent any potential danger to the monk's spiritual life that might arise from seeing her full form.)

Thereafter, the deva-daughter said, "Venerable Sirs, please strive in the practice of a monk without negligence," and after paying homage to the young monk, she departed and vanished.

In this way, the deities and Brahmas have great devotion and reverence for this Mahāsamaya Sutta.
412:
## Preaching the Dhamma According to Temperament

After the Blessed One preached the Mahāsamaya Sutta, in that very assembly:

(1) For the deities and Brahmas with a predominant temperament of lust (rāga-carita), He preached the Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta (where a created Buddha-image asked questions and the actual Buddha replied). At the end of that Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta discourse, one hundred thousand crores of deities and Brahmas attained the Fruit of Arahantship. The number of deities and Brahmas who attained the Fruits of Sotāpatti, Sakadāgāmī, and Anāgāmī was countless and very great.

(2) For the deities and Brahmas with a predominant temperament of anger (dosa-carita), He preached the Kalahavivāda Sutta in the same manner as before, and the deities and Brahmas attained liberation as before.

(3) For the deities and Brahmas with a predominant temperament of delusion (moha-carita), He preached the Mahāvyūha Sutta in the same manner as before, and the deities and Brahmas attained liberation as before.

(4) For the deities and Brahmas with a predominant temperament of speculative thought (vitakka-carita), He preached the Cūḷavyūha Sutta in the same manner as before, and the deities and Brahmas attained liberation as before.

(5) For the deities and Brahmas with a predominant temperament of faith (saddhā-carita), He preached the Tuvaṭṭaka-paṭipadā in the same manner as before, and the deities and Brahmas attained liberation as before.

(6) For the deities and Brahmas with a predominant temperament of intelligence (buddhi-carita), He preached the Purābheda Sutta in the same manner as before, and the deities and Brahmas attained liberation as before.
413:
(The detailed meaning of these six suttas should be extracted and noted from the Burmese translation of the Sutta Nipāta Pāḷi or, in particular, from the 'Mahāsamaya Sutta Pāḷi Nissaya and Commentary' written and compiled by the Most Venerable Pakokku Sayadaw Ashin Nandiya.)

## Here ends Chapter 22.
414:
## Chapter 23
## The Fifth Vassa Residence in Vesālī

The Buddha, having performed the Buddha's duties such as establishing seven hundred million devas and brahmas in the Fruit of Arahantship and establishing countless devas and brahmas in the lower Paths and Fruits while preaching the Mahāsamaya Sutta, Sammāparibbājanīya Sutta, etc., at the Great Assembly of the five hundred Arahant prince-monks as mentioned before, spent the fifth Vassa (rainy season retreat) at the Kūṭāgāra Hall (the Gabled Hall) in the Mahāvana forest near the city of Vesālī.

## Two Types of Mahāvana Forests

(In this regard, there are two types of Mahāvana forests: the Mahāvana forest near Kapilavatthu and the Mahāvana forest near Vesālī. The Mahāvana forest near Kapilavatthu, where the Mahāsamaya Sutta was preached, is contiguous with the Himalayas and extends boundlessly towards the Great Ocean. The Mahāvana forest near Vesālī is not like that; it is a large forest with definite boundaries.)

## King Suddhodana Attaining Arahantship and Entering Parinibbāna under the White Parasol in the Kapilavatthu Palace during that Vassa

While the Buddha was spending his fifth Vassa in the Mahāvana forest of Vesālī, his father, King Suddhodana, within the golden palace of Kapilavatthu...
415:
...attained the Fruit of Arahantship under the auspicious white parasol and entered Parinibbāna on that very day*.

## The Request of Mahāpajāpati Gotamī and the Permission for the Bhikkhunī Order

(Even when the Buddha first visited Kapilavatthu, his foster mother Mahāpajāpati Gotamī went to the Nigrodhārāma monastery and requested permission for women to enter the Buddha's Dispensation and ordain as nuns. At that time, the Buddha refused her request three times.

That refusal was because he considered: "If I allow women to ordain only after they have requested it many times with great effort, they will think, 'The status of a Bhikkhunī was obtained only after difficult and wearying requests,' and thus women will observe the rules well and respectfully." It was with the intention of granting permission after giving it due weight that he initially refused and prohibited it.

Thus, although Mahāpajāpati Gotamī requested three times during that first visit to Nigrodhārāma in Kapilavatthu, she did not receive permission and had to return to the palace in disappointment).

Now, when the Buddha was spending his fifth Vassa in the Mahāvana forest of Vesālī, the occasion for a second request arose again. That reason was:

* The scene of King Suddhodana attaining Arahantship and entering Parinibbāna is described in detail in the Tathāgata Udāna Dīpanī. In this text, it is written briefly as it appears in the Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 1, page 263: "Tassmiṃ samaye Suddhodanamahārājā setacchatta-tassa heṭṭhā arahattaṃ sacchikatvā parinibbāyi."
416:
After the five hundred Sakyan princes had attained Arahantship as previously described, their five hundred former wives sent messages and letters to them, as they had done before, to ascertain their intentions and to urge them to return to lay life. Those five hundred monks replied, "It is no longer possible for us to live in a household; it is no longer appropriate for us to do so." 

Those five hundred former wives then thought, "It is no longer proper for us to go to another's house (to remarry). Let us go to the Great Foster Mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and request her to plead with the Blessed One until He grants permission for women to be ordained as nuns, and then we shall ordain." They went to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and spoke with one voice, "O Great Mother, please plead with the Blessed One on our behalf so that He may grant us permission to enter the Dispensation and be ordained as nuns."

Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī had previously requested the Blessed One once (while He was staying at the Nigrodhārāma monastery) to allow women of the royal family to be ordained in this Dispensation, but she had not received permission. Therefore, on this second occasion, she summoned a barber and had her hair (and the hair of the five hundred Sakyan princesses) shaved off. They donned saffron-dyed robes and, within the royal palace itself, she herself took the form of a nun dedicated to the Blessed One and caused the five hundred Sakyan princesses to do the same.
417:
Together with those five hundred Sakyan princesses (aspiring nuns), she made arrangements to travel from the royal palace of Kapilavatthu to the Mahāvana forest in the city of Vesālī, where the Blessed One was staying.

The distance between Kapilavatthu and Vesālī was very great, being fifty-one yojanas. When they were planning the journey, the Sakyan and Koliyan kings consulted and thought, "These princesses and royal ladies are very delicate; they will not be able to travel on foot." Thus, they prepared over five hundred golden palanquins for the royal ladies to ride in.

However, those royal ladies reflected, "If we travel by vehicle, it would be a sign of disrespect to the Blessed One." Considering this, they traveled the fifty-one yojana distance only on foot. The kings of the two nations also arranged sufficient guards for the front and rear of the royal ladies and sent along carts fully loaded with provisions. They dispatched royal attendants with the order, "At every stage and stopping place, you must prepare food and sustenance for the royal ladies."

Because they were very delicate and had to walk the long distance of fifty-one yojanas, large swellings and blisters formed on their feet, breaking and reforming until both feet were swollen and inflamed, as if strewn with clear water-blisters. Thus, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, along with the five hundred Sakyan princesses, reached the gateway of the Kūṭāgāra Hall in the Mahāvana forest of Vesālī.
418:
When she arrived at the gateway, she stood outside with swollen feet, a dust-covered body, and a tearful face, being in great distress of both body and mind. (She did not dare to enter the monastery grounds suddenly.)

(In this regard: The thought occurred to Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, "I have taken the form of a nun on my own, even though the Blessed One has not granted permission. The fact that I have taken this form of a nun is now famous and well-known throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. If the Blessed One grants permission for ordination, it will be well. But if He does not grant permission, I shall be greatly ridiculed." Thinking thus, she did not dare to enter the monastery and stood weeping outside the gateway.)

The Venerable Ānanda saw Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī standing outside the gateway, weeping, with swollen feet, a dust-covered body, and a tearful face, in great distress of both body and mind. He asked her, "O Great Mother, why is this? Has there been some disaster for the Sakyan and Koliyan royal families? Why has the Great Mother come to such a wretched state? Why are you standing outside the gateway weeping, with swollen feet, a dust-covered body, and a tearful face, in great distress of both body and mind?"

Then Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī replied, "O Venerable Ānanda, it is because the Blessed One does not grant permission for women of the royal family to be ordained as nuns in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation that I am standing here outside the gateway in such great distress, weeping."
419:
When she had replied thus, the Venerable Ānanda spoke words of encouragement, saying, "Great Mother, if that is the case, please wait here for a moment until I have pleaded with the Blessed One to obtain permission for women of the royal family to be ordained as nuns in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation." Then the Venerable Ānanda went to the presence of the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat in a suitable place, addressing the Blessed One:

"Exalted Blessed One, because the Blessed One does not grant permission for women of the royal family to be ordained as nuns in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī is standing outside the gateway weeping, with swollen feet, a dust-covered body, and a tearful face, in great distress of both body and mind. Exalted Blessed One, I beg of You, may women of the royal family be allowed to receive ordination as nuns in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation."

When he had pleaded thus, the Blessed One replied, forbidding it: "Enough, Ānanda. Do not desire the ordination of women of the royal family in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation." Although forbidden, the Venerable Ānanda did not lose heart and pleaded a second time in the same manner. The Blessed One also replied and forbade it as before. A third time, the Venerable Ānanda pleaded in the same manner.
420:
The Blessed One also replied and forbade it in the same manner.

## Pleading by Changing the Approach

Then the thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda, "The Blessed One does not grant permission for women of the royal family to be ordained as nuns in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation. It would be well if I were to change the reason and plead with the Blessed One in another way to obtain permission for women of the royal family to be ordained as nuns in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation." Then the Venerable Ānanda asked the Blessed One:

"Exalted Blessed One, are women of the royal family capable, after having ordained as nuns in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation, of realizing the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala), the Fruit of Once-returning (Sakadāgāmi-phala), the Fruit of Non-returning (Anāgāmi-phala), and the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahatta-phala)?"

When he asked thus, the Blessed One replied, "Ānanda, women of the royal family are capable, after having ordained as nuns in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation, of realizing the Fruit of Stream-entry, the Fruit of Once-returning, the Fruit of Non-returning, and the Fruit of Arahantship."

Then the Venerable Ānanda said:

"Exalted Blessed One, if women of the royal family are capable of realizing the four Noble Fruits after having ordained as nuns in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation..."
421:
"Exalted Blessed One, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī has been of great service to the Blessed One. She is the Blessed One's own maternal aunt. She was the one who cherished, embraced, and nurtured the Blessed One from the time He was a tiny infant. She was the one who bathed Him with scented water two or three times a day and fed Him. When the Blessed One's mother, Mahāmāyā Devī, passed away, she was the one who nursed the Blessed One with her own milk." (After Mahāmāyā Devī gave birth to the Bodhisatta, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī gave birth to Prince Nanda two or three days later. At that time, the Great Mother entrusted her own son, Prince Nanda, to nurses, while she herself became the chief nurse for the Bodhisatta and nursed Him with her own milk; that is why he spoke thus.)

"Exalted Blessed One, I beg of You, may women of the royal family be allowed to receive ordination as nuns in this Dhamma-Vinaya Dispensation."

When he had pleaded thus, the Blessed One granted permission for the Bhikkhunī Dispensation by teaching the Eight Heavy Rules (Garudhamma) as follows:

"Ānanda, if Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī accepts and follows the Eight Heavy Rules, then the acceptance of those Eight Heavy Rules
422:
shall itself constitute her full ordination as a nun. The Eight Heavy Rules are as follows:

(1) A nun even of a hundred years' standing must perform the duties of paying homage, rising to greet, saluting with joined palms, and showing proper respect to a monk who has been ordained even that very day. This rule is to be revered, respected, and honored, and not to be transgressed as long as life lasts.

(2) A nun must not spend the rains retreat in a monastery where there are no monks nearby. This rule is to be revered, respected, and honored, and not to be transgressed as long as life lasts.

(3) Every fortnight, a nun must desire and follow two things from the Order of Monks: (a) asking the date of the Uposatha, and (b) approaching for exhortation. This rule is to be revered, respected, and honored, and not to be transgressed as long as life lasts.

(4) After the rains retreat, a nun must perform the 'Invitation' (Pavāraṇā) before both the Order of Monks and the Order of Nuns with respect to three matters: what has been seen, what has been heard, and what has been suspected (of an offense). This rule is to be revered, respected, and honored, and not to be transgressed as long as life lasts.

(5) A nun who has committed a serious offense (Saṅghādisesa) must undergo the Mānatta discipline for fifteen days (a fortnight) before both the Order of Monks and the Order of Nuns. This rule is to be revered, respected, and honored, and not to be transgressed as long as life lasts.
423:
(6) A bhikkhunī who has trained for two years in the six rules (sikkhamānā) without violation, breach, or spot, must seek ordination from both the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. This rule is to be revered, respected, and honored, and not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
(7) A bhikkhunī must not, for any reason, abuse or revile a monk. This rule is to be revered, respected, and honored, and not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
(8) From this day forward, the admonition of monks by bhikkhunīs is forbidden (meaning they must not speak admonition); the admonition of bhikkhunīs by monks is not forbidden (meaning they must speak admonition). This rule is to be revered, respected, and honored, and not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts (it must be followed).
(These are the Eight Heavy Rules - Garudhamma.)
"Dear Ānanda, if the foster-mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī accepts and follows these Eight Heavy Rules, that acceptance of the Eight Heavy Rules shall serve as her higher ordination as a bhikkhunī."
Having thus preached the Eight Heavy Rules, the Buddha granted permission for the Bhikkhunī Order.
424:
Then, the Venerable Ānanda, having learned these Eight Heavy Rules in the presence of the Buddha, returned to the foster-mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī and said to her:
"Great Foster-mother, if you accept and follow these Eight Heavy Rules, that acceptance itself will be your higher ordination as a bhikkhunī. (The Eight Heavy Rules are as follows):"
(1) A bhikkhunī even of a hundred years standing must perform the duties of bowing, rising to welcome, saluting with joined palms, and showing proper respect to a monk ordained that very day. This rule is to be revered, respected, and honored, and not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts. (It must be followed).
(Pe...) 
(8) From this day forward, the admonition of monks by bhikkhunīs is forbidden (meaning they must not speak admonition); the admonition of bhikkhunīs by monks is not forbidden (meaning they must speak admonition). This rule is to be revered, respected, and honored, and not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts. (= It must be followed).
"Great Foster-mother, if you accept and follow these Eight Heavy Rules..."
425:
"...that acceptance itself will be your higher ordination as a bhikkhunī."
Thus he informed her.
Then the foster-mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī said, "Venerable Ānanda, just as a young man or woman, youthful and fond of ornaments, having washed their head, would receive a garland of lotuses, jasmine, or blue lilies with both hands and place it respectfully upon their head; even so, I accept and will follow these Eight Heavy Rules as rules not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts."
Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Buddha, paid homage respectfully, and sat in a suitable place. He reported, "Venerable Sir, the foster-mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī has accepted the Eight Heavy Rules as rules not to be transgressed for as long as life lasts."
(In this context, the joyful and respectful acceptance of the Eight Heavy Rules was indeed the foster-mother's higher ordination. There was no need to enter the boundary (sīmā) or recite the formal act (kammavācā); at the very moment of acceptance, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī became a bhikkhunī. This type of ordination is called 'Aṭṭhagarudhamma-paṭigga-haṇa-upasampadā'.)
426:
## Permission for the Ordination of Bhikkhunīs
Then the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī approached the Buddha, paid homage respectfully, and stood in a suitable place. She addressed the Buddha, "Exalted Son, how should I act and manage regarding these five hundred Sakyan princesses?"
Then the Buddha preached the Dhamma to the foster-mother Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. After hearing the Dhamma, Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī paid homage, showed respect, and departed. Then the Buddha, having preached the Dhamma concerning the matter requested by Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, addressed the monks:
"Monks, I allow monks to give higher ordination to bhikkhunīs."
Thus He laid down the training rule. According to this rule, the monks gave higher ordination to the five hundred Sakyan princesses, making them the pupils (saddhivihārinī) of Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī. In this way, those five hundred Sakyan bhikkhunīs, because they received ordination from only one side (the Bhikkhu Saṅgha) as the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha was not yet fully established, were known as "Ekatoupasampanna" bhikkhunīs.
After being ordained as bhikkhunīs, the Elder Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī, upon hearing the Saṅkhitta Sutta (from Aṅguttara Nikāya, 3.106)...
427:
...attained the fruit of Arahantship. As for the five hundred Sakyan bhikkhunīs, they later heard the Nandakovāda Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya, 3.314), and according to their individual dispositions, some became Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), some Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), some Non-returners (Anāgāmī), and some became Arahants.
(Note: Although the stories of the ordinations of Queen Yasodharā, Princess Janapadakalyāṇī, Queen Khemā, the merchant's wife Dhammadinnā, and the Elder Bhaddā Kāpilānī should follow here, their accounts will be presented in the section on the Saṅgha Ratana.)
## Subduing Saccaka the Paribbājaka
While the Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in the Great Wood (Mahāvana) near the city of Vesālī, He subdued Saccaka the Paribbājaka and achieved victory. The biography and account of this Saccaka Paribbājaka will be extracted and presented from the Commentary on the Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka (Catukka Nipāta) and the Commentary on the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta (Mūlapaṇṇāsa).
