In ancient times, in the city of Vesālī, seven thousand seven hundred and seven (7,707) Licchavī princes ruled in rotation. All these Licchavī princes had a strong desire to inquire into and investigate strange and profound doctrines. At that time, a male wandering ascetic (Paribbājaka) skilled in five hundred doctrines arrived in Vesālī; the Licchavī princes supported him. Similarly, a female wandering ascetic (Paribbājikā) skilled in five hundred doctrines also arrived in Vesālī.
428:
The Licchavī princes arranged a debate for these two. Since both were equal in wisdom, neither could defeat the other, and it ended in a draw. Then a thought occurred to the Licchavī princes: "A child born of these two will surely be exceptionally skilled in doctrines." Subsequently, they said, "You two are equal in matters of doctrine. Why wander about to various towns and villages? Stay here in our city of Vesālī." Having said this, they married the two, provided them with a house, and honored them.
Later, from the union of that Paribbājaka and Paribbājikā, four daughters and one son were born in succession. The names of the four daughters were, in order: (1) Saccā, (2) Lolā, (3) Avadhārikā, and (4) Paṭicchādā. The young son was named Saccaka. (However, the Commentary on the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta gives the daughters' names as 1. Saccā, 2. Lolā, 3. Paṭācārā, and 4. Ācāravatī).
When these five siblings reached the age of discretion, they mastered one thousand (1,000) doctrines—five hundred from their mother's side and five hundred from their father's side. The parents advised the four daughters:
"Dear daughters, if any layman is able to resolve and refute your doctrines, you should submit yourselves to him and serve as his wife."
429:
"If any monk is able to resolve and refute your doctrines, you should ordain as monastics under that monk."
Thus they gave their advice.
Later, when the parents passed away, the young brother Saccaka Paribbājaka, being superior in wisdom to his four elder sisters, learned the one thousand doctrines from his parents as well as many other external doctrines. He did not go elsewhere but remained in Vesālī, teaching the young princes. Fearing that his belly might burst because it was so full of wisdom, he wandered about with iron plates bound around his stomach.
The four elder sisters of Saccaka, thinking, "This Jambudīpa is the island famous for the Jambu (rose-apple) tree," each took a rose-apple branch. To challenge others in debate, they wandered from city to city and region to region. Wherever they arrived, they would plant the rose-apple branch in a mound of sand or earth at the city gate and leave instructions: "Whoever is capable of finding fault in our doctrine, let him trample and crush this rose-apple branch." Then they would enter the city or village.
Wandering thus from village to village and city to city, they eventually reached the city of Sāvatthī. They planted the rose-apple branch at the city gate and said, "Whether layman or monk, whoever is able to point out a fault in our doctrine, let him [trample this mound]..."
430:
“Trample it with your feet so that it is scattered, and crush the rose-apple branch with your very feet,” they told the children who had approached, and then they entered the city of Sāvatthī for alms.

## The Prowess of the Venerable Sāriputta

At that time, the Venerable Sāriputta, the Chief Disciple of the Right Hand of the Blessed One, having swept the areas in the Jetavana Monastery that had not yet been swept, having filled the empty pots with drinking and utility water, and having attended to the sick monks, entered the city of Sāvatthī for alms late in the day. Upon seeing the rose-apple branch planted at the city gate, he questioned the children about it. The children reported the matter in full to him.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta said to the children, “Children, if that is so, trample and crush that rose-apple branch.” The children said, “Venerable sir, we do not dare to trample or crush it. We are afraid.” The Venerable Sāriputta said, “Children, do not be afraid. If they ask you, ‘Who caused our rose-apple branch to be crushed?’, you should (boldly) tell them, ‘The Elder Sāriputta, the great disciple of the Blessed One, caused it to be trampled and crushed. If the female wanderers wish to compete in a debate of doctrines, let them go to the presence of the Elder who resides in the Jetavana Monastery.’” When the Venerable Sāriputta had spoken thus, the children...
431:
...having heard the words of the Elder, (becoming enthusiastic), they trampled and crushed the rose-apple branch and threw it away. The Venerable Sāriputta, after wandering for alms, returned to the Jetavana Monastery.

The four female wanderers also came out of the city and asked the children, “Who caused our rose-apple branch to be crushed?” The children reported the matter to them.

The four female wanderers re-entered the city and, each taking responsibility for one street, proclaimed, “A person named Sāriputta, a disciple of the Blessed One, says he will engage in a debate of doctrines with us. Let the citizens who wish to listen come forth!” A great crowd of citizens came out in a commotion. Together with that crowd, the four female wanderers went to the Jetavana Monastery.

The Venerable Sāriputta, considering that “the arrival of women at our dwelling place is not pleasant,” sat ready in the middle of the monastery. The wanderers approached and asked the Venerable Sāriputta, “Did you cause our rose-apple branch to be crushed?” When the Venerable Sāriputta replied, “Yes, I caused it to be crushed,” the wanderers said, “We shall engage in a debate of doctrines with you.” Then the Venerable Sāriputta asked, “Very well, engage in the debate. Who do you wish to ask (first) and who should answer?” The wanderers said, “The matter of questioning...
432:
...falls to us.” Then the Venerable Sāriputta said, “You are women. You ask first.”

The four female wanderers stood at the four directions and asked one thousand doctrines they had learned from their parents. The Elder answered every question they asked without any confusion or difficulty, as if cutting a lotus stalk with a sword. Having answered thus, he invited them again, saying, “Ask further.” Then the four female wanderers, (their pride humbled), said, “Venerable sir, we only know this much.”

Then the Venerable Sāriputta said, “Wanderers, I have answered the one thousand doctrines you asked. I shall ask you only one question. Will you answer that question?” When he asked this, the four female wanderers, seeing the Elder's stature, did not dare to answer boldly, “Ask, venerable sir, we shall answer,” but instead humbly said, “Speak, venerable sir; if we know it, we shall answer.” Then the Venerable Sāriputta, as a preamble, said, “Wanderers, this question I am about to ask is (not yet a high-level problem); it is the very first question taught to noble youths who have been ordained as novices (sāmaṇera).” He then asked, “Ekaṃ nāma kiṃ? = What is the one?”
433:
The four female wanderers did not see even a hint of the answer to the question asked by the Elder. The Elder said again, “Wanderers, answer.” When the wanderers confessed, “Venerable sir, we do not see even a hint of the answer to that question,” the Venerable Sāriputta asked, “I have answered the thousand doctrines you asked, but you cannot answer even one of my questions. This being so, who has won and who has lost?” The wanderers replied, “Venerable sir, you have won and we have lost.” Then the Elder asked, “In that case, what will you do now?” The wanderers, reporting the advice given by their parents (as mentioned before), replied, “We shall take ordination as nuns in your presence, venerable sir.”

Then the Venerable Sāriputta said, “It is not proper for you women to be ordained in our presence. However, take our message, go to the nunnery (bhikkhunī monastery), and take ordination there.” The four female wanderers agreed, took the Elder's message, went to the community of nuns, and were ordained. (According to the Jātaka Commentary, they were ordained in the presence of the Elder Nun Uppalavaṇṇā). After being ordained, they practiced the Dhamma diligently and without negligence, and before long...
434:
...they attained Arahantship. (Regarding this incident, the Blessed One preached the Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka found in the Catukka Nipāta. That Jātaka should be noted in the 550 Jātaka stories).

(Note: This incident of the four female wanderers occurred at a later time when the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, after the Bhikkhunī Order had been permitted at the request of Mahāpajāpati Gotamī while the Blessed One was staying in the Mahāvana forest in Vesālī. However, it is described here because it is connected to the story of Saccaka the Wanderer).

## About Saccaka the Wanderer

Saccaka the Wanderer, who was the younger brother of the four female wanderers mentioned above, resided in Vesālī as a royal teacher, instructing the princes in various arts and sciences.

At that time, the Blessed One was residing in the Gabled House Hall (Kūṭāgārasālā) in the Mahāvana forest near Vesālī. Then Saccaka the Wanderer, who was the son of a Nigaṇṭha, a skilled debater, one who claimed to be a scholar, and one whom the people regarded as a saint, spoke thus in the assembly at Vesālī:

“I do not see any recluse or brahmin, any head of a group, any teacher of a group, even one who claims to be an Arahant and a Fully Enlightened One, who, if I were to challenge them in debate, would not tremble, shake, and sweat from the armpits.
435:
Even if I were to challenge a mindless post in debate, even that post would tremble and shake; what then of a human being?”

Thus he boasted. (Saccaka the Wanderer was one who wandered about thinking, “I will find fault with the doctrine of the recluse Gotama.”) Then, Saccaka the Wanderer, who was walking about for exercise, saw the Venerable Assaji entering Vesālī for alms in the morning and thought:

“I am one who wanders about thinking of finding fault with the doctrine of the recluse Gotama. However, I have not yet criticized it, thinking, ‘I do not yet know the doctrine of that recluse Gotama.’ Indeed, a criticism is well-placed only when one knows the doctrine of another for oneself. This person I see now is the one known as the Elder Assaji, a disciple of the recluse Gotama, and he is one who is skilled in the doctrine of his teacher. I shall question this Elder Assaji, and after firmly establishing their doctrine, I shall speak words of criticism regarding the doctrine of the recluse Gotama.”

Having thought thus, he approached the Venerable Assaji, and after exchanging pleasantries, he stood in a suitable...
436:
...place and asked the Venerable Assaji, “O Assaji, how does the recluse Gotama discipline his disciples? What part of the recluse Gotama’s instruction (anusāsanī) to his disciples is frequent?”

Then the Venerable Assaji said to Saccaka the Wanderer:

“O Saccaka of the Aggivessana clan, the Blessed One disciplines his disciples in this way. This following part of the Blessed One’s instruction (anusāsanī) to his disciples is frequent:

‘Monks, form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, mental formations are impermanent, the sixfold consciousness is impermanent. Form is not-self, feeling, perception, mental formations, and the sixfold consciousness are not-self. All formations are impermanent, all phenomena are not-self.’

O Saccaka of the Aggivessana clan, the Blessed One disciplines his disciples in this way; this aforementioned part of the Blessed One’s instruction to his disciples is frequent.”

[Special Note: Here, the Venerable Assaji answered Saccaka the Wanderer only regarding the points of impermanence and non-self.]
437:
He did not answer the point regarding suffering (dukkha). (Please re-read the answer). The reason for omitting the point of suffering in the reply is clearly explained in the Commentary as follows:

If the Venerable Assaji had stated, "Material form is suffering, feeling is, perception is, mental formations are, and the sixfold consciousness is suffering," it would have provided an opportunity for accusation. There are instances where the Path and Fruition (Magga and Phala) are also referred to as suffering in the sense of the suffering of conditioned states (saṅkhāra-dukkha). If Saccaka the Paribbājaka were answered with the point of suffering included, he might have asked Venerable Assaji, "O Assaji, for what purpose do you lead the monk's life?" If Venerable Assaji then replied, "We lead the monk's life for the sake of the Path and Fruition," Saccaka would have criticized him, saying, "O Assaji, your Dispensation (Sāsana) is not one that leads to liberation from the round of rebirth; rather, this so-called Dispensation of yours is merely a place of great slaughter and oppression. This Dispensation of yours is just a kind of Ussada Hell. Therefore, there is no such thing as a desire for happiness in your minds. You all merely wander about exerting effort only to experience suffering."

Therefore, thinking, "It is not appropriate to speak in figurative terms (pariyāya-kathā) to this Saccaka the Paribbājaka who holds views outside the Dispensation; I shall speak to him only in direct, literal terms (nippariyāya) so that he finds no foothold for criticism," Venerable Assaji answered only the points of impermanence and non-self, starting with "Bhikkhus, material form is impermanent," and so on. (From Ma-ṭha, 2, 172-3).

Then Saccaka the Paribbājaka said to Venerable Assaji, "O Assaji, we have heard words that are not fit to be heard. We have heard that the Ascetic Gotama speaks in this manner. Perhaps at some time we might meet that Master Gotama; perhaps some conversation might take place. When we meet and speak, we might be able to dissuade him from that lowly false view."
438:
Thus he spoke boastfully. At that time, five hundred Licchavī princes were assembled in the meeting hall (Santhāgāra) for some business. Then Saccaka the Paribbājaka thought, "Previously, because I did not know the doctrine of the Ascetic Gotama, I did not speak words of criticism regarding his doctrine. Now, however, having heard it from his great disciple (Venerable Assaji), I know his doctrine well. These five hundred Licchavī princes, who are my disciples, are also assembled in the meeting hall. I shall go together with these five hundred Licchavī disciples and speak words of criticism against the Ascetic Gotama regarding his doctrine."

Having so planned, he went to the meeting hall where the five hundred Licchavī princes were assembled and said to them:

"O Licchavīs, come forth! O Licchavīs, come forth! Today there will be a great debate between me and the Ascetic Gotama. If the Ascetic Gotama admits to me what his disciple Assaji—who is one of the five famous monks of the group of five (Pañcavaggī)—admitted to me (regarding impermanence and non-self):

(1) Just as a strong man might seize a long-haired ram by its hair and pull it, drag it, and toss it about, even so shall I
439:
refute the Ascetic Gotama in debate, pulling him, dragging him, and tossing him to and fro.

(2) Just as a strong worker in a tavern might throw a large coarse mat into a deep pool and, seizing it by the corner, pull it, drag it, and toss it about, even so shall I refute the Ascetic Gotama in debate, pulling him, dragging him, and tossing him to and fro.

(3) Just as a strong drunkard, wishing to clean a wine-strainer (or a wine-pot), would seize it by the edge and shake it down, shake it up, and shake it repeatedly, even so shall I refute the Ascetic Gotama in debate, shaking him down, shaking him up, and shaking him repeatedly.

(4) Just as a great royal elephant, sixty years of age, whose strength has not yet diminished, would descend into a deep lake and play the game of 'washing hemp fibers,' even so shall I play the 'hemp-washing game' with the Ascetic Gotama.

(Note: Regarding this, people used to bundle hemp stalks into sheaves to make hemp thread and soak them in water.
440:
After three days, those hemp stalks would be well-softened by the water. Then, people would take sour gruel, liquor, and other food and drink, go to that place, firmly grasp the bundles of hemp stalks, and beat them against three planks placed to the right, to the left, and directly in front, alternating between them. While doing so, they would eat and drink sour gruel and liquor merrily. For those people, this was a great and joyful game.

A king's great elephant, seeing this game and wishing to imitate it, would descend into deep water and, taking water with its trunk, spray it over its head, its back, its two sides, and between its thighs, alternating and turning about. Based on this, such a game is called 'Sāṇadhovika' or the 'hemp-washing game').

"O Licchavīs, come forth! O Licchavīs, come forth! Today there will be a great debate between me and the Ascetic Gotama."

Thus he spoke and invited them. Among the Licchavīs who were thus invited: (1) Some foolish Licchavīs said, "How could the Ascetic Gotama refute Saccaka the Paribbājaka in debate? Only Saccaka the Paribbājaka will be able to refute the Ascetic Gotama in debate." (2) Some wise Licchavīs said, "What kind of person is Saccaka the Paribbājaka that he could refute the Blessed One in debate?

##
441:
On the contrary, only the Blessed One will be able to refute Saccaka the Paribbājaka in debate."

Then Saccaka the Paribbājaka, surrounded by the five hundred Licchavī princes, went to the Kūṭāgāra Hall in the Great Wood (Mahāvana). It was the time of the blazing midday sun. At that time, many monks, having finished their fine meal, were walking to and fro (caṅkama) to dispel the drowsiness (thina-middha) that arises from food. (Alternatively, those monks were 'daytime meditators' (divāpadhānika). For such daytime meditators, if they walk in the afternoon, bathe, warm themselves, and then sit down to practice the Dhamma, they can achieve great concentration. Therefore, those daytime meditators were walking in the open air during the heat of the midday sun).

Then Saccaka the Paribbājaka went to where those monks were and asked, "Friends, where is the Master Gotama staying now? We wish to see that Master Gotama."

On that day, at dawn, the Blessed One had entered the Attainment of Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) and, spreading the net of his Omniscient Knowledge (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) over the ten thousand world systems, looked for beings worthy of liberation. He saw, "Tomorrow, Saccaka the Paribbājaka will come
442:
bringing a large company of Licchavī princes, wishing to speak words of criticism against my doctrine." Having seen this, he performed his morning ablutions early, went on alms round in the city of Vesālī surrounded by the community of monks, and upon returning from the alms round, he thought, "Today I shall stay in a place where it will be comfortable for a large assembly to sit." Thus, without entering the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi), he sat for the day's rest at the foot of a well-shaded tree in the Great Wood.

The monks who were wearers of rag-robes (paṃsukūlika) and daytime meditators, who had just been asked by Saccaka, had only recently returned from attending to the Blessed One. Therefore, as soon as Saccaka the Paribbājaka asked, they pointed with joined palms towards the Blessed One who was staying at a distance and said:

"O Saccaka the Paribbājaka of the Aggivessana clan, the Blessed One has entered the Great Wood and is sitting for the day's rest at the foot of a certain tree."

Then Saccaka the Paribbājaka, together with the vast and immeasurable assembly of Licchavīs (the princes and the people of Vesālī), entered the Great Wood, went to the tree where the Blessed One was staying, exchanged pleasant greetings, and sat down in a suitable place. (It was mentioned earlier that there were five hundred Licchavī princes; those five hundred Licchavīs were the disciples of Saccaka. In particular,)
443:
In the city of Vesālī, the news was heard: "Saccaka has gone to the Blessed One, leading five hundred Licchavī princes, desiring to engage in a debate of views." Thinking, "Let us listen to the debate between these two great scholars," a vast multitude of the people of Vesālī followed along with Saccaka. Thus, the assembly was immeasurably large.

Among that assembly (who came with Saccaka): (1) Some paid homage to the Blessed One with deep respect and sat down at a respectful distance (free from the six faults of sitting). (2) Some exchanged pleasantries and memorable words with the Blessed One and sat down at a respectful distance. (3) Some extended their joined palms towards the Blessed One and sat down at a respectful distance. (4) Some announced their name and lineage to the Blessed One and sat down at a respectful distance. (5) Some remained silent and sat down. (The specific attitudes of these five groups were previously explained in the section "King Bimbisāra Visiting the Buddha" in the Great Chronicle of Buddhas, Vol. 2, pp. 581, 582).

Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta, having sat down at a respectful distance, addressed the Blessed One: "If the Venerable Gotama would grant me the opportunity to ask a question, I would like to ask the Venerable Gotama about a certain matter." The Blessed One replied: "Saccaka of the Aggivessana lineage...
444:
...ask whatever you desire." This was an invitation given by the Omniscient Buddha (an invitation not shared by Paccekabuddhas or disciples).

Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta asked: "How does the Venerable Gotama discipline his disciples? And what part of the Venerable Gotama's instruction (anusāsanī) is most frequent among his disciples?"

The Blessed One then said to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta:

"O Saccaka of the Aggivessana lineage, I discipline my disciples in this way. This part of my instruction is frequent among my disciples:

'Monks, form is impermanent, feeling is impermanent, perception is impermanent, formations are impermanent, the sixfold consciousness is impermanent. Monks, form is not-self, feeling is not-self, perception is not-self, formations are not-self, the sixfold consciousness is not-self. All formations are impermanent. All things are not-self.'

O Saccaka of the Aggivessana lineage, I discipline my disciples in this way. This part of my instruction is frequent among my disciples."

Thus the Blessed One spoke.
445:
Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta said, "O Venerable Gotama, a simile occurs to my mind." When the Blessed One granted him permission, saying, "O Saccaka of the Aggivessana lineage, let the simile that occurs to you be clear (speak it boldly)," Saccaka said to the Blessed One:

"O Venerable Gotama, just as all seeds and all plants that reach growth, increase, and full development do so depending on the earth and established upon the earth; or just as all tasks that must be performed by physical strength are performed depending on the earth and established upon the earth; even so, O Venerable Gotama, this person who has form as self (clinging to form as self) is established upon form and produces both wholesome and unwholesome deeds. This person who has feeling as self (clinging to feeling as self) is established upon feeling and produces both wholesome and unwholesome deeds. This person who has perception as self (clinging to perception as self) is established upon perception and produces both wholesome and unwholesome deeds. This person who has formations as self (clinging to formations as self) is established upon formations and produces both wholesome and unwholesome deeds. This person who has the sixfold consciousness as self (clinging to the sixfold consciousness as self)...
446:
...is established upon the sixfold consciousness and produces both wholesome and unwholesome deeds."

Thus he stated his doctrine of self with a simile. (By these words, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta meant: "These five aggregates are the foundation for these beings, like the earth. These beings are established upon these five aggregates and perform both wholesome and unwholesome kamma. The Venerable Gotama and his followers reject such a self which is so obvious to the world and instead teach and speak of not-self." He presented this simile with great confidence to make his point firm).

This simile presented by Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta was indeed very strong and memorable. No one other than the Omniscient Buddha would be able to break it down, destroy it, and point out the flaws in his doctrine. Indeed, there are two types of persons: (1) Buddha-veneyya—those to be tamed by the Buddha, and (2) Sāvaka-veneyya—those to be tamed by the disciples. Disciples and Buddhas can both tame the Sāvaka-veneyya to realize the truth. However, disciples cannot tame the Buddha-veneyya to realize the truth; only the Buddhas can tame them. Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta was a Buddha-veneyya. Therefore, no one besides the Buddha was capable of refuting his doctrine and pointing out its faults. Thus, the Blessed One himself, in order to show the faults in Saccaka's doctrine, said:
447:
"Saccaka of the Aggivessana lineage, do you say: 'Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, formations are my self, the sixfold consciousness is my self'?"

Then Saccaka the Nigaṇṭhaputta thought: "The ascetic Gotama is making me state, establish, and admit my doctrine of self very firmly in the midst of this assembly. If any fault arises later, it will press upon me alone. Now, I will also cast this doctrine of self upon the heads of the people of Vesālī."

Having thought thus, he said: "O Venerable Gotama, I say: 'Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, formations are my self, the sixfold consciousness is my self.' And this great multitude of the people of Vesālī also says the same."

Thus he spoke, involving the whole multitude (like a thief seeking companions in death). The Blessed One, however, was hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands of times more skillful and superior in the matter of debate than Saccaka. Therefore, thinking, "This Saccaka desires to free himself and cast the blame upon the heads of the multitude. I will not allow him to escape in any way. I will separate him from the multitude...
448:
...and subdue Saccaka alone," the Blessed One thought and then said:

"Saccaka of the Aggivessana lineage, what will the great multitude do for you? I urge you, Saccaka of the Aggivessana lineage, explain only your own doctrine."

(The meaning is: This multitude did not come to debate or point out faults in my doctrine. You alone are the one who gathered the people of Vesālī and came to point out faults in my doctrine. Therefore, explain only your own doctrine; do not pile the blame on the heads of the uninvolved multitude). Then Saccaka, unable to avoid it, admitted directly:

"O Venerable Gotama, I do say: 'Form is my self, feeling is my self, perception is my self, formations are my self, the sixfold consciousness is my self.'"

(From here on, he will be referred to simply as Saccaka).

Thus, after the Blessed One had made Saccaka admit his own doctrine, He said:

"Saccaka, since you admit that the five aggregates are the self, I will ask you a question in return. You should answer as you please.

Saccaka, what do you think of this? Would an anointed king, such as King Pasenadi of Kosala or King Ajātasattu of Magadha, the son of Queen Vedehī, have the power in his own realm to execute those who should be executed, to fine those who should be fined, or to banish those who should be banished?"
449:
Then Saccaka replied to the Blessed One:

"O Venerable Gotama, an anointed king, such as King Pasenadi of Kosala or King Ajātasattu of Magadha, the son of Queen Vedehī, would have the power in his own realm to execute those who should be executed, to fine those who should be fined, or to banish those who should be banished.

Indeed, O Venerable Gotama, even the oligarchic groups like the rulers of the Vajjī and the rulers of the Malla have the power in their own realms to execute those who should be executed, to fine those who should be fined, or to banish those who should be banished. What then need be said of an anointed king like King Pasenadi of Kosala or King Ajātasattu of Magadha, the son of Queen Vedehī?"
450:
“O Master Gotama, power is possible; it is indeed fitting for power to be exercised,” he replied. (In this instance, the Blessed One prepared this line of reasoning to strongly suppress Saccaka’s doctrine of self. Saccaka, being unskilled, provided the very reason to dismantle his own doctrine, like someone sharpening a weapon to be used against himself, by citing the rulers of the Vajjī and Malla states and emphasizing, “It is indeed fitting for power to be exercised.”) 

Then the Blessed One said to Saccaka the Wanderer: 
“Saccaka, what do you think? You say, ‘Form is my self.’ Can you exercise power over that form, saying, ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus’?” 

Thus He questioned him pointedly. When this was asked, Saccaka the Wanderer remained silent without giving an answer. 

(In this regard: Saccaka the Wanderer realized his mistake, thinking, “The ascetic Gotama has brought forth an argument to break my doctrine. Because I am unskilled, I have highlighted the very point the ascetic Gotama used. Now I am utterly ruined. If I say I can exercise power over form, these Licchavī princes will rise and say, ‘O Saccaka, you say you can exercise power over your form. If you can indeed exercise power over your form,
451:
why are you not as beautiful and radiant as these Licchavī princes who are as handsome and inspiring as the Tāvatiṃsa gods?’ If I say I cannot exercise power over form, the ascetic Gotama will rise and blame me, saying, ‘O Saccaka, you said before you could exercise power over form, but now you deny it.’ Thus, if I say ‘I can exercise power,’ I will be at fault; if I say ‘I cannot exercise power,’ I will also be at fault.” Thinking thus, he remained silent without giving an answer.) 

For the second time, the Blessed One said to Saccaka the Wanderer: 
“Saccaka, what do you think? You say, ‘Form is my self.’ Can you exercise power over that form, saying, ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus’?” 

Even at this second questioning, Saccaka the Wanderer remained silent without giving an answer. 

Specifically, if one is asked a question by the Blessed One up to three times and does not answer (thereby harassing the Blessed One by not answering a legitimate question), by the power of the law of nature (dhamma-niyāma), the head of the one who does not answer may split into seven pieces. The Buddhas, however, have fulfilled the perfections for four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand world-cycles for the benefit of beings, and are thus possessors of great compassion.
452:
Therefore, the Blessed One did not ask a third time immediately but changed the course of the conversation: 
“Saccaka, answer now. Now is not the time for you to remain silent. Saccaka, if anyone is asked a legitimate question by a Blessed One up to three times and does not answer, his head will split into seven pieces right here.” 

At that moment, Sakka, the King of Gods, in the form of a yakkha, holding a flaming, glowing iron thunderbolt (Vajira), stood in the air above Saccaka, as if threatening him, “If this Saccaka does not answer the Blessed One’s legitimate question for the third time, I will split his head into seven pieces right here.” Only the Blessed One and Saccaka saw Sakka in the form of a yakkha holding the thunderbolt. (No one else in the assembly saw him.) 

[Note: Why did Sakka come holding the thunderbolt? Like the Blessed One, he had compassion for Saccaka, thinking, “I will frighten him by manifesting a terrifying form to make him abandon his wrong view.”
453:
He stood in the air directly in front of Saccaka, not with the intent to actually split his head. Indeed, no harm ever comes to anyone in the presence of the Blessed One. (From Ma-Ṭī, 2, 206). 

Why did Sakka come in the form of a yakkha? He came to make Saccaka abandon his wrong view. (Alternatively) When Sahampati Brahma came to request the Buddha to teach, Sakka accompanied him and promised: “Venerable Sir, please teach the Dhamma. We will make those who do not follow or listen to your authority comply. Let the Wheel of Dhamma be on your side, and let the Wheel of Authority be on ours.” Therefore, he came today intending to frighten Saccaka into answering the question. (From Ma-A, 2, 179).] 

Seeing Sakka in the form of a yakkha, large drops of sweat poured from Saccaka’s entire body, and his stomach churned with a loud noise. Saccaka looked around to see if others saw it, but he did not see even a single person’s hair standing on end. Then he thought, “These people do not see the yakkha; thus, this fear is mine alone. If I say ‘Great Yakkha!’, they will say, ‘Are you the only one with eyes? Only you see a yakkha. You didn’t see a yakkha before, but only when debating the ascetic Gotama do you see one!’” Having considered this, he thought, “There is now no other refuge but the ascetic Gotama.” Terrified, with his hair standing on end,
454:
seeking the Blessed One as his shelter, hiding place, and refuge, Saccaka said to the Blessed One, “Let Master Gotama ask me; I will answer.” 

Then the Blessed One said to Saccaka the Wanderer: 
“Saccaka, what do you think? You say, ‘Form is my self.’ Can you exercise power over that form, saying, ‘Let my form be thus, let my form not be thus’?” 

“No, Master Gotama,” Saccaka replied. 

“Saccaka, consider well! Consider and then answer. Your former statement and your latter statement do not agree.” Having said this, the Blessed One asked Saccaka: 

“Saccaka, what do you think? You say, ‘Feeling is my self.’ Can you exercise power over that feeling, saying, ‘Let my feeling be thus, let my feeling not be thus’?” 

“No, Master Gotama,” Saccaka replied. 

“Saccaka, consider well! Consider and then answer. Your former statement and your latter statement do not agree.” Having said this, the Blessed One asked Saccaka:
455:
“Saccaka, what do you think? You say, ‘Perception is my self.’ Can you exercise power over that perception, saying, ‘Let my perception be thus, let my perception not be thus’?” 

“No, Master Gotama,” Saccaka replied. 

“Saccaka, consider well! Consider and then answer. Your former statement and your latter statement do not agree.” Having said this, the Blessed One asked Saccaka: 

“Saccaka, what do you think? You say, ‘Mental formations are my self.’ Can you exercise power over those mental formations, saying, ‘Let my mental formations be thus, let my mental formations not be thus’?” 

“No, Master Gotama,” Saccaka replied. 

“Saccaka, consider well! Consider and then answer. Your former statement and your latter statement do not agree.” Having said this, the Blessed One asked Saccaka: 

“Saccaka, what do you think? You say, ‘The six types of consciousness are my self.’
456:
Can you exercise power over those six types of consciousness, saying, ‘Let my consciousness be thus, let my consciousness not be thus’?” 

“No, Master Gotama,” Saccaka replied. 

“Saccaka, consider well! Consider and then answer. Your former statement and your latter statement do not agree,” said the Blessed One. 

Then, the Blessed One, wishing to discipline Saccaka with the “Te-parivaṭṭa-dhamma-desanā” (the teaching repeated in three rounds for each point), asked: 

(a) “Saccaka, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?” 

Saccaka replied, “Impermanent, Master Gotama.” (I) 

“Is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?” 

When the Blessed One asked this, Saccaka replied, “It is suffering, Master Gotama.” (II) 

“Is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as ‘This is mine’ (through craving), ‘This I am’ (through pride), or ‘This is my self’ (through wrong view)?”
457:
When the Blessed One asked this, Saccaka the wanderer replied, "It is not fit, Master Gotama." (III)

(b-c-d) "Saccaka, what do you think about this? Is feeling... perception... mental formations..."

(e) "Saccaka, what do you think about this? Is the sixfold consciousness—that is, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing—permanent or impermanent?"

When asked thus, Saccaka the wanderer replied, "Impermanent, Master Gotama." (I)

"Is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?"

When the Blessed One asked this, Saccaka the wanderer replied, "It is suffering, Master Gotama." (II)

"Is it fit to regard that sixfold consciousness, which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, thus: 'This consciousness is mine (through craving), this consciousness I am (through conceit), this consciousness is my self (through wrong view)'?"

When the Blessed One asked this, Saccaka the wanderer replied, "It is not fit, Master Gotama." (III)
458:
In this way, just as a skilled snake-doctor (Alampāyana) might make the very snake that bit a person suck back its own venom from the wound, so too, in the midst of the Licchavī assembly, the Blessed One made Saccaka the wanderer—who had previously asserted that the five aggregates are permanent, pleasant, and self—admit with his own mouth that the five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and non-self. (The venom of the 'self' doctrine that had issued from Saccaka's mouth was thus extracted by making him admit 'non-self' in the midst of the assembly).

Through this sequence of discourse, the Blessed One made Saccaka the wanderer openly admit in the midst of the assembly that "the five aggregates are impermanent, suffering, and non-self." Now, wishing to further discipline and subdue Saccaka so that he would sit with his head bowed and face downcast, the Buddha questioned him again as follows:

"Saccaka, what do you think about this? Suppose a person clings to suffering, is attached to suffering, is immersed in suffering, and regards suffering (the five aggregates) thus: 'This suffering is mine (through craving), this suffering I am (through conceit), this suffering is my self (through wrong view).' Could such a person, indeed, fully understand suffering (through the three types of full understanding)?"
459:
"Or could he dwell having exhausted the suffering that is the five aggregates?"

When asked thus, Saccaka the wanderer replied, "Master Gotama, how could that be possible? Master Gotama, it is certainly not possible." Then the Blessed One continued to Saccaka:

"Saccaka, what do you think about this? This being so, are you not one who clings to suffering (the five aggregates), is attached to suffering, is immersed in suffering, and regards that very suffering thus: 'This suffering is mine (through craving), this suffering I am (through conceit), this suffering is my self (through wrong view)'?"

When asked thus, Saccaka the wanderer admitted, "Master Gotama, how could it be otherwise? O Master Gotama, I do so regard it." Then the Blessed One said to Saccaka:

"Saccaka, it is as if a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, were to take a sharp axe and enter a forest. There he might see a young banana tree, straight and tall, without a core. He would cut it at the root and the tip..."
460:
"...and after cutting it, he would peel the leaf-sheaths. Peeling it, he would not even find softwood, let alone heartwood.

Saccaka, in the same way, when you are cross-examined, questioned, and rebuked by me concerning your own doctrine, you are found to be empty, hollow, and utterly defeated.

Saccaka, you said in the assembly at Vesālī: 'I do not see any leader of a group, leader of a sect, teacher of a sect, even one who claims to be an Arahant, a Fully Enlightened One, who would not shake, tremble, and sweat from the armpits if I were to challenge them in debate. Even a mindless post would shake and tremble if I challenged it in debate; how much more a human being?' Saccaka, now some drops of sweat are falling from your forehead, soaking through your outer robe and falling to the ground. But on my body, Saccaka, there is no sweat now."

Having said this, the Blessed One revealed his golden-hued body to the assembly.

[Note: It cannot be said that there is no sweat at all in a physical body (upādinnaka-kāya); therefore, the Buddha spoke with reference to that specific time (there is no sweat now). Regarding the phrase 'revealed his golden-hued body,' the Blessed One did not reveal his entire body...]
461:
[...The Buddhas, whose bodies are always covered with robes fastened with a belt, usually preach to the assembly in that manner. At that time, however, the Blessed One took hold of his robe at the throat and opened it about four finger-breadths, then let it fall. As soon as he lowered the robe about four finger-breadths, golden rays of light (pīta-rasmi) burst forth in clusters, like a stream of molten red gold from a crucible or like lightning from a dark red cloud. These rays circled his noble head, which was like a golden drum, in a clockwise direction and ascended into the sky.

Why did the Blessed One do this? He did this to dispel the doubts of the multitude. To elaborate: if the Blessed One had not revealed it, the people might have doubted, thinking, "The recluse Gotama says, 'I have no sweat,' but we clearly see drops of sweat on Saccaka's body. The recluse Gotama, however, remains wrapped in a thick double-layered robe; how can we know whether there is sweat inside or not?" He did this to remove such doubts from the people.]

When the Blessed One had spoken, Saccaka the wanderer sat silent, dejected, with his neck drooping and head bowed, brooding and at a loss for words.

## The Speech of Prince Dummukha Licchavī

Then the Licchavī prince named Dummukha, seeing Saccaka sitting silent, dejected, with his neck drooping and head bowed, brooding and at a loss for words, said, "Venerable Blessed One, a simile has occurred to me."
462:
When he said this, the Blessed One said, "Dummukha, let the simile occur to you." Then Prince Dummukha said to the Blessed One:

"Venerable Blessed One, suppose there is a pond near a village or town, and in that pond there is a crab. Then a crowd of boys and girls might go out from that village or town to the pond, enter the water, pull the crab out, and place it on dry land. Venerable Blessed One, whenever that crab extends a leg, those boys and girls would cut it off, break it, or smash it with a stick or a shard. Venerable Blessed One, thus that crab, with all its legs cut, broken, and smashed, would be unable to return to the pond as before. In the same way, Venerable Blessed One, all of Saccaka's distorted doctrines, his wriggling and stirrings, have been cut, broken, and smashed by the Blessed One. Venerable Blessed One, now Saccaka is unable to approach the Blessed One again for the purpose of debating doctrines."

When he had spoken, Saccaka the wanderer said to Prince Dummukha, "Stop, Dummukha!"
463:
"Stop, Dummukha! (Dummukha, you are a harsh-spoken person). We are not conferring with you; we are conferring with Master Gotama."

(Note: While Prince Dummukha was presenting the simile to the Blessed One, the other Licchavī princes thought, "This ascetic has long looked down on us during his teaching. Now is the time to see the enemy's back. We should each bring a simile and strike Saccaka the wanderer down, like hitting a man already floored by a fist with a pestle, so that he never dares raise his head in the assembly again." Saccaka sensed their intention and thought, "All these Licchavī princes are waiting for their chance with heads raised and lips moving. If they all get to present their similes, I will never be able to raise my head again. I will rebuke Dummukha now and cut off the others so they cannot speak, and then I will question the recluse Gotama." Thus, he rebuked Dummukha as mentioned above).

Then Saccaka the wanderer, cutting off the others so they could not intervene, said to the Blessed One:

"Master Gotama, let the talk of us and other recluses and brahmins be."
464:
(Let it be). (All those words) are merely words spoken at random, like the incoherent babbling of one who is delirious. To what extent, Master Gotama, is a disciple of Master Gotama one who follows the teaching, one who follows instructions, one who has crossed over doubt, is free from 'how' and 'why' (uncertainty), has attained confidence (in knowledge and vision), and dwells in the Dispensation of the Blessed One without needing to rely on others?"

Thus he asked. Then the Blessed One said to Saccaka the Nigantha-son:

"Saccaka, here a disciple of mine views any kind of form whatsoever—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form as it really is with right wisdom through insight-knowledge and the knowledge of the Path thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.' He views any kind of feeling... (p)... any kind of perception... (p)... any kind of mental formations... (p)... any kind of consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all these six groups of consciousness as they really are with insight-knowledge and the knowledge of the Path thus: 'This group of consciousness is not mine, this group of consciousness I am not, this group of consciousness is not my self.'
465:
Saccaka, to this extent, a disciple of mine is one who follows the teaching, one who follows instructions, one who has crossed over doubt, is free from 'how' and 'why' (uncertainty), has attained confidence (in knowledge and vision), and dwells in the Dispensation of the Blessed One without needing to rely on others."

Thus the Blessed One replied.

(In the terminology of the Dispensation, the three lower Fruitions of the Supramundane are called the 'plane of the trainee' (sekha-bhūmi), the dwelling place of the noble trainees. The Fruition of Arahantship is called the 'plane of the non-trainee' (asekha-bhūmi), the dwelling place of the Arahant. Indeed, the four Fruitions are called the 'plane of the Noble Ones' (ariya-bhūmi), the dwelling place of the Noble Ones. By the previously mentioned words 'he views,' indicating that the action of viewing is not yet completed, the plane of the trainee was taught. Now, wishing to ask about the plane of the non-trainee, Saccaka asks the following question, and the Blessed One answers. In this upcoming exchange, Saccaka the Nigantha-son does not understand the technical terms 'plane of the trainee' and 'plane of the non-trainee'; however, he perceives that with the extent of knowledge described as 'viewing' (still in progress), the monk's task is not yet finished. Therefore, he continues to ask about the plane of the non-trainee as follows.)

"Master Gotama, to what extent is a monk an Arahant—one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden (of the aggregates, defilements, and volitional formations), attained his own goal (the Fruition of Arahantship), whose fetters of existence are
466:
totally destroyed, and who is liberated through right knowledge?"

Thus he asked. Then the Blessed One said to Saccaka the Nigantha-son:

"Saccaka, here a monk views any kind of form whatsoever—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all form as it really is with right insight-wisdom and the wisdom of the Path thus: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self,' and having so seen it, he is liberated through non-clinging. He views any kind of feeling... (p)... any kind of perception... (p)... any kind of mental formations... (p). Any kind of consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all these six groups of consciousness as they really are with insight-knowledge and the knowledge of the Path thus: 'This group of consciousness is not mine, this group of consciousness I am not, this group of consciousness is not my self,' and having so seen this group of the six types of consciousness, he is liberated through non-clinging.

Saccaka, to this extent, a monk is an Arahant—one whose taints are destroyed, who has lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden (of the aggregates, defilements, and volitional formations), attained his own goal (the Fruition of Arahantship), whose fetters of existence are
467:
totally destroyed, and who is liberated through right knowledge."

After answering thus, the Blessed One continued to describe the virtues of that Arahant:

"Saccaka, a monk whose mind is thus liberated is endowed with three excellences: excellence in vision, excellence in practice, and excellence in liberation. Saccaka, a (Arahant) monk whose mind is thus liberated, performs acts of respect, reverence, and veneration only toward the Blessed One, thinking:

'That Blessed One, our Teacher, is himself enlightened (having penetrated the Four Noble Truths) and he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the enlightenment of sentient beings who are like lotuses ready to bloom.

That Blessed One, our Teacher, is himself tamed and he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the taming of sentient beings who are like lotuses ready to bloom.

That Blessed One, our Teacher, is himself at peace (having stilled all defilements) and he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the peace of sentient beings who are like lotuses ready to bloom.

That Blessed One, our Teacher, has himself crossed over the four floods and he teaches the Dhamma so that sentient beings who are like lotuses ready to bloom may also cross over the four floods.

That Blessed One, our Teacher, has himself attained Nibbāna (the cooling of defilements) and
468:
he teaches the Dhamma so that sentient beings who are like lotuses ready to bloom may also attain Nibbāna.'"

Thus He spoke.

Buddho bodhāya desesi,
Danto yo damathāya ca,
Samathāya santo dhammaṃ,
Tiṇṇova taraṇāya ca.
Nibbuto nibbānatthāya,
Taṃ lokasaraṇaṃ name.

Buddho = Our Blessed One, the Supreme Buddha, the pinnacle of the world. Buddho = Because He has personally and clearly realized the Noble Truths. Bodhāya ca = And in order that all those worthy of liberation may likewise realize them. Danto = Because He is himself tamed. Damathāya ca = And in order that all those worthy of liberation may likewise be tamed. Santo = Because He has himself stilled all defilements. Samathāya ca = And in order that all those worthy of liberation may likewise be at peace. Tiṇṇova = Because He has himself crossed over the rough waters of the four floods. Taraṇāya ca = And in order that all those worthy of liberation may likewise be able to cross over. Nibbuto = Because He has attained Nibbāna, the cooling of defilements.
469:
Nibbānatthāya ca = And in order that all those worthy of liberation may likewise be cooled and at peace. Dhammaṃ = The profound Dhamma of the four Truths. Desesi = He has taught out of compassion. Lokasaraṇaṃ = To that Supreme Buddha, the pinnacle of the world, who is the unique refuge of the three worlds. Taṃ Buddhaṃ = To that Blessed One known as the Omniscient Buddha. Namo—namāmi = I pay homage, bowing my head with joined palms in devotion, humbling my pride through body, speech, and mind, O Blessed One.

## Inviting the Blessed One for a Meal

When the Blessed One had finished teaching, culminating in the Fruition of Arahantship, Saccaka the Nigantha-son said to the Blessed One:

"O Master Gotama, we were mistaken in thinking we could attack Master Gotama in debate. (Thus) we were indeed those who disparage virtues. We were harsh in speech and arrogant in our words.

O Master Gotama, to use an analogy to make it clear: a man might find safety even after attacking a rogue elephant. But there is no safety at all for a man who attacks Master Gotama. (1)

O Master Gotama, a man might find safety even after attacking a great mass of blazing fire.
470:
But there is no safety at all for a man who attacks Master Gotama. (2)

O Master Gotama, a man might find safety even after attacking a snake with swift poison, a snake with fierce poison. But there is no safety at all for a man who attacks Master Gotama. (3)

O Master Gotama, we were mistaken in thinking we could attack Master Gotama in debate. (Thus) we were indeed those who disparage virtues. We were harsh in speech and arrogant in our words."

Thus he spoke.

[Note: By the phrase "there is no safety at all for a man who attacks Master Gotama," it means that no one who attacks Master Gotama in debate is able to leave with their own doctrine intact and unshaken as it was originally; they only return with their own doctrine shattered and destroyed. Indeed, the Blessed One does not harm the life of anyone, unlike rogue elephants, great fires, or poisonous snakes.

Furthermore, Saccaka the Nigantha-son did not use these three analogies merely to praise the Blessed One, but rather to praise himself. (For example), when a king has oppressed, tortured, or killed an enemy, he might say of that killed enemy, "That man was indeed a brave man."]
471:
Just as one might praise an enemy, saying, 'He is endowed with such power,' yet indirectly praises oneself, so too did Saccaka the Wanderer (Paribbājaka) praise the Blessed One with three similes. However, by saying, 'We have approached the Blessed One—who is difficult for ordinary people to approach, like an intoxicated bull elephant, like a great blazing forest fire, or like a venomous cobra with its hood raised—with the intent to challenge his doctrine; therefore, in this world, we alone are the brave, the wise, and the learned,' he was indirectly praising only himself. [This is a point of special note.]

After Saccaka the Wanderer had indirectly praised himself in this manner, he addressed the Blessed One, saying, 'May the Venerable Gotama, together with the Saṅgha of monks, accept my meal tomorrow for the sake of merit.' The Blessed One accepted the invitation of Saccaka the Wanderer by remaining silent.

Then Saccaka the Wanderer, knowing that the Blessed One had accepted, said to the Licchavī princes, 'Listen to my words, O Licchavīs! I have invited the ascetic Gotama together with the Saṅgha of monks for tomorrow’s meal for the sake of merit. Bring to me whatever food you think is suitable for the ascetic Gotama.' Then, when the night had passed, the Licchavī princes sent about five hundred pots of rice to Saccaka the Wanderer. Saccaka the Wanderer then had choice hard and soft foods prepared in his own park and sent word to the Blessed One that it was time, saying, 'Venerable Gotama, it is time for the meal; the meal is ready.'
472:
Then the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, approached the park of Saccaka the Wanderer and sat down on the prepared seat together with the Saṅgha of monks. Then Saccaka the Wanderer personally served and satisfied the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with choice hard and soft foods until they refused more.

Then Saccaka the Wanderer, knowing that the Blessed One had finished his meal, sat down in a suitable place and addressed the Blessed One:

'O Venerable Gotama, may the root merit of this gift (the future resultant aggregates) and the great secondary benefits (such as the five regalia of a king, etc.) be for the happiness of the donors (the Licchavī princes).'

(Saccaka said this thinking, 'I have served the ascetic Gotama and his disciples with the food provided by the Licchavī princes; therefore, this merit belongs only to the Licchavī princes.') However, the meal was actually given to the Blessed One and the Saṅgha by Saccaka the Wanderer, not by the Licchavī princes. (The Licchavīs gave the food to Saccaka, and it was Saccaka who then offered it to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha). Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to correct Saccaka's view and understanding, said:

'Saccaka, the gift given to a recipient who is not yet free from passion, hatred, and delusion (referring to yourself) will be for the benefit of the donors (the Licchavīs).'
473:
'Saccaka, the gift given by you to a recipient who is free from passion, hatred, and delusion (referring to me) will be for your own benefit.'

The Buddha said this so that Saccaka might gain a wholesome tendency (vāsanā) for the future.

## Preaching the Mahāsaccaka Sutta
What has been described above is the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta. The Blessed One did not preach only this Cūḷasaccaka Sutta to Saccaka the Wanderer; he also preached the Mahāsaccaka Sutta at another time. In that Mahāsaccaka Sutta, he preached in detail the analysis of the development of the body (kāya-bhāvanā) and the development of the mind (citta-bhāvanā), as well as the confused person and the unconfused person. For the details of the Mahāsaccaka Sutta, one should refer to the Myanmar translation of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa Pāḷi (starting from page 308).

## Saccaka’s Benefit of Wholesome Tendency
The Blessed One preached these two suttas, the Cūḷasaccaka Sutta and the Mahāsaccaka Sutta, to Saccaka the Wanderer. The Cūḷasaccaka Sutta consists of one recitation section (bhāṇavāra). The Mahāsaccaka Sutta consists of one and a half recitation sections. Thus, even after hearing such extensive teachings totaling two and a half recitation sections, Saccaka did not attain the Paths and Fruits, nor did he ordain as a monk, nor did he even establish himself in the Refuges.
474:
One might ask: why did the Blessed One preach such extensive Dhamma to Saccaka the Wanderer if this was the case?

The brief answer is: He preached it so that Saccaka would gain a wholesome tendency (vāsanā) for the Dhamma in the future. The detailed answer is: The Blessed One, through his knowledge of the future (anāgataṃsa-ñāṇa), saw that 'Saccaka the Wanderer does not have the supporting conditions (upanissaya) to attain the Paths and Fruits in this present life during my time. However, more than two hundred years after my Parinibbāna, the Sasana will flourish on the island of Sri Lanka (Sīhaḷadīpa). At that time, this Saccaka the Wanderer will be reborn into a family of ministers in Sri Lanka. Upon reaching maturity, he will ordain, master the Tipiṭaka, develop insight (vipassanā), and attain Arahantship together with the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), becoming the great Arahant Mahāthera named Kāḷabuddharakkhita.' Seeing this future event, the Blessed One preached the extensive Dhamma of two and a half recitation sections to Saccaka the Wanderer so that he would have the wholesome tendency for the Dhamma later on.

When the sun of the Sasana shone on the island of Sri Lanka, Saccaka the Wanderer passed away from the celestial realm and was reborn into a family of ministers in the village that served as the alms-resort (gocara-gāma) for the Dakkhinagiri Monastery. When he reached the age for ordination, he became a monk, mastered the word of the Buddha known as the Tipiṭaka, became a leader of a group (gaṇa), and, surrounded by many disciple monks, went to pay respects to his preceptor (upajjhāya).
475:
At that time, the preceptor of the group-leader Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita, intending to rebuke his resident pupil (saddhivihārika), remained without even speaking face-to-face with the Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita, who had arrived after mastering the Tipiṭaka.

Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita rose at dawn, went to the presence of his preceptor, the Mahāthera, and asked, 'Venerable Sir, I have come to you after completing my scriptural studies, yet you do not even speak to me face-to-face. What fault do I have?' Then the preceptor Mahāthera asked, 'Buddharakkhita, do you think that merely by mastering the word of the Buddha—the five Nikāyas and the Tipiṭaka—you have reached the summit of a monk's duty?' When the pupil Buddharakkhita asked, 'Venerable Sir, if that is so, what should I do?', the preceptor Mahāthera replied, 'You must cut off the obstruction of the group (gaṇa-palibodha), abandon the expansion of the remaining defilements, go to Cetiyapabbata Monastery, and strive in the Dhamma of a monk.'

Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita, abiding by the advice of his preceptor Mahāthera, practiced the Dhamma of a monk with great effort and became an Arahant who had attained the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-patta). He became a famous person of great merit, honored by kings, and resided at Cetiyapabbata Monastery itself, surrounded by a large assembly of monks.
476:
## The Story of King Tissa Listening to the Dhamma
At that time, King Tissa was observing the Uposatha and staying in the cave named Rāja at Cetiyapabbata. The King instructed the monk who served Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita, saying, 'Venerable Sir, when my master, the noble Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita, answers a question or preaches the Dhamma, please inform me.' On a certain day of a Dhamma assembly, Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita, surrounded by a large assembly of monks, ascended to the courtyard of the cetiya named 'Kaṇṭaka,' paid homage to the cetiya, and stood at the foot of a black plum tree.

Then, a certain Elder who practiced the dhutaṅga of alms-round (piṇḍapātika) asked Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita a question regarding the Kāḷakārāma Sutta (from the Catukka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya). When Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita asked the piṇḍapātika Elder, 'Friend, is today not the day for listening to the Dhamma?', the piṇḍapātika Elder replied that it was indeed so. Then Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita said, 'Friends, if that is so, bring a small bench—a Dhamma-preaching seat. Let us listen to the Dhamma right here; let us hold a Dhamma assembly.' Thereupon, they prepared a Dhamma seat (dhammāsana) for the noble Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita at the foot of that very black plum tree.

Elder Kāḷabuddharakkhita, after reciting the introductory verses of the Dhamma, began to preach the Kāḷakārāma Sutta found in the Catukka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Pāḷi. The young monk who was the attendant of the Elder also—
477:
He had the King informed according to the instructions given. 

King Tissa arrived at the place where the Dhamma was being preached even before the introductory verses of the Dhamma were finished. Upon arrival, he stood at the edge of the assembly in the guise of an ordinary person, listening to the Dhamma while standing throughout the three watches of the night. When the Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita concluded the sermon, the King uttered words of appreciation and praise (Sādhu). Recognizing that it was the King, the Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita asked, “At what time did you arrive, Great King?” When the King replied, “I arrived just as you were reciting the introductory verses of the Dhamma, Bhante,” the Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita remarked, “Great King, you have indeed performed a difficult task.” King Tissa then said, “Bhante, this act (of standing all night to listen to the Dhamma) is not a difficult task. Indeed, from the moment you began preaching the Dhamma, my mind did not wander to any other object even for a single word or phrase. If it had, may I not even possess sovereignty over a piece of land the size of a goad-stick in this island of Laṅkā.” Thus, he made a bold and solemn declaration.

## The Infinite Nature of the Buddha’s Virtues

In that Kāḷakārāma Sutta, the virtues of the Buddha were preached. Therefore, King Tissa asked the Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita, “Bhante, are the virtues of the Buddha only this many, or are there other virtues of the Buddha as well?” “Great King...
478:
The virtues that have not yet been preached are incomparably more numerous than the virtues of the Buddha I have just revealed,” replied the Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita.

Then the King requested, “Bhante, please provide a simile.” The Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita said, “Great King, just as in a vast field of hill-paddy about a thousand 'pe' in extent, the grains of rice remaining in the rest of the field are far more numerous than the grains of rice contained in a single ear of paddy; in the same way, the virtues of the Buddha I have now revealed are but a few (like the grains in a single ear), while the remaining virtues are far more numerous (like the grains in the rest of the vast field).” (1)

Again, King Tissa requested, “Bhante, please provide another simile as well.” The Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita said, “Great King, if one were to place the eye of a needle directly into the flowing current of the great River Ganges, the water flowing through the eye of the needle would be very little, while the remaining water in the current would be vast. In the same way, the virtues of the Buddha I have now revealed are but a few (like the water passing through the eye of a needle), while the remaining virtues are far more numerous (like the water in the rest of the great River Ganges).” (2)
479:
Then again, the King requested, “Bhante, please provide another simile as well.” The Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita asked, “Great King, in this world, there are small birds called rain-birds (or swallows) that fly and roam joyfully in the sky. Those birds are very small. What do you think, Great King? Is the space covered by the spread wings of that bird in the sky greater, or is the remaining space of the sky greater?” The King replied, “Bhante, what are you saying? The space in the sky covered by the spread wings of that small bird is insignificantly small, while the remaining space of the sky is vast.” The Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita then said, “Great King, in the same way, the virtues of the Buddha I have now revealed are but a few (like the space covered by the wings of a swallow), while the remaining virtues are far more numerous (like the vastness of the remaining sky).” (3)

At that time, King Tissa said, “Bhante, you have preached well by comparing the infinite virtues of the Buddha with the infinite sky. We are greatly devoted to you, Bhante. However, we are unable to make an offering that is worthy and suitable for you. We offer to you, Bhante, the kingship of this island of Laṅkā, which is three hundred yojanas in circumference. This gift is but a poor man’s humble offering to you, Bhante.”
480:
(In this context, King Tissa’s kingship or royal splendor was that of a regional monarch. The Dhamma discourse regarding the virtues of the Buddha preached by the Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita was of priceless value. Therefore, the King referred to his own kingship and royal splendor as a “poor man’s humble offering”).

The Venerable Kāḷabuddharakkhita also said, “Great King, you have performed an act of your faith and devotion. As for us, we return the kingship and royal splendor you have offered to us back to you. Rule the country and exercise kingship in accordance with the Dhamma.” Thus, he gave the royal splendor back to King Tissa.

(Dhamma Instruction: Following the practice of this Arahant Kāḷabuddharakkhita, if rulers who govern a country offer worldly possessions, royal requisites, or royal splendor that are unsuitable for monks out of great faith in the Dhamma, those offerings should be returned to the royal donors.)

Note: In this chapter concerning the fifth Vassa, it was intended to write about the Buddha’s second visit to the island of Laṅkā to preach to the Naga kings Cūḷodara and Mahodara, who were uncle and nephew. However, as I wish to present the Buddha’s three visits to Laṅkā together in one place, I will not write about it here but will explain the three events together when reaching the chapter on the eighth Vassa.

## Here ends Chapter 23.
481:
## Chapter 24
## The Buddha Spending the Sixth Vassa at Mount Makula

The Buddha, having spent the fifth Vassa in the Mahāvana forest of Vesālī as mentioned before, and having provided the deathless nectar of the Dhamma to the devas, humans, and brahmas who were ready for liberation during that Vassa, traveled on a journey (cārikā) to various towns and villages such as Sāvatthī and Rājagaha to benefit the world of beings when the fifth Vassa ended, providing them with the deathless nectar of the Dhamma.

## Two Types of Journeys

There are two types of the Buddha's journeys: (1) Turitacārikā = an urgent or fast journey; (2) Aturitacārikā = a regular journey from town to town and village to village, traveling a set distance such as one or two leagues (yojana) daily.

Among them, even if a place is many leagues away, if the Buddha sees a person who is ready for liberation, the type of journey he takes urgently to liberate that person is called "Turitacārikā." This Turitacārikā journey should be understood in instances such as going to meet the Venerable Mahākassapa. Indeed, when the Buddha went to meet the Elder Mahākassapa, he traveled and waited at a distance of three gāvutas (approx. 9 miles) in just a moment. Also, to liberate the ogre Āḷavaka...
482:
He traveled a distance of thirty yojanas in a single moment. The same was true for the liberation of the robber Angulimāla. To liberate King Pukkusāti (who had come to be ordained), he traveled a distance of forty-five yojanas in a single moment. To liberate King Mahā Kappina, he traveled a distance of one hundred and twenty yojanas in a single moment. To liberate the wealthy cattle-owner Dhaniya and his wife, he traveled a distance of seven hundred yojanas in a single moment. Such rapid journeys are called Turita-cārikā.

When the Buddha had spent the Vassa in various towns and villages and the retreat ended, he would depart from those places and travel one or two yojanas a day through the sequence of villages and market towns. He would benefit the people by going on alms round and preaching the Dhamma in those villages and towns. Such beneficial travel is called Aturita-cārikā.

## Three Types of Circuits

The Buddha, while performing this Aturita-cārikā, would travel in one of the following three types of circuits: (1) Mahā-maṇḍala = the largest circuit, (2) Majjhima-maṇḍala = the middle circuit, and (3) Anto-maṇḍala = the smallest circuit.
483:
Among these three types of circuits: (1) The Mahā-maṇḍala circuit is nine hundred (900) yojanas. (2) The Majjhima-maṇḍala circuit is six hundred (600) yojanas. (3) The Anto-maṇḍala circuit is three hundred (300) yojanas.

(1) To clarify further: When the Buddha had spent the Vassa in various towns and villages and the retreat ended, if there was no special reason to wait for beings ready for liberation in that place, he would perform the Pavāraṇā on the full moon day of Thadingyut. On the first waning day, surrounded by a large assembly of monks, he would travel one or two yojanas a day. This travel would continue until the full moon of Waso the following year, lasting for nine (9) months.

During such travel, the towns and villages where the Buddha arrived would be the center, and for a hundred yojanas in all four directions—front, back, left, and right—there would be a great and bustling commotion. Only those who arrived first would have the opportunity to invite the Buddha. Offerings and honors from the other two circuits would flow into this Mahā-maṇḍala. In this Mahā-maṇḍala circuit, the Buddha would stay for one or two days in various villages and towns, benefiting the people by accepting material offerings such as alms-food, and by preaching the Dhamma, he would increase the people's wholesome deeds leading to the end of the cycle of rebirth (vivaṭṭanissita-kusala). He would complete the journey in a period of nine months.
484:
(= This means he traveled on a journey for nine months).

The straight distance of that nine-month journey is exactly three hundred (300) yojanas. Taking that three hundred yojanas as the center, the multitude of people within three hundred yojanas to the left and three hundred yojanas to the right performed meritorious deeds such as offering alms-food and other material requisites to the Blessed One, and listening to the Dhamma preached by the Blessed One. Thus, he had already traveled to those regions within three hundred yojanas to the left and three hundred yojanas to the right. Therefore, it was said previously: "(1) The circumference of the Mahāmaṇḍala (Great Circle) is nine hundred (900) yojanas."

(2) During the rainy season retreat (Vassa), if the monks' Samatha and Vipassanā (tranquillity and insight), or concentration and wisdom, have not yet matured, the Blessed One does not perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony on the full moon day of Thadingyut. Instead, he extends the period until the full moon day of Tazaungmon. Only on that full moon day of Tazaungmon does he perform the Pavāraṇā. Then, on the first waning day of that month, surrounded by a company of monks, he sets out on a journey and resides within the circumference of the Majjhimamaṇḍala (Middle Circle). For other reasons as well, when the Blessed One wishes to travel within the Majjhimamaṇḍala, he stays in various villages and market towns where he spent the Vassa for the full four months (until the full moon of Tazaungmon) before setting out on his journey. As mentioned before, the offerings and honor that occur in the other two circles are also present in the Majjhimamaṇḍala.
485:
The Blessed One, favoring the world (the multitude of people) in the same manner as before, completes his journey in a period of eight months (= This means he traveled on a journey for eight months).

The straight distance of that eight-month journey is exactly two hundred (200) yojanas. Taking that two hundred yojanas as the center, the multitude of people within two hundred yojanas to the left and two hundred yojanas to the right performed meritorious deeds such as offering material requisites and listening to the Dhamma. Thus, he had already traveled to those regions of two hundred yojanas each to the left and right. Therefore, it was said previously: "(2) The circumference of the Majjhimamaṇḍala is six hundred (600) yojanas."

(3) Although the Blessed One resides for the four months of the rainy season (until the full moon of Tazaungmon), if the beings to be liberated in those villages and market towns have not yet matured in their spiritual faculties (indriya), he waits for the maturation of those faculties. He continues to stay in those same locations for one more month (until the full moon of Nadaw), or two months (until the full moon of Pyatho), or three months (until the full moon of Tabodwe), or four months (until the full moon of Tabaung). Only then, surrounded by a large company of monks, does he set out on a journey (within the Antomaṇḍala). As mentioned before, the offerings and honor that occur in the other two circles are also present in the Antomaṇḍala.
486:
The Blessed One, favoring the world in the same manner as before, completes his journey in a period of seven months, or six months, or five months, or four months (= This means he traveled on a journey for seven, six, five, or four months).

Because the time for such a journey of seven, six, five, or four months is short, the straight distance is one hundred (100) yojanas. As in the previous manner, since he had already traveled to the regions of one hundred yojanas each to the left and right, it was said previously: "(3) The circumference of the Antomaṇḍala (Inner Circle) is three hundred (300) yojanas."

In this way, when the Blessed One travels in any one of these three circles, he does not travel for the sake of obtaining robes, alms-food, lodgings, or medicines (the four requisites). Rather, he reflects and considers: "The poor, the ignorant, the elderly, and the sick will never be able to come to my presence. If I travel on a journey, all these aforementioned people will have the opportunity to see the Buddha. Among those people, some will gain clarity of mind in me; some will make offerings with flowers, scents, and so on; some will offer even a single ladle of alms-food; some will abandon and discard wrong views and become those with right view (Sammādiṭṭhi). Such occurrences will be for their long-term...
487:
...welfare and happiness." Thus, he travels on a journey solely out of compassion for the multitude of people. (From the Commentary to the Dīgha Nikāya, Vol. 1, p. 216).

After the Blessed One spent his fifth Vassa at the Mahāvana forest in the city of Vesālī, when the Vassa was over, for the sake of favoring the world of beings, he traveled to Sāvatthī, Rājagaha, and various other villages and market towns (by way of one of the three aforementioned circles). Having nourished them with the cooling water of Dhamma, the medicine of the Deathless, he spent his sixth (saṭṭha) Vassa at the Makuḷa Mountain monastery, which had a fence of star-flower (chayā) trees, near the ocean. There he resided, nourishing the devas, humans, and Brahmās who were ready for liberation with the cooling water of Dhamma, the medicine of the Deathless.

## The Story of the Rājagaha Treasurer's Sandalwood Alms-bowl

After the Blessed One spent his sixth Vassa at the Makuḷa Mountain monastery, he rose from that retreat and traveled by stages until he reached the city of Rājagaha, where he resided at the Veḷuvana Monastery.

While the Blessed One was residing at the Veḷuvana Monastery in Rājagaha, one day the Treasurer of Rājagaha wished to play in the waters of the Ganges. To ensure safety upstream and downstream from his bathing place, and to prevent the loss of any ornaments that might accidentally slip off due to forgetfulness, he had nets cast around the four sides in the shape of a casket. He then played freely in the Ganges with his attendants.
488:
At that time, the roots of a red sandalwood tree growing on the upper bank of the Ganges were eroded by the water, causing the tree to fall and float away. As it drifted, it struck various rocks and crags along the way, breaking into fragments and becoming scattered. One piece of red sandalwood, about the size of a water pot, having been struck against rocks and buffeted by various waves, became a smooth and polished block of wood. As it continued to float down, it became entangled in the nets set around the Rājagaha Treasurer's bathing place, surrounded by water weeds. The Treasurer's attendants took that block of red sandalwood and presented it to him.

At that time, the Rājagaha Treasurer was neither a person of right view nor a person of wrong view; he was simply a person of neutral disposition, uncommitted to any religion. Thus, he had the sandalwood block brought to his house and ordered it to be cut and planed with the tip of an adze. Upon realizing it was high-quality red sandalwood with the color of lac and a fragrant, delightful scent, he thought: "I have many kinds of sandalwood in my house. What use should I make of this sandalwood block I have just obtained?" After considering this, the following thought occurred to him:

"In this world, there are many who claim, 'We are Arahants, we are Arahants.' I do not know for certain, by distinguishing and analyzing, even a single person who is truly an Arahant. I will have a lathe set up in my house and...
489:
...have this block of red sandalwood turned into an alms-bowl. (I will use the shavings, but the bowl itself I will offer). After placing this red sandalwood bowl in a mesh bag, I will have it suspended in the air at a height of about sixty (60) cubits by joining bamboo poles together. Then I will announce: 'Let the person who is truly an Arahant come through the air and take this sandalwood bowl.' I will support, along with my wife and children, the Arahant who can fly through the air by means of psychic power and take this sandalwood bowl (according to my announcement)."
