This was his thought. According to his plan, the Treasurer had the red sandalwood block placed on a lathe and carved into an alms-bowl. He then placed the bowl in a mesh bag, had bamboo poles erected in stages, and hung the bowl sixty cubits high in the air. He then announced: "Let the person in this world who is truly an Arahant come through the air and take this bowl."

## The Six Heretical Teachers

At that time in the city of Rājagaha, there were six heretical teachers who lived as great sect leaders, claiming themselves to be Arahants. These six heretical teachers were:

(1) The teacher Pūraṇa Kassapa: His personal name was Pūraṇa. His clan name was Kassapa. Combining both name and clan, he was called the teacher Pūraṇa Kassapa.
490:
The brief history of this teacher is as follows: A certain wealthy man had ninety-nine (99) household slaves, and this man was the hundredth (100th) to be born. Therefore, they named him Pūraṇa (= meaning 'The Filler' or 'Master Hundred-Filler'). Because he was considered an auspicious slave, even when he did his work poorly, no one would say anything about it. Even if he did no work at all, no one would say he was not working.

Nevertheless, he became arrogant and thought, "Why should I live in this treasurer's house?" and ran away. While he was fleeing, thieves robbed him of his clothes. Because he was someone who did not even understand or know that he should cover himself with leaves or grass, he entered a village just as he was born (without any clothes). The villagers saw him and, through misplaced devotion, praised him, saying, "This monk is an Arahant! He is one of few desires! There is no one like this monk!" They brought cakes, alms-food, and other offerings and approached him. He thought, "These gains have come to me because I do not wear clothes." From then on, even when he obtained cloth, he would not wear it at all. Pūraṇa adopted this very practice of not wearing clothes as his monkhood. Five hundred other men also became his disciples and accepted this form of monkhood, which is the practice of not wearing clothes. In this way, Pūraṇa Kassapa became a great sect leader in the world.
491:
He became famous as a great teacher and a Buddha.

(Note: If one examines the brief account of this teacher Pūraṇa Kassapa, it is seen that initially, he did as he pleased and, after encountering the danger of thieves, ended up without clothes. It was this lack of clothing that foolish people admired, designating him as an Arahant. When the multitude designated him as an Arahant, Pūraṇa Kassapa, despite not possessing any good practice, adopted the persona of a great teacher and a Buddha as the people had designated. Then, as a leader of a sect, he felt the need for a personal doctrine. Consequently, he invented a new, erroneous, and haphazard doctrine based on whatever came to his mind. The other five sectarian teachers followed a similar path. The six types of doctrines invented by these six sectarian teachers should be noted as extracted from the Sāmaññaphala Sutta of the Sīlakkhandhavagga Pāḷi.)

(2) Makkhali Gosāla: His original name was Makkhali. Because he was born in a village named Gosāla (or alternatively, in a cowshed where cattle were kept during the rainy season), he gained the second name Gosāla. Combining the two names, he is called "Makkhali Gosāla."

A brief summary of his background is that he, like Pūraṇa, was a slave. One day, while this slave was carrying a pot of oil across a muddy area, his master warned him, "Tāta mā khali—Dear man, do not slip (be careful)." Even as he was being warned, he was heedless, slipped and fell. Fearing his master, he attempted to flee to freedom.
492:
When his master ran to him and grabbed the edge of his garment, he stripped off the cloth and fled naked to freedom. (The remaining events are similar to those of Pūraṇa Kassapa).

(3) Ajita Kesakambala: He was also a sectarian teacher. His original name was Ajita. He was known as Kesakambala because he wore a blanket woven from human hair. Combining the two names, this sectarian teacher is called "Ajita Kesakambala."

(4) Pakudha Kaccāyana: He was also a sectarian teacher. His original name was Pakudha. His lineage was the Kaccāyana lineage. Thus, combining the name and lineage, this teacher is called "Pakudha Kaccāyana." He was one who completely avoided cold water. Whether after defecating, after eating, or when smeared with any impurity, he did not perform cleansing with cold water. He only performed cleansing if he obtained hot water or rice-scum (vinegar). If he happened to cross a river or step over water on a path, he would think, "My virtue is now broken," and would proceed only after making a mound of sand and undertaking the precepts.

(5) Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta: He was also a sectarian teacher. During the time when the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna lived as wanderers (paribbājakas),
493:
they lived with this teacher. His original name was Sañjaya, and because he was the son of a man named Belaṭṭha, the two names were combined, and he was called "Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta."

(6) Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta: He was also a sectarian teacher. He was known as Nigaṇṭha because he used to say, according to his own views and perceptions, "We have no defilements that bind or harass us; we are free from the bonds and harassment of defilements." (In reality, he was not free from the bonds and harassment of defilements). His father was named Nāṭa. Because he was the son of Nāṭa, he was also called Nāṭaputta in relation to his father. Combining the two names, this teacher was called "Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta."

(This is an account extracted from the Sīlakkhandhavagga Commentary, pages 130, 131, and the Vinaya Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā, Volume III, pages 382, 383).

When the merchant of Rājagaha had the sandalwood bowl hung in the sky at the height of sixty cubits using successive bamboo poles and announced, "If there is a true Arahant in the world, let him come through the air by means of meditative absorption (jhāna) and take this bowl," first, the teacher Pūraṇa Kassapa came to the merchant and said, "Merchant, I am indeed an Arahant and one possessed of psychic power. Give the bowl to me." The merchant of Rājagaha replied, "Venerable sir, if your reverence
494:
is indeed an Arahant and possessed of psychic power, I have already offered my bowl to the Arahant who has psychic power; please take it down only by means of psychic power." He replied cleverly and skillfully. (Since Pūraṇa Kassapa was neither an Arahant nor possessed of psychic power, he could not take the bowl and went away giving up).

On the second day, Makkhali Gosāla; on the third day, Ajita Kesakambala; on the fourth day, Pakudha Kaccāyana; and on the fifth day, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta came in order and spoke just as Pūraṇa Kassapa had. The merchant of Rājagaha also replied cleverly and skillfully in the same manner as before, and those teachers also could not take the bowl and went away giving up.

On the sixth day, the teacher Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta said to his disciples, "Go, students, and tell the merchant of Rājagaha: 'This bowl is suitable only for our teacher. Do not let our teacher come through the air for the sake of a mere, insignificant wooden bowl. Give your bowl to our teacher.'" Having given these instructions, he sent his disciples to the merchant of Rājagaha.

When the disciples went and spoke to the merchant as their teacher had instructed, the merchant of Rājagaha spoke firmly, "Only he who is able to come through the air and take it, let him take it." Since Nāṭaputta himself wished to go, he gave his disciples the following signal:
495:
"I will lift one hand and one foot and act as if I am about to fly into the sky. You must then say, 'Teacher, what are you doing? Do not display the hidden quality of the Fruit of Arahantship to the people for the sake of a wooden bowl,' and you must pull me by my hands and feet and make me fall to the ground."

This was the signal he gave.

After giving that signal, Nāṭaputta went to the merchant and said, "Merchant, your bowl is not at all suitable for others. Merchant, do not let me fly into the sky for the sake of a mere, insignificant wooden bowl (meaning, do not make me fly into the sky because of a trivial wooden bowl). Give the bowl to me." The merchant of Rājagaha replied briefly and firmly, "Venerable sir, please take it only by flying into the sky."

Then Nāṭaputta said, "If that is the case, move aside, move aside," and after making his disciples move away, he lifted one hand and one foot, saying, "I shall fly into the sky." Then his disciples said, "O teacher, what kind of things are you doing? What benefit is there for you teachers in displaying the hidden quality of the Fruit of Arahantship to the people for the sake of a worthless wooden bowl?" (speaking as previously signaled), and they pulled their teacher by his hands and feet and made him fall to the ground. While still on the ground where he had fallen,
496:
Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta said to the merchant of Rājagaha, "O merchant, these disciples do not allow me to fly into the sky. (You see for yourself). Just give me the bowl." The merchant, without losing his composure, replied, "Venerable sir, please take it only by ascending into the sky."

In this way, although the six sectarian teachers tried for six days, they did not obtain the bowl.

## Ven. Moggallāna and Ven. Piṇḍola

Then, on the seventh day, the two great elders, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, thinking, "We shall enter the city of Rājagaha for alms," left the Veḷuvana Monastery. While they were robing themselves on a certain flat rock near the city of Rājagaha, some drunkards (toddy-tappers) spoke these offensive words:

"Friends, in the past, the six sectarian teachers traveled around saying, 'We are Arahants.' It has been seven days today since the merchant of Rājagaha planted bamboo poles sixty cubits high and placed a sandalwood bowl, saying, 'If there is an Arahant, let him come through the air and take it.' There is not a single person who can fly into the sky claiming, 'I am an Arahant.' Only today do we know well that there are no Arahants in the world."

Thus they spoke mockingly and offensively. Hearing those words, the Elder Mahāmoggallāna said to the Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, "Friend Bhāradvāja, do you hear what these drunkards
497:
(toddy-tappers) are saying? These drunkards, intoxicated with toddy, are speaking offensively as if they are sweeping away the entire Dispensation (Sāsana) of the Buddha. You, friend, are also one of psychic power and great majesty. Go and fetch that sandalwood bowl by traveling through the air."

The Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja said to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna, "Friend Moggallāna, you are the one who is praised and famous with the title of Etadagga as the foremost and greatest among those with psychic power. I want you, friend, to take that bowl. Only if you do not take it, will I take it." (He spoke thus out of respect and deference to the Elder Mahāmoggallāna). Then the Elder Mahāmoggallāna gave his kind permission, saying, "Friend, you take it yourself."

## Ven. Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja
## Taking the Sandalwood Bowl by Psychic Power

When the Elder Mahāmoggallāna gave his permission, the Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for supernormal knowledge (abhiññā). Emerging from that jhāna, by means of the process of supernormal knowledge (abhiññā-javana-vīthi), he caused the great flat rock (where they had robed themselves), which was three gāvutas in size, to rise into the sky like a tuft of cotton wool neatly trimmed at the edges, and he made it circle seven times above the city of Rājagaha. That great rock appeared like a massive lid or cover over the great city of Rājagaha, which was three gāvutas in extent.
498:
498
The people of the city, terrified and trembling, thinking "The great stone slab has covered and crushed us!", put winnowing trays and such on their heads and hid in whatever places they could find. On the seventh circuit, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja split the stone slab and revealed himself. When the multitude saw the Elder, they pleaded, "O Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, please hold your great stone slab firmly; do not let all of us people perish!" The Elder (while the people were watching) kicked and cast away the stone slab with the edge of his foot. The stone slab went and settled back in its original place.

When the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja stood in the air above the merchant's house, the merchant of Rājagaha saw the Elder, prostrated himself on the ground, and pleaded, "Please descend, Venerable Sir." He invited the Elder, who had descended from the sky, to sit in his house. Then, he brought down the bowl from the sky, filled it with the four sweet foods (catumadhu), and offered it to the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja.

## The Multitude Gathering and Following

When the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja took the bowl and headed towards the Veḷuvana monastery, all the people who had missed the miracle because they were away in the fields and farms gathered and pleaded, "Venerable Sir, please show the miracle to us as well," and followed closely behind the Elder. The Elder, to those various people who followed...
499:
Performing a miracle of psychic power, he arrived at the Veḷuvana Monastery.

## Prohibiting the Display of Miracles and Prescribing Training Rules
The Buddha, hearing the tumultuous noise of those people, asked the Venerable Ānanda, "Dear Ānanda, whose tumultuous noise is this?" The Venerable Ānanda replied, "Exalted Buddha, the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja flew into the sky and took down the sandalwood bowl of the Treasurer of Rājagaha. Having heard this news, a great crowd of people followed closely behind the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. This noise is the tumultuous sound of those people speaking."

Then, the Buddha had the Saṅgha of monks assembled regarding this matter and asked the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, "Dear Bhāradvāja, is it true that you took down the bowl of the Treasurer of Rājagaha by means of a miracle of psychic power?" When he replied that it was true, the Buddha rebuked the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja in many ways. After delivering a Dhamma discourse, he prescribed the training rule: "Monks, a miracle of psychic power should not be displayed. Whoever displays one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)." He further instructed, "Monks, break that sandalwood bowl into small pieces. Once broken, distribute them among the monks to be ground for eye-ointment. Monks, a wooden bowl should not be carried or used."
500:
He further prescribed the training rule: "For a monk who carries or uses one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."

## The Sectarians Speaking Provocative Words
When the sectarians (titthiyas) heard the news that "The Buddha has prescribed a training rule for his disciple monks not to display miracles of psychic power," they consulted among themselves, saying, "The disciples of the ascetic Gotama do not transgress the training rules prescribed by him even for the sake of their lives. Now we have found a good opportunity." They then went around the large and small streets of the city, boasting, "In the past, out of a sense of protecting our own dignity, we did not display our qualities of psychic power to the public for the sake of a wooden bowl. Only the disciples of the ascetic Gotama displayed them (without shame). The ascetic Gotama, being wise himself, had that bowl broken into pieces (to hide the evidence) and prescribed a training rule for his disciples. Now, we shall compete in a display of miracles with the ascetic Gotama."

## The Buddha Declaring He Will Perform a Miracle
When King Bimbisāra heard of this matter, he went to the Buddha and they engaged in a dialogue as follows:

(King Bimbisāra): "Exalted Buddha, have you prescribed a training rule for your disciples not to perform miracles of psychic power?"
501: (The Blessed One): "Yes, it is so, Great King." (The King): "Now the sectarians are going around saying they will compete with you in displaying psychic miracles. What shall be done now, Lord?" (The Blessed One): "If those sectarians perform psychic miracles, I too shall perform psychic miracles." (The King): "But has not the Blessed One promulgated a rule?" (The Blessed One): "Great King, I did not promulgate the rule for myself; I promulgated it only for my disciples." (The King): "Is it possible to promulgate a rule specifically for others, excluding yourself?" (The Blessed One): "Great King, if that is so, I shall ask you in return. Are there not mango trees and mango fruits in your garden?" (The King): "There are, Exalted Buddha." (The Blessed One): "Great King, if other people were to pick and eat the mangoes in that garden, what would you do?" (The King): "They would be punished, Lord." (The Blessed One): "But do you yourself have the right to eat those mangoes?"
502: (The King): "Yes, Exalted Buddha. There is no need to punish me; I would only be eating my own property." (The Blessed One): "Great King, just as your authority extends throughout this realm of three hundred yojanas, so too my authority extends throughout the hundred thousand million universes (āṇā-khetta). There is no rule promulgated for me; there is a rule promulgated for other disciples. I shall perform the display of psychic miracles." (The King): "Exalted Buddha, when will you perform the display of psychic miracles?" (The Blessed One): "Great King, four months from today, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, I shall perform the display of psychic miracles." (The King): "Exalted Buddha, in what place will you perform it?" (The Blessed One): "Great King, I shall perform it near the Kaṇḍamba tree in the city of Sāvatthī." (The word "Kaṇḍamba" literally means a white mango tree. The "Kaṇḍamba-rukkha" mentioned by the Blessed One refers to the mango tree planted by the gardener named Kaṇḍa. It should be specially noted here that the Blessed One indicated a place 45 yojanas away and a time four months distant because Sāvatthī is the place where all Buddhas perform their psychic miracles, and also to allow a large number of people to assemble.)
503:
## The Pretense and Actions of the Sectarians
When the sectarians heard the Buddha's bold declaration to King Bimbisāra (that he would perform a miracle near the Kaṇḍa mango tree in Sāvatthī on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, four months from now), they thought, "We are now utterly ruined. However, (without losing our composure), let us follow closely behind the ascetic Gotama as he travels to Sāvatthī. When people see us and ask, 'Why are you doing this?', we will tell them, 'We have challenged the ascetic Gotama to a contest of miracles. The ascetic Gotama is now fleeing (out of fear of us). We are following him closely without letting him out of our sight to prevent his escape.' If we act and speak in this way, we will receive many gains and offerings." Thus they consulted and spoke.

## The Buddha's Journey from Rājagaha to Sāvatthī
The issue regarding the display of miracles arose around the full moon day of Phagguna in the year 108 of the Great Era (Mahā Sakkarāj). Around the 1st waning day of Phagguna, the Buddha went for alms in Rājagaha and then departed from the city, traveling on a journey toward Sāvatthī accompanied by a large group of monks.

The sectarians also departed right behind the Buddha. Wherever the Buddha took his meal, they also took theirs.
504:
When the Buddha continued his journey, they also continued theirs. Wherever the Buddha stayed for the night, they also slept, and after having breakfast the next morning, they set out together. When people along the way asked, "Why are you following the Buddha so closely like this?", they spoke pretentiously as they had previously planned. A great multitude of people followed along continuously, thinking, "We shall witness the miracle of psychic power."

## Preparations from Both Sides in Sāvatthī
The Buddha, continuing his journey, eventually arrived and stayed at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. The sectarians, having arrived in Sāvatthī along with the Buddha, spoke to and preached to their respective lay supporters. Upon receiving one hundred thousand pieces of money, they used that capital to build a pavilion (maṇḍapa) with pillars made of khadira wood. They decorated and covered their pavilion elaborately with blue lotuses and stayed there, boasting, "We shall display miracles in this pavilion."

King Pasenadi of Kosala approached the Buddha and said, "Exalted Buddha, the sectarians have had a miracle pavilion built. I also wish to build a miracle pavilion for the Exalted One, Lord." When he said this, the Buddha replied, "Great King, do not build one. The one who will build the pavilion for me..."
505:
"The donor is ready," the Buddha said. "Greatly Blessed One, who else but I would be able to build a pavilion for the Buddha?" King Pasenadi of Kosala asked. "Great King, Sakka, the King of Devas, will build it," the Buddha replied. When the King asked, "In what place will the miracle be performed?", the Buddha replied, "Great King, it will be performed near the Kaṇḍamba mango tree."

As soon as the sectarians heard the news that "the Buddha will perform a miracle near a mango tree," they became very frightened and trembling. They consulted with their supporters and bought up all the mango trees within a league of Sāvatthī and cut them down. They even went so far as to uproot and throw away mango sprouts that had just germinated that very day.

## About the Kaṇḍamba White Mango Tree

Then, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, the Buddha, surrounded by a company of monks, departed from Jetavana Monastery to enter Sāvatthī for alms.

King Pasenadi's gardener was named Kaṇḍa. This gardener, Kaṇḍa, saw a large, ripe mango fruit inside an old red ants' nest on a mango tree in the royal garden. He chased away the crows that were swarming around, drawn by the scent and flavor of the mango, and took the fruit.
506:
With the intention of presenting it to the King, he carried it along. On the way, he encountered the Buddha and thought:

"If the King were to receive and eat this mango, he might give me a reward of eight (or at most sixteen) kahāpaṇas. That reward of eight (or sixteen) kahāpaṇas given by the King would not be enough to sustain me for a lifetime. If I offer this mango to the Buddha, it will be able to bring me welfare and happiness throughout the boundless cycle of saṃsāra."

Having made up his mind with faith, he offered the mango to the Buddha right there on the road. When the Buddha looked at the Venerable Ānanda, the Venerable Ānanda, being perceptive of the Buddha's signs, offered the Buddha the stone bowl presented by the Four Great Kings. The Buddha tilted the stone bowl and accepted the mango offered by the gardener Kaṇḍa, and then showed his intention to sit down at that very spot.

Venerable Ānanda spread out a robe. Then, for the Buddha who was seated on that robe, Venerable Ānanda prepared the mango into a beverage and offered it. After the Buddha drank the mango juice, he said to the gardener Kaṇḍa, "Layman Kaṇḍa, dig the earth and plant this mango seed right here." The gardener Kaṇḍa...
507:
...did exactly as the Buddha had instructed. The Buddha then washed his hands over the mango seed.

## The Great Mango Tree Growing Instantly

Immediately after the Buddha washed his hands, a large mango sprout with a stem the size of a plow-pole emerged from the ground in an instant. Even as people watched, it grew rapidly into a great mango tree fifty cubits in height. There were four large branches in the four cardinal directions—East, West, South, and North—and one large branch at the top; thus, there were five main branches, each fifty cubits long. In that very moment, the great mango tree was covered with blossoms and fruits, and the entire tree was filled with clusters of ripe mangoes.

The monks who came later followed along eating the ripe mangoes from that tree (yet the mangoes were never exhausted). King Pasenadi of Kosala, having heard the news that "a great mango tree of such wonderful and extraordinary nature has grown and is shining brightly," issued a royal decree that "no one shall cut this mango tree" and stationed guards there.

Because that great mango tree was planted by the gardener named Kaṇḍa, it became famous as the "Kaṇḍambarukkha = the mango tree planted by the gardener Kaṇḍa." It was with reference to this very tree that the Buddha had replied to King Bimbisāra and King Pasenadi of Kosala when they asked...
508:
"I will perform the Twin Miracle near the Kaṇḍamba mango tree," he had said. The heretics (Titthiyas), not knowing the reason, bought, chopped down, and uprooted all mango trees within a league around Sāvatthī, not leaving even a sprout, so that the Buddha would not be able to perform the miracle.

Afterwards, drunkards, having enjoyed eating the ripe mangoes from that mango tree planted by Kaṇḍa the gardener, shouted, "Hey, you ruined heretics! Fearing that 'the ascetic Gotama will perform a miracle near the Kaṇḍamba mango tree,' you uprooted every single mango tree within a league of Sāvatthī, not even leaving a sprout that grew today. The Kaṇḍamba mango tree mentioned by the Buddha is not the white mango tree you thought; it is this very mango tree planted by Kaṇḍa the gardener!" Saying this, they surrounded the heretics and pelted them with the mango seeds they had finished eating.

## The Wind God Destroying the Heretics' Pavilion and the Defeat of the Heretics

Sakka, the King of Devas, commanded the Wind God, "Blow down the heretics' pavilion, uproot the pillars, and cast them into an unclean place." The Wind God did as Sakka commanded.

Then, Sakka again commanded the Sun God, "Lower the orb of the sun and make it scorching hot." The Sun God also did as Sakka commanded.
509:
Sakka then commanded the Wind God, "Go and stir up a whirlwind; specifically, blow a whirlwind at the site of the heretics' pavilion." The Wind God did as Sakka commanded. Consequently, the heretics' entire bodies, which were dripping with sweat, became covered and encrusted with clouds of dust. At that time, the heretics resembled large red anthills.

Then Sakka ordered the Rain God, "Rain down very large hailstones with a clattering sound." The Rain God did as Sakka commanded. Then the heretics' entire bodies resembled brindled red cows.

Since their pavilion was destroyed, the sun was very hot, the whirlwind was intense, and the hailstones were falling rhythmically, the group of heretics, having no refuge and their pride fallen, fled in all directions.

## Pūraṇa Kassapa Drowning in Water with a Noose Around His Neck

While the six heretical teachers were fleeing in all directions, a farmer who was a lay supporter and attendant of Pūraṇa Kassapa thought, "Now it is time for our masters to display their miracles. I will go and watch the miracle." He unyoked his oxen, took the pot in which he had brought gruel early in the morning, the rope, and the goad, and came to the festival of miracles. Seeing Pūraṇa Kassapa running in great haste, he said, "Venerable sir, I have come to behold your miracle..."
510:
The teacher Pūraṇa Kassapa said, "What use is your miracle? Just give me this jar and rope you have in your hand." Taking the jar and rope given by that disciple farmer, the teacher went to the bank of a flowing stream, filled the jar with sand, tied it to his neck with the rope he had brought, and jumped into a deep pool of the swift-flowing stream. As bubbles rose to the surface, he passed away and was reborn in the Great Avīci Hell.

As much suffering as arises,
For the fools who do not understand,
Just as much happiness is for the wise;
This is the nature of the world.

To those who are greatly lacking in wisdom and intelligence, long-lasting suffering reaches them. But to the noble ones who are the banners of wisdom and possess superior intellect, the Dhamma is held in hand, and benefits abound, resulting in abundant happiness; such is the nature of the world.

## Disciples Requesting the Buddha at the Miracle Site

As for the Buddha, the teacher of gods and humans, the pinnacle of the three worlds, the Omniscient One, Sakka, the King of Devas, reflected in the evening: "It is my responsibility to build a jeweled pavilion for the Buddha." Knowing this, he sent the celestial architect Vissakamma to create a great pavilion made of the seven kinds of jewels, twelve leagues wide and covered with blue lotuses. In that pavilion, the Buddha's disciples—monks and laypeople—assembled together.
511:
When it reached the afternoon and evening, the Buddha, in order to perform the miracle, departed from the Gandhakuṭī cell and sat upon a jeweled throne one league in size inside the jeweled pavilion created by Vissakamma, under a divine white umbrella three leagues in size.

Ever since the full moon day of Phagguna, the Buddha had told King Bimbisāra, "Four months from today, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, I will perform a miracle near the Kaṇḍamba mango tree in Sāvatthī." Having heard this news through successive reports and wishing to witness the Twin Miracle, the fourfold assembly of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen gathered in Sāvatthī. With the Buddha at the center, they extended twelve leagues in each of the four directions—front, back, left, and right. From one end of the assembly to the other, it was twenty-four leagues. In circumference, it was seventy-two leagues. All the devas and brahmas living in the ten thousand world systems of the field of birth (jāti-khetta) also assembled simultaneously.

## The Request of the Woman Garaṇī

In that assembly, a greatly powerful female lay disciple named "Garaṇī," who was established in the fruit of Anāgāmī, stood before the Buddha, and with palms joined in reverence, she addressed him: "Greatly Blessed One, while a daughter like me is present, there is no need for the Buddha to undergo the hardship of performing this task."
512:
512
“I shall perform a display of miracles,” she requested. The Buddha asked, “Dear daughter Gharaṇī, in what manner will you perform the display of miracles?” Then the laywoman Gharaṇī, an Anāgāmī, replied:

“Exalted Buddha, I shall transform the existing earth within this universe into water, making the entire universe a single expanse of water. Then, diving into the water like a water-hen, I shall manifest myself at the eastern edge of the universe. Likewise, I shall manifest myself at the western edge, the northern edge, and the southern edge of the universe. Similarly, I shall manifest myself in the center.

(At that time) when someone asks, ‘Who is this woman?’, others will reply, ‘This is the laywoman named Gharaṇī, a daughter of the Buddha and an Anāgāmī.’ (Then, all the assembled spectators) will say, ‘This power is merely the initial power of a single girl, a daughter of the Buddha. As for the power of the Buddha himself, it is beyond imagination.’ When this happens, the heretics will not even dare to look back, but will turn away and flee.”

Thus she requested. Then the Buddha said, “Dear daughter Gharaṇī, I well know that you are capable of performing such a
513:
513
display of miracles. However, this bundle of flowers (the task of the Great Miracle) is not bound for you.” Having been refused by the Buddha’s words, the laywoman Gharaṇī thought, “The Buddha does not grant me permission; there must be someone else capable of performing a miracle superior to mine,” and she stood in a suitable place.

The Buddha reflected, “If I ask these sons and daughters of mine, they will speak boldly and brilliantly like lion kings in the midst of this assembly, which is twenty-four leagues in length and breadth. In this way, the virtues of my sons and daughters will become manifest.” Thinking thus, he asked other male and female disciples respectively, “How will you perform a display of miracles?” Those disciples replied, “I shall do it in such and such a way, Venerable Sir,” making various bold declarations in the presence of the Buddha.

## The Request of Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika

Among those disciples who made such bold declarations, the lay devotee Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika said, “Exalted Buddha, while a noble son and lay devotee who has attained the stage of Anāgāmī like myself is present, there is no need for the Buddha to undergo such exertion. Let me perform the display of miracles.”
514:
514
When he requested thus, the Buddha asked, “Dear son Anāthapiṇḍika, in what manner will you perform the display of miracles?” The lay devotee Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika, an Anāgāmī, replied:

“Exalted Buddha, I shall create a physical form of a Mahābrahmā twelve leagues in height. Then, in the midst of this assembly, I shall strike my arms (as a sign of power) with a sound as great and intense as a thunderous roar of a great storm.

At that time, when the multitude of people ask, ‘What sound is this?’, (the assembly) will answer, ‘It is the sound of the Buddha’s son, the young merchant Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika, an Anāgāmī lay devotee, striking his arms in the guise of a Brahmā.’ Then the heretics will say, ‘This power is merely the initial power of a single young lay devotee, a son of the Buddha. As for the power of the Buddha himself, it is beyond imagination.’ Thus, they will be terrified and, not daring to even look back, will turn away and flee.”

Thus he requested. Then the Buddha said, “Dear son Anāthapiṇḍika, I know of such power of yours. You may remain standing,” and he did not grant permission.
515:
## The Seven-Year-Old Sāmaṇerī Named Cira's Petition

Then, a seven-year-old novice nun named Cira, who possessed the analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), paid respectful homage to the Blessed One and petitioned, "Exalted Buddha, please allow me to perform a miracle." When the Blessed One asked, "Dear daughter Cira, in what manner will you perform the miracle?" the young novice nun Cira replied:

"Exalted Buddha, by my psychic power, I will bring these three great mountains—Mount Meru, Mount Cakkavāḷa, and Mount Himavanta—and place them in a row at this site of the miracle festival. After arranging them in a row, I will fly freely and unhindered from one mountain to another like a young swan.

When the multitude of people see me and ask, 'Who is this little girl?' the assembly will answer, 'This is the young novice nun named Cira.' Hearing this, the heretics will say, 'This power is merely that of a seven-year-old novice nun at the start of the festival; the power of the Blessed One must be beyond imagination.' They will be terrified and, not even daring to look askance at the Exalted One, they will flee away."
516:
...she submitted. (From this point onwards, the similar words of the disciples' replies should be understood in the same manner; they will not be written in detail, only the exceptional points will be presented). To that young female novice named Cirā, the Buddha also said, "Dear daughter, I know your power," and as before, He did not grant her permission to perform the miracle.

## Cunda, the Seven-Year-Old Arahant Novice
## His Request

Then, another seven-year-old novice named Cunda, who possessed the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), paid homage to the Buddha and requested, "Exalted Buddha, may I be allowed to perform a miracle?" When the Buddha asked, "Dear Cunda, in what manner will you perform the miracle?" the young novice Cunda replied:

"Exalted Buddha, I shall take hold of the trunk of the great Jambu tree, which stands like a banner of Jambudīpa, shake it, bring the Jambu fruits, and feed this entire assembled congregation. I shall also bring the Parichattaka flowers from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and give them to this congregation."

To this young novice Cunda as well, the Buddha spoke as before and did not grant permission.

517
## The Request of Uppalavaṇṇā Therī

Then, Uppalavaṇṇā Therī paid respectful homage to the Buddha and (as before) requested permission to perform a miracle. When the Buddha asked, “How will you perform it?”, Uppalavaṇṇā Therī replied:

“Exalted Buddha, I shall create an assembly twelve leagues in size, and appearing in the form of a Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti) surrounded by a retinue of thirty-six leagues, I shall come and pay homage to the Buddha.”

To that Uppalavaṇṇā Therī, the Buddha also said, “I know of your power,” and as before, he did not grant permission to perform the miracle.

## The Request of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna

Then, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and the Buddha engaged in the following dialogue regarding the performance of the miracle:

(Venerable Moggallāna): “Exalted Buddha, let me perform the display of miracles.”

(The Buddha): “Dear son Moggallāna, in what manner will you perform the display of miracles?”

(Venerable Moggallāna): “Exalted Buddha, I shall place Mount Meru, the king of mountains, between my teeth
518:
518
and chew it in the midst of the assembly as if it were a tiny mustard seed.”

(The Buddha): “What other kind of miracle will you perform?”

(Venerable Moggallāna): “I shall fold this great earth like a reed mat and, placing it between my fingers, I shall display it.”

(The Buddha): “What other kind of miracle will you perform?”

(Venerable Moggallāna): “I shall cause this great earth to spin like a potter’s wheel and let the multitude of people eat the nutritious essence of the soil from beneath this earth.”

(The Buddha): “What other kind of miracle will you perform?”

(Venerable Moggallāna): “I shall place this great earth on my left palm and, placing these beings on another continent, I shall display it.”

(The Buddha): “What other kind of miracle will you perform?”

(Venerable Moggallāna): “Exalted Buddha, I shall make Mount Meru like an umbrella handle and, lifting the great earth like an umbrella canopy, I shall place it on the summit of Mount Meru. Then, like a monk holding an umbrella,
519:
519
holding it with one hand, I shall walk back and forth in the sky and display it.”

The Buddha said, “Dear son Moggallāna, I know of your power,” and he did not grant permission to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna to perform the miracle. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna also reflected, “The Buddha must surely perceive a miracle to be performed in this assembly that is superior to mine,” and he stood in a suitable place.

Thereafter, the Buddha said to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, “Dear son Moggallāna, this bundle of flowers is not a bundle of flowers intended for you. Indeed, I am one who can bear a burden like no other; there is no one else who can bear my burden. It is not surprising that now, having become a Buddha, there is no one else who can bear my burden. Even when I was born as a brute animal while my perfections (pāramīs) were still immature, there was no one who could bear my burden.” Having said this, at the request of the Venerable Moggallāna, he preached the Kaṇha-usabha Jātaka in detail (as found in the Ekanipāta, 3-Kuruṅgavagga, 9th Jātaka, Jātaka Commentary Vol. 1, page 209).

## The Creation of the Jeweled Walkway

After preaching the Kaṇha-usabha Jātaka, he created a jeweled walkway ten thousand world systems in length, stretching from east to west. The manner of its creation was as follows: in the ten thousand world systems aligned from east to west,
520:
He created a great jewel walkway (ratana-caṅkama) spanning ten thousand world-systems, using ten thousand Mount Sinerus as the pillars of the walkway, arranged in a sequence. The eastern end of this great jewel walkway touched the edge of the easternmost world-system (among the ten thousand world-systems), and the western end touched the edge of the westernmost world-system. The width of this great jewel walkway was twelve yojanas. On both sides (south and north), He created a very delightful golden ground as the boundary of the walkway. In the center, He created golden roofs over the beams, rafters, and crossbeams made of the ten kinds of jewels. The railings surrounding the walkway were made entirely of gold. Rubies and pearls were strewn as sand within the jewel walkway.

At that time, the assembly of people in the four directions—front, back, left, and right—extended for twelve yojanas each; in a straight line, it was twenty-four yojanas. The assembly of devas and brahmas was immeasurably large. In the midst of such a vast assembly of humans, devas, and brahmas, the Buddha performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya). To make it understandable, I shall further present from the Pāḷi text how the Buddha performed the Twin Miracle on that jewel walkway:

(1) From the upper part of His body, flames of fire burst forth, and from the lower part of His body, a stream of water flowed out. (Alternating again) from the lower part of His body, flames of fire burst forth, and from the upper part of His body, a stream of water flowed out.

(2) From the front of His body, flames of fire burst forth, and from the back of His body, a stream of water flowed out. (Alternating again) from the back of His body, flames of fire burst forth, and from the front of His body, a stream of water flowed out.

(3) From His right eye, flames of fire burst forth, and from His left eye, a stream of water flowed out. (Alternating again) from His left eye, flames of fire burst forth, and from His right eye, a stream of water flowed out.

(4) From His right ear, flames of fire burst forth, and from His left ear, a stream of water flowed out. (When observed again after closing the eyes, it changed) from His left ear, flames of fire burst forth, and from His right ear, a stream of water flowed out.

(5) From His right nostril, flames of fire burst forth, and from His left nostril, a stream of water flowed out. (Alternating again) from His left nostril, flames of fire burst forth, and from His right nostril, a stream of water flowed out.

(6) From His right shoulder, flames of fire burst forth, and from His left shoulder, a stream of water flowed out. (Alternating again) from His left shoulder, flames of fire burst forth, and from His right shoulder, a stream of water flowed out.

(7) From His right hand, flames of fire burst forth, and from His left hand, a stream of water flowed out. (Alternating again) from His left hand, flames of fire burst forth...

...and from His right hand, a stream of water flowed out.

(8) From His right side, flames of fire burst forth, and from His left side, a stream of water flowed out. (Alternating again) from His left side, flames of fire burst forth, and from His right side, a stream of water flowed out.

(9) From His right foot, flames of fire burst forth, and from His left foot, a stream of water flowed out. (Alternating again) from His left foot, flames of fire burst forth, and from His right foot, a stream of water flowed out.

(10) From the ten fingers and ten toes, flames of fire burst forth, and from the spaces between the ten fingers and ten toes, a stream of water flowed out. (Alternating again) from the spaces between the ten fingers and ten toes, flames of fire burst forth, and from the ten fingers and ten toes, a stream of water flowed out.

(11) From each single hair of His body, flames of fire burst forth, and from other single hairs, a stream of water flowed out.

(12) From each single pore, flames of fire burst forth, and from other single pores, a stream of water flowed out.

From the respective parts of His body, the six-colored rays—namely, Nīla (blue), Pīta (yellow), Lohita (red), Odāta (white), Mañjeṭṭha (crimson), and Pabhassara (brilliant)—burst forth in pairs...
523:
...in strands, and in clusters, radiating brilliantly.

[A special note here: Due to the power of the meditative attainment of the fire-kasiṇa (tejokasiṇa-jhāna-samāpatti), flames of fire burst forth from the upper part of the Buddha's body, and due to the power of the meditative attainment of the water-kasiṇa (āpokasiṇa-jhāna-samāpatti), a stream of water flowed out from the lower part of His body. (This means that to emit flames, He had to enter the fire-kasiṇa attainment, and to emit water, He had to enter the water-kasiṇa attainment). The same applies to the alternating creations.

In this miracle, the flames of fire did not mix with the stream of water, nor did the stream of water mix with the flames; they remained distinct and pure. Since two types of consciousness cannot arise simultaneously, the creation of flames occurred at one moment, and the creation of water occurred at another. Although there was a temporal gap, because the intervals of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) between thought-processes (vīthi) are minimal for the Buddha, because the occurrence of consciousness is extremely rapid, and because He had reached the pinnacle of the five masteries (vasībhāva), the beings who beheld the miracle perceived the flames and the water as occurring at the same time, the same moment, and simultaneously. It was that rapid.

Those pairs of fire and water, after emerging from the Buddha's body, ascended as far as the highest point of existence (bhavagga) and descended to the edges of the world-systems within the ten thousand world-systems of the field of birth (jātikhetta).]

## Displaying the Miracle of the Opening of the Worlds

The Buddha, having performed the Twin Miracle of water and fire, also performed the Miracle of the Opening of the Worlds (Loka-vivaraṇa). The manner of performance was as follows: Having entered the...
524:
...fourth fine-material sphere functional jhāna (rūpāvacara-kiriya-catuttha-jhāna) with the white-kasiṇa (odātakasiṇa) as the object, He made the resolution: "Let there be light throughout the ten thousand world-systems." Simultaneously with this resolution, from the great earth up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm (including the earth itself), everything became filled with a single expanse of light.

At that time, the people of the human world, while standing or sitting in their own places, could see all the devas and brahmas from the Cātumahārājika heaven up to the Akaniṭṭha Brahma realm. They saw various devas and brahmas in their respective diverse and numerous abodes, palaces, mansions, ponds, gardens, thrones, couches, and excellent vehicles, moving about, wandering, and enjoying themselves with delight and joy. They saw them shining brilliantly with their divine power and the radiance of their celestial mansions. They saw them enjoying great celestial pleasures with relish.

Among the brahmas in the sixteen realms of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara), they saw some brahmas enjoying the bliss of meditative attainment (samāpatti) as calmly and steadily as statues cast from a mass of jewels. They saw other brahmas gathering with those of like mind, discussing and consulting on various subtle and profound points of the Dhamma. All of this was clearly visible even to the natural eye due to the power and majesty of the Buddha's miracle.
525:
Similarly, in the eight great hells located within the great earth, in the sixteen subsidiary Ussada hells surrounding each of the four sides of every great hell, and in the Lokantarika hells located in the dark spaces between every three world-systems, the people could clearly see, even with their natural eyes, the denizens of hell suffering immense torments according to their respective realms and kamma, all due to the power and majesty of the Buddha's miracle.

Furthermore, all the devas and brahmas living in the ten thousand world-systems of the field of birth (jātikhetta) approached the Buddha with great divine power. Filled with overflowing awe and devotion, they paid homage with palms joined in reverence (añjalī) raised to their foreheads. They praised Him by composing and reciting verses (gāthā) related to the Buddha's virtues, clapped their hands in joy, laughed merrily, and spoke words of great delight.

Along with all of this, the multitude of people beheld with devotion the wonderful Twin Miracle of fire and water and the six-colored rays.

## The Radiance of the Six-Colored Rays

(1) Nīla (Blue) Rays: Due to the power and majesty of the Buddha's Knowledge of the Twin Miracle (Yamaka-pāṭihāriya-ñāṇa) while performing the miracle of fire and water, the six-colored rays radiated forth. From the places where His hair and beard grew, and from the dark portions of His eyes, the blue rays (nīla-raṃsī) radiated forth. Due to the power of these blue rays, the entire sky became like the color of eye-lotion...

...as if sprinkled with powdered sapphire, as if covered with blue pea flowers and blue lotuses, and like a blue sapphire fan being waved, they remained covered with sapphire-colored light.

(2) Pīta-raṃsī (Golden Rays): From the skin and the golden-yellow parts of the eyes, the Pīta rays (rays having a golden hue) radiated and emerged. By the power of these Pīta rays, all the surrounding directions became exquisitely beautiful, as if poured with liquid gold, as if spread with golden robes, and as if sprinkled with saffron powder and Mahāleghā flowers, being enveloped in a golden glow.

(3) Lohita-raṃsī (Red Rays): From the flesh, the blood, and the reddish parts of the eyes, the Lohita rays (red rays) radiated and emerged. By the power of these Lohita rays, all the surrounding directions became exquisitely beautiful, as if dyed with vermilion powder, as if poured with well-boiled lac resin, as if wrapped and covered all around with layers of red blankets, and as if sprinkled with Muiswe, Kathit (Erythrina), and Le-gaung-yan flowers.

(4) Odāta-raṃsī (White Rays): From the bones, the teeth, the canine teeth, and the white of the eyes, the Odāta rays (rays having a white color) radiated and emerged. By the power of these Odāta rays, all the surrounding directions, as if from silver pots...

...were continuously pouring and sprinkling streams of milk; as if silver ceilings, silver leaves, silver plates, and silver foils were spread and draped in layers; as if silver fans were being waved; and as if covered with flowers such as Thin-khwe, Kumudra lotuses, water lilies, jasmine, and Kyat-yone (Spanish jasmine), they became exquisitely beautiful.

(5) Mañjeṭṭha-raṃsī (Crimson Rays): From the palms of the hands, the soles of the feet, and other slightly reddish parts of the body, the Mañjeṭṭha rays (crimson or madder-colored rays) radiated and emerged. By the power of these Mañjeṭṭha rays, all the surrounding directions became exquisitely beautiful, as if a net of coral were spread out, and as if sprinkled with red flowers known as Leik-su-shwe (or Leik-sa-ywe).

By the power of these Pabhassara rays, all the surrounding directions became exquisitely beautiful, as if filled with clusters of morning stars, and as if filled with flashes of lightning and the like. These aforementioned six-colored rays, like streams of liquid gold, liquid silver, and liquid ruby flowing continuously from the mouth of a mechanical tube...

...flew upwards from the universe, reaching the highest plane of existence (Bhavagga), and then sank back down to fall upon the edge of the universe. Thus, the entire universe became like a great golden house, exquisitely beautiful and adorned with jeweled shields and arrows, shining with a single continuous radiance.

## Preaching the Dhamma While Walking on the Jeweled Walkway
On that day, the Blessed One walked upon that jeweled walkway, which stretched ten thousand universes in length from east to west. While performing the Twin Miracle of water and fire, he also preached the Dhamma suitable to the temperaments of the multitude at intervals. When he wished to preach the Dhamma, the Blessed One temporarily ceased the miracle to give the people a rest. At that moment, the multitude shouted "Sādhu" in applause. While the people were applauding, the Blessed One contemplated the mental states of that vast assembly. He contemplated the mental state of each individual through the sixteen modes (as mentioned in the Cittānupassanā teaching). The minds of the Buddhas have such rapid transitions.

After thus thoroughly contemplating the mental states of the people, and knowing well the specific miracle that would inspire their faith and the method of preaching that would suit their inclinations (ajjhāsaya) and dispositions, he again displayed the miracle that would inspire their faith.
529:
529
He also preached the Dhamma discourse that was suitable and appropriate to the inclinations and dispositions of the various people. When the Dhamma was thus preached and the Twin Miracle was displayed in accordance with the inclinations and dispositions of the beings, a great triumph of Dhamma-realization (Dhammābhisamaya) occurred, in which many beings perceived the Four Noble Truths and were liberated.

## Creating the Created Buddhas (Nimmitabuddha)
In that vast assembly, the Blessed One contemplated to see if there was any person who could grasp his intention and ask questions. Finding no such person, he created Nimmitabuddhas (created Buddha-images). Upon creating them, he increased their number sequentially—one, two, three, four, and so on—creating countless Nimmitabuddhas.

The original Buddha (Pakati-dhātusāra) answered the questions asked by the Nimmitabuddhas, and the Nimmitabuddhas answered the questions asked by the original Buddha. In terms of postures, some Nimmitabuddhas were standing, some were walking, some were reclining, and some were sitting; thus, many Nimmitabuddhas existed in all four postures.

At that time, the six-colored rays of the original Buddha, the six-colored rays of the Nimmitabuddhas...

...the flames of fire, the streams of water, and the countless Nimmitabuddhas were all intermingled throughout the sky. They made the sky exceedingly beautiful, performing in a way that was incomparable and beyond the reach of the disciples (Sāvakas).

Many Brahmas, Devas, and humans uttered words of praise. The entire sky was filled with the songs of the Devas. Devas and Brahmas showered divine flowers. With thousands of divine and human musical instruments playing together in a great roar, it was as if a single great festival was being celebrated.

## Twenty Crores of Brahmas, Devas, and Humans Attaining Liberation
When the Blessed One displayed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya)—which is an unshared (asādhāraṇa) supreme knowledge not common to Paccekabuddhas or disciples—and preached the Dhamma at intervals according to the temperaments of the audience, twenty crores of humans, Devas, and Brahmas attained liberation by realizing the Four Noble Truths through witnessing the miracle and hearing the Dhamma.

At this point, for the sake of the monks and laypeople who have great and sharp faith, I shall now write and present the Pali and meaning of the "Yamaka Pāṭihāriya Vandanā" (Adoration of the Twin Miracle) from the Mahānamakkāra text.

## Adoration Verse of the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya Vandanā Gāthā)
## Pali and Meaning
Kaṇḍambammūle parahitakaro yo munindo nisinno,
Accheraṃ sīghaṃ nayanasubhagaṃ ākulannaggijālaṃ.
Dujjaladdhaṃsaṃ munibhijahitaṃ pāṭiheraṃ akāsi,
Vande taṃ seṭṭhaṃ paramaratijaṃ iddhidhammehupetaṃ.
(Kusumitalatāvellitā verse of 18 syllables)

*Parahitakaro*: He who has accomplished the five duties of a Buddha without fail for forty-five years for the welfare and happiness of others, the venyeya beings. *Yo Munindo*: Which Blessed One, who is the supreme Lord of Sages, including householder sages and others. *Kaṇḍambammūle*: Near the mango tree which shines with the name of the man Kaṇḍa. *Nisinno*: While seated there with a joyful smile, wishing to make the host of heretics flee to distant places. *Accheraṃ*: Worthy of being marveled at, causing the world of humans and Devas to applaud and snap their fingers in wonder, shaking the highest Brahma realm (Bhavagga), because of witnessing such an unprecedented event. *Sīghaṃ*: Although the creation of the stream of water and the creation of the flames of fire occurred at different times, it was so rapid that the Brahmas, Devas, and humans who saw it perceived it as happening simultaneously at the same moment. *Nayanāsubhagaṃ*: Exquisitely beautiful and magnificent, causing a surge of joy to overwhelm the eyes of the Devas and humans who beheld it. *Dujjaladdhaṃsaṃ*: Capable of destroying the net of false views (micchā-diṭṭhi) of the heretics (vitaṇḍī) who are outside the liberating Dispensation (Sāsana)...

## Ascending to the Tāvatiṃsa Heaven
While performing the Twin Miracle, the Buddha reflected: "Where did the Buddhas of the past spend the rains retreat after performing the Twin Miracle?" He saw that they used to spend the rains retreat in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and preach the Abhidhamma to their mothers, who had become devas. He then intended to lift his right foot and place it on the summit of Mount Yugandhara. At that moment, Mount Yugandhara, which is forty-two thousand yojanas high, moved of its own accord to receive his right foot. Then, when he lifted his left foot, the summit of Mount Sineru, which is eighty-four thousand yojanas high from the ground, moved of its own accord to receive his left foot.
535:
(In this matter: No one saw Mount Yugandhara and Mount Sineru bending down beneath his feet. For the Buddha, there was no such thing as taking unnaturally long strides across such vast distances of yojanas. This is purely a matter of psychic power; it is inconceivable and should not be speculated upon.)
In this way, the Buddha reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven from the human world in just two steps. (The Tāvatiṃsa heaven is situated on the summit of Mount Sineru; thus, reaching the summit of Mount Sineru means reaching the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.)
## Sakka’s Wrong Thought
As soon as Sakka, the King of Devas, saw the Buddha, he thought:
"The Buddha will likely spend this rains retreat here in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven on the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone seat. It will be of great benefit to many devas and Brahmās. Specifically, if the Buddha spends the three months of the rains retreat on this Paṇḍukambala stone seat, no other deva or Brahmā would be able even to place a hand upon it. This Paṇḍukambala stone seat is sixty yojanas long, fifty yojanas wide, and fifteen yojanas high; it is very large. Even if the Buddha sits on that Paṇḍukambala stone seat (throughout the rains), it will be like a small cāvadī bird resting in the middle of a large winnowing tray; the space used will be small, while the unused space will be vast, making it seem almost empty."
536:
...he had such a wrong and misguided thought. The Blessed One, knowing Sakka's thought, spread his double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) to cover the entire stone slab. Sakka thought simply, "Even if he can spread the robe to cover the entire stone slab, the Blessed One himself will likely sit only on a small portion." The Blessed One, knowing Sakka's thought, sat cross-legged filling the entire Paṇḍukambala stone slab, just as a senior monk who observes the dhutaṅga of wearing refuse-rag robes (paṃsukūla) might sit on a small stool.

Then Sakka, realizing his own fault, thought, "Not knowing one's own measure is indeed a great disadvantage. We cannot fully know what kind of person a Buddha is. We cannot fully know the extent of a Buddha's virtues. I have had such a wrong thought and misconception even toward the Blessed One, who is endowed with all these inconceivable virtues." Thus, acknowledging his fault, he paid respectful homage to the Blessed One.

## The Multitude Weeping Because They Could Not See the Buddha, etc.

At that time, while the people in the human world were watching, thinking, "We shall behold the Twin Miracle," the multitude suddenly lost sight of the Blessed One...

It was as if a thousand moons and a thousand suns had set. "What is the reason?" they asked one another—
Gato nu cittakūṭaṃ vā, kelāsaṃ vā yugandharaṃ.
Na no dakkhemu sambuddhaṃ, lokajeṭṭhaṃ narāsabhaṃ.
No: We. Lokajeṭṭhaṃ: To the one who is the leader and chief of the three worlds. Narāsabhaṃ: To the one who is the supreme person, the bull among men. Sambuddhaṃ: To the Buddha, the Lord of the World known as the Omniscient One. Na dakkhemu: We no longer see him even as we were beholding him. So sambuddho: That Buddha, the Lord of the World known as the Omniscient One. Cittakūṭaṃ vā: To Mount Cittakūṭa. Gato nu: Has he traveled there, thinking, "I shall seek a remote place far from these noisy and talkative people"? Kelāsaṃ vā: Or to the silver mountain Kelāsa? Gato nu: Has he traveled there? Yugandharaṃ vā: Or to Mount Yugandhara? Gato nu: Has he traveled there, thinking, "I shall seek a remote place far from these noisy and talkative people"?—
Reciting this verse, the people wept.
Some other people said: "The Buddha delights in and enjoys secluded places. The Buddha might have thought, 'Though I am one who delights in seclusion, I have performed such a marvelous display of psychic power in the midst of this vast assembly,' and out of great modesty, he might have gone to a place where people cannot see him."
