"Now we can no longer behold that Buddha," they said, and—
Pavivekarato dhīro, nayimaṃ lokaṃ punehiti.
Na no dakkhemu sambuddhaṃ, lokajeṭṭhaṃ narāsabhaṃ.
Dhīro: The Buddha, the Master of Omniscient Wisdom. Pavivekarato: Because he approaches and delights only in places secluded from the five-fold sense objects. Imaṃ lokaṃ: To this human world, which is filled with the five-fold sense objects and is very hot, offering no place of coolness. Na puna ehiti: He will not return again. No: We. Lokajeṭṭhaṃ: To the one who is the leader and chief of the three worlds. Narāsabhaṃ: To the one who is the supreme person, the bull among men. Sambuddhaṃ: To the Buddha, the Lord of the World known as the Omniscient One. Na dakkhemu: We no longer see him even as we were beholding him.—
Reciting this verse, they wept.
The multitude of people asked the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: "Venerable Sir, where is the Buddha now?" Although the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna himself knew (that the Buddha was in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven), he thought, "Let the virtues of others be known," and said, "Ask the Venerable Anuruddha." When the people asked the Venerable Anuruddha, he replied: "He has gone to spend the rains retreat on the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone seat spread at the foot of the Parichattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, to preach the Abhidhamma Piṭaka to the assembly of devas and Brahmās,
539:
headed by the deva who was his mother." When the people asked, "When will he return?" the Venerable Anuruddha replied: "After preaching the Abhidhamma for the three months of the rains, he will return on the full moon day of Thadingyut, the Great Pavāraṇā day."
The people consulted one another, saying, "We will not leave without beholding the Buddha," and they built leaf-huts right there. The vast sky itself became the roof for those people. The great earth itself swallowed all the bodily waste discarded by those people, so that no bodily waste of such a large assembly could be found. Everywhere, the ground remained clean.
The Buddha had already instructed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna beforehand: "Dear son, you must remain to preach the Dhamma to this assembly; the lay devotee Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika will provide food and sustenance to this assembly." Therefore, throughout the three months of the rains, the lay devotee Cūḷa Anāthapiṇḍika provided gruel, rice, hard food, soft food, betel, medicine, tea, perfumes, flowers, and ornaments—all human necessities—completely and without lack. According to the Buddha's prior instruction, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna preached the Dhamma to that assembly throughout the three months of the rains retreat.
540:
## The Gathering of Devas and Brahmas from Ten Thousand World-Systems
## Approaching the Presence of the Blessed One

When the Blessed One resided for the Rains Retreat on the Paṇḍukambala stone throne at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to preach the Abhidhamma, devas and Brahmas from the ten thousand world-systems of the Jātikkhetta (the field of birth) gathered around and approached him to listen to the Abhidhamma Dhamma. Among those many devas and Brahmas, not a single one could surpass or equal the Blessed One in terms of physical appearance and radiance; indeed, the Blessed One alone outshone and excelled all the devas and Brahmas in splendor.

While the Blessed One sat there, outshining all the devas and Brahmas with his own bodily radiance, the deva Santusita, who had been his mother, descended from his abode in the Tusita realm and sat down respectfully on the right side in front of the Blessed One.

## The Story of the Deva Aṅkura and the Deva Indaka

After the deva who was the former mother had sat down, the deva Indaka also came into the presence of the Blessed One and sat on the right side. The deva Aṅkura sat on the left side. As more and more powerful devas and Brahmas arrived, this deva Aṅkura had to move back further and further to give way, eventually finding a place twelve yojanas away from the Blessed One. The deva Indaka, however, remained in his original place without having to move at all.
541:
## A Brief Account of the Deva Aṅkura

Aṅkura was a prince who lived during a time outside the Buddha's dispensation (after the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha had disappeared). He was the son of Prince Upasāgara, the son of King Mahāsāgara of Uttaramadhurā, and Princess Devagabbhā, the daughter of King Mahākaṃsa of Asitañjana, which was a fief city of King Kaṃsa in the Uttarāpatha region. They had eleven children: a daughter named Princess Añjanādevī and ten sons, including Prince Vāsudeva. The youngest son was named Prince Aṅkura.

When Prince Aṅkura reached adulthood (after his elder brothers, Vāsudeva and others, had conquered the entire Jambudīpa with their discus weapons), he gave his allotted share of the kingdom to his eldest sister, Princess Añjanādevī. He himself requested only tax exemption within the territories ruled by his brothers and sister and lived happily by engaging in trade and commerce.

At one time, Prince Aṅkura was traveling with five hundred carts for trade when he lost his way in a desert and faced great hardship due to the depletion of food and supplies. In that desert, there was a tree-deity who could provide all necessary items from his right hand alone. This tree-deity was a grateful person (kataññū) who recognized the kindness Prince Aṅkura had shown him in a previous human life.
542:
Recognizing the past kindness, the tree-deity pointed with a single finger of his right hand and provided all the necessary supplies to the prince and his followers. When Prince Aṅkura asked about his past merit, the tree-deity replied: "In my previous life as a human, I was a poor tailor living near the house of the wealthy man Asayha in the city of Roruva. When the wealthy Asayha gave great alms, I would joyfully and with faith stretch out my right hand to point the way to the alms-hall for the recipients who arrived. Due to that merit, all human necessities such as food, drink, and clothing flow continuously from my right hand as desired."

Inspired by that tree-deity, Prince Aṅkura, upon reaching the capital of Dvāravatī, gave such immense alms that the entire Jambudīpa ceased its plowing (due to the abundance). Because the kings received no taxes, the elder brothers requested Prince Aṅkura to give alms more moderately. Consequently, Prince Aṅkura moved to the Dakkhiṇāpatha region and, in the Damila country near the ocean, he gave great alms for ten thousand years, arranged in rows of hearths over a distance of twelve yojanas. Upon passing away from that life, he was reborn as a deva in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven with his original name, Aṅkura.

Although Prince Aṅkura gave such great alms for a long period, because it was outside the Buddha's dispensation and he gave only to immoral recipients, it was like seeds sown in poor soil.
543:
The results did not flourish as much as they should have. (This is a summary of the story of the deva Aṅkura. For a detailed account, one should refer to the Aṅkura-peta-vatthu, the 9th story of the 2nd Ubbarivagga in the Peta-vatthu Pāḷi of the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka.)

## A Brief Account of the Deva Indaka

Regarding the deva Indaka, while Aṅkura was enjoying celestial bliss in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as mentioned, during the time of our Buddha, a youth named Indaka, with a mind full of faith and devotion, offered a single spoonful of alms-food to the Venerable Anuruddha Mahāthera who had come for alms.

When the youth Indaka later passed away, due to the power of sowing the seed of merit—the gift of a spoonful of alms-food—in the fertile field of the Buddha's dispensation, he was reborn as a powerful deva named Indaka in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. He then outshone and excelled the deva Aṅkura with ten attributes: (1) celestial appearance, (2) celestial sound, (3) celestial fragrance, (4) celestial taste, (5) celestial touch, as well as (6) longevity, (7) greatness of retinue, (8) beauty of form, (9) great happiness, and (10) sovereignty.

Therefore, at this present Abhidhamma assembly, because the deva Aṅkura did not possess great power, every time more powerful devas and Brahmas arrived,
544:
he had to give up his seat and move, eventually finding a place twelve yojanas away from the Blessed One. The deva Indaka, however, being powerful, was able to remain in his first-taken seat near the Blessed One (without having to move elsewhere).

The Blessed One, looking at both the deva Aṅkura and the deva Indaka, wished to make known the great fruit of alms given to noble recipients in his dispensation. He intended to ask: "Aṅkura, you gave great alms for ten thousand years, with hearths arranged over twelve yojanas, yet now, having come to this assembly of the Buddha's Abhidhamma teaching, why do you have to stay at a distance of twelve yojanas?"

*Mahādānaṃ tayā dinnaṃ, aṅkura dīghamantaraṃ.*
*Atidūre nisinnosi, āgaccha mama santike.*

O deva Aṅkura, well-known by name! You have given great alms, with hearths arranged over twelve yojanas, with faith for a long period of ten thousand years. (Now, in this profound assembly of the Abhidhamma discourse), why do you sit so far away, twelve yojanas from me, moving back every time powerful devas and Brahmas arrive? Come here to my presence, under the shadow of my feet.
545:
*Āgaccha-āgacchāhi* = Come quickly without delay.

The Blessed One uttered this verse. (The sound of the Blessed One questioning the deva Aṅkura reached down to the earth, and the people in the human world heard that voice. From Dhammapada Aṭṭhakathā 2, 143.)

When questioned by the Blessed One in this way, the deva Aṅkura's reply in one and a half verses (6 padas), along with the half-verse added by the Saṅgītikāraka Elders, are recorded in the Pāḷi Canon as follows:

*Codito bhāvitattena, aṅkuro etadabravi.*
*Kiṃ mayhaṃ tena dānena, dakkhiṇeyyana suññataṃ.*
*Ayaṃ so indako yakkho, dajjā dānaṃ parittakaṃ.*
*Atirocati amhehi, cando tārāgaṇe yathā.*

Being questioned and urged by the Blessed One, who has developed both body and mind, the deva Aṅkura, who performed deeds outside the dispensation, spoke this reply with hands raised in worship: "Venerable Blessed One, what is the use of that merit of mine, which was performed with effort outside the dispensation, but was entirely void of noble recipients called 'virtuous ones' (*sīlavanta*)?"

"This deva Indaka here, in your presence, gave only a small gift of a single spoonful of alms-food to the great Elder Anuruddha with bright faith. Because of that, just as the moon in its silver palace outshines and excels the many groups of stars and constellations with its radiance,
546:
he outshines and excels us, whose power is small because our alms were chosen outside the dispensation, with his ten kinds of celestial power."

When Aṅkura had spoken thus, the Blessed One asked the deva Indaka: "Indaka, you sit near my right side without moving. Why is it that you can remain in your seat without having to move (when powerful devas arrive)?" The deva Indaka replied: "Venerable Blessed One, I am like a farmer who sowed a few seeds in fertile soil; I am one who obtained the perfection of the 'fertile field' of the recipient." Then, wishing to clarify the quality of a noble recipient, he said:

*Ujjaṅgale yathā khette,*
*bījaṃ bahumpi ropitaṃ.*
*Na phalaṃ vipulaṃ hoti,*
*napi toseti kassakaṃ.*

"Venerable Blessed One, just as many seeds sown with great effort in barren, salty, or high parched land where nutrients are distant, cannot produce abundant fruit, and thus cannot satisfy the farmer who works the land for a living;"
547:
*Tatheva dānaṃ bahukaṃ,*
*dussīlesu patiṭṭhitaṃ.*
*Na phalaṃ vipulaṃ hoti,*
*napi toseti dāyakaṃ.*

"In the same way, alms given outside the dispensation, sown and established in recipients who are immoral (*dussīla*), no matter how many times they are multiplied in number, cannot have great and abundant fruit. They cannot satisfy the donor who gives the alms, O Blessed One."

*Yathāpi bhaddake khette,*
*bījaṃ appampi ropitaṃ.*
*Sammā dhāraṃ pavecchante,*
*phalaṃ toseti kassakaṃ.*

(Just as even a few seeds sown in a good field...)
548:
Just as in a good field,
Endowed with nutrients and essence,
A seed sown with effort,
Even if small and insignificant,
When the rain falls correctly and timely—
Every fifteen days for the best soil,
Every ten days for medium soil,
Every five days for poor soil—
The fruit, being successful and full,
Delights the farmer who works the land;

In the same way,
Towards the virtuous ones (sīlavantesu),
Abounding in the grace of virtue,
Towards the Steadfast ones (tādisu) endowed with concentration,
An act of service or merit performed,
Even if small, yields great fruit.
It can clearly manifest like a seed sown in fertile soil, O Blessed One.

Indaka the deva spoke these four verses. When Indaka had spoken thus, the Blessed One addressed Aṅkura the deva: "Aṅkura, regarding what is called 'giving' (dāna), it is proper to give only after selecting and investigating these two: the excellence of the object to be given and the excellence of the recipient.
549:
When giving after such selection and investigation, that dāna can yield great fruit, like a seed sown in a good field. As for you (having encountered a time of decline outside the Dispensation), you were unable to give with such careful selection. Therefore, your dāna did not yield as much fruit (as Indaka's)." Wishing to clarify this meaning, the Buddha spoke:

Giving should be done after selection,
Where the gift yields great fruit.
Having given after selection,
Donors go to heaven.

Giving after selection is praised by the Sugata;
Those who are worthy of offerings here in the world of living beings—
Gifts given to them yield great fruit,
Like seeds sown in a good field.

"O Aṅkura, famous donor deva... giving with faith to those recipients known as virtuous ones yields great fruit. One should give after selecting (those virtuous recipients). Because of giving after selection, donors reach the celestial realm.

Giving after selecting the best of these two—the object to be given and the recipient—
550:
is praised by the Buddhas. In this world where beings live long, there are those noble recipients known as the virtuous. Gifts given with faith to those noble recipients yield great fruit, abounding in prosperity from the human and celestial realms up to Nibbāna, just like the five kinds of seeds sown in fertile soil.

After saying this, wishing to expand the teaching to lead them further to the attainment of the Path and Fruition, the Buddha continued to preach these four verses:

Fields are ruined by weeds;
This generation is ruined by lust.
Therefore, indeed, to those free from lust,
A gift given yields great fruit.

Fields, the grounds where the five kinds of seeds are sown, are often plagued by the defect of weeds. This generation of humans, devas, and brahmas is plagued by the defect of lust (rāga). Therefore, a gift given with faith to the noble ones who are free from lust yields great fruit, abounding in prosperity from the human and celestial realms up to Nibbāna.
551:
Fields are ruined by weeds;
This generation is ruined by hatred.
Therefore, indeed, to those free from hatred,
A gift given yields great fruit.

Fields, the grounds where the five kinds of seeds are sown, are often plagued by the defect of weeds. This generation of humans, devas, and brahmas is plagued by the defect of hatred (dosa). Therefore, a gift given with faith to the noble ones who are free from hatred yields great fruit, abounding in prosperity from the human and celestial realms up to Nibbāna.

Fields are ruined by weeds;
This generation is ruined by delusion.
Therefore, indeed, to those free from delusion,
A gift given yields great fruit.

Fields, the grounds where the five kinds of seeds are sown, are often plagued by the defect of weeds. This generation of humans, devas, and brahmas is plagued by the defect of delusion (moha). Therefore, a gift given with faith to the noble ones who are free from delusion yields great fruit, abounding in prosperity from the human and celestial realms up to Nibbāna.
552:
Fields are ruined by weeds;
This generation is ruined by desire.
Therefore, indeed, to those free from desire,
A gift given yields great fruit.

Fields, the grounds where the five kinds of seeds are sown, are often plagued by the defect of weeds. This generation of humans, devas, and brahmas is plagued by the defect of desire (icchā)—the attachment and longing for the five cords of sensual pleasure. Therefore, a gift given with faith to the noble ones who are free from desire yields great fruit, abounding in prosperity from the human and celestial realms up to Nibbāna.

At the conclusion of this teaching, Aṅkura the deva and Indaka the deva were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The teaching also became beneficial for many devas and brahmas.

(This is the story of Aṅkura the deva and Indaka the deva.)

## Here ends Chapter 24.
553:
## Chapter 25: Spending the Seventh Vassa in Tāvatiṃsa Heaven and Preaching the Abhidhamma

Thus, after the Blessed One established the deities Aṅkura and Indaka in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala), he spent the seventh rainy season in that very Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Sitting cross-legged on the Paṇḍukambala stone slab, in the midst of the assembly of deities and Brahmās who had arrived from the ten thousand world systems of the field of birth (jāti-khetta), led by the deity who was his former mother (Santusita deva), he preached the noble Abhidhamma Dhamma for the full three months of the rainy season, day and night without ceasing, in the manner of "Kusalā dhammā, akusalā dhammā, abyākatā dhammā," like a great celestial river flowing steadily.

(A special note here: Even when preaching a discourse of appreciation for a meal, the Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas, though slightly extended, is equal in volume to the Dīgha Nikāya or Majjhima Nikāya. The Dhamma teaching of the Buddhas to the assembly that arrives in the afternoon is equal in volume to the two great Nikāyas, the Saṃyutta Nikāya and Aṅguttara Nikāya. This is because for the Buddhas, the interval of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) between one cognitive process (vīthi) and another is very brief (only about two moments of bhavaṅga). Their lips are perfectly aligned. The opening of their lips (or the movement of their tongue) is very smooth and precise. Their tongue is very soft, thin, and long. Their voice possesses the eight qualities and is extremely sweet and pleasant to hear. Therefore, their speech (voice) is as follows:

"When people of a hundred and one races utter one word, Ānanda speaks eight words rapidly. When the famous Elder Ānanda speaks one word..."
554:
"...the Blessed One, the peerless and swift one, matches it with sixteen words. When ordinary worldly people speak one word, the Buddha, the Lord of Sages, speaks one hundred and twenty-eight words."

As described, his speech is very rapid. Therefore, the volume of the Dhamma teaching when preaching the appreciation for a meal or to the assembly in the afternoon is about the size of two great Nikāyas. The noble Abhidhamma Dhamma preached throughout the three months of the rainy season is indeed beyond perception and comparison.

## How the Buddha Sustained His Body While Preaching the Abhidhamma

Here, if it is asked, "How did the Buddha's physical body (upādinnaka-kāya), which can only be sustained by partaking of food and drink, endure while he preached the Abhidhamma continuously for the three months of the rainy season?" the brief answer is: "It was sustained only because he was nourished with food and drink." The detailed answer is:

For the Buddhas, those various times were already well-defined and personally realized. Therefore, while preaching the Abhidhamma, the Buddha would contemplate the time in the human world. Having contemplated thus, when the time for alms arrived, the Buddha would create a created image (nimmita-buddha) as his representative and resolve, "Let the manner of holding the robe, the manner of holding the bowl, the voice, and the entire appearance of this created image be exactly like mine. Let him preach this much of the Dhamma in my stead."
555:
Taking his bowl and robes, he proceeded to Lake Anotatta. At Lake Anotatta, the deities offered the Buddha a betel-vine tooth-stick. After using the tooth-stick and bathing in Lake Anotatta to cleanse his body, he stood on the Manosilā plateau. There, he donned his well-dyed double-layered robe and took the dark stone bowl with four rims (which had become a single bowl), offered by the Four Great Kings during his stay at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree (the seventh week of the seven locations). He then went to Uttarakuru for alms. After receiving alms from Uttarakuru, he sat gracefully at the bank of Lake Anotatta, partook of the meal, and proceeded to the Sandalwood Forest for his day's rest.

The Venerable Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma, also went to that Sandalwood Forest. After performing his duties for the Buddha, he sat in a place free from the six faults. At that time, the Buddha gave a summary and guidance to the Venerable Sāriputta, saying, "Sāriputta, I have preached this much of the Dhamma." When the Buddha gave this guidance, it was for the Chief Disciple, the Venerable Sāriputta, who had attained the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā-ñāṇa), like pointing out the great ocean with an outstretched hand while standing on the shore. Thus, for the Elder, through hundreds, thousands, and hundreds of thousands of methods, the Dhamma preached by the Buddha
556:
...the Dhamma that was preached became clear. He understood it in detail.

(After resting during the day in the Sandalwood Forest, the Blessed One would go to Tāvatiṃsa heaven to preach the Abhidhamma at the time he would normally preach to the people of Sāvatthī who came to listen in the afternoon. Because the rays, the voice, and the manner of speaking of the natural Buddha and the created Buddha were indistinguishably similar, only the powerful deities and Brahmās knew when the natural Buddha went to the human world or when he returned and exchanged places with the created image; the lesser deities and Brahmās did not know.)

## Ven. Sāriputta Preaching the Abhidhamma Again to the Five Hundred Monks Who Were Formerly Bats

The Venerable Sāriputta also brought the Abhidhamma Dhamma, which the Blessed One preached daily (in the briefest way), and preached it again (in a medium way, neither too brief nor too detailed) to his five hundred resident pupils (saddhivihārika).

The past merit of those five hundred monks is as follows: In the time of Kassapa Buddha, they were born as small bats. While they were hanging in a cave, they took the sound of the Abhidhamma as an object of their attention (nimitta) from two monks who were Abhidhamma-bearers reciting the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. (Although they did not even know what the waxing or waning moon was), by merely taking the sound of the Abhidhamma as an object, they passed away and were reborn in the celestial realm.
557:
(Those five hundred small bats did not know it was the Abhidhamma Dhamma; they did not know about the aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), or truths (sacca); they did not even know the waxing or waning of the moon. However, because the sound of the Abhidhamma they heard was a very noble kamma-nimitta, they were able to focus on that good object of the Abhidhamma sound at the time of death and were thus reborn in the celestial realm.)

Those five hundred deities, who were formerly bats, did not fall into the lower realms for the entire interval between the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha and this Buddha (one Buddhantara). They were reborn from one celestial life to another. In the time of this Buddha, they were born in the human world. Having developed faith and devotion during the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya), they ordained under the Venerable Sāriputta. The Venerable Sāriputta took the Abhidhamma Dhamma as it was preached daily by the Buddha and taught it daily (in a medium method) to his five hundred co-resident pupils who were formerly bats.

The completion of the Buddha's preaching of the Abhidhamma in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and the completion of the five hundred monks' learning of the full seven books of the Abhidhamma under the Venerable Sāriputta occurred simultaneously at the same time.

Every day, as mentioned before, when the Buddha finished his meal in the Sandalwood Forest,
558:
"Dear Sāriputta, today I have preached the Abhidhamma in such and such a manner and to such an extent. The created Buddha-image (nimmitarūpa) has also preached the Abhidhamma to such an extent. You, dear son, should teach it to your five hundred disciple monks." After giving this brief instruction, the Buddha himself returned to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and continued preaching the Abhidhamma personally, following on from where the created Buddha-image had finished.

In this way, the preaching of the Abhidhamma was completed on the full moon day of Thadingyut (Assayuja), marking the end of the three-month rainy season retreat. At that time, eighty crores (800 million) of deities and Brahmas realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation. The mother-deity (Santusita deva) was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala).

## The Multitude of People from Sāvatthī
## Moving and Gathering at the City of Saṅkassa

That multitude of people, residing in Sāvatthī and covering an area of thirty-six yojanas, approached the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna on the ninth day of the waxing moon of Thadingyut and said, "Venerable Sir, it would be well to find out the day the Blessed One will descend to the human world. Indeed, if we do not get to pay homage to the Blessed One, we will not return; only after paying homage will we return." Hearing these words, the Venerable Moggallāna replied, "Very well, lay devotees," and then, diving into the earth at that very spot, he reached the foot of Mount Meru.
559:
He made a resolution: "Let the multitude see me as I ascend from within Mount Sineru to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven." Then, appearing clearly to the people like a crimson thread threaded through a precious gem, he ascended from the middle of Mount Sineru to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

The people saw the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna clearly, saying, "Now he has ascended one league, now two leagues," and so on. The Elder reached the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as if he were carrying the Buddha's feet on his head. After respectfully paying homage to the Buddha, he asked, "Exalted Buddha, the multitude of people wish to return to their homes only after seeing the Blessed One. When will you descend to the human world, Lord?"

The Buddha asked, "Moggallāna, where is your elder brother Sāriputta now?" The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied, "Exalted Buddha, the Venerable Sāriputta is spending the rainy season in the city of Saṅkassa."

The Buddha then said:
"Moggallāna, seven days from today, on the full moon day of Assayuja, the day of the Great Pavāraṇā, I shall descend at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa. Let those who wish to see me come to that place. From Sāvatthī to the gate of Saṅkassa is thirty leagues. In such a
560:
"On such a long journey, there is no need at all to carry provisions. Tell those people, dear son, to come without provisions, just as they would go to the monastery at the head of the city or village to listen to the Dhamma after observing the Uposatha on an Uposatha day."

The Elder replied, "Very well, Blessed One," and returning to Sāvatthī, he informed the people exactly as the Buddha had instructed.

## Descending to the Gate of Saṅkassa City via the Three Stairways
## 

When the rainy season retreat ended, on the full moon day of Thadingyut, the Blessed One addressed Sakka, the King of Devas, saying, "Lay devotee Sakka, I shall now return to the human world." Sakka then created three stairways: a golden stairway, a ruby stairway, and a silver stairway. The bases of these three stairways were established at the gate of Saṅkassa city, while their tops were on the summit of Mount Meru. Among these three stairways, (1) the golden stairway on the right was for the deities, (2) the silver stairway on the left was for the Great Brahmas, and (3) the ruby stairway in the middle was for the Blessed One.

The Blessed One stood on the summit of Mount Meru, and as he was about to descend from the celestial realm to the human world, he performed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) of water and fire and looked up towards the sky. At that moment, the space up to the Akanittha Brahma realm became open and unobstructed, appearing as a single expanse. Then...
561:
he looked downward, and the space down to the Avīci hell became open and unobstructed, appearing as a single plain. Then, he looked toward the cardinal and intermediate directions, and thousands of surrounding world systems became open and unobstructed, appearing as a single plain. Thus, the deities and Brahmas could see the humans, and the humans could clearly see the deities and Brahmas.

The Buddha emitted the six-colored rays. On the day he descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven to the human world, after beholding the Buddha's glory, there was not a single person among the multitude thirty-six leagues in circumference who did not aspire for Buddhahood.

The deities descended following him on the golden stairway on the right. The Great Brahmas descended following him on the silver stairway on the left. The Buddha himself descended on the central jeweled stairway. The deity Pañcasikha, holding the Beluva lute, stood on the right side and descended while playing the lute in worship of the Buddha. The deity Suyāma, holding a yak-tail fan, followed on the right side in worship. The deity Santusita, swinging a jeweled circular fan, likewise followed on the right side in worship. Sakka, blowing the Vijayuttara conch, followed on the right side in worship. In this manner, the deities living in the remaining world systems also performed various acts of worship.
562:
—they descended, following Him. From the silver stairway on the left, the Great Brahma also descended, holding a white parasol in honor of the Buddha.

The Blessed One, accompanied by this retinue of devas and Brahmas, descended and stood at the gate of Saṅkassa city. The vast multitude gathered in Sāvatthī, having finished their morning meal on the Great Pavāraṇā day of the full moon of Thadingyut, set out saying, “Today we shall behold the Blessed One at the gate of Saṅkassa city.” They reached the gate of Saṅkassa in a short time without exhaustion, as if they were merely entering a village monastery.

## Preaching the Sāriputta Sutta

As soon as the Blessed One descended from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven and set His right foot on the ground at the head of the stairway in the human world, the Elder Sāriputta was the first to pay homage and worship Him. Thereafter, the rest of the assembly paid their respects to the Blessed One. The spot where the Buddha first set His right foot upon descending from the stairway at the gate of Saṅkassa city later became famous as the “Acala-cetiya-ṭhāna” (The Station of the Unshakable Shrine).

After performing the Twin Miracle and spending the Rains Retreat in Tāvatiṃsa heaven preaching the Abhidhamma for three months, the place where the Buddha first set His right foot upon descending to the Saṅkassa city gate via the three stairways is one of the “Avijahita-ṭhāna” (Unforsaken Places) that all Buddhas do not abandon. (This means that every Buddha, after preaching the Abhidhamma in Tāvatiṃsa heaven—)
563:
—customarily sets His right foot first at this very spot at the gate of Saṅkassa city when descending to the human world via the three stairways.)

## The Four Unforsaken Places (Avijahita-ṭhāna)

In this context, it is appropriate to briefly note the four Unforsaken Places (Avijahita-ṭhāna).

The permanent places that all Buddhas do not abandon are called “Avijahita-ṭhāna.” There are four such places:

(1) The place where the Mahābodhi tree and the Aparājita Throne (The Unconquerable Throne) arise, where all Buddhas attain victory over the five Maras. (This means that the Aparājita Thrones of all Buddhas arise in the exact same spot where our current Buddha’s throne arose; the location never changes.)

(2) The place in the Isipatana Migadāya (Deer Park) where the first sermon, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, is preached. (Every Buddha preaches the first sermon in the same location in the Isipatana Migadāya where our current Buddha preached it. They do not preach it elsewhere.)

(3) The place at the gate of Saṅkassa city where the right foot is first set when descending from Tāvatiṃsa heaven to the human world after preaching the Abhidhamma. (Every Buddha customarily sets His right foot first at this very spot when descending from Tāvatiṃsa heaven after preaching the Abhidhamma.)

(4) The place where the four legs of the Blessed One’s bed (gandhakuṭī-mañca) are positioned within the Gandhakuti (Fragrant Chamber) of the Jetavana Monastery. (In the case of our—)
564: Buddha's personal bed stood, the four legs of the personal beds of all Buddhas are placed; there is no change in location). The area of the monastery grounds varied in size according to the era. To clarify further: (a) For Vipassī Buddha, a merchant named Punabbhasumitta purchased land one yojana in extent by covering it completely with gold bricks and built a great monastery. (b) For Sikhī Buddha, a merchant named Sirivaḍḍha purchased land three gāvutas in extent by covering it completely with gold staffs (gold rods) and built a great monastery. (c) For Vessabhū Buddha, a merchant named Sotthija purchased land half a yojana (two gāvutas) in extent by covering it completely with gold plowshares (or gold bowls) and built a great monastery. (d) For Kakusandha Buddha, a merchant named Accuta purchased land one gāvuta in extent by covering it completely with gold blocks cast in the shape of elephant hooves and built a great monastery. (e) For Koṇāgamana Buddha, a merchant named Ugga purchased land half a gāvuta (forty usabhas) in extent by covering it completely with gold bricks and built a great monastery. (f) For Kassapa Buddha, a merchant named Sumangala purchased land twenty usabhas in extent by covering it completely with gold tortoise figures and built a great monastery. (g) For our Buddha, the merchant Sudatta (Anāthapiṇḍika) purchased land eight karīsas in extent by covering it completely with gold coins (kahāpaṇas) and built the great Jetavana Monastery.
565:
—Blessed One, these statements are extracted from the Buddhavaṃsa Commentary (page 351) and the Vinaya Cūḷavagga Commentary (Vin. A. 4, page 63).

Although the grounds of the Jetavana Monastery may vary in extent according to the era, the site of the Gandhakuti remains unchanged; it is always built in the same location.

(This concludes the note on the four Unforsaken Places.)

## Devas and Humans Love and Cherish the Buddhas

As mentioned before, when the Blessed One stood having first set His right foot at the head of the stairway, the Elder Sāriputta was the first to behold and pay homage to Him, saying, “Exalted Buddha, today all humans and devas love, cherish, and adore You; they aspire for and pray for the attainment of Buddhahood.” The Blessed One replied to the Elder Sāriputta, “Dear Sāriputta, it is only natural that all Brahmas, devas, and humans should favor, respect, and love the Buddhas who are endowed with such qualities.” Then, wishing to preach the Dhamma, He spoke this verse:

Ye jhānappasutā dhīrā,
nekkhammūpasame ratā.
devāpi tesaṃ pihayanti,
sambuddhānaṃ satīmatā.

Sāriputta = Dear Sāriputta. Ye dhīrā = Those wise ones who possess Omniscience. Jhānappasutā = Who are devoted to and practice the two types of jhāna (meditation on objects and meditation on characteristics)—
566:
They delight in, enjoy, and strive with the five kinds of mastery (vasībhāva). Nekkhammūpasame = in the ultimate Nibbāna, the certain escape from all suffering. Ratā = they constantly rejoice and delight in entering the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). Satīmataṃ = to those Fully Enlightened Ones who are always possessed of constant mindfulness. Tesaṃ sambuddhānaṃ = to those Lords of Wisdom. Devāpi = even the deities and Brahmas of the upper realms. Pihayanti = they admire and aspire with great joy, saying, "It would be wonderful if we too could become a Supreme Buddha, which is so rare to encounter."

He preached this verse. (The Dhammapada Commentary states that at the end of this verse, thirty crores of humans, deities, and Brahmas attained liberation, and the five hundred disciple monks of the Venerable Sāriputta were established in Arahatship. This does not agree with the Sutta Nipāta Commentary). According to the Sutta Nipāta Commentary:

## of the Venerable Sāriputta

While standing at the head of the stairway, the Blessed One reflected and considered thus:

"In this assembly, the Elder Moggallāna is renowned as the foremost and most excellent in psychic powers (iddhipāda). The Elder Anuruddha is renowned as the foremost and most excellent in divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). The Elder Puṇṇa is renowned as a preacher of the Dhamma (dhammakathika). However, this assembly does not yet know the Elder Sāriputta as being so superior and noble in any particular virtue."
567:
“It would be well if I were to make Sāriputta’s virtue of wisdom clearly known.” Having thus reflected, He asked the Elder Sāriputta a series of questions: questions pertaining to worldlings (puthujjana), questions pertaining to those in training (sekha, the lower noble disciples), and questions pertaining to those beyond training (asekha, the Arahants). The Elder answered all the questions—those of the worldlings, the learners, and the non-learners—exactly as the Blessed One asked them. At that time, the multitude clearly recognized the Elder Sāriputta as “a person of superior and noble wisdom.”

## Preaching the Parosahassa Jātaka

Thereafter, the Blessed One remarked, “Sāriputta is not only superior in the virtue of wisdom now; he was also superior in the virtue of wisdom in the past.” He then related the Parosahassa Jātaka (Ekaka Nipāta, 10-Litta Vagga, 9th Jātaka, Jā. I, page 430). The summary of the Parosahassa Jātaka is as follows:

In the past, over a thousand noble ascetics lived at the foot of a mountain, subsisting only on wild roots and fruits of the forest. When their teacher fell ill, among the disciples who were attending to him, the eldest disciple said to the others, “I shall go and find suitable medicine for our teacher. Until I return, do not neglect to care for him.” He then set out toward the human paths to search for medicine.
568: Before the eldest disciple could return, the teacher passed away. Shortly before his death, when the other disciples questioned him regarding his attainments in jhāna, the teacher, referring to the Ākiñcaññāyatana (the third formless jhāna), replied, "Natthi kiñci" (There is nothing). (To enter the Ākiñcaññāyatana jhāna, one must focus on the concept of non-existence—that there is not even a little bit of the first formless jhāna—and repeatedly meditate, "Natthi kiñci, natthi kiñci." It was with reference to this that the teacher replied, "Natthi kiñci"). The disciples, however, did not understand the teacher's intention and misunderstood, thinking, "Our teacher has no attainment of jhāna at all." Consequently, they did not perform the funeral rites for the teacher's physical remains at the cemetery with proper respect, but lived with indifference. (A special point to note here: The Great Bodhisatta teacher, who had attained the Ākiñcaññāyatana jhāna, replied "Natthi kiñci" when asked by his disciples and was then reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma realm—the second Rūpāvacara jhāna realm. Indeed, although Great Bodhisattas attain the formless (arūpa) jhānas, they are not reborn in the four formless realms because those realms are "abhabbaṭṭhāna"—places where Bodhisattas are not reborn). Later, when the eldest disciple returned with the suitable medicine and found that the teacher had passed away, he asked the other disciples, "Did you ask the teacher anything?" The disciples replied, "Yes, we did. The teacher said, 'Natthi kiñci' (There is nothing). Our teacher..."
569:
569
They spoke according to their own views, saying, 'He passed away without attaining even a single jhāna.'

When the chief disciple ascetic heard their words, he replied truthfully, 'You do not understand the meaning of the words spoken by the Great Teacher at all. Our Great Teacher was one who attained the Ākiñcaññāyatana jhāna (the third formless jhāna).'

Although the chief disciple ascetic spoke the truth repeatedly, those ascetics remained unable to believe him. The Bodhisatta, the King of the Ābhassara Brahmas, became aware of this and thought, 'These fools, blind in wisdom, do not believe the words of my chief disciple. I shall make the truth clear to these fools who are blind in wisdom.' Having so resolved, he descended from the Ābhassara Brahma realm to the human world. Standing in the air above the monastery grounds with great majesty, and wishing to praise the power of the chief disciple's wisdom, he recited this verse:

Parosahassampi samāgatānaṃ,
Kandeyyuṃ te vassasataṃ apaññā.
Eko va seyyo puriso sapañño,
So bhāsitassa vijānāti atthaṃ.

Even if more than a thousand fools were to gather and lament for a hundred years, they would certainly not understand the reason behind the Teacher's words. A single wise man who discerns the meaning of what is spoken is far more excellent and worthy of praise than those thousand fools.
570:
570
Reciting this verse, the Great Being stood in the air, preached the Dhamma to make the assembly of ascetics understand, and then returned to the Brahma realm. Those ascetics also attained jhānas and meditative attainments (samāpatti) and, at the end of their lives, were reborn in the Brahma realm.

After the Blessed One had delivered this religious discourse, he connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, Sāriputta was the chief disciple ascetic, and I myself was the Mahā Brahma of the Ābhassara realm.'

(This is the summary of the Parosahassa Jātaka; if a detailed account is desired, it should be noted from the Ekanipāta Jātaka stories.)

## Preaching the Sāriputta Sutta
After the Blessed One had preached this Parosahassa Jātaka, the Venerable Sāriputta Mahāthera, for the benefit of his five hundred resident pupils (saddhivihārika), wished to ask about suitable places, resorts, and practices. He began by reciting eight verses of praise, starting with 'Na me diṭṭho ito pubbe.' Wishing to answer those questions, the Blessed One preached thirteen verses, starting with 'Vijigucchamānassa yadidaṃ phāsu.'*

## Summary of the Sāriputta Sutta
I (Sāriputta) have never before seen, nor heard from anyone else, the Teacher, the Blessed One, the leader of the Order, who speaks pleasant words and who, having descended from the Tusita heaven into his mother's womb, dwells adorned with such a collection of wonderful and extraordinary miracles. (1)

Having abandoned all delusion, being the peerless and unique one, he has attained delight in jhāna and delight in Nibbāna. The inhabitants of the three realms—Brahmas, devas, and humans—see the Lord Buddha, who possesses the five eyes, as he truly is. (2)

I (Sāriputta) have come to this place wishing to ask questions for the sake of many disciples to the Blessed One, who is the leader of the Order, who is free from the two dependencies of craving and views, who is entirely unshaken by worldly conditions, who performs no deceptive or miraculous tricks, and who has arrived at the gate of this city of Saṅkassa. (3)

For a monk who, loathing and fearing the dangers of birth and so forth, resorts to and dwells in secluded lodgings such as the foot of a tree, a cemetery, or a mountain cave where it is quiet from people—how many objects of fear are there in those various lodgings, both good and bad, at which the monk must remain unshaken and unafraid? (a), (4-5)
572:
572
For the noble monk who journeys toward the destination of Nibbāna, a place he has never reached before, how many dangers are there in the secluded forest lodgings at the edge of towns and villages that he must overcome? (b). (6)

What are the words that the noble monk should speak? (c). What are the resorts (pastures) in this world where that noble monk should frequent? (d). What are the practices to be followed by that noble monk whose mind is intensely directed toward the work of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna)? (e). (7)

What training (sikkhā) should that noble monk well undertake so that, with a concentrated mind, mature wisdom, and clear mindfulness, he may blow away and remove his own impurities of defilements, just as a goldsmith blows away the dross of gold? (f). (8)

(Thus, Venerable Sāriputta praised the Blessed One with three verses and asked about suitable lodgings, resorts, habits, and practices for the benefit of the five hundred disciple monks with five verses. The Blessed One answered with the following thirteen verses.)

Dear Sāriputta, for the monk of good family who, loathing and fearing the dangers of birth and so forth, dwells in a secluded lodging and desires the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa), I shall preach to you the Dhamma for living happily and the Dhamma to be practiced, according to what I have personally realized (not by mere conjecture). (1)
573:
573
Dear Sāriputta, a monk who is wise, whose mindfulness is clear, and who practices within the four boundaries (virtue, sense-restraint, moderation in eating, and wakefulness) should not fear these five types of dangers: (1) the danger of contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and flies; (2) the danger of contact with snakes, scorpions, and centipedes; (3) the danger of being overwhelmed and oppressed by evil people; (4) the danger of wild beasts such as four-legged lions and tigers; (5) the danger of being questioned, spoken to, or oppressed by those with external (bāhiraka) views who do not have faith in the Triple Gem. Even if he encounters various terrifying objects from these five sources, he should not be startled or afraid.

(With this half-verse, the answer is given to question (a): 'How many objects of fear are there for the noble monk who resorts to seclusion?' The answer states that there are five such dangers: gadflies/mosquitoes, snakes/scorpions, evil people, wild beasts, and those with external views.)

Furthermore, the noble monk who seeks and strives for the noble and faultless Right Practice (sammā-paṭipatti) that leads to Nibbāna should also overcome and master the following internal enemies in addition to the five external dangers: (2-3)

Even if he is oppressed by (1) the touch of illness, (2) the touch of hunger and thirst, (3) the touch of internal and external cold weather, and (4) the touch of hot weather,

Although that noble monk is oppressed in various ways by those four types of internal contacts, he must not allow (5) the ten forms of misconduct—briefly, the collection of unwholesome states (akusala)—which are the innermost enemies, to arise. Instead, he must exert firm and steadfast effort (sammappadhāna-vīriya). (4)

(With this half-verse, the answer is given to question (b): 'How many internal dangers must the noble monk who resorts to seclusion overcome?' Having answered questions (a) and (b), the answers to the remaining questions (c), (d), (e), and (f) are given collectively in the following nine verses.)

The noble monk should by no means commit theft. He should by no means speak lies. He should constantly radiate loving-kindness (mettā) toward beings who still have craving (tasa) and those who are free from craving (thāvara). He should recognize and abandon the collection of unwholesome states—briefly, the ten forms of misconduct—which cause the mind to be turbid, knowing, 'This collection is the army of Māra.' (5)

(By this verse, four practices are preached: not stealing, not lying, practicing mettā, and abandoning unwholesome states.)

He should not follow the will of anger (kodha) or excessive pride (atimāna).

He should uproot the six states that are the fundamental causes of anger and pride (namely: ignorance, unwise attention, the conceit 'I am', lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, and restlessness). Furthermore, he should master pleasant and unpleasant objects so that he can overcome them. (That is, he should live in such a way that pleasant and unpleasant objects do not affect him.) (6)

(By this verse, four practices are preached: not being angry, not being proud, uprooting the six fundamental causes of those two, and not letting pleasant or unpleasant objects exist for him.)

The noble monk, placing clear comprehension (sampajañña) at the forefront and holding onto the joy (pīti) obtained by practicing the ten recollections (anussati), should remove the previously mentioned internal and external enemies.

(By this statement, a skillful means is shown: by putting clear comprehension first and developing the meditation of recollections, one should endure and overcome the five external dangers and five internal enemies with the joy resulting from that meditation.)

By that same skillful means, he should overcome discontent (arati) in the secluded forest monastery and discontent in the meritorious work of meditation. He should also overcome the following four causes of lamentation. (7)

## The Four Causes of Lamentation
(1) Thinking and worrying, 'What food shall I get to eat today?' (Shall I eat rice? Shall I eat barley cake? Shall I eat sweets? Shall I eat fish? Shall I eat meat?)
576:
(2) Thinking, "Where shall I eat today?" (i.e., whether at the King's palace, a Brahmin's house, a wealthy merchant's house, or a poor person's house); (3) Thinking, "I slept miserably last night" (i.e., on a wooden plank, or on a mat of woven bamboo, or on a small piece of leather, or on a bed of grass, leaves, or straw); (4) Thinking, "Where shall I sleep comfortably tonight?" (i.e., on a couch, or on a bench, etc.)—these four types of thoughts and anxieties are called the four causes of weeping. A noble monk who practices the Three Trainings should be free from all impediments (palibodha) such as attachment to family (kula), group (gaṇa), dwelling (āvāsa), and the four requisites (paccaya). He should abandon these four causes of weeping: the two anxieties regarding food and the two anxieties regarding lodging. (8)

(The meaning is that if these four types of anxieties exist, one may lose heart and weep. A noble monk must abandon these four causes of weeping by ensuring that no impediments—attachments to donors, the Saṅgha, dwellings, or the four requisites—arise. To prevent the four causes of weeping from arising, one must cut off the impediments.)

In this Dispensation, when a noble monk receives alms-food at the time for alms and robes at the time for robes in accordance with the Dhamma,
577:
he should know moderation in receiving and consuming them for the sake of increasing contentment (santoṣa).

(Knowing moderation in receiving means: weighing these three factors—the quantity of the gift, the degree of the donor's faith and desire to give, and one's own capacity. (a) If the gift is abundant but the donor's desire to give is small, one should receive only a little out of consideration for the donor's desire. (b) If the gift is small but the donor's desire to give is great, one should receive only a little out of consideration for the smallness of the gift. (c) If both the gift and the donor's desire are great, one should know one's own capacity and receive only what is sufficient. These three ways of receiving are called "paṭiggahana-mattaññutā" (moderation in receiving). Consuming the four requisites after reflecting upon them (paccavekkhaṇā) is called "paribhoga-mattaññutā" (moderation in consumption).)

Having secured himself from unwholesome states regarding the four requisites (through the two types of moderation mentioned), that noble monk, while restraining and guarding his four postures within the town or village, should not speak harsh words even if he is insulted or provoked by others. (9)

(The meaning is: one must receive and use the four requisites obtained according to the Dhamma in line with the two types of moderation. One must remain restrained in the four postures while in towns or villages. Even if people insult or provoke him, he must not respond with harsh speech.)

A noble monk should be one with downcast eyes (i.e., not looking here and there). He should not be one who wanders aimlessly (i.e., not traveling frequently to various places). He must strive and exert himself to attain the Jhanas not yet attained and to master the fivefold mastery (vasī-bhāva) of the Jhanas already attained. He should be one who is very wakeful.
578:
(During a day and night, he should sleep mindfully for only about 4 hours during the middle watch, and spend the remaining time practicing the monk's Dhamma through the two postures of walking and sitting.) (By striving thus), he should develop the equanimity of the fourth Jhana and, with a very concentrated mind, abandon and cut off sensual thoughts (kāma-vitakka) and the like, the objects of those thoughts such as sensual perceptions (kāma-saññā), and remorse (kukkucca) such as the fidgeting of hands and feet. (10)

When a noble monk is admonished with words of blame by those who desire his welfare, such as his teachers and preceptors (upajjhāya), saying, "Friend, this action of yours is not proper," etc., he should remain mindful and feel satisfied and appreciative toward those teachers and preceptors. He should never harbor a mind of resentment or hostility toward his fellow monks; he must destroy such feelings. He should speak only blameless words. He must not speak beyond the limits of the training rules or the appropriate time. He should not even think of doing anything that would lead to accusations by the public. (The meaning is: if one's virtue, conduct, view, or livelihood is corrupted, the public will speak words of accusation, blame, and reproach. Therefore, let alone doing such things, one should not even think of committing acts that corrupt virtue, conduct, view, or livelihood which would lead to public reproach.) (11)

Dear Sāriputta, furthermore, there are five kinds of "dust" in the world: lust for forms (rūpa-rāga), lust for sounds (sadda-rāga), lust for smells (gandha-rāga), lust for tastes (rasa-rāga), and lust for tangibles (phoṭṭhabba-rāga). Regarding these five kinds of dust,
579:
a noble monk, being clearly mindful, must practice and develop the Three Trainings to abandon them. By practicing in this way, the noble monk will be able to overcome those five kinds of lust or dust. (12)

(The meaning is: to abandon the five kinds of lust or dust, one must practice the Three Trainings. Only one who strives thus can overcome the five kinds of dust; others cannot.)

(That monk who practices the Three Trainings to abandon the five kinds of lust will, in due course) be able to dispel sensual desire for the five sense objects. Being clearly mindful and having a mind liberated from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth, that monk, at the appropriate time, investigates and contemplates the collection of conditioned things (saṅkhāra) as impermanent (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anatta) without distortion and with clarity. Having a concentrated heart, he will be able to burn away and abandon the darkness of the defilements. (13)

In this way, the Blessed One answered the questions asked by the Venerable Sāriputta, culminating in the Fruit of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred monks who were disciples of the Venerable Sāriputta attained the Fruit of Arahantship, and thirty crores of devas and humans realized the Four Noble Truths and attained liberation.

## Special Note
Before this Sāriputta Sutta was preached, in the section highlighting the great wisdom and virtues of the Venerable Sāriputta, in the Dhammapada Commentary Vol. 2, page 148, and in the Jātaka Commentary Vol. 4, page 267, in the explanation of the Sarabhamiga Jātaka—
