"Ye ca saṅkhāta-dhammāse, ye ca sekhā puthū idha; tesaṃ me nipako iriyaṃ, puṭṭho pabrūhi mārisa."

When the Blessed One asked for the detailed meaning of this brief verse to be explained, it is said that although the Venerable Sāriputta had no doubt about the question itself, he had doubt about the Blessed One's intention. Only after the Blessed One gave a hint did he answer by way of the aggregates (khandha), and so forth.

The commentators mentioned this point to show that the Chief Disciples cannot answer questions within the Buddha's range (Buddha-visaya), citing the Bhūta Sutta from the Nidānavagga Saṃyutta (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1, 281).

It was not intended to show that the Blessed One asked for the detailed meaning of that verse while standing at the head of the stairway. Indeed, the Blessed One preached that Bhūta Sutta at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī.

Therefore, to avoid confusing the readers' understanding, that matter is not mentioned in this text (in the section on standing at the head of the stairway). For the same reason, it was not mentioned in the commentary to the Sāriputta Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta (to avoid confusing the understanding).

(This is a special note.)

## While the Blessed One was Residing at the Jetavana Monastery
## The Accusation by Ciñcamāṇavikā

As previously mentioned, the Blessed One preached many Dhamma discourses at the gate of Saṅkassa city, leading thirty crores of deities and humans, along with the five hundred disciple monks of the Venerable Sāriputta, to the realization of the Four Noble Truths...
581:
and attain liberation, He traveled from the city of Saṅkassa to the region of Sāvatthī. While residing and delighting in the Jetavana Monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī, He continued to distribute the nectar of the Dhamma to the veneya beings (those teachable) who arrived.

While He was residing there, a great incident occurred involving an improper accusation against the Blessed One by a wicked female wanderer named Ciñcamāṇavikā. The detailed account of how it happened is as follows:

During the first twenty years of His Buddhahood (Paṭhama-bodhi), the disciples of the Blessed One increased day by day like the rising tide. As they increased, an incomparably vast number of humans, devas, and Brahmas reached the stages of the Noble Ones (the four Fruits) according to their perfections (pāramī) and merit. Consequently, the fame and virtues of the Blessed One, such as being an 'Arahant,' spread throughout the universe, and great gains and honor (lābha-sakkāra) arose for the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha. As for the heretics (titthiya), their influence, fame, and gains diminished day by day, like fireflies when the sun rises.

Those heretics, longing for gains and honor to arise, would stand along the roads and say to the people:

"Lay followers, is only the ascetic Gotama truly a Buddha? We, too, are truly Buddhas."
582: 582 "Is only the offering made to the ascetic Gotama of great fruit? The offering made to us is also of great fruit. (Therefore) give to us as well; perform meritorious deeds"—even though they spoke such words of solicitation, they did not receive the four requisites, gains, or honor. Thus, they gathered in a secluded place and consulted one another, saying, "By what means or trickery can we cause the ill-repute of the ascetic Gotama to arise among the people and cause his gains and honor to be ruined?" At that time, there was a female wandering ascetic named Ciñcamāṇavikā in the city of Sāvatthī. Because she had taken conception through moisture-birth (saṃsedaja) in a tamarind tree, she was named Ciñcamāṇavikā (the young woman of the tamarind tree).* She possessed a noble appearance like a goddess and had reached the pinnacle of grace and beauty; rays of light flickered and radiated from her body. When the heretics (titthiyas) were thus consulting, one cruel, wicked, and fierce heretic suggested, "Let us cause the ill-repute of the ascetic Gotama to arise by using the female wandering ascetic Ciñcamāṇavikā as a means, and let us ruin the gains and honor of that ascetic Gotama." When he spoke thus, all the remaining heretics unanimously agreed, saying, "This means and trickery is indeed a good way to cause the loss of the ascetic Gotama's gains." *Ciñcamāṇavikā: A female wandering ascetic so named because she was born by way of moisture-birth in a tamarind tree. — Commentary on the Mahāpaduma Jātaka, Jātaka-ṭīkā.
583:
"This is indeed a good strategy," they all agreed in unison. Then, the female wandering ascetic Ciñcamāṇavikā went to the monastery of the heretics and stood there paying her respects, but the heretics remained silent and did not speak to her. Thinking to herself, "What fault could I have committed?", she said three times, "Noble ones, I pay my respects to you with devotion." She then asked directly, "Noble ones, what fault do I have? Why do you remain silent without speaking to me?" The heretics spoke words of blame, saying, "Sister Ciñca, do you not know that the ascetic Gotama is oppressing and harrassing us, causing our gains and offerings to dwindle as he wanders about?" When they said this, Ciñcamāṇavikā replied, "Noble ones, I did not know of this matter. What task should I perform and carry out in this regard?" The heretics gave her the responsibility, saying, "Sister Ciñca, if you desire our well-being, then by using yourself as a means, create a bad reputation for the ascetic Gotama and destroy his gains, offerings, and honor."
## Ciñca's Strategy
Ciñca replied, "Very well, noble ones. Let this be my responsibility to carry out. Noble ones, do not remain anxious with various thoughts."
584: 584 ...she spoke words of bold responsibility and departed from the monastery of those heretics. Being clever and skilled in feminine wiles, from that time on, when the people of Sāvatthī had finished listening to the Dhamma and were leaving the Jetavana Monastery, she would wear a robe the color of a red insect, hold perfumes and flowers, and head towards the Jetavana Monastery. When many people met her on the way and asked, "O Ciñcamāṇ, where are you going at this time near dusk?" Ciñcamāṇ would speak suspicious words, saying, "What benefit is it to you to know where I am going?" She would then sleep in the heretics' monastery near the Jetavana Monastery. Early in the morning, when the lay devotees (upāsakas) were coming out from the city of Sāvatthī, saying, "Let us be the first to pay homage to the Blessed One," she would enter the city of Sāvatthī, making it appear as if she had spent the night within the Jetavana Monastery. When the people met her and asked, "O Ciñcamāṇ, where did you sleep last night?" she would speak suspicious words, saying, "What benefit is it to you to know where I slept? Even if you know where I slept, it is of no benefit to you; do not seek to know." In this manner, she went and spoke daily. When about half a month or a month had passed, and she was asked by people on the road as before, Ciñcamāṇ began to make accusations, saying, "I have been staying the night in the same Gandhakuṭī with the ascetic Gotama within the Jetavana Monastery." By speaking thus, she caused doubt and speculation in the minds of ordinary worldlings (puthujjanas) who heard those words, thinking, "Could this matter be true? Or could it be untrue?"
585:
She caused people to have doubts and speculations, wondering, "Is it true or is it not true?" After three or four months had passed, she wrapped her belly with coarse cloths to show the appearance of a pregnant woman. Over that, she wore a bright red robe and accused the Buddha, misleading the ignorant masses by saying, "I have conceived this child because of the ascetic Gotama."
## The Great Accusation in the Midst of the Fourfold Assembly
In this manner, when eight or nine months had passed, Ciñca tied a wooden disc shaped like a half-egg to her belly to look like a truly advanced pregnancy. Over it, she wore a bright red robe. She struck the backs of her hands and feet with a cow's jawbone to make them appear swollen as if she were near childbirth, and she made her eyes, ears, and nose appear weary and exhausted. In the evening, while the Blessed One was seated on the Buddha-throne of Dhamma preaching to the fourfold assembly, she went to the place where the Dhamma assembly was being held. Standing directly in front of the Blessed One, Ciñca said:
"Great ascetic, you preach the Dhamma to the masses. Your lips are indeed very smooth. As for me, I have conceived a child because of you, and now I am one with an advanced pregnancy. You, great ascetic, do not consider a house for my childbirth, nor do you consider butter, oil, and such; you just remain indifferent. If you do not perform these tasks yourself, you should at least have entrusted one of your supporting lay devotees, such as King Kosala, the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, or..."
586:
...the female lay supporter Visākhā, saying, 'Please perform and look after what should be done for this Ciñca.' But you said no such thing. You, great ascetic, only think of enjoying yourself, but you are one who does not think of caring for the child in the womb."
Thus, like a woman attempting to destroy the orb of the moon with a lump of dung, she spoke words of great accusation and abuse against the Blessed One in the midst of the fourfold assembly. The Blessed One paused his ongoing Dhamma discourse and, making a bold voice like a lion king, said:
"Sister Ciñca, only you and I know whether the words you have just spoken are true or false."
Ciñca, without backing down, accused him again, saying, "It is true, great ascetic. It is precisely because only you and I know that this advanced pregnancy has occurred."
## Sakka Descending to Resolve the Problem
At that moment, the Sakka's throne, the Paṇḍukambala emerald stone, showed signs of heat. When Sakka reflected on the cause, he realized, "The wicked woman Ciñca is accusing and abusing the Blessed One with false words." Thinking, "I will clear this matter in the midst of the great crowd of people," he came to the place where the Blessed One was preaching, accompanied by four deities.
587:
The four deities took the form of young mice and simultaneously gnawed through the strings of the wooden disc that Ciñca had tied. The wind also blew up the robe that Ciñca was wearing. When the strings of the wooden disc broke and fell, they landed on Ciñca's feet, and both her toes were instantly crushed.
## The Earth Swallowing Ciñca
All the people listening to the Dhamma said, "Phooey! You wicked woman! You are accusing and abusing the Blessed One!" They surrounded her, spat on her head, and, holding stones, sticks, and clods of earth, they dragged Ciñca out of the Jetavana monastery. Then, as soon as Ciñca passed beyond the sight of the Blessed One, this great earth split and provided a hole. From that hole, the flames of the Avīci Hell rose up. Ciñca was surrounded and covered by the terrifying flames of Avīci, as if she were wrapped in a red blanket given as a gift of love by her relatives, and she went through that hole to be reborn in the Great Avīci Hell.
From that time on, because the masses knew of the wickedness of the heretics, the gains, offerings, and honor of the heretics decreased and declined even more than before. As for the Blessed One, his gains, offerings, and honor increased immeasurably more than before.
## Preaching the Mahāpaduma Jātaka
On the following day, in the circular pavilion of the Dhamma hall where the Dhamma assembly was held, the monks were saying, "Friends..."
588:
...Ciñca has reached great ruin and loss by accusing and abusing with false words the Blessed One, who is endowed with such extensive and great virtues and is worthy of receiving the highest offerings." Thus, they initiated a conversation about Ciñca's story. The Blessed One came to that place and asked, "Monks, for what purpose are you gathered here in conversation now?" When the monks replied that they were gathered for this particular conversation (the story of Ciñca), the Blessed One said, "Monks, it is not only now that Ciñca has reached ruin by accusing and abusing me with false words; in the past also, she reached ruin by accusing me with false words." He then preached in detail the Mahāpaduma Jātaka of the Dvādasanipāta.
## Mahāpaduma Jātaka of the Dvādasanipāta
Monks, in the long past, while King Brahmadatta was reigning in the city of Vārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of that king's chief queen. When he was born, because he had a face as beautiful as a newly blossomed Paduma lotus, they named him "Prince Mahāpaduma."
When the Bodhisatta, Prince Mahāpaduma, reached the age of maturity, he went to the city of Takkasilā, mastered all the arts and sciences, and upon his return, his mother, the chief queen, passed away. His father, King Brahmadatta, appointed another woman as the chief queen and for his eldest son, Prince Mahāpaduma...
589:
He conferred the position of Viceroy upon him.

At a later time, as he wished to go and suppress a rebellion that had broken out at the border of the country, the King said to the Queen Consort, "O Queen Consort, you shall remain comfortably here in this golden palace. I shall go to suppress the rebellion that has arisen at the border."

When he said this, the Queen Consort replied, "I do not wish to remain in this golden palace; I will also go along with you."

The King, after explaining the hardships of the battlefield, spoke words of encouragement: "O Queen Consort, until I return, remain in this golden palace without boredom. I shall leave orders for my son, the Viceroy Mahāpaduma, to attend to all matters concerning your care without negligence." Having arranged things as he had spoken, he went to the border, drove the rebel enemies away, and after organizing the entire district to be prosperous and peaceful, he returned to the royal city. He built a temporary leaf-hut palace outside the city and resided there for a while.

The Bodhisatta, the Viceroy Mahāpaduma, knowing that his royal father had returned, had the entire city decorated and the golden palace cleaned and prepared. Then, he went alone to the presence of the Queen Consort. When the Queen Consort saw the beauty and grace of the Bodhisatta Prince Mahāpaduma, her heart was filled with lust. The Bodhisatta paid respects to the Queen Consort and said, "O Mother,
590:
what service shall I perform for you?"

Then the Queen said to the Bodhisatta Viceroy, "Do not call me mother." She rose from her seat, took the Bodhisatta by the hand, and gave the command, "Come up onto the bed."

When the Bodhisatta Viceroy asked, "For what reason?", the Queen Consort spoke (shameless words of lust), "Before the King arrives, let the two of us enjoy ourselves with sensual pleasures."

Then, the Bodhisatta Prince Mahāpaduma, as one who guards the Dhamma, spoke these firm words of refusal:

"O Mother Queen, you are indeed my mother (in the absence of my own mother). You are also one who has a husband as her lord. I have never even looked with sensual desire or broken my restraint toward women who have a protective husband as their lord. Such being the case, how could I, who guards and controls my senses, perform such a vile and loathsome act with you, O Queen?"

When she had spoken two or three times and the Bodhisatta Prince did not follow her desire, she asked in an authoritative tone, "Will you not obey my word?"

The Bodhisatta Prince also answered boldly, "Indeed, I will not obey."

The Queen then spoke threateningly, "If that is so, I shall speak slanderous words to the King and have your head cut off so that it falls like a vessel."
591:
The Bodhisatta Prince replied, "Do as you wish regarding slander before the King; (I simply will not follow your desire)." Having shamed the Queen, he departed.

The Queen became frightened and thought, "If the Viceroy tells his father about this matter first, my life will be no more. I myself will speak slanderous words first." Thinking thus, she stopped eating, put on soiled clothes, made scratches with her nails all over her body, and gave instructions to her attendants: "If the King asks where the Queen is, tell him she is unwell." Then, pretending to be seriously ill, she lay down upon her bed.

The King, after circling the city in a clockwise direction, ascended to the golden palace. Not seeing the Queen, he asked the attendants, "Where is the Queen?" When he heard the attendants' reply, "She is unwell, Your Majesty," he entered the royal chamber where the Queen was staying and asked, "O Queen, what kind of illness has befallen you?"

The Queen pretended not to hear the King's question. Only when he asked a second and third time did she speak in a suggestive and indirect manner: "Great King, why do you insist on asking so urgently? (I am so ashamed); please be silent. Other women who have a husband as their lord and master are not like me."
592:
The King said, "Who has oppressed you? Tell me quickly. I shall cut off the head of the person who oppressed you so that it falls like a bowl." When he spoke these words of royal rage, the Queen began her slanderous speech, saying, "Great King, whom did you leave to guard the city when you went away?" The King replied, "I went after leaving my son, the Crown Prince Mahāpaduma, to guard the city." Then the Queen spoke slander to the utmost, saying, "Great King, that son, Crown Prince Mahāpaduma, whom you trusted to guard the city, came to my bedchamber. Although I pleaded with him gently, saying, 'Dear son, do not do this; I am your mother,' he did not listen. He said, 'Setting aside the King, there is no other king but me. I will keep you in the house and enjoy myself with sensual pleasures.' He spoke overbearingly, grabbed me by my hair, and dragged me here and there. Finally, when I did not follow his words, he pushed me down and went away after beating and striking me as he pleased."
## The King's Rage
## Ordering the Execution of Prince Mahāpaduma
The King, without investigating or reflecting, became violently angry like a poisonous cobra or a hooded snake. He summoned the executioners and gave the command, "Men, go! Capture and bind Prince Paduma and bring him here!" The executioners, as if overwhelming the entire city, went to the Crown Prince's palace, captured and beat the Crown Prince, bound his hands tightly behind his back, and placed a wreath of red oleander flowers around his neck.
593:
and led him away, treating him as one about to be executed.

The Bodhisatta Viceroy, well aware that "This is the work of the Queen," followed them while lamenting, "O executioners, I have not committed any fault against the King; I am an innocent man."

The whole city was in an uproar, and the citizens gathered and spoke to one another, "The King, having mistakenly listened to a woman's words, is going to have the Viceroy Mahāpaduma killed." They prostrated themselves at the feet of the Bodhisatta Viceroy and cried out loudly, saying, "O Lord Viceroy, this criminal punishment is not at all fitting or appropriate for you, Lord Viceroy."

Then the King's men, the executioners, brought the Viceroy before the King and showed him. As soon as the King saw him, unable to control his mind, he gave the absolute command: "This Prince Paduma, though not the king, acts with the pride and manner of a king. Though he is my son, he has wronged the Queen Mother. Go! Throw him headfirst down the Corapapāta cliff (where thieves are thrown) and let him meet his end."

The Bodhisatta Prince said, "Royal Father, it is certain that I have not even a tiny bit of such fault. Do not destroy or kill me by mistakenly listening to a woman's words."
594:
Even though he pleaded thus, the King would no longer listen to the words of his son, the Viceroy.

Then, sixteen thousand palace women wailed and lamented loudly, "O dear Mahāpaduma, to have to suffer such an unfitting criminal punishment!"

All the princes, ministers, brahmins, wealthy merchants, and others pleaded, presenting reasons: "Great King, Prince Mahāpaduma is a man of good conduct. He is one who will protect the royal lineage and inherit the throne. You should not destroy or kill Prince Mahāpaduma, the heir to the throne, by believing a woman's words without consideration or reflection. A king must be one who acts with investigation and reflection." They then recited these seven verses to the King:

(1) Nādatthā parato dosaṃ,
aṇuṃthūlāni sabbaso.
Issaro paṇaye daṇḍaṃ,
sāmaṃ appaṭivekkhiya.

(O Great King). A ruler who governs a country should not inflict punishment, such as cutting off hands or feet or execution, in a fit of rage without personally seeing the fault of another, and without personally investigating and examining all faults, whether small or large.
595:
(In the time of King Mahāsammata, there was no such thing as a fine exceeding one hundred pieces of silver. There were no punishments such as cutting off hands or feet or execution beyond the punishments of whipping, rebuke, or banishment. It was only later, during the reigns of cruel and violent kings, that such punishments arose. The ministers made this plea with reference to those punishments.)

(2) Yo ca appaṭivekkhitvā,
daṇḍaṃ kubbati khattiyo.
Sakaṇṭakaṃ so gilati,
jaccandhova samakkhikaṃ.

If a khattiya, a lord of the land and water, should thoughtlessly inflict punishments such as cutting off hands or feet or execution without investigation, that king is truly said to have swallowed a meal mixed with the thorns of evil misconduct and ignorance, just as a man blind from birth might swallow a disgusting meal mixed with flies.

(3) Adaṇḍiyaṃ daṇḍayati,
daṇḍiyañca adaṇḍiyaṃ.
Andhova visamaṃ maggaṃ,
na jānāti samāsamaṃ.

A king who mistakenly punishes one who should not be punished, and does not punish one who should be punished, is like a blind man on a rough path who does not know the difference between the level and the uneven.
596:
Adaṇḍiya—(karoti) = Without restraint, thinking "I am the king," he acts only according to his own desires, his heart filled with pride. So = That lord of the land, the king. "Visamaṃ maggaṃ = An uneven, rough, and harsh path. Paṭipanno = Having gone astray and reached suffering. Andhova = Like one born blind." Samāsamaṃ = Between the even path of the ten-fold good conduct and the uneven path of the ten-fold bad conduct. Na jānāti = Because he does not distinguish or know, he follows the wrong path and reaches great suffering in the four lower realms.

(4) Yo ca etāni ṭhānāni,
aṇuṃ thūlāni sabbaso.
Sudiṭṭhamanusaasayya,
sa ve vohāritumarahati.

Yo ca = And whichever lord of the land, the king. Etāni ṭhānāni = These many circumstances where punishment should or should not be applied. (Daṇḍiyesupi = Even in the many circumstances where punishment is deserved.) Sabbaso-sabbāni = All matters entirely. Aṇuṃ thūlāni = Various matters, both small and large. Sudiṭṭhaṃ = Having seen clearly with the eye of wisdom. (Katvā = Having acted after considering with the eye of wisdom.) Anusāseyya = If he should judge according to the Dhamma without error. Sa-so = That king, whose wisdom shines. Ve = Indeed. Vohārituṃ = To rule and administer the country. Arahati = Is worthy and fit according to cause and reason.
597:
(5) Nekantamudunā sakkā,
ekantatikkhena vā.
Attaṃ mahante ṭhapetuṃ,
tasmā ubhayamācare.

(Mahārāja = O Great King). Ekantamudunā vā = By practicing only extreme gentleness. Ekantatikkhena vā = Or by practicing only extreme harshness. Attaṃ = Oneself. Mahante = In the great position of authority and sovereignty. Ṭhapetuṃ = To remain firmly established. Na sakkā = It is not possible. Tasmā = Therefore. Ubhayaṃ = Both gentleness and harshness. (Rājā = A person who rules the country). Ācare-ācareyya = Should practice, distinguishing with the power of wisdom when to be gentle and when to be harsh.

(6) Paribhūto mudu hoti,
atitikkho ca veravā.
Etañca ubhayaṃ ñatvā,
anumajjhaṃ samācare.

(Mahārāja = O Great King). Mudu = A king who is consistently and solely gentle in nature. Paribhūto = Is despised and oppressed by the citizens and the army. Hoti = It is so. Atitikkho ca = And a king who is excessively fierce and sharp in anger. Veravā = Is hated by the whole country and has many enemies. Hoti = It is so. Etañca ubhayaṃ = These two points: that being too gentle leads to being despised, and being too harsh leads to many enemies. Ñatvā = Having understood and distinguished this in the mind. Anumajjhaṃ = The practice which is the middle between gentleness and harshness.
598:
Or the middle path that is neither too soft nor too harsh. Samācare-samācareyya = One should practice.

(7) Bahumpi ratto bhāseyya,
duṭṭhopi bahu bhāsati.
Na itthi kāraṇā rāja,
puttaṃ ghātetumarahati.

Rāja = O Great King... Rattopi = Even a person oppressed by intense lust. Bahuṃ = Many kinds of words. Bhāseyya = Would speak, urged by lust. Duṭṭhopi = Even a person who is fiercely angry. Bahuṃ = Many kinds of words. Bhāsati = Speaks, urged by anger. (Tasmā = Therefore, because people oppressed by lust and anger speak many kinds of words). Itthikāraṇā = Because of a queen who is perverse and of bad conduct, whose mind is filled with lust and anger. Puttaṃ = The Crown Prince named Mahāpaduma, the heir to the throne. Ghātetuṃ = To execute without consideration. Na arahati = It is not proper or fitting.

Although they spoke in various ways showing cause and reason, the ministers were unable to make the king listen to their words. The Bodhisatta, Crown Prince Mahāpaduma, also spoke various words of entreaty, but he was unable to make his father the king listen to his words.
599:
The king, who was foolish and blind with ignorance, insisted on his authority, saying, "Go, throw him (Prince Paduma) into the Corapapāta abyss right now."

(8) Sabbova loko ekato,
itthī ca ayamekikā.
tenāhaṃ paṭipajjissaṃ,
gacchatha pakkhipatheva taṃ.

Sabbova loko = All the citizens and people. Ekato-(ṭhito) = Stand on one side, following the prince's favor. Ayaṃ ca itthī = But this queen, the Chief Consort. Ekikā = Is left alone with a small face. Tena = Because all the people show such favoritism. Ahaṃ = I, the head of the great country, the king. Paṭipajjissaṃ = Will follow only the words of the queen. Gacchatha = Go. Taṃ = That traitorous Prince Paduma. Pakkhipatheva = Throw him into the Corapapāta abyss immediately this very moment.

He uttered this eighth verse of command. When the king issued this absolute command, not a single one among the sixteen thousand court women could remain calm; they wept bitterly. All the city dwellers raised their arms and lamented in various ways, weeping and following with their hair disheveled. The foolish king, thinking, "These people might
600:
prevent the act of throwing this prince into the abyss," went out himself with his retinue. While the multitude of people were weeping, he had the Bodhisatta, the Crown Prince, held upside down—head down and feet up—and then cruelly ordered him to be thrown into the Corapapāta abyss.

## The Bodhisatta's Power of Loving-kindness
At that time, due to the power of the Bodhisatta's loving-kindness, the mountain deity appeared in person and comforted the Bodhisatta, saying, "Mahāpaduma, do not be afraid." The deity then embraced him with both hands, held him to his chest, letting the divine touch permeate the Bodhisatta's entire body. Then, descending the mountain, the deity placed the Bodhisatta upon the hood of the Naga King who lived at the foot of the mountain.

The Naga King took the Bodhisatta, Prince Mahāpaduma, to the Naga realm and shared half of his splendor and wealth with the Bodhisatta prince. After the Bodhisatta had lived happily in the Naga realm for a full year, he said to the Naga King, "I shall go to the human world." When the Naga King asked, "Where do you wish to go?", the Great Being replied, "I shall go to the Himalayas and become an ascetic." The Naga King agreed, saying, "Very well," and brought the Bodhisatta to the Himalayas in the human world. He provided the Bodhisatta with the requisites and utensils of an ascetic and returned to his own Naga realm. The Bodhisatta, Prince Mahāpaduma, entered the Himalayas, became an ascetic, and developed the meditative absorptions (jhāna) and higher knowledges (abhiññā).
601:
He lived happily in the Himalayas, sustaining himself on forest roots and fruits.

Then one day, a hunter from Vārāṇasī reached the Bodhisatta's dwelling place. Recognizing the Bodhisatta, he asked, "O Great King, are you not Prince Mahāpaduma?" When the Bodhisatta replied, "Yes, friend," the hunter paid homage to the Great Being Mahāpaduma and stayed there for two or three days. Upon returning to Vārāṇasī, he reported to the king, "O Lord, your son Prince Mahāpaduma has become an ascetic in the Himalayas and is living in a leaf-hut. I stayed with Prince Mahāpaduma for two or three days and have now returned." The king asked, "Did you see him yourself?" and the hunter replied, "Yes, I saw him, O King."

The king, surrounded by a large army of soldiers, went to that place. He built a temporary leaf-palace at the edge of the forest and set up camp. Then, surrounded by his ministers, he went to the leaf-hut. He saw the Bodhisatta sitting at the entrance of the hut like a statue of pure gold. He paid homage and sat in a suitable place. The ministers also sat down after exchanging polite conversation. The Bodhisatta invited the king (to partake of his fruits and spring water) and engaged in polite conversation.

Afterward, the king, wishing to ask the Bodhisatta, "My son, although I had you
602:
thrown head-first into the very deep Corapapāta abyss, how is it that you, my son, are still alive?", uttered the ninth verse:

(9) Anekatāle narake,
gambhīre ca suduttare.
Pātito giriduggasmim,
kena tvaṃ tattha nāmari.

Tāta = My son. Anekatāle = As deep as many palm trees. Gambhīre ca = Fearfully deep. Suduttare = Difficult to cross or escape from. Narake giriduggasmim = In the abyss called Corapapāta, which is difficult to traverse and hard to escape. Pātito = Although you were thrown head-first. Tvaṃ = You, my son. Kena = By what means or for what reason. Tattha = In that extremely fearful abyss. Nāmari = Did you not die but remain alive?

Then the son and the father answered and questioned each other as follows:

(10) Nāgo jātaphaṇo tattha,
thāmavā girisānujo.
Paccaggahi maṃ bhogehi,
tenāhaṃ tattha nāmariṃ.

Tāta = O father, lord of all... Tattha = In that extremely fearful abyss. Thāmavā = Endowed with great strength and power. Girisānujo = Born and raised in the mountain valleys. Nāgo = The Naga King.
603:
Jātaphaṇo = Having a hood created by great psychic power. Maṃ = Me (your son). Paccaggahi = Received me from the hands of the mountain deity. Tena = By that means and for that reason. Ahaṃ = I (your son). Tattha = In that extremely fearful abyss. Nāmariṃ = Did not die but remained alive.

(This is the verse spoken by the son in reply.)

When the Bodhisatta Mahāpaduma, the ascetic, replied thus, the father king was filled with great joy and said, "My son, because I was blind with ignorance and foolish, I took the woman's words as truth and committed this wrong against you, my son, who are endowed with such virtue. Please be compassionate and forgive your father's wrongdoings." Saying this, he bowed at the Bodhisatta's feet. The Bodhisatta Mahāpaduma, the ascetic, said, "Great King, please rise. I forgive your fault. From this time forward, do not be one who acts without investigation and consideration." When he spoke these words of forgiveness and satisfaction, the father king, wishing to say, "My son, only if you return to the country, accept your father's inheritance of the kingdom, and rule under the white parasol, will it truly mean you have forgiven your father," uttered this verse:

(11) Ehi taṃ paṭinessāmi,
rājaputta sakaṃ gharaṃ.
Rajjaṃ kārehi bhaddante,
kiṃ araññe karissasi.

"Come, I will take you back, O Prince, to your own home. Rule the kingdom, venerable one; what will you do in the forest?"
604:
“O Prince Mahāpaduma of noble lineage! Come, I shall lead you back to the golden palace of Bārāṇasī, your own inheritance and birthplace. May you be blessed. Rule the kingdom of Bārāṇasī with great glory. What can you do in this great forest, far from human habitation, to benefit the people?”

With this verse, the King pleaded and invited him to return to the kingdom and rule. Then the Great Being replied:

(12) “Just as a man who has swallowed a fishhook would extract it along with blood; having extracted it, he would be at ease—even so do I see myself.”

“O dear Father, just as a man who inadvertently swallows a fishhook should quickly vomit it out along with the red blood before it reaches his vital organs; and having quickly vomited it out, he would certainly be at ease in both body and mind—even so, I, the son named Mahāpaduma, see myself.”
605:
“I see myself in the same way as that man who, having swallowed a fishhook, finds immediate relief by quickly vomiting it out.”

When he replied thus, the King asked again:

(13) “What do you call the fishhook? What do you call the blood? What do you call that which is extracted? Being asked, please tell me this.”

“O dear son, what do you mean by the term ‘fishhook’? What do you mean by the term ‘with blood’? And what do you mean by ‘that which is quickly vomited and extracted’? O son, you who are asked because I wish to know the answer to these deep problems, please explain this to me.”

Then the Great Being, the hermit Mahāpaduma, replied:

(14) “Sensual pleasures I call the fishhook; elephants and horses I call the blood; renunciation I call that which is extracted. Know this thus, O Khattiya.”
606:
“O King, ruler of the land! I, your son Mahāpaduma, declare the five cords of sensual pleasure to be the piercing fishhook. I declare the various forms of wealth and luxury, such as elephants, horses, and chariots, to be the red blood. I declare the renunciation of these five senses to be the act of quickly vomiting them out. O Father, may you understand this profound meaning with your wisdom.”

Having thus clarified the King's question, he gave an exhortation to his father, saying: “Great King, as I have stated, there is no longer any need for me to act as the King of Bārāṇasī. My special advice to you, Father, is to rule righteously, without violating the Ten Royal Virtues and avoiding the four prejudices (agati).”

## The King Returns to the City and Punishes the Queen

Although the father invited his son to the golden palace many times, he did not succeed. Lamenting and weeping, he returned to the city. On the way, he asked his ministers: “O ministers, because of whom have I been separated from such a virtuous son?”
607:
The ministers replied in unison: “Great King, it is because of the Chief Queen that you have been separated and parted from such a virtuous son.” Upon reaching the kingdom, the King ordered the Queen to be seized and thrown head-first into the Corapapāta (Robbers' Cliff). He then entered the city and ruled righteously.

The Buddha, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said: “Monks, thus in the past, this Ciñcamāṇavikā also slandered and spoke maliciously against me, and she came to great ruin.” He then concluded the Jātaka with this final verse:

(15) “Ciñcamāṇavikā was the mother, and Devadatta was my father. Ānanda was the wise Naga, and Sāriputta was the deity. I was the Prince. Thus you should remember the Jātaka.”

“Monks, at that time, Ciñcamāṇavikā was the stepmother queen; my brother-in-law Devadatta was the King; Ānanda was the wise Naga King; Sāriputta was the deity guarding the mountain; and I, the Buddha, was Prince Mahāpaduma. Thus you should remember this Mahāpaduma Jātaka.” (This is the Mahāpaduma Jātaka.)
608:
The Buddha, having preached this Mahāpaduma Jātaka in detail, said: “Monks, for those who have abandoned the single law of truth-telling, who abide in falsehood (musāvāda), and who have discarded the happiness of the three realms—human, celestial, and Nibbāna—to be attained in the afterlife, there is no evil they would not dare to do.” He then spoke this verse of Dhamma:

“For the person who has transgressed one law (truth), who speaks lies, and who has disregarded the next world, there is no evil that is not to be done.”

“O monks! For a creature who violates the single Dhamma of truth, who habitually speaks falsehood, and who has turned away from the three types of happiness in the next world, there is not a single evil deed they would not dare to commit.” (This means that one who dares to commit the evil of lying dares to commit any kind of evil.)

At the conclusion of the teaching, many in the audience attained the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and other stages.

(This is the detailed account of the accusation by the wicked woman Ciñcamāṇavikā.)
609:
## The Past Karma of the Wicked Woman Ciñcamāṇavikā
## Being Falsely Accused in This Manner
The past karma of the wicked woman Ciñcamāṇavikā being falsely accused in this manner is as follows:
In a life beyond the period of four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons (before receiving the definite prophecy), the Bodhisatta associated with evil friends and was one who practiced much improper reflection (ayoniso manasikāra). At that time, he committed the grave unwholesome karma of false accusation (ariyūpavāda) against a noble Arahant Elder named Nanda, who was a disciple of the Buddha named Sabbābhibhū, by falsely accusing him of misconduct with a woman.
Due to that unwholesome karma, he suffered greatly in hell for many long years. Afterwards, in many human lives, he was also falsely accused. Due to the remnants of that unwholesome karma, even in this final life as a Buddha, he had to endure such a shameful and false accusation by the wicked woman Ciñcamāṇavikā in the midst of the fourfold assembly.
Regarding this matter, in the first volume of the Apadāna Pali (pages 346-7), 39th Avaṭaphalavagga, 10th Pubbakamma-pilotika-buddha-apadāna:
"Of the Buddha Sabbābhibhū,
There was a disciple named Nanda.
By falsely accusing him, in hell,
I wandered for a long time."
610:
The Buddha himself preached this, starting with those words. The full Pali and Burmese versions should be noted from that Pali text and the Burmese translation of the Piṭaka.

(This is the past kamma of the false accusation by the wicked woman Ciñcamāṇavikā.)

## The Accusation by the Female Wanderer Sundarī

As previously mentioned, the heretics (titthiyas) of external sects, due to the decline of their gains and offerings, resorted to malicious efforts. Just as they used the wicked female wanderer named Ciñcamāṇavikā to falsely accuse and disgrace the Buddha, on another occasion, while the Buddha was residing in Sāvatthī, they also used a female wanderer named Sundarī to disgrace him. I shall now describe that event (as it appears in the Udāna Pali, 4th Meghiyavagga, 8th Sundarī Sutta, and its Commentary).

When the Buddha was dwelling in the Jetavana monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī, he and the community of monks were respected, revered, honored, and venerated by humans and deities, easily obtaining the four requisites: robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicine. Conversely (like the opposite side of a scale), the heretics of external sects became scarce in the four requisites. (The Buddha and the Sangha were abundant in offerings like a great river formed by two merging streams, due to their great past merits and their righteous conduct in the present life.)
611:
The heretics, however, were scarce in offerings and respect because they lacked past merit and their conduct in the present life was not righteous.

At that time in Sāvatthī, there was a female wanderer named Sundarī, who was more beautiful and attractive in form and figure than other female wanderers, and she was in the prime of her beauty. Because she was so beautiful, she was called Sundarī. However, as beautiful as she was, her conduct was base; she did not guard or restrain her body, speech, or mind.

The heretics, unable to bear and jealous of the abundance of the four requisites for the Buddha and the Sangha, met and consulted as follows:

“Since the appearance of the Ascetic Gotama, we have suffered great ruin. Not only have our offerings become scarcer day by day, but no one even recognizes our existence anymore. On what basis do the people have such extreme faith in the Ascetic Gotama and make such excellent offerings to him?”

While they were considering and discussing the fundamental reason for the Buddha's abundance of offerings, a heretic teacher in that meeting said:

“Sirs, the Ascetic Gotama is descended from the lineage of Mahāsammata, an unbroken Khattiya lineage...”
613:
613
In this way, the various great heretical teachers, being ignorant of the Buddha’s incomparable perfections (pāramī), generosity (cāga), and conduct (cariya), spoke in various ways according to their own perceptions about the reasons why the multitude of people loved and honored the Buddha. When they tried to think of and search for any grounds that would cause the people to lose faith in the Buddha, they could not find a single reason. They then took counsel together, thinking, “By what means can we cause ill-repute for the Monk Gotama and destroy his gains and honors?” Among those heretical teachers, one who had a cruel, wicked, and vile plan said:

“O Sirs, in this world, there is not a single man who is not attached to or does not lust after the pleasures associated with women. This Monk Gotama is young and as beautiful as a celestial being. If he meets a woman whose beauty matches his own, he will surely be lustful and attached. Even if he is not lustful or attached, he will become someone suspected by the multitude. Come, let us send the female wanderer Sundarī to the Monk Gotama so that his ill-repute may spread throughout the whole earth.”

Upon hearing the words of this heretical teacher’s suggestion, all the other heretics agreed, saying, “This point you have conceived is an excellent one. If we act according to this suggestion, the Monk Gotama, being oppressed by ill-repute,
614:
614
will not even be able to lift his head and will flee to some other direction.” Having reached a consensus, they went together to the female wanderer Sundarī to send her according to the heretical teacher’s plan.

When Sundarī the female wanderer saw those heretics, she asked, “Venerable sirs, why have you come gathered together?” The heretics did not say a single word in reply but sat together in a secluded, hidden spot at the edge of the monastery grounds. Although Sundarī went to that place and repeatedly called out and questioned them, she received no answer. She then asked, “What fault do I have toward you, sirs? Why do you not give me an answer?” The heretics replied, “We do not give you an answer because you remain indifferent while we are being oppressed.” Sundarī asked, “Who is harassing and oppressing you, sirs?” The heretics then spoke accusingly, “Do you not see the Monk Gotama wandering about, harassing us and causing our gains and honors to perish and become scarce?” Sundarī asked plainly, “In this matter, what help must I provide?” The heretics then spoke bindingly, “Sister, can you truly shoulder and perform what is for the benefit of us, your relatives?”

(In this context: They flattered the female wanderer by calling her a close relative simply because she, too, did not lead a household life. How very frightening!)
615:
615
Then, Sundarī the female wanderer, becoming enthusiastic, said, “Sirs, what deed must I perform? Is there any deed I cannot do? If it is a matter that will benefit you, my relatives, I have already surrendered my very life.” (That female wanderer Sundarī was like a deer whose leg is caught in a vine; according to her own words, she could no longer escape by any means.) Then the heretics said, “Sister, you have spoken words of great benefit, saying, ‘If it is a matter that will benefit you, my relatives, I have already surrendered my very life.’ You, sister, are in the prime of youth and have reached a state of great beauty and grace. Therefore, using yourself as the cause, strive and act as best as you can to bring about the ill-repute of the Monk Gotama.” After giving her these flattering instructions, they sent her off, saying, “Go in and out of the Jetavana Monastery constantly.”

Sundarī, the foolish female wanderer—like one who wishes to play with a flower garland on a saw, like one who wishes to seize a wild elephant in rut by its trunk, or like one who wishes to receive Death with her forehead—accepted the heretics' words, saying, “Very well, sirs.” She applied perfumes and ointments, chewed fragrant betel to sweeten her breath, and taking advantage of the time when the multitude of people had finished listening to the Buddha’s Dhamma teaching and were returning to the city, she headed toward the Jetavana Monastery. When people she met on the way asked, “Where are you going?” she replied:

“I am going to the Monk Gotama. I am one who stays with the Monk Gotama in the same
616:
616
Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭī).” Having spoken such offensive and implicating words, when she reached the vicinity of the Jetavana Monastery, she did not dare enter the monastery but slept in another heretical park. Early in the morning, she descended onto the road to the Jetavana Monastery and headed toward the city of Sāvatthī. When the multitude of people she met on the way asked, “Little Sundarī, what is it? Where have you been?” she made her accusation, saying, “I have been staying with the Monk Gotama in the same Perfumed Chamber, and after having delighted and pleased that Monk Gotama with sensual pleasures, I am returning.”

After two or three days had passed, when the multitude of people had seen Sundarī frequently going to the Jetavana Monastery and were likely to be misled, the heretics gave money to some drunkards and said, “Go, kill Sundarī and throw her body into the ditch between the old flowers and rubbish near the Monk Gotama’s Perfumed Chamber, then return.” The drunkards did exactly as the heretics had instructed. Afterward, the heretics made a great commotion, saying, “We cannot find our young disciple Sundarī.” They went to King Kosala and reported, “Great King, our young disciple Sundarī the female wanderer has disappeared miserably; we cannot find her.” When the King asked, “Where do you have suspicion?” the heretics replied, “Great King, we have suspicion regarding the Jetavana Monastery.” The King then said, “If that is the case,
617:
617
search the Jetavana Monastery.”

Then the heretics took their disciples and supporters, went to the Jetavana Monastery, and under the guise of searching for Sundarī, they cleared away the flower rubbish. They pulled out the corpse (utuja-rūpa) of Sundarī from the ditch where they had originally placed it. Placing it on a litter, they brought it into the city and spoke to King Kosala in a convincing manner, saying, “The disciples of the Monk Gotama, thinking they would cover up the evil deed committed by their teacher, killed young Sundarī and threw her among the piles of flower rubbish.” The King, without due reflection, issued a summary decree, saying, “If that is the case, go and proclaim it throughout the entire city.”

Encouraged by the King’s uninvestigated and unreflective decree, the heretics placed Sundarī’s corpse on a small litter and carried it through the city of Sāvatthī from one main road to another, and from one junction to another, telling the multitude of people:

“O friends and mothers, look at the deed of the Sakyan monks! These Sakyan monks are shameless, they are immoral, they are of wicked nature, they are speakers of falsehood, and they are practitioners of unholy conduct (incest/sexual misconduct). Yet, these monks (pretending to be virtuous) claim: ‘We are practitioners of the Dhamma, we are of good conduct, we are practitioners of the holy life,
618:
618
speakers of truth, possessed of virtue, and of good nature.’ For these monks, there is no monkhood at all; there is no holy life at all. For these monks, monkhood has perished; the holy life has perished. Where can there be monkhood in the nature of these monks? Where can there be the holy life? These monks are devoid of monkhood; they are devoid of the holy life. How is it that a man, after performing a man’s business, must kill the woman? (How terrible! That a man would do a man's deed and then kill a weak woman!)”

Thus they spoke words of blame and reproach.

At that time, when the citizens of Sāvatthī saw the monks, they followed the propaganda taught and spread by the heretics, saying:

“These Sakyan monks are shameless, they are immoral, they are of wicked nature. They are speakers of falsehood. They are practitioners of unholy conduct. Yet, these monks (pretending to be virtuous) claim: ‘We are practitioners of the Dhamma, we are of good conduct, we are practitioners of the holy life, speakers of truth, possessed of virtue, and of good nature.’ For these monks, there is no monkhood at all; there is no holy life at all. For these monks, monkhood has perished;”
619:
The holy life has vanished. Where is the monkhood in these monks? Where is the holy life? These monks have fallen away from monkhood; they have fallen away from the holy life. Why would a man, after having his way with a woman, kill her?"
Thus, they reviled, scolded, harassed, and annoyed the monks with harsh words that were completely unsuitable for the ears of the virtuous.
Then, many monks, returning from their alms round in Sāvatthī, went to the Blessed One, paid homage, and sat down to one side. 
"Venerable Sir, now the people of Sāvatthī, upon seeing monks, say: 'These Sakyaputta monks are shameless, immoral, of evil nature, speakers of lies, and practitioners of unchastity. Yet these monks claim (pretending to be virtuous) "We are practitioners of Dhamma, practitioners of good conduct, practitioners of the holy life, speakers of truth, virtuous, and of good nature." There is no monkhood for these monks; there is no holy life for these monks. The monkhood has vanished for these monks; the holy life has vanished. In these monks...'
620:
...where is the monkhood? Where is the holy life? These monks have fallen away from monkhood; they have fallen away from the holy life. Why would a man, after having his way with a woman, kill her?' Thus, Venerable Sir, they revile, scold, harass, and annoy us with harsh words completely unsuitable for the ears of the virtuous."
When they had reported this to the Blessed One, the Blessed One said:
"Monks, this noise will not last long. It will last for only seven days, and after seven days have passed, it will disappear. Therefore, monks, when you see those people who revile, scold, harass, and annoy you with harsh words unsuitable for the ears of the virtuous, you should counter them with this verse:
Abhūtavādī nirayaṃ upeti,
Yo vāpi katvā na karomi cāha.
Ubho'pi te pecca samā bhavanti,
Nihīnakammā manujā parattha.
(One who speaks what is not true—claiming to have seen, heard, met, or known when they have not—goes to hell. One who, having done an evil deed, says 'I did not do it' also goes to hell. Both these people of base actions, after passing away from this life, become equal in the next world...)
621:
...(in the state of woe, Niraya). Counter them with this verse."
Thus he spoke.
Then the monks, having learned the verse from the Blessed One, whenever they saw those people who reviled, scolded, harassed, and annoyed them with harsh words unsuitable for the ears of the virtuous, they countered them exactly as the Blessed One had taught:
Abhūtavādī nirayaṃ upeti,
Yo vāpi katvā na karomi cāha.
Ubho'pi te pecca samā bhavanti,
Nihīnakammā manujā parattha.
(One who speaks what is not true—claiming to have seen, heard, met, or known when they have not—goes to hell. One who, having done an evil deed, says 'I did not do it' also goes to hell. Both these people of base actions, after passing away from this life, become equal in the next world (in the state of woe, Niraya).)
They countered them with this rebuttal verse.
## The People Gain Right Understanding
When the people heard the Dhamma verse spoken in rebuttal by the monks, it occurred to them:
"These Sakyaputta monks certainly did not commit this murder, which the heretics (titthiyas) from outside the Dispensation have been shouting and proclaiming, spreading propaganda throughout the city.
622:
If one considers the matter carefully, although we accused these monks with harsh words unpleasant to the ears of the virtuous, they showed no sign of agitation. Not only that, they did not abandon their two qualities of patience (khanti) and gentleness (soracca), but remained patient and delighted only in their habitual meritorious deeds. Furthermore, these Sakyaputta monks, to those of us who accused them without investigation or reflection, preached only the Dhamma, saying 'The speaker of untruth goes to hell,' and so on, making a solemn declaration so that we might believe them. To let us know clearly that they are innocent, they said, 'As does he who, having done a deed, says "I did not do it," goes to hell,' making a solemn declaration so that we might believe them."
Thus, right understanding, right vision, and the power of reflection arose in them. Indeed, immediately after hearing that verse taught by the Blessed One, it occurred to those people: "We did not see this matter with our own eyes. As for what is heard, some is true and some is false. What should be especially considered is that those heretics only wish for the harm and misfortune of the monks. Therefore, believing those heretics, we should not speak of this matter one-sidedly. Indeed...
623:
...monks are difficult to know." Thus, a sense of shame and dread (saṃvega) entered their hearts. Therefore, that noise did not last long; it lasted only seven days and disappeared after seven days had passed.
## The Full Revelation of the Heretics' Murder
King Pasenadi also sent royal spies throughout Sāvatthī to investigate and reveal the murderers of the female wanderer Sundarī. Then, those murderous drunkards, having received the blood money from the heretics, drank liquor and, becoming intoxicated, began to quarrel with one another. One murderous drunkard said to another, like the proverb "When the palm wine is drunk, the stolen buffalo appears": "You struck and killed the female wanderer Sundarī with a single blow, threw her into the flower-refuse heap, and now you are drinking liquor with the blood money. Just you wait, just you wait!" When the royal spies heard this, they arrested the murderous drunkards and presented them to King Pasenadi.
The King interrogated them, "Did you kill the female wanderer Sundarī?" and the murderous drunkards replied, "Yes, Great King." Again, the King asked, "Who told you to kill her?" and they replied, "The heretics from outside the Dispensation told us to kill her...
624:
...Great King." Thus they replied truthfully. The King had the heretics brought before him, interrogated them, and made them confess the truth. Then he decreed:
"You heretics must go around the city proclaiming: 'Desiring to cast blame and disgrace upon the Ascetic Gotama, we deliberately had the murderers kill her. There is no fault at all in the Ascetic Gotama, nor is there any fault in the disciples of the Ascetic Gotama. In this matter of killing the female wanderer Sundarī, the fault is entirely ours.'"
The heretics had to act according to the King's command. Then the people had even greater faith in the Blessed One and the Community of Monks than before. Towards the heretics, however, they showed increased loathing and disgust. The heretics suffered the punishment for the murder. From then on, the offerings, respect, and honor towards the Blessed One and the Sangha became exceedingly great.
## The Blessed One's Inspired Utterance
Then, many monks approached the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Sir, it is wonderful! It is marvelous!
625:
Venerable Sir, the Blessed One, the Master, spoke most truly and excellently when he said: 'Monks, this noise will not last long; it will last for only seven days; after seven days have passed, this noise will disappear.' Venerable Sir, now that noise has indeed disappeared."
Then the Blessed One, knowing well that for a wise and virtuous person endowed with the strength of patience, there is nothing that cannot be endured even when fools speak words of accusation and abuse that are extremely hard to bear, felt repeated bursts of joyful rapture (pīti). As if the momentum of that rapture could not be contained within and overflowed, he uttered this inspired utterance:
Tudanti vācāya janā asaññatā,
Sarehi saṅgāmagataṃva kuñjaraṃ.
Sutvāna vākyaṃ pharusaṃ udīritaṃ,
Adhivāsaye bhikkhu aduṭṭhacitto.
(As warriors with arrows prick a great elephant that has entered the battlefield to conquer every fight, so do foolish, uncultured, and unrestrained people, who have no control over body, speech, or mind...)
626:
*Bhikkhu* = the wise person who contemplates the dangers of Saṃsāra. *Vācāya* = with the spear of false and fabricated speech. *Tudanti* = they pierce (by those foolish and wicked people). *Sutvāna* = upon hearing. *Pharusaṃ vākyaṃ* = the harsh and abusive words, like the blade of a saw. *Udīritaṃ* = that have been spoken unjustly. *Bhikkhu* = the wise person who contemplates the dangers of Saṃsāra. *Aduṭṭhacitto* = being free from a malicious mind, constantly reflecting on the *Kakacūpama* instruction. *Adhivāsaye* = should endure and practice with patience.

(The *Kakacūpama* instruction refers to the advice given by the Buddha in the *Kakacūpama Sutta* of the *Mūlapaṇṇāsa Pāḷi*, which states that even if enemies were to sever one's limbs with a double-handled saw, one should remain patient and not give way to anger.)

He then uttered this solemn utterance (*Udāna*).

## The Past Karma of Being Accused by the Female Ascetic Sundarī

Regarding this accusation by the female ascetic Sundarī, a question may arise: "Why did the Buddha, knowing that the heretics (*titthiyas*) were plotting and acting in such a way, not inform the monks that 'the murder of this female ascetic Sundarī is the work of the heretics'?" The answer is:

There is no benefit in telling such things to the Noble Ones (*Ariyas*), for the Noble Ones never had any doubt from the beginning regarding the Buddha and the Saṅgha in this matter. Among the worldlings (*puthujjanas*), however, if the Buddha had spoken the truth of the matter, those who did not believe would have
627:
only increased their unwholesome states (*akusala*), leading to their long-term harm and suffering. Therefore, the answer is that He did not speak or explain it prematurely.

Alternatively, it is not the custom (*āciṇṇa*) of the Buddhas to predict such events before they occur. The Buddha does not typically point out the perpetrator in matters involving unwholesome criminal acts but tends to teach in a way that is grounded in the Dhamma (*dhammādhiṭṭhāna*). (Consider again the verse of refutation). Furthermore, the unwholesome karma that has found the opportunity to yield its bad results for the Blessed One cannot be prevented by any means. Therefore, He remained indifferent to the public accusations against Himself and His disciples, as well as to the murder of the female ascetic Sundarī, which was the cause of those accusations.

A further question may arise: "What was the past unwholesome karma of the Blessed One, who had respectfully fulfilled the vast accumulation of merits for four *asaṅkheyyas* and a hundred thousand aeons, that led Him to be so harshly accused?" The answer is:

In a past life, when the Buddha was a Bodhisatta, He was a drunkard named Munāḷi. He associated only with wicked people and wandered about as one who frequently engaged in unwise attention (*ayoniso manasikāra*). One day, while the drunkard Munāḷi was watching a
628:
Paccekabuddha named Surabhi who was donning his robes to enter the city for alms, a woman happened to cross the path near the Paccekabuddha. Because the drunkard Munāḷi was prone to unwise attention, he falsely accused him, saying, "This monk is habituated to the ignoble practice of sexual misconduct."

Due to that unwholesome karma, he suffered in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years. As a remaining result (*vipākasesa*) of that false accusation, even after becoming a Buddha in this final life, He had to endure the false accusations of the people because of the female ascetic Sundarī.

Just as He was falsely accused due to past unwholesome karma, all the sufferings that befell Him—such as the false accusations by corrupt and wicked women like Ciñcamāṇavikā (referring to the twelve *Pubbakamma-piloti*)—are the remaining results of past unwholesome deeds. These unwholesome karmas are called "*Kamma-pilotika* = harsh unwholesome deeds" (commonly known as the "Twelve *Wut*" [Cycles of Karma]) in the *Apadāna Pāḷi* (Vol. 1, p. 346).

(This concludes the account of the past karma regarding the accusation by the female ascetic Sundarī.)
