## Chapter 26
## Observing the Eighth Vassa in the City of Susumāragira

As previously mentioned, after the Blessed One had observed the seventh (*sattama*) Vassa on the *Paṇḍukambala* emerald stone throne in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, preaching the Abhidhamma, He descended to the human world at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa via the triple stairway. At the head of the stairway, He taught various discourses such as the *Sāriputta Sutta*, leading many devas, humans, and Brahmās to the attainment of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*). Thereafter, He proceeded to the city of Sāvatthī, where He held a great festival of the Dhamma. He then spent the eighth (*aṭṭhama*) Vassa residing in the great forest named Bhesakaḷā, near the city of Susumāragira in the Bhagga country.

(The country where the Blessed One now observed His eighth Vassa is the Bhagga country, which is one of the sixteen great countries (*Mahājanapada*) in the Middle Country (*Majjhima Desa*). The capital city, Susumāragira, was so named because when the city was being founded, the sound of a crocodile (*susumāra*) was heard from the nearby river, which was taken as an omen. The great forest near the city where the Blessed One stayed was named "Bhesakaḷā" because it was the domain of an ogress named Bhesakaḷā [applying the name of the inhabitant to the place]. This forest was a sanctuary where animals were granted safety.)
630:
## The Householder Couple Nakulapitā and Nakulamātā
## Their Attainment of the Stage of Sotāpanna

While the Blessed One was residing in the Bhesakaḷā Grove near the city of Susumāragira, surrounded by a company of monks, the householder Nakulapitā and the householder-wife Nakulamātā, along with the citizens of Susumāragira, came to the presence of the Blessed One to listen to the Dhamma and pay their respects. Upon seeing the Blessed One for the first time, both husband and wife immediately perceived Him as their own son, thinking, "This is our son." They prostrated themselves at the feet of the Blessed One and spoke words of both affection and reproach (as if speaking to an eldest son from whom they had been truly separated in this very life), saying, "Dear son, where have you been wandering and living for so long, abandoning us, your parents?"

(Special Note: In the past, the householder Nakulapitā had been the biological father of the Blessed One for five hundred births, His uncle for five hundred births, His elder uncle for five hundred births, and His maternal uncle for five hundred births. Similarly, the householder-wife Nakulamātā had been His mother for five hundred births, His maternal aunt for five hundred births, His elder maternal aunt for five hundred births, and His paternal aunt for five hundred births. Thus, because the latent element of loving-kindness and affection had followed them throughout the long cycle of Saṃsāra, both of them, upon seeing the Blessed One, perceived Him as their son and were unable to remain in their normal state of composure.)

When the desires of the householder couple were fulfilled and they regained their mindfulness, the Blessed One, seeing that the householder couple now possessed a neutral mind, free from both hatred and attachment...
631:
preached the Dhamma to the two of them. At the conclusion of the discourse, both of them were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (*Sotāpatti-phala*).* (From Aṅguttara Commentary 1, 307-9)

## About Prince Bodhi

The story of Prince Bodhi appears in the commentary to the *Bodhirājakumāra Sutta* of the *Majjhima Paṇṇāsa* (page 222 onwards) and in the *Dhammapada Commentary*, Volume 2, Chapter 12 (*Attavagga*), in the story of Bodhirājakumāra (page 85 onwards). I shall write it here in this *Mahā Buddhavamsa* by consulting those texts.

Prince Bodhi was the son of King Udena. Having learned from his father, King Udena, he became an expert in the art of elephants and the use of the goad. (The detailed story of King Udena should be taken from the Burmese translation of the *Dhammapada Commentary* by Venerable Candajoti; here, I shall present only a summary.)

While King Parantapa was reigning in the city of Kosambī, the Chief Queen, who was heavily pregnant, was sitting with the King on an open terrace basking in the sun, wrapped in a red woolen blanket. A *Hatthilinga* bird (an elephant-bird), mistaking her for a piece of meat, snatched the Queen and flew up into the sky. The Queen thought, "If I make a sound now, it will drop me," and so she followed silently without making a sound.

* The story of the householder Nakulapitā and his wife will also be described in the chapter on the *Saṅgha Ratana*.
632:
The *Hatthilinga* bird placed the Queen in the fork of a tree at the foot of a mountain, which was its usual feeding place. When the Queen clapped her hands and made a loud noise, the bird was frightened and flew away. It was in that very tree fork that the Queen gave birth to her child. Because it rained heavily throughout the three watches of the night, the poor Queen had to remain sitting, wrapped only in her blanket.

Not far from that tree lived a hermit. Hearing the Queen's voice, the hermit came to the foot of the tree at dawn. After inquiring about her lineage, he made a ladder, helped the Queen down from the tree, and took her to his hermitage, where he fed her gruel. The child was named "Udena" because he was born amidst the rainy season (*utu*) and the mountain mist (*megha*).

One day, when the hermit returned from the forest, the Queen went out to meet him. (Anxious about her future living conditions), she displayed feminine charms and caused the hermit to fall from his virtue (*sīla*). While the two of them were living together, King Parantapa passed away in Kosambī. The hermit, observing the stars in the sky at night, knew that King Parantapa had died. He asked the Queen, "Your King has passed away. Do you wish for your son to remain here in this forest, or do you wish for him to rule the kingdom of Kosambī, which is his father's property?" When the Queen consulted her son and told him everything from the beginning, she learned of his desire to rule under the white parasol and informed the hermit accordingly.
633:
The hermit was well-versed in the elephant-charming mantra. From whom did this hermit obtain that lore? He obtained it from Sakka, the King of Devas. To clarify: in the past, Sakka approached the hermit and asked, "Venerable sir, what causes you such fatigue?" When the hermit replied that there was danger from elephants, Sakka gave the hermit the elephant-charming mantra and a lute, instructing him: "If you wish the elephants to flee, play this lute string and recite this mantra; if you wish to call the elephants, recite this mantra."

When the hermit gave this mantra lore to the prince, the prince climbed a banyan tree, and when the elephants arrived, he played the lute string and recited the mantra that makes elephants afraid; the elephants fled in terror.

Having personally witnessed the power of the mantra lore, on the following day, he recited the mantra to call the elephants. The great leader of the elephants came and bowed its shoulder for the prince to mount. While standing upon the shoulder of that great elephant, the prince selected strong young elephants capable of fighting in war. Then, he requested from his mother her woolen blanket and signet ring (as evidence), paid obeisance to his parents, and departed from the forest. In due course, he entered various villages and market towns, gathering a force of men by saying, "I am the son of King Parantapa; let those who desire wealth and position come to me." He then surrounded the city with a great army and said, "I am the son of the late King Parantapa. Give me the throne, my father's inheritance." To those who did not believe him,
634:
he showed his mother's woolen blanket and signet ring to make them believe he was the prince, and thus he easily gained the throne and ruled as king. Because King Udena was extremely fond of capturing elephants, whenever he was told, "There are fine elephants in such-and-such a place," he would go quickly without delay to capture them.

King Caṇḍapajjota thought, "I will learn the elephant-lore from King Udena." He had a large wooden elephant made, placed brave soldiers inside it, and captured King Udena when he came out to catch the elephant. He then sent his daughter, Vāsuladattā, to learn the elephant mantra lore from King Udena. Later, King Udena formed a romantic bond with King Caṇḍapajjota's daughter, Vāsuladattā, took her away, and lived with her in his own city. From Queen Vāsuladattā, Prince Bodhi was born. Prince Bodhi learned the elephant-charming mantra lore from his father, King Udena, and became a master of elephant-lore. He resided in the city of Sumsumāragira in the Bhagga country.

## Prince Bodhi
## The Reason for Building the Kokanuda Palace

Prince Bodhi had a palace named "Kokanuda" built, which was unique on earth, unlike other palaces, and so magnificent it seemed as if it were about to fly into the sky. He asked the master carpenter, "Have you ever built this kind of palace elsewhere, or is this craftsmanship your first
635:
work?" When the master carpenter replied, "Your Majesty, it is my first such work," Prince Bodhi thought, "If this master carpenter were to build such a palace for someone else, my Kokanuda Palace would no longer be an object of wonder and praise for all people. Therefore, it would be proper if I were to execute this master carpenter, or cut off his hands and feet, or gouge out both his eyes. Only by doing so will he be unable to build such a palace for anyone else." Thus, he conceived a cruel and wicked plan.

Prince Bodhi revealed his cruel plan to his very close friend, a young man named Sañjikāputta. Being a thoughtful and compassionate person, Sañjikāputta reflected, "Without a doubt, this prince will certainly destroy the master carpenter. A great artisan is of inestimable value. Let not such an inestimably valuable artisan perish while I am watching. I must give this artisan a sign of warning." Having so reflected, he went to the master carpenter and asked, "Is your work on the palace finished, or is it not yet finished?" When the master carpenter said, "It is finished," Sañjikāputta warned him, saying, "Teacher, Prince Bodhi wishes to destroy you. Be careful and protect yourself."
636:
The master carpenter replied, "O friend, you have done a very noble deed by telling me this. In this matter, I will act with careful consideration of all that needs to be done." Later, when Prince Bodhi asked, "Well, master carpenter, is the work to be done on this Kokanuda Palace finished?" he replied, "Your Majesty, it is not yet finished; there is still much work to be carried out." When the prince asked, "What kind of work remains?" he cleverly replied, "Your Majesty, I will explain later. For now, please have wood sent to me quickly." When the prince asked, "What kind of wood do you wish to have sent?" he replied, "Your Majesty, I wish for light and dry wood, such as *yamane* wood and the like." Believing him, the prince had that light and dry wood sent.

Thereafter, the master carpenter said to Prince Bodhi, "Your Majesty, from this time on, please do not come to me. The reason is that I am about to perform very delicate carpentry work, and if I have to converse with another person, the work may be delayed or go awry. Furthermore, at meal times, only my wife will bring the food." He spoke so convincingly that the prince agreed, saying, "Very well."
637:
The master carpenter also stayed in a chamber, carving and shaping those light woods according to his plan. He constructed a large "flying vehicle" in the shape of a Garuḍa bird, large enough for his family to reside within. When it was time for his meal, he instructed his wife (the carpenter's wife) who brought the food, "Sell everything we have in the house and bring the gold and silver." Prince Bodhi, to prevent the master carpenter from escaping, had guards stationed around the Kokanuda Palace. When the Garuḍa-shaped "flying vehicle" was completed, the master carpenter told his wife, "Bring all the children today." After eating his morning meal, he had his wife and children sit inside the belly of the wooden bird, and then he piloted the flying vehicle out through the window and escaped. While the guards stationed by Prince Bodhi were lamenting and saying, "O Lord, the carpenter has escaped!", he traveled through the air, descended in the Himavanta (Himalayas), founded a new city, and became king, becoming famous as "King Kaṭṭhavāhana."

## Prince Bodhi's Invitation to the Saṅgha Led by the Buddha
## For the Palace-Warming Ceremony

Prince Bodhi planned to celebrate the palace-warming ceremony of the Kokanuda Palace. He invited the Blessed One and had the palace smeared and decorated with the four kinds of perfumes. Starting from the first step of the ground-level staircase, he spread a large white cloth as a foot-cloth. (The Prince was one who had no children;)
638:
therefore, he spread it thinking, "If I am to have a son or a daughter, the Blessed One will step on this white cloth.")

When the Blessed One arrived, the prince paid obeisance with the fivefold prostration, received the alms-bowl, and said, "Please enter, Bhante." The Blessed One did not enter. The prince requested a second and a third time. When requested for the third time, the Blessed One looked at the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda, knowing well by the Blessed One's look that he would not step on the white cloth, said to the prince, "Prince, have the white cloths removed. The Blessed One will not step on the white cloth; the Blessed One is compassionate toward future generations." Thus, he had the white cloths removed.

(In this matter, I shall briefly explain the intention of Prince Bodhi, his past karma, and the reason why the Blessed One did not step on the white cloth, drawing from the Majjhima Nikāya Commentary, Vol. 3, pp. 222-3):

**The Prince's Intention:** Prince Bodhi was one who had no children. He had heard that if one performs an *adhikāra* (extraordinary) meritorious deed for the Buddhas, one can obtain what the heart desires. Therefore, the prince had the white cloth spread with the intention: "If I am to have children, the Blessed One will step on my white cloth. If I am not to have children, he will not step on it."
639:
At that time, the Buddha, contemplating whether children would be born to this prince, saw that they would not.

The Prince's Past Kamma: In a past life, while living on a small island, this Prince Bodhi, together with his wife who shared the same unwholesome intention, had killed and eaten small birds. If the prince's wife (the queen) in this present life were someone other than the wife from that past life, he might have been able to have children. However, now, both the prince and the queen had shared the same unwholesome intention in that past life and had committed the evil deed of killing and eating small birds (pāṇātipāta). Therefore, the Buddha clearly saw that children would not be born to the prince.

Reasons for Not Stepping on the Cloth: (1) Due to the aforementioned past unwholesome kamma of the prince, even if the Buddha were to step on the white cloth, children would not be born. Nevertheless, if the Buddha were to step on the white cloth, the prince might hold a wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi), thinking: 'It is widely known in the world that if one performs a great act of merit (adhikāra) for the Buddhas, one can obtain whatever one wishes for; I have performed a great act of merit for the Buddha, yet I have not obtained children. This word that is famous in the world is merely empty and vain.' (This is one reason).

(2) The ascetics (titthiyas) would also speak words of blame, saying: 'The monks wander about stepping on white cloths; there is nothing these monks would not dare to do.' (This is another reason).

(3) At the present time while the Buddha is still alive, among the monks who would have to step on the white cloth, there are many monks with higher knowledge (abhiññā) who clearly perceive the thoughts of others. These monks with higher knowledge would step on it if they knew it was appropriate, and would not step on it if they knew it was not.
640:
Even though they would truly step or not step based on their knowledge, in the future after the Buddha's Parinibbāna, the spiritual support (upanissaya) for beings to attain the Paths and Fruits—which is a special merit—will become weak. Therefore, they will not know what will happen in the future. If the monks of the future, who will be weak in spiritual support and will not know what will happen in the future, step on the white cloth, it would be well if the wish (of the owner of the cloth) were fulfilled; but if it were not fulfilled, the people (of the future) would become dissatisfied, thinking: 'In the past, during the time of the Buddha, if one performed merit for the Saṅgha and made a wish, every wish was granted. Now, however, such wishes are no longer granted. It seems that only the monks of the Buddha's time fulfilled the practice (paṭipatti); the monks of our present time are unable to fulfill the practice.' (This is another reason).

The Buddha remained silent without stepping on the cloth because of these three aforementioned reasons. The Venerable Ānanda, referring to the third of the stated reasons, said, 'The Buddha has regard for the generations to come.'

The prince then had the white cloths removed and invited the Buddha into the palace. After offering rice gruel and hard food, he addressed the Buddha: 'Venerable Sir, a thought has arisen in my mind: "Happiness is not to be gained easily; indeed, happiness is to be gained only through suffering (effort)."' When he said this, the Buddha replied: 'Prince, in my mind too, while I was still a Bodhisatta before becoming a Buddha, the same
641:
thought arose.' Having said this, the Buddha preached in detail the events starting from how he practiced austerities (dukkharacariya) up to the point where he preached the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta* to the five monks (Pañcavaggiya) and established them in the Fruit of Arahantship.

## Prince Bodhi Taking Refuge

When the Buddha preached about how the five monks were established in the Fruit of Arahantship, Prince Bodhi asked the Buddha: 'Venerable Sir, if a monk finds a leader (a teacher) such as the Buddha, within how long a time can he realize the Fruit of Arahantship and dwell in happiness?' Then the Buddha said: 'Prince, if that is the case, I will ask you a question in return; you may answer as you please. Prince, what do you think of this? Are you not skilled and proficient in the art of elephant-riding and the use of the hook?' The prince replied: 'Venerable Sir, I am indeed skilled and proficient in the art of elephant-riding and the use of the hook.'

Again, the Buddha asked:

'Prince, what do you think of this? Suppose in this world
