642:
a man were to come, thinking, "Prince Bodhi is skilled and proficient in the art of elephant-riding and the use of the hook; I will learn the art of elephant-riding and the use of the hook from him." Specifically, if that man:

(1) Lacked faith (saddhā) = having so little faith that he could not reach what should be reached,
(2) Was not free from illness = having so much illness that he could not reach what should be reached,
(3) Was a pretender and deceitful = being so deceitful and hypocritical that he could not reach what should be reached,
(4) Lacked energetic effort = being so lazy and deficient in effort (viriya) that he could not reach what should be reached,
(5) Lacked wisdom = having so little wisdom (paññā) that he could not reach what should be reached—

If he were such a person, would that man be able to learn the art of elephant-riding and the use of the hook from you until he is proficient?'

When asked thus, Prince Bodhi replied: 'Venerable Sir, if he possessed even one of these five factors, that man would not be able to learn the art of elephant-riding and the use of the hook from me until he is proficient; what need is there to mention one who possesses all five? He certainly
643:
would not be able to learn, Venerable Sir.'

Then the Buddha changed the scenario and asked:

'Prince, what do you think of this? Suppose in this world a man were to come, thinking, "Prince Bodhi is skilled and proficient in the art of elephant-riding and the use of the hook; I will learn the art of elephant-riding and the use of the hook from him." Specifically, if that man:

(1) Possessed faith (saddhā) = having great faith enough to reach what should be reached,
(2) Was free from illness = being healthy and physically fit enough to reach what should be reached,
(3) Was not a pretender and not deceitful = being honest and upright enough to reach what should be reached,
(4) Possessed energetic effort = having great persistence and effort (viriya) enough to reach what should be reached,
(5) Possessed wisdom = having great wisdom (paññā) enough to reach what should be reached—

If he were such a person, would that man be able to learn the art of elephant-riding and the use of the hook from you until he is proficient?'
644:
When asked thus, Prince Bodhi replied: 'Venerable Sir, if he possessed even one of these five factors, that man would be able to learn the art of elephant-riding and the use of the hook from me until he is proficient; what need is there to mention one who possesses all five? He certainly would be able to learn, Venerable Sir.'

## Padhāniyaṅga = Factors of a Person Striving in Meditation
## The Five Qualities

Then the Buddha said:

'Prince, in the same way, there are five factors for a person striving in meditation (to achieve success in meditation). The five are:

(1) Prince, in this Dispensation (Sāsana) of mine, a monk is endowed with faith (saddhā). He has faith in the Enlightenment (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa and sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) of the Buddha, thinking: "For this and that reason, the Blessed One is an Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One... (peyyāla) ... the Blessed One."

(2) He is free from illness and suffering. He is endowed with a digestive fire (pācaka) that is neither too cold nor too hot, but moderate and suitable for striving in meditation.

(3) He is not a pretender and not deceitful. He shows himself as he really is to the Buddha or
645:
to his wise fellow practitioners.

(4) He is one who has initiated effort (viriya) to abandon unwholesome states and to fulfill wholesome states; he is strong, firm in his exertion, and does not neglect his effort in wholesome states that are blameless.

(5) He is wise (paññā). He is endowed with the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa)—the wisdom that can perceive the arising and passing away of mind and matter—which is noble, penetrative of defilements, and leads to the complete destruction of the two kinds of suffering, the cycle of rebirth and defilements.

Prince, these aforementioned qualities (being endowed with faith, being free from illness, being honest and upright without pretense, having energetic effort, and being endowed with the knowledge of rise and fall) are the five factors for a person striving in meditation (to achieve success in meditation). They are the five Padhāniyaṅga. Prince, if a monk endowed with these five Padhāniyaṅga finds a leader (a teacher) such as the Buddha, he can realize the Fruit of Arahantship and dwell in happiness within seven years.

Prince, seven years is too long. Let alone that, if a monk endowed with these five Padhāniyaṅga finds a leader (a teacher) such as the Buddha...'
646:
646
Even within a period of six years (peyyāla), five years, four years, three years, two years, or even one year, he can realize the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala) and dwell in bliss.

“Prince, one year is too long. Let that be. If a monk endowed with these five factors of striving (padhāniyaṅga) finds a leader like the Blessed One to guide him, he can realize the fruit of Arahatship and dwell in bliss within seven months. Prince, seven months is too long. Let that be. If a monk endowed with these five factors of striving finds a leader like the Blessed One to guide him, he can realize the fruit of Arahatship and dwell in bliss within six months (peyyāla), five months, four months, three months, two months, one month, or even half a month (15 days).

Prince, half a month (15 days) is too long. Let that be. If a monk endowed with these five factors of striving finds a leader like the Blessed One to guide him, he can realize the fruit of Arahatship and dwell in bliss within seven days (peyyāla), six days, five days, four days, three days, two days, or even one day.

Prince, one day is too long. Let that be. A monk endowed with the five factors of striving—
647:
647
—if he finds a leader like the Blessed One to guide him, being instructed in the evening, he will attain the higher Dhamma (the Path and Fruit) in the morning; being instructed in the morning, he will attain the higher Dhamma in the evening.”

Thus did the Buddha reply.

(In this regard, concerning the five factors of striving—

“Faith, health, being upright and honest, great exertion, and the wisdom that sees the arising and passing of mind and matter; these five are the causes for attaining the Path.”

This summary verse by Ledi Sayadaw should be memorized. All these five factors are mundane (lokiya) states. Among them, regarding having faith (saddhā), there are four types of faith: (1) Āgama-saddhā, (2) Adhigama-saddhā, (3) Okappana-saddhā, and (4) Pasāda-saddhā. Among these four:

(1) The faith of the Omniscient Bodhisattas is called Āgama-saddhā because it has come down unbroken since the time they made the aspiration for Buddhahood.

(2) The faith of the Noble Disciples (ariya-sāvaka) is called Adhigama-saddhā because it is attained and remains unbroken from the moment they realize the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa).

(3) When the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha are mentioned, the conviction that enters into the qualities of the Triple Gem—such as “The Blessed One is indeed the Sammāsambuddha; the Dhamma is well-expounded (svākkhāta); the Saṅgha is of good conduct (suppaṭipanna)”—to such an extent that no one can shake or disturb it, is called Okappana-saddhā.

(4) Mere devotion and clarity of mind towards the Triple Gem is called Pasāda-saddhā.

In the context of these five factors of striving, the type of faith required is “Okappana-saddhā.” This special point should also be noted.)
648:
648
When the Blessed One had thus preached the Dhamma from his own direct experience, Prince Bodhi praised the Buddha with words of faith and devotion, saying: “It is wonderful, O Blessed One! It is wonderful, O Dhamma! It is wonderful how the Dhamma is preached, being excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end, endowed with the perfection of all three parts, such that one instructed in the evening can attain the higher Dhamma in the morning, and one instructed in the morning can attain the higher Dhamma in the evening.”

While Prince Bodhi was thus praising the Blessed One with words of faith, the young man Sañjikāputta spoke disparagingly to Prince Bodhi, saying: “This Prince Bodhi says only this: ‘It is wonderful, O Blessed One! It is wonderful, O Dhamma! It is wonderful how the Dhamma is preached, being excellent in the beginning, middle, and end.’ Even though he speaks thus, he does not approach the ascetic Gotama, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha as his refuge.”

Thereupon, Prince Bodhi said:

“Friend Sañjikāputta, do not say such a thing. Friend Sañjikāputta, do not say such a thing. Friend Sañjikāputta, I have heard, noted, and received this matter from the presence of my mother—

Friend Sañjikāputta, once the Blessed One was staying at the Ghositārāma monastery in the city of Kosambī.
649:
649
At that time, while my mother was pregnant with me, she went to the Blessed One, paid homage, sat down, and said to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable Sir, this boy (or this girl) who is in my womb goes to the Blessed One, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha for refuge. May the Blessed One remember this boy (or girl) as a lay follower (upāsaka/upāsikā) who has taken refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.’

Friend Sañjikāputta, at another time, while the Blessed One was staying in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, a deer sanctuary near the city of Susumāragira in the Bhagga country, my nurse carried me in her arms, went to the Blessed One, paid homage, stood there, and said: ‘Venerable Sir, this Prince Bodhi goes to the Blessed One, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha for refuge. May the Blessed One remember Prince Bodhi as a lay follower (upāsaka) who has taken refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.’

Friend Sañjikāputta, (my mother and my nurse having twice taken refuge on my behalf), I now for the third time go to the Blessed One, the Dhamma, and—
650:
650
—the Saṅgha for refuge. May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower (upāsaka) who has taken refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.”

Thus, addressing the young man Sañjikāputta, he took refuge in the presence of the Blessed One.

(Special Note: Regarding Prince Bodhi’s taking of refuge, one might ask whether it is possible for the Prince to have taken refuge merely by the mother and nurse speaking as described. The answer is: Since there is no such thing as “acittaka-saraṇagamana” (taking refuge without conscious intent), it was not yet a completed taking of refuge for Prince Bodhi at those times.

If that is so, was the refuge taken by the mother and nurse on behalf of the Prince in vain and without benefit? It was not without benefit. The refuge taken by the mother and nurse on behalf of the Prince served as a “guard” (asārakkha) placed for him. Therefore, after the Prince was born and reached the age of discretion, when his parents told him, “Dear son, we had you take refuge even while you were in the womb,” and reminded him by describing the virtues of the Triple Gem as they had seen and experienced them, the Prince reflected on the meaning of his parents' words. As soon as he became mindful, thinking, “I am a lay follower who has taken refuge,” the taking of refuge was then completed. The reason is—

When he mindfully remembered, “I am a lay follower who has taken refuge,” there clearly arose in the Prince’s continuum a mind inclined towards the Triple Gem, preceded by—
651:
651
—the recognition of the Triple Gem as his refuge. This is a special point to be noted.

These details regarding Prince Bodhi are extracts from the Pāḷi, Commentary (Aṭṭhakatha), and Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) of the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta in the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa.)

## Prince Bodhi Attaining Sotāpanna

Then Prince Bodhi, sitting in a place free from the six faults, respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One and asked:

“Venerable Sir, I am a long-standing lay follower of the Exalted Ones. I have taken refuge three times: once while in my mother’s womb, once as an infant, and now once more upon reaching the age of discretion. Being such a devoted lay follower, why did you not step upon my white cloth spreadings?”

Then the Blessed One asked, “Prince, with what thought or desire did you spread those white cloths?” The Prince replied, “I spread them with the thought: ‘If I am one who will obtain a son or a daughter, may the Blessed One step upon my cloth spreadings.’”

Then the Blessed One said, “Prince, it is precisely because you spread them with such a thought and desire that I did not step upon those white cloths.” Thereupon, Prince Bodhi asked again, “Venerable Sir, am I—
652:
652
—one who will not be able to obtain a son or a daughter?” The Blessed One replied, “Yes, Prince, that is so.”

When Prince Bodhi further asked, “For what reason can I not obtain children?” the Blessed One gave a brief hint, saying, “Prince, because in a past existence you were negligent (pamāda) and indulged in the five cords of sensual pleasure together with your wife, you cannot obtain children.” When Prince Bodhi asked, “Venerable Sir, at what time and in which life was I negligent and indulged in the five cords of sensual pleasure with my wife?” the Blessed One revealed the past life story of Prince Bodhi as follows:

Prince, in the long past, hundreds of people were crossing the ocean in a large ship when the ship broke apart and sank in the middle of the ocean. A husband and wife from that group of people clung to a plank and reached an island in the middle of the sea. All the other people perished in that ocean.

On that island, there lived a great number of birds. Those two, husband and wife, finding no other food and being extremely hungry, took bird eggs, roasted them on embers, and ate them. When the bird eggs were not enough to satisfy them, they caught young birds, roasted them, and ate them. In this manner, during their youth, middle age, and—
653:
The last stage of life = In all these three stages, they would poke out, roast, and eat bird eggs and young birds. Without reaching a state of mindfulness in even one of the three stages, both of them indulged in the craving for taste and sensual pleasures, remaining heedless.

Thus, the Blessed One revealed this past unwholesome kamma of Prince Bodhi:

"Prince, if you and your wife had reached a state of mindfulness in any one of the three stages of life, then in that stage of mindfulness, a son or a daughter would have been born to you in this life.

If not both, but if even one of you had been mindful, then because of that mindful person, a son or a daughter would have been born.

Prince, indeed, if one knows oneself to be dear (meaning, if one loves oneself), one should protect oneself by not being heedless in wholesome dhammas throughout the three stages of life. If one is unable to protect oneself in all three stages, one should certainly protect oneself in at least one of the stages."

Having said this, he uttered:

Attānañce piyaṃ jaññā,
rakkheyya naṃ surakkhitaṃ.
Tiṇṇamanyataraṃ yāmaṃ,
paṭijaggeyya paṇဍito.
654:
Rājakumāra = Prince Bodhi, the lay devotee. Paṇḍito = The wise person who considers the consequences. Attānaṃ = Oneself. Piyaṃ = As one who is loved and cherished in the whole world. Ce jaññā = If one truly knows. Naṃ = That self. Surakkhitaṃ = Having made it well-protected so that no danger comes in both the present and future lives. Rakkheyya = Should protect. Tiṇṇamanyataraṃ yāmaṃ = In any one of the three stages, namely the first, second, or third. Paṭijaggeyya = Should cleanse oneself so that the ten types of misconduct do not arise.

(In this verse, regarding the phrase "If a wise person knows himself to be dear, he should protect himself well-guarded": If a layperson, thinking "I will protect myself," enters a very secure room on the upper floor of a mansion and places guards all around, this is not called protecting oneself. Similarly, if a monk stays in a very secure cave with the windows closed, this is not called protecting oneself.

In truth, if a layperson strives to perform wholesome deeds such as generosity (dāna) and virtue (sīla) to the best of their ability, or if a monk strives with diligence in the duties of a monk, such as fulfilling major and minor duties, studying the scriptures (pariyatti), and practicing meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), then it is called protecting oneself.

Regarding the phrase "One should cleanse oneself in any one of the three stages": whether a layperson or a monk...)
655:
...as mentioned before, one must strive in the wholesome deeds and monastic duties relevant to them in all three stages of life. If one cannot strive in all three stages as mentioned, one must certainly strive and cleanse oneself in at least one of the three stages. To make it clearer:

If a layperson could not perform wholesome deeds in the first stage of life because time was spent in youthful play, they should be mindful and perform wholesome deeds in the middle stage. If they could not perform wholesome deeds in the middle stage because they had to care for their wife and children, they must certainly perform wholesome deeds in the last stage. Only such a person is said to cleanse themselves. For those who do not do so, they are not said to love themselves; they are only said to act in a way that leads them to the four lower realms (apāya).

Similarly, if a monk did not have the opportunity to practice meditation because he was busy studying, reciting, and performing major and minor duties in the first stage, he should be mindful and practice meditation in the middle stage. If he did not have the opportunity to practice meditation in the middle stage because he had to inquire and discuss the meanings, interpretations, and judgments of the scriptures he learned in the first stage, he must certainly be mindful and practice meditation in the last stage. A monk who acts in this way is said to cleanse himself. For those who do not do so, they are not said to love themselves; they are only said to cause themselves distress through later remorse. This special meaning should be noted.)

At the end of the teaching, Prince Bodhi was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). The teaching was also beneficial for the assembled audience.

(This is the story of Prince Bodhi.)
656:
## The Account of Mara Entering the Stomach of Venerable Mahāmoggallāna

On one occasion, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was staying in the Bhesakaḷā Grove, a sanctuary near the city of Sumsumāragiri in the Bhagga country. At that time, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna was walking in meditation (caṅkama) in the open air. Then, the evil Mara entered Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's stomach and sat inside the intestines, above the rectum. Then, a thought arose in Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's mind: "What is happening? My stomach feels as heavy as a heap of stones. It feels like the stomach of someone who has eaten bean rice, or like a bag filled with beans, or like wet, swollen beans."

Then, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reflected: "If this current heaviness in my stomach is due to a food-related ailment (indigestion), it is not suitable to continue walking in meditation in the open air." Having considered this, he stepped down from the meditation path, entered his dwelling, and sat down on the prepared seat.

After sitting down, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna reflected with wise attention: "Why is this happening?" (If the Venerable had reflected on his pure virtue and made a determination, "If there is undigested food eaten yesterday or the days before, or if there is an imbalance of phlegm, bile, or wind, let it all be digested; let there be comfort," and if he had rubbed his stomach with his hand, the evil Mara would have been crushed to powder. However, the Venerable did not do so; he only reflected with wise attention.)
657:
Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw the evil Mara (having created a small body) sitting inside the intestines above the rectum. He said to the evil Mara: "Get out, Evil One! Get out, Evil One! Do not harass the Buddha. Do not harass the disciple of the Buddha. Let it not be for your long-term harm and suffering."

(Just as harassing a child is considered harassing the parents, or harassing disciples is considered harassing the teachers and preceptors, or harassing a province is considered harassing the king, so too, harassing a disciple of the Buddha is considered harassing the Buddha himself. Therefore, the Venerable said, "Do not harass the Buddha.")

Then, a thought arose in the mind of the evil Mara: "This monk says 'Get out, Evil One! Get out, Evil One! Do not harass the Buddha. Do not harass the disciple of the Buddha. Let it not be for your long-term harm and suffering' without even knowing or seeing me. Even his teacher, the Buddha, might not be able to know me so quickly; how could this monk, who is a disciple, know me?"

Then, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said to the evil Mara: "Evil One, I know you by this very thought as well. Do not think, 'This monk does not know me.'"
658:
"Evil One, you are Mara. Evil One, a thought arose in your mind: 'This monk says "Get out, Evil One! Get out, Evil One! Do not harass the Buddha. Do not harass the disciple of the Buddha. Let it not be for your long-term harm and suffering" without even knowing or seeing me. Even his teacher, the Buddha, might not be able to know me so quickly; how could this monk, who is a disciple, know me?'"

Then, the evil Mara thought: "This monk truly knows and sees me, and that is why he says 'Get out, Evil One! Get out, Evil One! Do not harass the Buddha. Do not harass the disciple of the Buddha. Let it not be for your long-term harm and suffering.'" Having thought this, Mara exited from Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's mouth and stood outside the door-leaf.

Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw Mara standing outside the door-leaf and said to him: "Evil One, I see you here as well. Do not think, 'This monk does not see me.' Evil One, you are now standing outside the door-leaf."

Then, a thought arose in the Venerable's mind:

"The odor of human bodies causes distress to the sky-dwelling devas who reside a hundred yojanas away.
659:
(See Dīgha Nikāya 2, 260). Nevertheless, although this Mara is a celestial king from the Paranimmita-vasavatti heaven, very delicate and pure, and possessing great power and majesty, he entered my stomach and sat inside the intestines above the rectum. He must be someone who would greatly offend and destroy me. Since he can enter and sit in such a loathsome and disgusting place, what is there that he would not dare to do? Whom would he be ashamed of? (He would dare to do anything. He would not be ashamed of anyone).

In this world, if it is said, "You are my relative," there is no one who does not become softened. Therefore, I will now let this Mara know of our kinship and release him using only a gentle and subtle means."

After this thought, while revealing his own past unwholesome kamma, he preached the Dhamma of kinship to Mara, explaining that he was his uncle, as follows:

## Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's Past Misdeed

"Evil One, there is a special event that happened in the past (during the time of Kakusandha Buddha). In the time of that Blessed Kakusandha, I was a Mara named Dūsī. At that time, my sister was named Kāḷī. You are the son of my sister Kāḷī. (Therefore) you were my nephew (my sister's son)."
660:
(This statement was spoken by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna by way of lineage (paveṇī). To clarify further: in the human world, one who is of royal descent from the father’s or grandfather’s side succeeds to the throne and rules as a king. However, in the celestial world, there is no such thing as ruling by royal lineage. In truth, a being who possesses the merit worthy of becoming a celestial king becomes a celestial king in the celestial realm by the power of their own performed merit. They remain there until the end of their life span and then pass away (cuti). After that celestial king passes away, another being who possesses the merit worthy of becoming a celestial king becomes the king in that place due to their own performed wholesome kamma. In this way, the current Māra Vasavatti was the nephew of Māra Dūsī at that time; having passed away from that life and performed wholesome merit again, he has now become the one in the position of that Māra. It is not that the deity who was the nephew of Māra Dūsī at that time has remained without passing away until now.)

After the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna spoke to Māra about their kinship, mentioning that Māra was his nephew (sister’s son) at that time, he continued to preach in detail to Māra about how he himself was Māra Dūsī at that time, committed extremely grave unwholesome kamma, fell into hell, and suffered greatly. That detailed account should be noted from page 421 of the Burmese Translation of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa Pāḷi; here, it will be presented in brief:

“O Evil Māra, when I was Māra Dūsī, the Buddha Kakusandha was appearing in the world. The Buddha Kakusandha had a pair of chief disciples named the Venerable Vidhura and the Venerable Sañjīva.”
661:
## The Reason for Being Named Vidhura
“O Evil Māra, among the many disciples of the Buddha Kakusandha, the Venerable Vidhura was the most excellent and supreme in terms of Dhamma teaching and wisdom. For that reason, the name of that Elder became known as the Elder ‘Vidhura’. (Vidhura means the Elder who possesses wisdom.)

## The Reason for Being Named Sañjīva
“O Evil Māra, whether the Venerable Sañjīva was staying in the forest, at the foot of a tree, or in a secluded place, he used to enter the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) easily, without any hardship or fatigue. Once, while the Venerable Sañjīva was sitting at the foot of a tree in the attainment of cessation, many cowherds, goat-herds, farmers, and travelers saw him and thought, ‘Friends, how wonderful! How marvelous! This monk has passed away while sitting. Come, let us cremate the corpse of this monk.’ Having consulted and planned thus, they gathered as much grass, wood, and dried cow dung as they could find, piled it on the body of the Venerable Sañjīva, set it on fire, and departed.

(For Non-returners and Arahants who enter the attainment of cessation, according to the resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) made before entering the attainment: (1) Their personal requisites, which are separate from their body, cannot be destroyed by the five kinds of enemies. (2) While in the attainment, if the Buddha desires and sends a messenger monk to call them, they emerge from the attainment even before that messenger monk reaches their presence. This is due to their great respect for the Buddha. (3) If the Saṅgha desires them for some Saṅgha business and sends a messenger monk to call them,
662:
they emerge from the attainment even before that messenger monk arrives to call them; this is due to their great respect for the Saṅgha. (4) Before entering the attainment, they reflect upon their life-force (āyusaṅkhāra) and determine the time before the life-force ceases; therefore, there is absolutely no passing away or attaining Parinibbāna while in the attainment. As for the requisites attached to their body, even without a specific resolution, they cannot be destroyed by the five kinds of enemies due to the power of the attainment. Therefore, although the cowherds, goat-herds, farmers, and travelers set fire to the Venerable Sañjīva, not even a single thread of his robes could be burnt.)

“O Evil Māra, then, when that night had passed and the next morning arrived, the Venerable Sañjīva emerged from the attainment of cessation, stepped out from the glowing red embers which were like the color of Butea flowers and free from smoke, shook his robes, and entered the village for alms in the morning. O Evil Māra, those cowherds, goat-herds, farmers, and travelers who had set the fire the previous day saw the Venerable Sañjīva coming for alms and were astonished, saying, ‘Friends, how wonderful! How marvelous! Although this monk had passed away while sitting, he has now come back to life again!’ O Evil Māra, because of this reason—that people said ‘Paṭisañjīvito’ (he has come back to life)—the name of that Elder became known as the Elder ‘Sañjīva’. (Sañjīva means the Elder who has come back to life.)”
663:
## The Evil Intentions and
## Actions of Dūsī Māra

O evil Māra! At that time, a thought arose in the mind of Dūsī Māra: "I do not know the place of origin (regarding rebirth) or the destination (regarding death) of these monks who are virtuous and of good character. It would be well if I were to deceive the brahmin householders, saying, 'Come, sirs! You should abuse, revile, harass, and trouble these monks who are virtuous and of good character. When they are abused, reviled, harassed, and troubled by you, their minds may become perturbed. Because of such mental perturbation, Dūsī Māra might find an opportunity to act as an enemy without regard.'"

(Note: The intention of Dūsī Māra is presented here exactly as it appears in the Pali text and the Burmese Pitaka translation; it is not very clear. In fact, it means: "I do not know the place of origin or the destination of these monks who are virtuous and of good character. It would be well if I were to deceive the brahmin householders into saying to one another, 'Come, sirs! You should abuse, revile, harass, and trouble these monks whom people call virtuous and of good character,' and to act accordingly. If they are thus deceived and speak words of abuse, reviling, harassment, and trouble, the minds of those monks might become perturbed. Because of that mental perturbation, Dūsī Māra would be able to act as an enemy...")
664:
an opportunity to act as an enemy.’ Only if said in this way would it be consistent with the actual events.)

“O Evil Māra, after having such a thought, Māra Dūsī carried out the deception to make the brāhmaṇas and householders misunderstand, just as he had planned. (The details of the deception will become clear later.) O Evil Māra, then those brāhmaṇas and householders, being deceived by Māra Dūsī, spoke words of abuse, reviling, annoyance, and harassment to the virtuous and good-natured monks (in the following manner). The way they spoke was:

‘These low-born, dark-natured shaven-headed wretched monks, born from the instep of Brahma, say “We are meditators, we are meditators,” yet they remain brooding with drooping necks and downcast faces, being lazy, heavy, and dull.

For example, just as an owl broods while seeking a mouse among the branches; or as a jackal broods while waiting and seeking fish on a riverbank; or as a cat broods while waiting and seeking a mouse at a drain or a rubbish heap; or as a donkey broods at a drain or a rubbish heap when its back is sore; in the same way, these low-born, dark-natured shaven-headed wretched monks, born from the instep of
665:
Brahma, say “We are meditators, we are meditators,” yet they remain brooding with drooping necks and downcast faces, being lazy, heavy, and dull.’

Thus they spoke words of abuse, reviling, annoyance, and harassment.

“O Evil Māra, at that time, most people, after the breaking up of the body and passing away, were reborn in the four lower realms: hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), and the realm of asuras.

[In this context, regarding the statement that many people were reborn in the four lower realms, a special note should be made:

If Māra Dūsī had actually possessed the bodies of the people and committed the abuse, reviling, annoyance, and harassment (since the people would have had no desire to speak such words), the unwholesome kamma would not have accrued to the people; it would have accrued only to Māra Dūsī. (If unwholesome kamma had not accrued to the people, they would not have fallen into the lower realms.)

In truth, at that time, Māra Dūsī did not possess the bodies of the people, but rather, to make the hearts of those who saw them unpleasant, he showed the forms of women near the monks, the forms of men near the nuns, and various other incompatible (visabhāga) objects unsuitable for monks. The way he showed them was: at that time, Māra Dūsī showed illusions of monks catching fish with baskets, monks catching fish by casting nets, monks trapping birds by setting up birdlime sticks*, monks hunting animals in the forest with a pack of dogs, and monks taking women into liquor taverns (toddy shops or arrack shops).

* Birdlime stick (nhè-kaw) = a type of stick coated with sticky sap etc. to trap birds.]
666:
He showed visions of monks sitting, dancing, and singing, and of young men sitting and standing in the secluded places where the bhikkhunīs spend the night and day. (This was the deception of Dūsī Māra.)

When people went to the forest, the park, or the monastery, they saw these unpleasant sights. Upon returning home, they told others, “Sirs, these monks perform such improper and unseemly acts. If one gives to them, how can merit be gained? Do not give anything to these monks.”

In this way, whenever those people saw the monks, they uttered insults in every place, thus increasing unwholesome states and being reborn in the four woeful planes.

O Evil One, when Dūsī Māra thus deceived them (to cause loss of faith), the Blessed One Kakusandha addressed the assembly of monks, explaining that the insults of the brahmin householders were due to the deception of Dūsī Māra. He then gave the instruction to dwell developing the four Brahmavihāras: loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā). Following the Buddha’s instruction, the monks dwelt developing the four Brahmavihāra-jhānas.

O Evil One, then the thought occurred to Dūsī Māra: “Even though I act in this way, I cannot know the coming or going of these monks. What if I were to deceive the brahmin householders so that they show respect, honor, and veneration to the monks? If
667:
they are deceived and the brahmin householders show respect, honor, and veneration, then the minds of these monks might become corrupted. Because of that, Dūsī Māra would find an opportunity to do harm.” Having thought thus, he deceived the brahmin householders as he had planned, so that they would show respect, honor, and veneration to the monks. (The manner of deception will be explained later.)

O Evil One, when Dūsī Māra thus deceived them, those brahmin householders showed respect, deference, esteem, and veneration to the monks.

O Evil One, at that time, most people who died were reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.

[In this context, regarding the statement that many people reached a happy destination, the following should be noted:

Just as Dūsī Māra created various unpleasant visions to cause dissatisfaction in the previous section (the section on causing loss of faith), in this section (the section on causing faith), he created various pleasant visions to inspire faith. The manner of his creation was as follows:

Dūsī Māra created visions in places where many people could see: monks flying in the sky, standing in the sky, sitting cross-legged in the sky, sewing robes in the sky, teaching scriptures in the sky, spreading out robes in the sky to warm themselves, newly ordained monks traveling through the sky, and young novices standing in the sky plucking flowers.
668:
He created and showed such visions. (This was the deception of Dūsī Māra.)

When people went to the forest, the park, or the monastery, they saw such practices of the monks. Upon returning home, they told others, “Sirs, among the monks, even the youngest novices possess such great psychic power and majesty. Offerings given to these monks are of great fruit. Do give to these monks; do show them respect.”

At that time, the people showed respect, honor, and veneration to the Saṅgha with the four requisites—robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicine. Having performed much merit, they were reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.]

O Evil One, when Dūsī Māra thus deceived them (to inspire faith), the Blessed One Kakusandha addressed the assembly of monks, explaining that the brahmin householders’ respect and veneration with the four requisites were due to the deception of Dūsī Māra. He then gave this instruction: “Come, monks, dwell frequently contemplating the foulness of the body (asubha), perceiving the loathsomeness of food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā), perceiving non-delight in the entire world (sabbaloke anabhiratisaññā), and frequently contemplating impermanence in all conditioned things of the three planes (aniccānupassī).”

O Evil One, then the monks, following the instruction of the Blessed One Kakusandha, went to the forest, to the roots of trees, or to secluded places, and dwelt practicing the meditation on foulness, the meditation on the loathsomeness of food,
669:
the meditation on non-delight in the entire world, and the meditation on impermanence.

(In this regard: The Blessed One Kakusandha was then traveling throughout the entire island of Jambudīpa. He would visit even places where only two or three monks resided and, showing the respective benefits (as mentioned in Aṅguttara Nikāya 2, 433-434), he taught these four types of meditation. Those monks applied themselves diligently to these four meditations, developed insight (vipassanā), and attained the fruit of Arahantship.)

O Evil One, later on, the Blessed One Kakusandha, with the Elder Vidhura (his right-hand disciple) as his attendant monk, entered a village for alms. Then Dūsī Māra (having failed to find an opportunity to do harm despite deceiving the brahmin householders to either insult or revere the monks, now wished to destroy them through his own effort) possessed a young boy. He picked up a stone the size of a fist and directly struck the head of the Elder Vidhura. At that moment, the Elder Vidhura’s head was split open down to the skull.

O Evil One, even though his head was split and blood was flowing, the Elder Vidhura followed closely behind the Blessed One Kakusandha, step for step, without losing his composure. Then the Blessed One Kakusandha turned his whole body around with the gaze of an elephant (nāgavilokita) and said, “This Dūsī Māra truly knows no bounds.” O Evil One,
670:
at the very moment the Blessed One Kakusandha turned and looked, Dūsī Māra fell from that celestial world and passed away; he reached the Great Hell.

[In this regard: Concerning the phrase “looked with the gaze of an elephant”—when a noble elephant wishes to look back, it does not turn only its neck but turns its entire body to look. Similarly, the Blessed One turned his entire body to look. To clarify further:

The bones of ordinary people are joined end-to-end, and the bones of Paccekabuddhas are linked together. However, the bones of the Buddhas are not like that; the bones of the Buddhas are interlinked like rings. Therefore, when looking back, they cannot turn only the neck but must turn the entire body like a noble elephant. Thus, the Blessed One Kakusandha turned his entire body like a golden statue moved by a mechanical switch. Having turned and while still standing, he said, “When this Dūsī Māra does evil, he knows no bounds (he commits evil beyond measure).”

Regarding the statement “at the very moment the Blessed One Kakusandha turned and looked, Dūsī Māra fell from the celestial world and passed away,” it should not be understood that he passed away at that very spot in the human world where the Blessed One turned to look. Indeed, it is not the custom for a deva to pass away in a distant place (other than their own celestial realm). Therefore, it should be understood that Dūsī Māra returned to his own abode in the Vasavattī heaven and passed away from that deva world.

Furthermore, his passing away should not be understood as being caused by the Blessed One Kakusandha’s look. Indeed, the phrase “at the very moment the Blessed One Kakusandha turned and looked”
671:
is merely a phrase indicating the time of Dūsī Māra’s passing (it is not a phrase indicating that the look caused the death). In truth, because he had offended the Chief Disciple, the Elder of the Right, who was endowed with such vast and great virtues, the life of Dūsī Māra was cut off right there, as if severed by a large billhook. This should be carefully noted.]

O Evil One, the names of that Great Hell (where Dūsī Māra fell) are threefold: Saphassāyatanika, Saṅkusamāhata, and Paccatta-vedanīya.

[In this regard: For the beings in that Great Hell, iron spikes are driven into each of the six locations—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and the chest (the six sense bases)—causing unbearable suffering and pain. Thus, those hell-beings suffer agonizingly in the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and chest. These six types of suffering are called “saphassāyatana-dukkha.” Because it is a realm where this suffering exists, that hell is called the “Saphassāyatanika Great Hell.”

Saṅku = iron spike + samāhata = striking or torturing. Because it is a place where hundreds of iron spikes strike and torture, it is also called the “Saṅkusamāhata Great Hell.”

Paccatta = by its own nature + vedanīya = capable of causing painful feeling. Because it can cause painful feelings by its own nature, even without the actions of the executioners (hell wardens), it is also called the “Paccatta-vedanīya Great Hell.”]

O Evil One, then the hell wardens approached me and said, “Friend, when one iron spike meets another iron spike in your heart,
672:
672
‘Know that for me, who has been cooked in hell, it has been a thousand years.’

[In this regard: Concerning the statement ‘When one iron spike and another iron spike meet in the region of your heart,’ the following should be understood: The physical body of those who fall into that Great Hell is three gāvutas in size. The physical body of Dũsĩ Māra in that hell was also three gāvutas. When Dũsĩ Māra fell into that hell, the hell-warders themselves seized iron spikes, blazing and glowing, the size of palm trunks, and said, ‘With this intention, you planned and committed evil.’ Then, just as one pounds and grinds cake in a mortar, they pierced his heart and chest with the iron spikes. Fifty hell-warders pierced towards the feet, and fifty hell-warders pierced towards the head. As they proceeded in this manner, it took five hundred years to reach the extremities of the feet and the head.

Then, from those extremities of the feet and head, they pierced back again in the same manner, and it took another five hundred years to reach and meet at the heart and chest. (In total, it took a thousand years for the iron spikes to meet at the heart and chest; it is with this meaning in mind that it is said, ‘When one iron spike and another iron spike meet in the region of your heart.’)]

O Evil Māra! For many hundreds and thousands of years beyond counting, I was cooked in that Great Hell with great suffering. (And it did not end there.) For ten thousand years in the Ussada Hell, which is an annex of that Great Hell, I was cooked while experiencing what is called the final suffering (= meaning, as the final stage of suffering). (After suffering for countless years in the Great Hell, it was not over; when rising or being released from that Great Hell, in the annex of that Great Hell—)
673:
673
—in the Ussada Hell, I had to suffer for another ten thousand years. It is said that the suffering in that Ussada Hell is even more intense than the suffering in the Great Hell.)

O Evil Māra! For me, who was cooked in that hell, my body was like that of a human, but my head was like that of a fish. (Because a human head is round, the iron spike might slip when piercing; however, because a fish's head is long and flat, the iron spike cannot slip or miss. Therefore, the head was like that of a fish.)

After the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna had related the past events as stated, he exhorted and taught Māra with twenty-one verses in the following manner, so that Māra might feel dread and spiritual urgency (saᅃvega):

What kind of hell is it where Dũsĩ Māra was cooked for harassing the disciple Vidhura, the Arahant, and the Buddha Kakusandha?

The hell where Dũsĩ Māra was cooked for harassing the disciple Vidhura, the Arahant, and the Buddha Kakusandha, is one where there is piercing and torture with a hundred iron spikes. All those iron spikes, even without the torturers (= hell-warders), can cause suffering and pain by their own nature. The Great Hell where Dũsĩ Māra fell is of such a nature.

O Māra! You shall come to suffering because of harassing the monk who is a disciple of the Buddha, who clearly sees this kamma and the result of kamma. (a)
674:
674
Celestial mansions (vimāna) that last for an aeon stand in the midst of the ocean; they have the color of beryl, are delightful, and emit a brilliant radiance. In those mansions, many goddesses of various complexions dance and sing.

O Māra! You shall come to suffering because of harassing the monk who is a disciple of the Buddha, who clearly sees with knowledge these three things: the nature of these mansions, the luxury of the goddesses, and the cause of those luxuries. (b)

That monk, indeed, following the instruction and encouragement of the Buddha, shook the palace (Pubbārāma) of Visākhā, Migāra's mother, with his big toe while the assembly of monks was watching.

O Māra! You shall come to suffering because of harassing the monk who is a disciple of the Buddha, a possessor of higher knowledge (abhiā) who is able to shake this palace. (c)

That monk, supported by his psychic power, shook the Vejayanta Palace, the abode of Sakka, the King of Devas, with his big toe, and caused the host of devas to tremble with fear.

O Māra! You shall come to suffering because of harassing the monk who is a disciple of the Buddha, a possessor of higher knowledge who is able to shake the Vejayanta Palace with his big toe. (d)

That monk, in the Vejayanta Palace, the abode of Sakka, questioned Sakka: ‘Sakka, do you know the liberations through the destruction of craving?’ When questioned,
675:
675
Sakka, the King of Devas, replied and answered that monk according to the truth.

O Māra! You shall come to suffering because of harassing the monk who is a disciple of the Buddha, a master of psychic power and higher knowledge who is capable of asking such a question. (e)

That monk, near the Sudhammā Hall (in the Brahma realm), questioned a Brahma: ‘Friend, does that wrong view which you held previously—that there is no recluse or brahmin with great psychic power who can come to this Brahma realm—still exist in you now? Do you see the radiance of the Buddha's body, which blazes and glows, surpassing the radiance of the bodies, mansions, and ornaments of the Brahmas in the Brahma realm?’

The Brahma who was questioned replied and addressed that monk according to the facts: ‘Venerable sir, the wrong view I held previously no longer exists in me. I do see the radiance of the Buddha's body, which blazes and glows, surpassing the radiance of the bodies, mansions, and ornaments of the Brahmas in the Brahma realm. How could I now say, ‘I am permanent, I am eternal’?’

O Māra! You shall come to suffering because of harassing the monk who is a disciple of the Buddha, a master of psychic power and higher knowledge who is capable of asking such a question. (f)
676:
676
That monk (when subduing the Naga king Nandopananda) touched the peak of Mount Sineru and the four great continents—namely, the Southern, Eastern, Western, and Northern continents—with higher knowledge based on the meditative attainments of liberation (vimokkha-jhāna). (This refers to how, when subduing the Naga king Nandopananda, he covered and touched the peak of Mount Sineru and all four great continents with a created Naga body).

O Māra! You shall come to suffering because of harassing the monk who is a disciple of the Buddha, a possessor of such great higher knowledge. (g)

(In this regard: The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna spoke of himself as if he were another monk. This method is called in the scriptures ‘Aāpadesa-naya’ = the method of referring to oneself as another.

Regarding these seven points from (a) to (g) just mentioned, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna exhorted Māra while clearly demonstrating his own psychic power. Among those seven points:

Point (a) is spoken with reference to the Māratajjanĩya Sutta of the Mũlapaᅃᅃāsa Pāᄷi, which is currently being described. Point (b) is spoken with reference to the higher knowledge of the Venerable one who could travel to celestial realms and teach, as found in the Vimānavatthu and Petavatthu. Point (c) is spoken with reference to the Moggallāna Sutta on page 235 of the Mahāvaggasaᅃyutta Pāᄷi. Points (d) and (e) are spoken with reference to the Cũᄷataᅃhāsaᅃkhaya Sutta on page 320 of the Mũlapaᅃᅃāsa Pāᄷi. Point (f) is spoken with reference to the Saᅃyutta Nikāya, Sagāthāvagga Pāᄷi,
677:
677
page 146, the Aatarabrahma Sutta. Point (g) is spoken with reference to the section on subduing the Naga king Nandopananda in the Visuddhimagga Aᅡᅡhakathā, Volume II, page 27, Dasa-iddhikathā. This is a concluding note.)

Fire, indeed, does not make an effort saying, ‘I will burn only the fool.’ It is only because the fool strikes and touches the burning fire that the fire burns the fool. O Māra! In the same way, because you harass the Buddha, you will burn yourself, just like the fool who touches fire. (h)

Māra has increased unwholesome states (akusala) by harassing the Buddha. O Evil One! Do you perhaps think, ‘Evil does not bring me results’? (i)

O Evil One! For the one who does evil, the unwholesome evil increases as time goes on. O Māra! Be weary of harassing the Buddha. (Just as the desire of your uncle Dũsĩ Māra to oppress the monks in the past was the cause of his suffering in hell for a long time, so too is your current desire to oppress the monks. Therefore,) do not have the desire to oppress the monks. (j)

In this way, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna gave this exhortation to Māra in the Bhesakaᄷā Sanctuary Forest so as to cause him dread.
678:
Then Māra, feeling displeased, vanished instantly from that spot*.

## About the Brahmin Pañcaggadāyaka

The Blessed One spent His eighth Vassa (rainy season retreat) in the Bhesakaḷā Grove near the city of Susumāragira. After liberating those beings worthy of liberation through various Dhamma teachings such as the Bodhirājakumāra Sutta, He traveled on a journey, offering the cool nectar of the Dhamma to humans and devas. During that time, He was residing in the Jetavana Monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī.

In the city of Sāvatthī, there was a brahmin named Pañcaggadāyaka. This brahmin was known as Pañcaggadāyaka because he was accustomed to giving the "five first-fruits": the first-fruit of the field, the first-fruit of the heap, the first-fruit of the granary, the first-fruit of the pot, and the first-fruit of the plate. (Pañcagga = five first-fruits + Dāyaka = one who gives). The manner of giving these five first-fruits was as follows:

(1) From the fields he cultivated, he would first have the ripened stalks of Sāli rice, barley, and divine grain collected. He would prepare gruel, milk-rice, and parched rice cakes, and with the belief that "the wise one who gives the first-fruits can obtain the foremost benefits," he would offer these gifts of gruel, milk-rice, and parched rice cakes to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha. This was the brahmin's gift of the first-fruit of the field.

(2) When the crops were fully ripened, harvested, and threshed, he would take the first-fruits from the threshed heap of grain and, in the same manner, offer them to the Saṅgha led by the Buddha...

* This passage is extracted and written from the Pāḷi, Commentary, and Sub-commentary of the Māratajjaniya Sutta of the Mūlapaṇṇāsa Pāḷi.
679: This was the Brahmin's offering of the first-fruits of the heap. (3) After filling the granaries with grain, when the first granary was opened, he would set aside the grain first taken out and offer it in the same way. This was the Brahmin's offering of the first-fruits of the granary. (4) Every time a pot of rice or gruel was cooked in his house, he would take the first portion and offer it to the monks. If he had not yet made this offering, he would not even feed the children. This was the Brahmin's offering of the first-fruits of the pot. (5) Furthermore, when he was about to eat his own meal, if it was in the morning, he would first offer the first portion of the food to the Saṅgha before eating. If it was after noon, he would give it to beggars who came to his house (or at the very least to dogs if there were no beggars) before eating. He never ate without giving. This was the Brahmin's offering of the first-fruits of the meal. Thus, because he was accustomed to giving these five first-fruits, he became famous as the Brahmin Pañcaggadāyaka. One day, at dawn, the Buddha surveyed the world of beings with his Buddha-eye—the Knowledge of the Inclinations and Latent Tendencies of Beings (āsayānusaya-ñāṇa) and the Knowledge of the Maturity of the Faculties of Beings (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa). He saw the powerful merit and supporting conditions (upanissaya) of the Brahmin Pañcaggadāyaka and his wife for attaining the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga). After attending to his physical needs, he entered the Gandhakuṭī (Fragrant Chamber) early.
680: (In the monastery where the Buddha resided, when it was time for the morning alms round, all the monks in the monastery would gather at the Gandhakuṭī where the Buddha stayed. At that time, if the Buddha wished to enter for alms together with the monks, he would emerge from the Gandhakuṭī without being invited by anyone. If the Buddha wished to go for alms alone, he would not emerge, and the door of the Gandhakuṭī would remain closed. Then the monks, knowing that the Buddha wished to go for alms alone for a special reason, would enter the city or village for alms by themselves.) On that day, when the monks gathered near the Gandhakuṭī at the time for alms and saw that the door remained closed, they understood that the Buddha wished to enter the city alone. They circumambulated the Gandhakuṭī to the right and entered the city for alms. When it was time for the Brahmin Pañcagga's meal, the Buddha emerged from the monastery and entered the city of Sāvatthī. When the people saw the Buddha entering the city alone, they thought, "Today, there must surely be a being whom the Buddha will bless; that is why he has entered the city alone." Knowing this, no one came forward to invite the Buddha.
681: The Buddha gradually made his way and stood at the door of the Brahmin Pañcaggadāyaka's house. At that moment, the Brahmin was sitting and holding his food. The Brahmin's wife was standing and holding a fan to fan him. When the wife saw the Buddha, she thought, "If this Brahmin sees the Buddha, he will take the bowl of rice and offer all the food. If he does that, I will have to cook again." Thinking thus, with a mind of non-devotion and stinginess, she hid the Brahmin's view of the Buddha with a round palm-leaf fan. Knowing this, the Buddha emitted a radiance from his body. When the Brahmin saw the yellow radiance emitted by the Buddha, he looked up and wondered, "What is this?" and saw the Buddha standing at his door. The wife thought, "The Brahmin has seen the Buddha," and at that moment, she dropped the palm-leaf fan and went to the Buddha before the Brahmin could. She paid homage with the fivefold prostration. Knowing what was appropriate for the wife as she rose from her seat, the Buddha recited this verse: "Sabbaso nāmarūpasmiṃ, yassa natthi mamāyitaṃ. Asatā ca na socati, sa ve bhikkhūti vuccati." Yassa = In whom; sabbaso = in every way; nāmarūpasmiṃ = regarding the two phenomena of mind and matter; mamāyitaṃ = the attachment of craving and views as 'I' or 'mine'; natthi = does not exist in the least. Asatā ca = And because of the non-existence through the cessation of mind and matter; na socati = he does not grieve at all. Sa = That person; ve = indeed; vuccati = is called a Bhikkhu, a holy one, because of his ability to destroy the thick darkness of defilements.
682: The Buddha preached this Dhamma verse. At the end of the verse, the Brahmin's wife was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). The Brahmin also invited the Buddha into the house, had him sit on a noble seat, poured the water of donation, and offered the food prepared for himself, saying, "Magnificent Buddha, you are the supreme recipient of offerings in the world including the devas. I entreat you, Lord, please let this meal of mine be placed in your bowl." To bless the Brahmin, the Buddha accepted and partook of that meal. After the Buddha had finished his meal, knowing what was appropriate for the Brahmin, he preached this Dhamma verse: "Yadaggato majjhato sesato vā, piṇḍaṃ labhetha paradattūpajīvī. Nālaṃ thutuṃ nopi nipaccavādī, taṃ vāpi dhīrā muni vedayanti."
683: Paradattūpajīvī = A monk who lives depending on the requisites offered by others; labhetha = may receive through the faith and generosity of others; yaṃ piṇḍaṃ vā = whatever alms-food; aggato = from the first-fruits; majjhato = from the middle; sesato vā = or from the small amount remaining in the pot. (Yo = That noble person who is an Arahant); nālaṃ thutuṃ = is not at all worthy of praising with delight, thinking 'I have received the first-fruits,' because he has discarded the defilement of greed. (This means he does not praise even when receiving the first-fruits). Nopi nipaccavādī = Even when receiving the leftovers or remains, he does not speak disparagingly with a displeased heart or angry pride, thinking 'It is not proper to offer such coarse food to a monk like me.' Taṃ = That person who has discarded both these states of affection and aversion; dhīrāva = only the wise ones, starting with the Buddha; vedayanti = clearly know and recognize; muniṃ = as a Muni, a monk whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava). At the end of this Dhamma verse, the Brahmin Pañcaggadāyaka was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). (This is the story of the Brahmin Pañcaggadāyaka. This story is extracted from the commentary to the Muni Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta (Volume 1, page 256). The explanation differs from that in the Dhammapada Commentary.)
684:
## The Blessed One's Three Visits
## To the Island of Sīhaḷa

I shall briefly describe the account of the Blessed One's three visits to the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka), extracted from the first part of the Mahāvaṃsa:

After His Enlightenment, the Blessed One spent His first Vassa in the Isipatana Migadāya (Deer Park) near Bārāṇasī. From there, He proceeded to the Uruvelā forest. In the episode where He displayed miracles to the hermit Uruvelā Kassapa, on the day before the great alms-giving ceremony for the great hermit Uruvelā Kassapa by the people of the two kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha, the Blessed One perceived the hermit's desire that the Blessed One should not come to his great feast. Therefore, on the day of that great ceremony, the Blessed One went to the island of Uttarakuru for alms-round, and after taking His meal at Lake Anotatta, when night fell (in the ninth month after His Enlightenment), He proceeded to the island of Sīhaḷa.

At that time, in a place three yojanas long and one yojana wide near the riverbank in the center of Sīhaḷa—at the site of the present-day Mahānāgavana Garden—a great assembly of the Yakkhas (demons) of Sīhaḷa was being held. The Blessed One went to that assembly of Yakkhas and, standing in the air above the center of the assembly—at the site where the Mahiyangana Cetiya now stands—He caused the Yakkhas to be terrified and fearful by means of rain, fierce winds, and total darkness.
685: Then the Yakkhas, being greatly terrified, entreated the Blessed One for protection. The Blessed One said, "O Yakkhas, I shall dispel your fear and suffering; give me a place to dwell on this island." The Yakkhas replied, "O Noble One, who has quelled all suffering, we give this place to You. May You grant protection to all of us Yakkhas throughout this entire island of Sīhaḷa." The Blessed One withdrew the miraculous display of rain, fierce winds, and thick darkness. When the Yakkhas' fear was calmed, He descended from the sky, went to the place given by the Yakkhas, spread His leather rug (cammakhaṇḍa), and sat down. Then, the Blessed One spread that rug, which was burning with brilliant flames, all around. The Yakkhas, being severely tormented by the heat and terrified, stood clinging to the edges around the island. Then, the Blessed One, by His psychic power, brought the island of Giridīpa to this region of Sīhaḷa. Once all the Yakkhas had entered that island, He returned Giridīpa to its original location by His psychic power. In this way, when the Yakkhas were cleared from the island of Sīhaḷa, the Blessed One withdrew the brilliant, flaming leather rug. At that time, many righteous Devas
686:
They came and assembled on the island of Sīhaḷa. At that assembly, when the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to the devas, many crores of beings attained the realization of the Dhamma (Dhammābhisamaya). Countless devas established themselves in the Three Refuges and the Precepts.

## The Offering of the Hair Relics at the Request of the Great Deva Mahāsumana

The great Deva Mahāsumana, who resided on Mount Sumanakūṭa, after attaining the stage of Sotāpanna at that Dhamma assembly, requested the Blessed One to grant him something for worship. The Blessed One rubbed His head and gave a handful of hair relics to the great Deva Mahāsumana, and then He returned to the Uruvelā forest.

The great Deva Mahāsumana took those hair relics in a golden casket and placed them on a seat adorned with various jewels (at the site where the Mahiyangana Cetiya now stands). He then enclosed them within a stupa made of sapphire (indanilā) for worship.

When the Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, the Elder Sarabhu, a disciple of the Elder Sāriputta, miraculously brought the neck-bone relic from the sandalwood funeral pyre. He placed it within that stone stupa, and surrounded by a company of monks, he had it covered with red stones and renovated the stupa to a height of twelve cubits before departing.

Later, Prince Uddhacūḷābhaya, the younger brother of King Devānaṃpiyatissa, encased that old stupa and...
687:
...renovated it to a height of thirty cubits. Again, King Duṭṭhagāmaṇī encased that old stupa and renovated it to a height of eighty cubits. In this way, the Mahiyangana Cetiya was built and raised in height by successive generations.

(This was the first visit of the Blessed One to the island of Sīhaḷa.)

## The Visit to the Island of Nagadīpa

In the fifth year after His Enlightenment, while the Blessed One was residing in the Jetavana Monastery in the noble city of Sāvatthī, He saw that on the small island of Nagadīpa in Sīhaḷa, the Naga King Mahodara (the uncle) and the Naga King Cūḷodara (the nephew) were engaged in a great battle, having mobilized large Naga armies from both sides over a gem-set throne. On the morning of the new moon day of the month of Tagu (Caitra), the Blessed One took His bowl and robes and proceeded to the island of Nagadīpa out of compassion for the Nagas.

As for the Naga King Mahodara, he was at that time a powerful Naga king ruling over a Naga kingdom five hundred yojanas in extent within the great ocean.

The Naga king who ruled over Mount Vaḍḍhamāna had been given the Naga maiden named Kaṇhā, the sister of Naga King Mahodara, in marriage. From the Naga king of Mount Vaḍḍhamāna and Queen Kaṇhā, a son named Cūḷodara was born. Therefore, Naga King Cūḷodara and Naga King Mahodara were nephew and uncle.
688: The grandmother of the Naga King Cūḷodara (his mother's mother) had given the gem-set throne to his mother, the Naga Queen Kaṇhā, before she passed away. A great battle arose between the uncle, Naga King Mahodara, and the nephew, Naga King Cūḷodara, due to a dispute over the ownership of that gem-set throne, each claiming it as his own. The Naga King Cūḷodara and his army, who lived in the mountains, were also Nagas of great power. At that time, the tree deity (rukkha-devatā) named Samiddhisumana, who lived in a Rājāyatana tree (Lin-lun tree) near the gateway of the Jetavana Monastery, took his abode, the Rājāyatana tree, and with the Blessed One's permission, held it over the Blessed One's head like a parasol, and arrived at the island of Nāgadīpa where he had lived before. To clarify further: in his immediately preceding life, this Deva Samiddhisumana had been a human on the island of Nāgadīpa. At the place where the Rājāyatana Stupa now stands, he saw Paccekabuddhas taking their meal. Filled with intense faith and devotion, he offered branches to the Paccekabuddhas for cleaning their bowls. Due to that meritorious deed, when he passed away, he was reborn as the tree deity named Samiddhisumana in a Rājāyatana tree near the gateway of Prince Jeta's park in Sāvatthī. Later, when the great Jetavana Monastery was built, that Rājāyatana tree stood outside the monastery grounds.
689:
The Blessed One, considering the long-term welfare of the deity Samiddhisumana and the benefit of the island of Nagadīpa, brought the deity Samiddhisumana along with the Rājāyatana tree to Nagadīpa.

Sitting in the air in the midst of the battlefield of the two Naga kings, the Blessed One created a great darkness to cause fear in those Nagas. When the Nagas were greatly terrified, the Blessed One comforted them and displayed light once again. Seeing the Blessed One, the Nagas were filled with immense joy and respectfully prostrated at the Buddha's feet.

When the Blessed One preached the Dhamma of harmony to those Nagas, both Naga kings were exceedingly delighted and offered the gem throne to the Blessed One. The Blessed One descended to the ground, sat upon the gem throne, and partook of the celestial food and drinks offered by the two Naga kings. He then preached the Dhamma to the eighty crores of Nagas living on land and in water, establishing them in the Three Refuges and the Precepts.

## The Request of Maniakkhika Naga King

The Naga king Maniakkhika, who ruled in the region of Kalyāṇī and was the maternal uncle of the Naga king Mahodara, also arrived at Nagadīpa for the battle. This Naga king had already been established in the Three Refuges and the Precepts since the Buddha's first visit to the island of Laṅkā, having heard the Dhamma then. Maniakkhika Naga king...
690: addressed the Blessed One at the island of Nāgadīpa: "O Blessed One, You have shown us this great compassion. Had You not come, we would all have been turned to ashes. O Blessed One, I also desire Your special consideration and compassion. When You visit this island of Sīhaḷa again, I wish for You to visit and grace my dwelling place in Kalyāṇī." The Blessed One accepted the invitation to visit the island of Sīhaḷa again by remaining silent. He then caused the Rājāyatana Stupa to be established at that very spot, and entrusted the Rājāyatana tree and the gem-set throne to the Naga kings for their reverent worship, saying: "O Naga kings, worship the Rājāyatana tree and the gem-set throne, which are my use-relics (paribhoga-cetiya). Such worship will lead to your various forms of welfare and happiness." After giving this and other instructions and advice to the Nagas, He returned to the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī. (This was the Blessed One's second visit to the island of Sīhaḷa.)
691:
## The Third Visit to the Island of Sīhaḷadīpa
## and Entering into Attainments in Various Places

Then, when the third year arrived, the Naga King Maniakkhika approached the Blessed One, who was residing comfortably at the Jetavana Monastery in Sāvatthī, and once again invited the Blessed One to visit the island of Sīhaḷadīpa (Sri Lanka) together with the community of monks.

In the eighth year after his Enlightenment, while the Blessed One was residing at the Jetavana Monastery, on the day after the invitation by the Naga King Maniakkhika (the full moon day of Kason), when it was time for the meal, the Blessed One, surrounded by five hundred monks, robed himself at the Jetavana Monastery and traveled to the abode of the Naga King Maniakkhika in the Kalyāṇီ region of Sīhaḷadīpa.

The Naga King Maniakkhika, along with his retinue of Nagas, served celestial hard and soft foods to the Buddha, the King of Dhamma, and the five hundred monks of the retinue, within a jeweled pavilion constructed at the site where the Kalyāṇī Stupa now stands, on a jeweled throne.

After preaching the Dhamma to the assembly of deities and Nagas, headed by the Naga King Maniakkhika, at the site of the Kalyāṇī Stupa pavilion, the Blessed One traveled from that place through the air and placed a footprint (padacetiya) on the summit of Mount Sumana. At the foot of Mount Sumana, the Blessed One [with his] disciple monks...
692:
After spending the day there, the Buddha, accompanied by the five hundred monks, proceeded again to the region of Dīghavāpī.

At the site where the Dīghavāpī Cetiya would later stand, the Buddha sat down with his five hundred disciple monks and entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) so that in the future, devas and humans would hold that place in high esteem. Having arisen from that attainment, the Buddha then proceeded from that spot to the Mahāmeghavana Park.

Upon reaching the Mahāmeghavana Park, the Buddha sat at the site where the Great Bodhi Tree (Mahābodhi) now stands, together with his five hundred disciple monks, and again entered the attainment of fruition.

From there, he proceeded to the site of the Great Stupa (Mahācetiya) and entered the attainment of fruition with the five hundred monks. After arising from that attainment, he likewise entered the attainment of fruition with his five hundred disciple monks at the site where the Thūpārāma Cetiya now stands.

After arising from that attainment of fruition, the Buddha proceeded with his five hundred disciple monks to the site where the Stone Stupa (Silācetiya) now stands. There, he delivered a discourse of admonition and advice to the assembly of devas who had gathered there, and then returned to the excellent Jetavana Monastery in the city of Sāvatthī.

(This concludes the account of the Buddha’s third visit to the island of Sīhaḷa [Sri Lanka]. This is the account of the Buddha’s three visits to the island of Sīhaḷa.)

## Chapter 27
## The Story of Ghosaka the Great Merchant of Kosambī

(The story of Ghosaka the Great Merchant is described in detail in the first volumes of the Dhammapada Commentary and the Aṅguttara Commentary; in this Great Chronicle of Buddhas, it will be presented as concisely as possible.)—

Before the time of our Buddha’s appearance, a type of disease called ahivātaka (plague) broke out in the kingdom of Allakappa. When this disease occurred, ten, twenty, or thirty people in a single house would die at the same time. Those who fled and escaped to other countries survived. Knowing this, a man took his wife and child, and thinking, “I shall go to another country,” he departed from the kingdom of Allakappa. During the journey, the provisions they had brought from home were exhausted before they could cross the wilderness (the difficult part of the journey). Consequently, as their physical strength failed, the mother and father took turns carrying the young son.

At that time, a thought occurred to the father: “Our physical strength has diminished; if we continue to carry the child, we will not be able to cross this wilderness.” Thus, without letting the child’s mother know, the father pretended to stay behind for a call of nature, made the child sit on the path, and continued the journey alone. When the wife, while waiting for her husband to come, did not see the young son in his hands, she wept and lamented. She went to her husband and asked, “Lord, where is my son?”
694:
The husband said, “What is the use of your son? If we live, we can have more children.” Hearing this, the wife said, “This man is truly cruel!” and quarreled with him, saying, “You go on; I will not go together with a cruel and harsh person like you.” The husband then said, “My dear, I have acted thoughtlessly and wrongly; please forgive that fault,” and he went back to pick up the young son and carry him again. (Note well the evil deed of the father here.)

The husband, wife, and son—the three of them—crossed the wilderness and reached a cowherd’s hut in the evening. That day happened to be the day the residents of the cowherd’s hut had cooked thick milk-rice (curds) without any added water. When the people in the hut saw the three of them, they thought, “These three are extremely hungry,” and they filled a large pot with the milk-rice, poured a ladle full of ghee over it, and gave it to them.

While the couple ate the milk-rice, the wife ate only in moderation. The husband, however, ate beyond moderation; he could not digest the food and died of indigestion after only one night. Because of his attachment to the people living as cowherds, he took conception in the womb of a bitch in that cowherd’s hut at the moment of his death.

The bitch soon gave birth to a puppy. The cowherd, seeing the attractive puppy, enticed and fed it with lumps of rice.
695:
The cowherd took the puppy, who was very fond of him, wherever he went. 

One day, a Paccekabuddha arrived at the cowherd’s door for alms during the alms-round. When the cowherd saw the Paccekabuddha, he offered alms-food and requested the Holy One to reside nearby under his patronage. The Paccekabuddha resided in a forest not far from the cowherd’s hut. Whenever the cowherd went to the Paccekabuddha, he took the dog along. Along the way, in places where there were lions, leopards, tigers, and wild beasts, he would strike trees, bushes, and rocks to make the wild beasts flee. The dog noted and remembered the master’s methods.

One day, the cowherd stayed with the Paccekabuddha and said, “Venerable Sir, I may not be able to come to you every day. This dog is a clever animal. Please come to our house for alms whenever this dog comes to your presence as a sign.”

One day, the cowherd told the clever dog, “Dear son, go and invite the Paccekabuddha,” and sent him off. Upon hearing his master’s words, the clever dog went at the time for alms and crouched on his chest at the feet of the Paccekabuddha. The Paccekabuddha, knowing that “this clever dog has come to invite me,” took his bowl and robes and
696:
set out on the journey for alms. Wishing to test the clever dog, the Paccekabuddha took a wrong path. The dog then stood in front of the Holy One to block him and only moved away when the Paccekabuddha turned back to the path leading to the cowherd’s hut. When they reached the places where his master, the cowherd, used to strike trees, bushes, and rocks to drive away lions, leopards, tigers, and wild beasts, the clever dog would bark with a terrifyingly loud voice. Because of the dog’s roaring bark, the lions, leopards, tigers, and wild beasts fled.

When the Paccekabuddha finished his meal at the cowherd’s hut, he would feed the clever dog with large lumps of rice. Receiving these lumps of rice, the clever dog became even more attached to the Paccekabuddha than before.

At the end of the Rains Retreat (Vassa), the cowherd offered the Paccekabuddha cloth sufficient for making a triple robe (ticīvara) and said, “Venerable Sir, if you wish, please continue to reside here; if you wish to go elsewhere, you may do so.” The Paccekabuddha showed signs that he would depart for another place. After the cowherd escorted the Paccekabuddha and returned, the clever dog realized that the Paccekabuddha was leaving for good. Because of his great affection, he felt intense grief, his heart broke, and he died, being reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.
697:
At that time, because of the merit of having barked with a terrifyingly loud voice to drive away lions, leopards, tigers, and wild beasts while traveling with the Paccekabuddha in his life as a dog, whenever he spoke with other devas in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, his voice would resonate and cover the entire celestial realm. For this reason, that deva came to be known by the name “Ghosaka Devaputta.”

While Ghosaka Devaputta was enjoying celestial bliss in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, King Udena ruled in the city of Kosambī in the human world. (The story of King Udena has been written above.)

While King Udena was ruling in Kosambī, Ghosaka Devaputta passed away from the deva realm and took conception in the womb of a courtesan in Kosambī. When the mother, the courtesan, realized she had given birth to a son, she had him abandoned on a rubbish heap.

At that time, a foreman of the Great Merchant of Kosambī was going to the Merchant’s house early in the morning. Seeing the child surrounded by a flock of noisy crows, he thought, “This child must be one of great merit,” and entrusted the child to another man to be sent to his house before proceeding to the Merchant’s house.

The Great Merchant of Kosambī, when it was time to attend to the King, went to the golden palace. On the way, he met the Chaplain (Purohita) and asked, “Teacher, how are the constellations today?” The Chaplain, standing right there, examined and calculated the movement of the constellations and said,
698:
“Great Merchant, it is such-and-such a constellation. A boy born today under this constellation will surely attain the position of Great Merchant in the city of Kosambī.”

Upon hearing the Chaplain’s prediction, the Merchant said to his attendants, “Friends, the prediction of this great Chaplain is never of two kinds (it is always certain). My wife, the Merchant’s lady, is also heavy with child. Friends, go and find out whether she has given birth or not.” He sent them quickly to his house. The attendants went to the house, investigated, and returned saying, “My Lord Merchant, the lady has not yet given birth.” The Merchant then ordered again, “Friends, if that is so, go and search for a child born today in this city.”

While searching for a child born that day, the attendants found the child in the house of the Merchant’s foreman and reported it to the Merchant. The Merchant ordered, “Friends, if that is so, bring that foreman to me.” When the foreman arrived...

(Merchant)
“Is it true that there is a child born today in your house?”

(Foreman)
“It is true, my Lord Merchant.”

(Merchant)
“Give that child to us.”

(Foreman)
“I cannot give him, my Lord Merchant.”
699:
699

(The Treasurer)
"Well then, take this thousand pieces of money and give that child to me."

When he spoke thus, the foreman of the laborers, thinking, "This child may live or he may die; it is difficult to know whether he will live or die," accepted the thousand pieces of money and gave the child to the Great Treasurer.

## The Plan of the Great Treasurer of Kosambī

The Great Treasurer of Kosambī planned, "If my chief wife gives birth to a daughter, I will adopt this boy as my son and raise him. If she gives birth to a son, I will kill this boy," and so he kept the boy in his house. Then, after two or three days had passed, the chief wife gave birth to a son.

## The Cruelties of the Great Treasurer of Kosambī

(1) After the chief wife had given birth to a son, the Great Treasurer of Kosambī, plotting, "In this way, the cattle will trample and kill this boy Ghosaka (the son of a prostitute)," commanded his attendants and servants, saying, "Go and place this boy Ghosaka at the entrance of the cattle pen."
