The attendants and servants, according to the Treasurer's command, placed the boy Ghosaka at the entrance of the cattle pen.

At that time, the lead bull, coming out first from the gate of the pen, saw the boy and, thinking, "In this way, the other cattle shall not be able to trample this boy," [stood over him].
700:
700

Thinking thus, the bull stood still with the boy between its four legs. Then, the cowherds saw the boy Ghosaka and, consulting among themselves, said, "This boy must be one of great merit. Even animals recognize his virtues. Therefore, let us raise and care for this boy." They then took him to their homes.

(2) When the Great Treasurer of Kosambī investigated whether the boy was dead or alive, he heard the news that the cowherds had taken him. He again paid a thousand pieces of money to redeem the boy and, exercising his authority, ordered his attendants to abandon him in a cemetery.

At that time, a goatherd of the Treasurer was tending goats near the cemetery. Due to the boy's wholesome kamma and merit, a milch goat left the path and went to where the boy was, and after giving him milk, went to eat her food. When she returned from the cemetery, she likewise went to where the boy was and gave him milk again. The goatherd thought, "This goat left from this very spot in the morning as well; what could be the reason for this?" Upon investigating, he found the boy Ghosaka and thought, "This boy is surely one of great merit. Even animals recognize his virtues. I shall raise and care for this boy," and he took him to his home.

(3) On the following day, the Treasurer sent someone to see whether the boy Ghosaka was dead or still alive. When he heard the news that the goatherd had taken him,
701:
701

Having heard the news, he redeemed the boy as before by paying a thousand pieces of money. He then gave an order to his attendants, saying, "Tomorrow, a caravan leader will enter this city of Kosambī. Take this boy and leave him on the cart track. In this way, the wheels of the carts will run over and kill him."

According to the Treasurer's command, the attendants abandoned the boy on the cart track. The oxen yoked to the lead cart of the caravan leader saw the boy and stood perfectly still, like four great pillars firmly planted, without moving. When the caravan leader investigated the cause, he saw the boy and thought, "This boy is one of great merit. It is proper that I should raise and care for him," and he took the boy and went on his way.

(4) The Treasurer again sent someone to investigate whether Ghosaka had died on the cart track. Learning that the caravan leader had taken him, he paid another thousand pieces of money to the caravan leader to redeem the child. He then commanded his followers to throw the boy down a precipice not far from the city.

As the boy Ghosaka fell headlong down the precipice, he landed on top of a hut at a workshop of reed-makers. Due to the power of the boy's wholesome merit, that workshop hut felt as soft to the touch as a heap of cotton that had been beaten a hundred times. Then, the head reed-maker thought, "This boy is one of great merit;
702:
702

I should raise and care for him," and he took the boy to his home.

(5) The Treasurer again sent someone to investigate as before. Hearing that the head reed-maker had taken him, he paid a thousand pieces of money to the reed-maker to redeem the child and ordered him to be brought back to his house.

Later, both the Treasurer's own biological son and the boy Ghosaka reached the age of maturity. The Great Treasurer of Kosambī, still plotting the death of the boy Ghosaka, went to the house of his man, a potter, and consulted with him, saying, "Friend, in my house there is a certain wicked boy. It would be proper to kill this boy secretly by some means or other."

The potter covered both his ears and replied, "Lord Treasurer, it is not proper to speak such a heavy and sinful word."

Then the Treasurer thought, "This potter will not do it for nothing," and said, "O friend, take this thousand pieces of money. Take this thousand and simply carry out this work to completion." A bribe can cause even those who are not divided in mind to become divided. Thus, the potter, having received and accepted the bribe of a thousand pieces, said, "Lord Treasurer, on such and such a day, I will fire the kiln.
703:
703

At that time, please send that boy at such and such an hour," and they came to an agreement.

The Treasurer accepted the potter's words and, from that day on, counted the days. Knowing that the day mentioned by the potter was approaching, he called the boy Ghosaka and sent him, saying, "Dear son, we have need of many pots on such and such a day. Go to our potter and tell him, 'My father says there is a certain matter he has discussed with you; please complete that matter this very day.'"

Ghosaka accepted the Treasurer's words, saying, "Very well," and left the house.

## Envy of others leads to one's own suffering

At that time, the Treasurer's biological son saw the boy Ghosaka while he was playing marbles. He ran to him and asked for help, saying, "Brother, I have lost this many marbles while playing with these children. Please play for me so that I may win them back."

Ghosaka said, "I cannot play right now because my father, the Great Treasurer, has sent me to the potter on an urgent matter." The Treasurer's biological son then took the responsibility, saying, "Brother, I will go to the potter. You just play with these boys and win back the marbles I have lost."
704:
704

Then Ghosaka agreed, saying, "If that is so, go, my brother." He explained in detail to the biological son the matter his father had told him, and remained there playing marbles with the children.

The biological son went to the potter and delivered the message from his father in full. The potter said, "Very well, young man, I will complete the work." He then took the biological son into a room, locked him in, cut him into pieces with a sharp billhook, placed the pieces in a large jar, sealed the mouth of the jar, placed it among the unbaked pots, and fired the kiln.

Ghosaka, having won many marbles, sat waiting for his younger brother's return. But as the brother did not come, he wondered, "Why is my brother so long?" He went near the potter's house to look for him, but not seeing him anywhere, he thought, "He must have gone back home," and returned to the house alone.

The Great Treasurer saw Ghosaka returning from afar and wondered, "What could have happened? I sent this Ghosaka to the potter to be killed, yet he is now returning home." Without even waiting for Ghosaka to sit down, while he was still approaching, he asked, "How is it, dear son? Did you not go to the potter?"
705:
705

When asked, the boy Ghosaka replied, "Yes, father, I did not go." When asked again, "Why did you not go, dear son?", Ghosaka explained in full the reason for his return and how his younger brother had gone to the potter instead.

From the moment the Great Treasurer heard Ghosaka's words, he felt as if he were being crushed by the great earth. Crying out, "What kind of thing have you said, dear son?", and with a heart trembling violently, he rushed to the potter. Because it was a matter that should not and could not be spoken to others, he only whispered to the potter, "Look, friend! Look, friend!"

The potter spoke decisively, "Lord Treasurer, what is there to look at now? The work has been completed." The Treasurer then returned from that place and went home. From that time on, the Great Treasurer was afflicted with a severe mental illness.

(6) From then on, the Great Treasurer of Kosambī would no longer eat with the boy Ghosaka. Thinking, "I must look for an opportunity for this Ghosaka, the enemy of my son, to die by some means or stratagem," he wrote a letter. He called Ghosaka and said, "Take this letter. In such and such a village, there is our foreman. Go to that foreman, hand over this letter, and say, 'Carry out the matter in this letter quickly.' On the way, our friend..."
706:
706
There was a treasurer named Gāmaka-seṭṭhī (the village treasurer). The Treasurer of Kosambī gave instructions, saying, "Go to that treasurer's house, and after having a meal, go to the headman of the workers." By this time, the youth Ghosaka had reached the age of young manhood.

Ghosaka respectfully paid homage to the Great Treasurer, took the letter, and set out on his journey. Along the way, he reached the place of Gāmaka-seṭṭhī. After inquiring about the treasurer's house, he saw Gāmaka-seṭṭhī sitting outside the gateway having his beard trimmed. Ghosaka paid homage and stood there. When Gāmaka-seṭṭhī asked, "Young man, where have you come from?", he replied, "O father, I am the son of the Great Treasurer of Kosambī." Hearing this, Gāmaka-seṭṭhī was greatly delighted, thinking, "He is the son of my friend, the Great Treasurer of Kosambī."

At that moment, a maidservant of Gāmaka-seṭṭhī's daughter was about to go and fetch flowers for her. Gāmaka-seṭṭhī commanded the maid, "Dear girl, set aside your task of fetching flowers for a moment. Wash the feet of the youth Ghosaka and prepare a bed for him." The maid did as the treasurer commanded, then went to the market to buy flowers for the treasurer's daughter and returned home.

When the treasurer's daughter saw the maid, she became angry, saying, "You have spent a long time outside today," and scolded her, asking, "What have you been doing outside for such a long time?" Then the maid replied—
707:
707
"Do not speak so, my lady. I have never before seen a youth as handsome as this. He is said to be the son of your father's friend, the treasurer. I cannot fully describe the perfection of his beauty and appearance. While I was going to buy flowers, the treasurer told me, 'Wash this youth's feet and prepare a bed for him.' That is why I have spent such a long time outside."

(The daughter of Gāmaka-seṭṭhī had been the wife of the youth Ghosaka in their fourth previous life). Therefore, from the moment she heard the maid's words, she was so overwhelmed with love that she did not even know whether she was sitting or standing. (It means she was lost in thought, oblivious to her posture).

The treasurer's daughter took the maid and went to the place where the youth Ghosaka was reclining. Seeing the sleeping Ghosaka, she noticed the letter tied to the hem of his garment. Thinking, "What kind of letter is this?", she gently took the letter without waking the youth. After reading it, she realized, "This youth is carrying his own death warrant!" She tore up that letter and, before Ghosaka woke from his sleep, she wrote a new one:

"Manager of my workers, I have sent my son to you. My friend Gāmaka-seṭṭhī has a daughter who has reached marriageable age. You must quickly gather the wealth from the areas under our authority and,
708:
708
with a hundred units of every kind of property, you must ask for the daughter of Gāmaka-seṭṭhī for my son and perform the marriage ceremony on my behalf.

After the marriage ceremony is completed, I would like you to send me a detailed report along with an account of the wedding festivities conducted with such and such ceremonies and arrangements.

I shall recognize the gratitude due to you for what you have done in this matter (of my son's wedding).

The Great Treasurer of Kosambī
City of Kosambī"

Having prepared the new letter in this manner, she stamped it with the same seal and tied it back to the hem of his garment using the original method of tying, so that the handiwork appeared undisturbed.

The youth Ghosaka stayed at the house of Gāmaka-seṭṭhī for that day. The next day, after taking leave of Gāmaka-seṭṭhī, he went to the village of the headman and delivered the letter. After reading the letter, the headman gathered the villagers and said, "It is only you who do not hold me in high regard. My master, the Great Treasurer of Kosambī, has sent his eldest son (Ghosaka) to me to arrange his marriage with Gāmaka-seṭṭhī's daughter, providing a hundred units of every kind of property. Therefore, quickly gather and provide the wealth available in this place." Having said this, he arranged various wedding preparations. After sending word to Gāmaka-seṭṭhī and receiving his consent, he provided a hundred units of every kind of property and,
709:
709
after performing the marriage ceremony with great grandeur, he sent a letter to the Great Treasurer Ghosaka with a detailed account, saying, "I have learned the contents of the letter sent by my lord treasurer and have successfully carried out such and such tasks."

When the Great Treasurer of Kosambī heard this news, he felt as if he were on fire. Thinking, "Alas, now I have met with a terrible ruin!", he was overcome with great anxiety and fell ill with dysentery. (Yet, not giving up his scheme), he plotted inwardly, "I will somehow summon him (Ghosaka) and make sure he does not inherit my wealth." He then sent a message, saying, "Why has my son stayed away for so long since the marriage? Come back to your father quickly."

Upon hearing the message, the (innocent) youth Ghosaka prepared to return to his father. However, Gāmaka-seṭṭhī's daughter thought, "This simple and honest Ghosaka does not realize that he obtained this fortune because of me. It is better that I devise a plan to prevent him from going back." She then delayed him, saying, "My dear, do not be in such a hurry. One who goes to a village of relatives should only go after making all necessary arrangements for one's surroundings."

The Great Treasurer of Kosambī, knowing that Ghosaka was delayed, sent another message, saying, "Why is my son taking so long? I, your father, have reached a state of dysentery where there is no hope. It is proper for my son to come and see me while I am still alive."

710
At that time, the treasurer's daughter spoke openly to the youth Ghosaka, saying, "My dear, the Great Treasurer of Kosambī is not your father. You only think of him as your biological father. That Great Treasurer sent a letter to the headman to have you killed. I tore up that death warrant and changed it to a good message (for the marriage), planning so that you would obtain this treasurer's fortune. That Great Treasurer is not calling you out of sincerity; he calls you with the intention of making it clear that you are not his son. Wait until that treasurer dies."

Later, having heard the news that the Great Treasurer of Kosambī had passed away (though he had not yet died), Ghosaka and his wife, along with their retinue, went to the city of Kosambī. The treasurer's daughter (being a wise woman) warned Ghosaka outside the house, saying, "My dear, when you enter the house, do so only after placing guards throughout the entire house." She herself entered the house with the treasurer's son. Pretending to weep with her hands raised, she approached the Great Treasurer of Kosambī, who was lying in the dark, and struck him forcefully in the chest with her head. Since the treasurer was already weak, he passed away from the impact of the blow to his chest by the treasurer's daughter.
710:
Once again, she sent a message. This time, the treasurer's daughter spoke openly to the young Ghosaka: "My dear, the Great Treasurer of Kosambī is not your father; you only think of him as your biological father. That Great Treasurer of Kosambī sent a letter to the chief of the laborers to have you killed. I tore up and discarded that execution order, changed it to a good message for a marriage proposal, and planned for you to obtain this treasurer's wealth. The Great Treasurer is calling for you now, not out of sincerity, but with the intention of proving you are not his son. Wait until that Great Treasurer dies."

Later, having heard a false report that the Great Treasurer of Kosambī had died while he was still alive, Ghosaka and his wife, along with their retinue, went to the city of Kosambī. The treasurer's daughter, being a woman of wisdom, warned the young Ghosaka even before entering the house: "My dear, when you enter the house, place guards throughout the entire building for your protection before you go in." She herself entered the house together with the treasurer's son. Raising both hands as if in grief, she approached the Great Treasurer of Kosambī, who was lying in the dark, and struck him forcefully in the chest with her head. Since the Great Treasurer was already weak, he passed away and died from the impact of the blow to his chest by the treasurer's daughter.
711:
## Winning Over the Household Members
After performing the funeral rites for his father, the Great Treasurer, the young Ghosaka spoke privately to the household members, saying, "Friends and mothers, please speak of me as the biological son of the Great Treasurer." He then gave satisfying gifts and bribes to the internal staff of the Great Treasurer of Kosambī.

## Attaining the Position of Treasurer
Then, on the seventh day, King Udena, the ruler of Kosambī, reflected, "It is proper to find someone worthy of the position of Treasurer." He issued an order to his officials: "Friends, you must investigate whether the late Great Treasurer of Kosambī has a son." He sent them to the Treasurer's house to investigate. The internal staff of the Great Treasurer of Kosambī unanimously reported to King Udena that the Treasurer had a biological son named Ghosaka.

King Udena accepted this, saying, "Very well," and appointed the young Ghosaka to the position of Treasurer along with the official insignia. From that time on, the young Ghosaka became famous as "Ghosaka the Great Treasurer."

## Establishing a Daily Alms-giving of One Thousand
When he became the Great Treasurer, his wise wife, the Treasurer's lady, gave him a reminder: "O lord, although both of us are of humble origins, we have obtained this magnificent wealth of a Great Treasurer due to exceptional past merits. Now, let us perform meritorious deeds without negligence."
712:
The Great Treasurer Ghosaka accepted his wife's reminder, saying, "Very well, my lady." He then established a permanent alms-giving (nibaddhadāna) by donating one thousand coins every single day.

(This is the account of the Great Treasurer Ghosaka of the city of Kosambī).

## Observing the Ninth Vassa in Kosambī
At that time, there were three famous friends who were treasurers in the city of Kosambī: the Treasurer Ghosaka, the Treasurer Kukkuṭa, and the Treasurer Pāvārika. All three friends (during the time before the Buddha's enlightenment was known to them) supported and fed five hundred ascetics. These ascetics would stay with the three treasurers in Kosambī for the four months of the rainy season, and for the eight months of winter and summer, they would reside in the Himalayas (Himavanta).

After living this way for many years, one day, as the five hundred ascetics were traveling from the Himalayas to Kosambī, they became thirsty and exhausted in a great desert. At the end of the desert, they saw a large banyan tree and thought: "Judging by the appearance of this great banyan tree, there must certainly be a powerful tree deity residing here. It would be wonderful if this guardian deity of the banyan tree would give us water to drink and use."

The guardian deity of the banyan tree, knowing the thoughts and desires of the ascetics, thought, "I shall provide hospitality and assistance to these ascetics."

* This account of the Great Treasurer Ghosaka is extracted and written from the Aṅguttara Commentary, Volume I, page 321 onwards.
713:
By his own power, he caused a stream of water the size of a yoke-pole to flow from the fork of the banyan tree. Seeing the mass of water, which resembled a block of silver, the group of ascetics received the water in their bowls and used it. They thought, "The deity residing in this banyan tree has given us water to use. This place is a great forest, far from any village. It would be wonderful if the banyan tree deity would also offer us food."

The banyan tree deity then offered and served the ascetics suitable divine gruel, hard food, and so on.

Again, the ascetics thought, "The banyan tree deity has given us water and food to use. It would be wonderful if the banyan tree deity would show himself to us." Knowing the desire of the ascetics, the banyan tree deity revealed the upper half of his body. When the ascetics asked, "O deity, your splendor is indeed great. What merit did you perform to obtain such splendor?", the banyan tree deity replied, "I obtained this splendor by performing a small, not very great, merit." Indeed, the banyan tree deity obtained this splendor based on the merit of having observed the Uposatha for only half a day while in the human world.

To elaborate: In a previous life, this banyan tree deity was a laborer in the house of the treasurer Anāthapiṇḍika. In the treasurer's house, on Uposatha days, everyone, starting from the slaves and laborers, observed the Uposatha. One day, this laborer woke up early alone and went to work at his workplace. When the treasurer Anāthapiṇḍika was taking a census of the people who were to receive rations, that one laborer...
714:
...was found to have gone to the forest, so the treasurer gave him rations for his evening meal. The slave woman who cooked the rice prepared a portion for only one person and served it to the laborer when he returned from the forest.

The laborer thought, "On other days, at this mealtime, the whole house is noisy, but today it is very quiet. What is the reason for this?" and he asked the cook. When the cook replied, "Today, everyone in this house is observing the Uposatha; the treasurer gave rations only to you, brother," the laborer asked, "Mother, is that so?" When the cook replied, "Yes, master," the laborer urged her, saying, "Mother, please ask the treasurer whether it is possible or not for someone to undertake the Uposatha at this late hour of the evening."

When the cook went and asked, the treasurer replied, "It is not possible to observe the full-day Uposatha, but it is possible to observe the half-day Uposatha. (If one observes the half-day Uposatha in this way,) it is still called observing the Uposatha."

Upon hearing the treasurer's answer, the laborer did not eat his meal, but rinsed his mouth, undertook the factors of the Uposatha, and went to his place to sleep. Because there was no food at all in his body, he suffered from a wind ailment during the night, and at dawn, he passed away. Due to the result of the merit of having observed the half-day Uposatha, near the main road...
715:
...at the entrance of a great forest, he was reborn as the deity residing in the banyan tree mentioned here.

The banyan tree deity related all the aforementioned events to the ascetics. When the ascetics asked, "O banyan tree deity, you have spoken to us words never heard before, such as 'Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha.' Has the Blessed One appeared in the world?", the banyan tree deity replied that it was true. When the ascetics asked again, "Where is the Blessed One residing now?", he replied, "He is residing at the Jetavana Monastery, depending on the city of Sāvatthī for alms."

Then the ascetics said, "O banyan tree deity, remain here; we shall go to see the Buddha." Rejoicing, they left the forest and traveled by stages until they reached the city of Kosambī. The three treasurers welcomed them, saying, "The ascetics have arrived," and invited them, saying, "Venerable sirs, please accept our alms-food tomorrow." On the following day, they gave a great offering to the group of ascetics.

Immediately after finishing their meal, when the ascetics announced, "We shall be going," the three treasurers asked, "Venerable sirs, on previous visits, you stayed for one, two, three, or four months before moving elsewhere. On this visit, however, you arrived only yesterday and say you will leave today."
716:
"Why do you speak thus?" they asked. The ascetics replied, "It is true, treasurers. The Blessed One has appeared in the world, and life is uncertain. Therefore, we wish to go quickly." When the ascetics said this, the three treasurers requested, "Venerable sirs, if the Blessed One has appeared, we too shall follow. Please travel only together with us."

Then the ascetics said, "You laypeople have many busy affairs. You stay behind for now (and follow gradually later). We shall go ahead first." They left Kosambī and, without staying two days in any one place, traveled quickly and reached Sāvatthī. They went straight to the presence of the Blessed One at the Jetavana Monastery. Having heard the sweet Dhamma in the presence of the Blessed One, all five hundred ascetics were ordained as monks and attained Arahantship.

## The Three Treasurers Attain Stream-entry

After the ascetics had left, the three treasurers departed from Kosambī, each with five hundred carts filled with offerings. They reached Sāvatthī by stages, formed a wagon camp near the Jetavana Monastery, and built temporary pavilions. They then went to the Blessed One, paid homage respectfully with the fivefold prostration, and sat in a suitable place. The Blessed One...
717:
...preached the Dhamma to the three treasurers according to their temperaments. At the conclusion of the teaching, all three treasurers were established in the fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala). They invited the Buddha for the next day, and on the following day, they gave a great offering to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. In that manner, for half a month, they offered what was called "pavilion alms." When they requested the Blessed One to visit and grace their city of Kosambī, the Blessed One said, "O lay disciples, the Buddhas delight in solitude."

The three treasurers said, "We understand, Blessed One," and requested, "Venerable sir, please come when we send word and invite you." They respectfully paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and left Sāvatthī. Along the way, they had a rest house built at every league (yojana). Upon reaching Kosambī, they proclaimed, "The Blessed One has appeared in the world!" All three treasurers then spent a great deal of wealth in their respective gardens to build great monasteries for the Blessed One.

Among those three great monasteries, the one built by the treasurer Ghosaka became known as the "Ghositārāma" monastery. The one built by the treasurer Kukkuṭa was known as the "Kukkuṭārāma" monastery, and the one built by the treasurer Pāvāriya in his mango grove...
718:
The great monastery that was built was named "Pāvārikambavana".

When the three merchants had completed the construction of the great monasteries, they sent a messenger to the Blessed One, inviting him: "May the Blessed One favor us and travel to our city of Kosambī."

## Converting the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya and his Wife on the Way

While the Blessed One was traveling with a large company of monks, intending to go to Kosambī, he saw the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the attainment of the Fruit of Arahantship in the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya and his wife. Therefore, he diverted from his usual route and traveled to the market town of Kammāsadamma in the Kuru country.

At that time, the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya had been performing fire worship outside the village all night and was just entering the village early in the morning. On the following day, while the Blessed One was entering the village for alms, he allowed the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya to see him. Upon seeing the Blessed One, the Brahmin thought: "For a long time, I have been wandering in search of a young man whose beauty matches that of my daughter (Māgaṇḍiyā). Although I desired a young man of equal beauty, I only wanted one who had taken the form of a monk. This monk is indeed handsome and pleasant to look at; he is the only one suitable for my daughter." Having thought this, he hurried back home.
719:
(In the lineage of that Māgandiya the Brahmin, there had previously been a lineage of monks; therefore, upon seeing the monk, the Brahmin's mind was inclined to give his daughter to him.)

Māgandiya the Brahmin said to his wife, "O lady, I have never seen such a monk before. He has a golden complexion, a complexion like that of the Great Brahma. He is the only one suitable and worthy of my daughter. Adorn my daughter quickly." While the Brahmin's wife was adorning their daughter, the Blessed One left his footprints (pādacetī) at the place where he stood and entered the city for alms.

(Note: The footprints of the Buddhas appear only in the place where they have made a determination (adhiṭṭhāna) to tread; they do not appear elsewhere. Only those for whom the determination was made can see the footprints. Even if animals like elephants tread upon them, even if heavy rains fall, or even if the great Veramba winds blow, no one and nothing is able to erase those footprints. From Dhp-A, i, 129.)

Then, when the Brahmin came to that place together with his wife and daughter, the Buddha had already entered the village. Not seeing the Blessed One after looking here and there, he grumbled to his wife in dissatisfaction, "Lady, nothing you do is good. Because you took so long, that monk has departed."

When the Brahmin's wife asked, "O Brahmin, let him be gone; in which direction did he depart?" the Brahmin said:
720:
"He went in this direction," and while looking in the direction the Blessed One had gone, he saw the footprints (pādacetī) and said, "O lady, these footprints are the footprints of that man. He must have gone from this place."

At that time, the Brahmin's wife, seeing the footprints of the Blessed One, thought, "This Brahmin is indeed unwise; he does not even know the meaning of his own Vedic scriptures." Desiring to mock the Brahmin, she said, "O Brahmin, you are very unwise indeed. How could you even think of giving our daughter to such a noble man? The footprint of a man who is not free from lust, hatred, and delusion is not like this. Indeed, look carefully at this footprint of the Omniscient Buddha, who has broken open the roof of defilements in the world, O Brahmin.

Rattassa hi ukkuṭikaṃ padaṃ bhave,
Duṭṭhassa hoti avakaḍḍhitaṃ padaṃ.
Mūḷhassa hoti sahasānupīḷitaṃ,
Vivaṭacchadassa idamīdisaṃ padaṃ.

The footprint of one full of lust tends to be hollow in the middle.
The footprint of one full of hatred is as if dragged backward.
The footprint of one full of delusion is as if pressed down by the toes and heels.
This footprint seen now is only the footprint of the Omniscient Buddha, who has broken open the roof of defilements."
721:
Thus she spoke. Although the Brahmin's wife spoke so profoundly, the Brahmin did not listen and said, "Lady, you are very coarse; your words are very harsh." While the Brahmin and his wife were arguing with each other, the Blessed One, having finished his alms round and his meal together with the assembly of monks, came out and stood within the range of Māgandiya the Brahmin's sight.

Māgandiya the Brahmin saw the Blessed One coming from afar. After rebuking his wife, he said with great joy and satisfaction, "That man I spoke of is this very person!" Standing directly in front of the Blessed One, he said:

"O monk, I have been searching for you for a long time. In this entire Jambudīpa, there is not a single woman whose beauty is equal to my daughter's, nor is there a man in this Jambudīpa whose beauty is equal to yours. I wish to give my daughter to you to serve and care for you. Please take this daughter of mine."

He spoke directly and plainly. Then the Blessed One said to Māgandiya the Brahmin:

"O Brahmin, I did not even desire the three daughters of Māra, who came to tempt me and stood near me, speaking various words of love, possessing the noble appearance of the Vasavatti celestial realm.
722:
How then should I wish to take this daughter of yours, Māgandiyā?"

Having said this, he uttered this verse:

Disvāna taṇhaṃ aratiṃ ragañca,
Nāhosi chando api methunasmiṃ.
Kimevidaṃ muttakarīsapuṇṇaṃ,
Pādāpi naṃ samphusituṃ na icche.

Taṇhañca = the daughter of Māra named Taṇhā; aratiñca = the daughter of Māra named Arati; ragañca = the daughter of Māra named Ragā; disvāna = although I saw them clearly coming before me at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, assuming various beautiful forms (to capture me); methunasmiṃ = in the base practice called sexual union performed by two consenting people; chando api = not to mention the physical act, even the slightest desire of craving; (me = in me, the Buddha); nāhosi = did not arise even for a moment. Muttakarīsapuṇṇaṃ = filled with various loathsome things like urine and excrement; idaṃ = this physical form of the young girl Māgandiyā; disvāna = having seen; chando = the desire of craving; kimeva ahosi = how could it possibly arise? Naṃ = that young girl Māgandiyā; pādāpi = even with the foot; samphusituṃ = just to touch for the sake of union; na icche = as both types of sensuality (objective and subjective) are absent in me, I truly have no desire at all.
723:
...he recited this verse, not as if speaking directly to the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya, but as if speaking to someone else.

## The Grudge of the Maiden Māgaṇḍiyā

The Brahmin's daughter, Māgaṇḍiyā, thought: "If he did not want me, he should have simply said 'I do not want you' honestly. But now, this ascetic Gotama has spoken harshly and dismissively, saying that my body is full of repulsive excrement and urine, and that he would not even want to touch it with his foot. Let it be; when I reach a position of power, I will seek an opportunity for this ascetic Gotama's death." Thus, with wrong thoughts, she harbored a grudge (āghāta) against the Blessed One.

## The Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya and his Wife Attaining Arahantship after becoming Anāgāmīs

Disregarding the grudge of the maiden Māgaṇḍiyā and considering what was suitable for their temperaments, the Blessed One preached the Dhamma to the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya. (The Dhamma preached to the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya should be noted from the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta of the Sutta Nipāta, Burmese translation). At the conclusion of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta, both the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya and his wife were established in the Fruit of Anāgāmī. They reflected, "Now, there is no benefit for us in living the household life." They entrusted their daughter Māgaṇḍiyā to her uncle (her father's younger brother), also named Māgaṇḍiya, and both of them ordained as monastics. Through diligent practice, they exhausted all taints (āsava) and became Arahants.
724:
## Accepting the Three Great Monasteries of Kosambī

After converting the Brahmin Māgaṇḍiya and his wife, the Blessed One continued his journey and arrived at Kosambī accompanied by a large company of monks.

When the three merchants heard the good news of the Blessed One's arrival, they went out in a grand manner to welcome the Saṅgha led by the Buddha. They escorted them to the monasteries. Upon arrival, they paid homage with the fivefold prostration (pañcapatiṭṭhita) and sat in a suitable place. They addressed him: "Venerable Sir, we have built these three great monasteries dedicated to you. Venerable Sir, for the benefit of the Saṅgha of the four quarters, please accept these three great monasteries out of compassion." At the request of the three merchants, the Blessed One accepted the three monasteries. The merchants then invited the Blessed One for the next day's meal for the sake of merit, paid their respects, and returned home.

(Following this, the stories of Khujjuttarā, Queen Sāmāvatī, and Queen Māgaṇḍiyā are to be written. However, the stories of Khujjuttarā and Sāmāvatī will be written in the section on the Saṅgha Ratana. The story of Queen Māgaṇḍiyā should be noted from the Burmese translation of the Dhammapada Commentary. In this chapter of this book, only the points that would otherwise be unclear will be briefly mentioned.)
725:
The Blessed One, after accepting the three great monasteries built and donated by the three merchants as mentioned, entered and resided for the ninth Rains Retreat (vassa) in that very city of Kosambī.

## The Evil Deed of Queen Māgandiyā
At the time the Blessed One was observing the Rains Retreat in Kosambī, the young girl Māgandiyā had become one of the chief queens of King Udena. To make it clear: after Māgandiya the Brahmin and his wife entrusted their daughter Māgandiyā to the uncle, Cūḷa Māgandiya the Brahmin, and went to ordain, King Udena consulted with Cūḷa Māgandiya. By the king's power, he brought the girl Māgandiyā to the golden palace, consecrated her, and gave her a separate palace building to reside in along with five hundred attendants. Thus, at the time the Blessed One was observing the ninth Rains Retreat in Kosambī, Māgandiyā was already a chief queen of King Udena.

As soon as Queen Māgandiyā heard the news that the Blessed One had arrived in Kosambī, following her previous grudge, she summoned some wretched, starving drunkards. Giving them bribes, she instructed them, "You all must abuse the Monk Gotama in this way and that way," and sent them off.

When the Blessed One, surrounded by the assembly of monks, entered the city of Kosambī to receive alms as invited by the three merchants, the drunkards employed by Queen Māgandiyā followed the monks and...
726:
...and they spoke various words of insult to the Blessed One. 

Then the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, let us not stay in this city where we are being insulted; let us go to another city." The Blessed One replied, "Ānanda, those known as Buddhas are never shaken or disturbed by the eight worldly conditions (lokadhamma). This sound of insult will not last beyond seven days; it will fall back only upon those who insult. Do not be anxious with various thoughts." (This is a brief explanation from the Aṅguttara Commentary. For the detailed account, one should refer to the Dhammapada Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 308, Nagavagga, the commentary on the Attadaṇḍa Vatthu). 

## The Outstanding Devotion of the Three Wealthy Merchants 

The three wealthy merchants of the city of Kosambī invited the Blessed One into the city with great honor and offerings, and they gave great alms. (The Blessed One resided in rotation at the three great monasteries built and donated by the three merchants. If he resided at the Ghositarāma monastery today, he would go to the house of the merchant Ghosaka for alms the next day. If he resided at the Kukkuṭārāma monastery today, he would go to the house of the merchant Kukkuṭa for alms the next day. If he resided at the Pāvārikambavana monastery today, he would go to the house of the merchant Pāvārika for alms the next day). (Dhp-A. 1, 133-4).
727:
After the three wealthy merchants had each taken turns giving great alms for one month, a thought arose in their minds: 

"Buddhas arise in the world to show compassion, protect, and uplift all people. Let us also give the opportunity to other people to perform meritorious deeds." 

Then, the three merchants gave the opportunity to the citizens of Kosambī to perform meritorious deeds. From that time on, the townspeople also gave great alms according to their streets, neighborhoods, and associations. 

## The Great Dispute in the Saṅgha 

While the Blessed One was staying and dwelling at the Ghositarāma monastery in Kosambī, two monks—one a bearer of the Vinaya (Vinayadhara) and the other a bearer of the Suttas (Suttantadhara)—lived in the same dwelling. One day, the Sutta-bearer monk entered the toilet (vaccakuṭī) and, having left some water remaining in the rinsing vessel, came out unmindfully. The Vinaya-bearer monk entered the toilet afterward and, seeing the remaining water, came out and asked the Sutta-bearer monk, "Friend, did you leave this remaining water?" When the Sutta-bearer monk honestly admitted, "Yes, friend," the Vinaya-bearer monk asked, "Friend, do you not know that there is an offense (āpatti) in leaving this remaining water?"
728:
"No, friend, I did not know," said the Sutta-bearer monk. Then the Vinaya-bearer monk said, "Friend, there is an offense in leaving water inside the vessel." The Sutta-bearer monk replied, "If there is an offense, friend, I shall confess it." The Vinaya-bearer monk then said, "Friend, if you did it unintentionally and through forgetfulness, there is no offense." Because of this statement, the Sutta-bearer monk came to hold the view that there was no offense regarding the dukkhaṭa (wrongdoing) incurred by leaving the remaining water. 

(In this matter: The Vinaya-bearer monk spoke saying "there is no offense" because he considered that "on one hand, there should be no offense if one leaves the water without intention or through forgetfulness." In reality, however, whether there is intention or not, if one leaves the remaining water, a dukkhaṭa offense is indeed incurred). 

The Vinaya-bearer monk then told his own disciples disparagingly, "This Sutta-bearer monk does not even know when he has committed an offense." When the disciples of that Vinaya-bearer monk saw the disciples of the Sutta-bearer monk, they spoke mockingly, "Your preceptor (upajjhāya) does not know an offense even when he has committed one." The disciples of the Sutta-bearer monk went to their teacher and reported the matter. The Sutta-bearer monk then spoke in rebuttal, "This Vinaya-bearer monk previously said there was no offense, and now he says there is an offense; this Vinaya-bearer monk speaks a falsehood." 

The disciples of the Sutta-bearer monk went and said, "Your preceptor, the Vinaya-bearer monk, is a liar,"
729:
and in this way, they caused the dispute between each other to increase. Subsequently, the Vinaya-bearer monk, finding an opportunity and gathering his faction, performed the Ukkhepaniyakamma (Act of Suspension) against the Sutta-bearer monk for "not seeing an offense" (āpattiyā adassane)—a disciplinary act of the Saṅgha to exclude him. 

The Sutta-bearer monk, who was subjected to the Act of Suspension, was also a person endowed with great learning and other virtues. He approached the monks who were his close friends and said, "Friends, that matter is not an offense; it is not an offense. I am one who has not committed an offense; I am not an offender. (Even though they performed the Act of Suspension against me), in reality, I am not one against whom the Act of Suspension should be performed; I have been subjected to the Act of Suspension through an illegal act (adhamma). May you, venerable sirs, be my faction for the Dhamma and Vinaya." Because of this, he gained a faction of monks who were his close friends. He also sent messengers to the monks who were his close friends living in the countryside and districts, and thus he also gained a faction of monks in the countryside. 

Then, the Ukkhittānuvattaka monks (the follower monks of the suspended Sutta-bearer monk) went to the Ukkhepaka monks (the monks who performed the suspension) and said to them, "Friends, that matter is not an offense; it is not an offense. This Sutta-bearer monk is one who has not committed an offense; he is not an offender. (Even though you performed the Act of Suspension against our teacher,
730:
...(even though they did so), he is not truly one against whom the act of suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma) was performed. It was merely an act of suspension performed through an illegal procedure (adhamma)." Thus they argued.

Then the monks who performed the suspension (ukkhepaka) said to the followers of the suspended monk (ukkhittānuvattaka): "Friends, that matter is indeed an offense (āpatti), not a non-offense. That monk who is a master of the Suttas (Suttantadhara) is indeed one who has committed an offense, not one who has not. That Suttantadhara monk is indeed one against whom the act of suspension was performed, not one against whom it was not. The act of suspension was performed through a legal procedure (dhamma). Friends, do not follow the example of that suspended monk; do not follow or surround him." Even though they were told this, those followers of the suspended monk continued to follow the example of the Suttantadhara suspended monk as before. They continued to follow and surround him consistently.

## The Blessed One Visiting Both Sides to Preach the Dhamma

Then, an obscure monk approached the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, and sat in a suitable place. He reported all the aforementioned matters to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "The Saṅgha of monks is divided! The Saṅgha of monks is divided!" He spoke these serious words twice. Then, rising from his seat, he went to the monks who performed the suspension and sat on the prepared seat.

("The Saṅgha of monks is divided! The Saṅgha of monks is divided!"—regarding these words, at that time the Saṅgha was already divided...)
731:
Having sat down, the Blessed One said to the Ukkhepaka monks: 

"Monks, do not think 'I know, I am capable' and consider that another monk should be subjected to the Act of Suspension (i.e., expelled) for a trivial matter. 

Monks, a certain monk commits an offense but holds the view that it is not an offense. Other monks, however, hold the view that it is an offense. Monks, if those monks who hold the view that it is an offense know regarding that monk who holds the view that it is not an offense: 'This venerable one is of great learning, one who has mastered the Pali texts, a bearer of the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Pātimokkha, a wise man, skilled and proficient, conscientious, scrupulous, and desirous of the three trainings. If we perform the Act of Suspension—the act of expulsion for not seeing an offense—against this monk, and (1) if we perform the Uposatha without this monk, separately from this monk, there will arise disputes, malice, and offensive speech in the presence and absence of the Saṅgha, leading to the schism of the Saṅgha, the conditions for schism, the discord of the Saṅgha, and separate acts.' If they know this, monks...
732:
...monks, those monks who regard the schism of the Saṅgha as a serious matter should not perform the Act of Suspension—the act of expulsion for not seeing an offense—against that monk who holds the view that it is not an offense. 

Monks, a certain monk commits an offense but holds the view that it is not an offense. Other monks, however, hold the view that it is an offense. Monks, if those monks who hold the view that it is an offense know regarding that monk who holds the view that it is not an offense: 'This venerable one is of great learning, one who has mastered the Pali texts, a bearer of the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Pātimokkha, a wise man, skilled and proficient, conscientious, scrupulous, and desirous of the three trainings. If we perform the Act of Suspension—the act of expulsion for not seeing an offense—against this monk, and (2) if we do not perform Pavāraṇā with this monk, but perform Pavāraṇā separately from this monk, (peyyāla - etc.), 

(3) if we do not perform Saṅghakamma with this monk, but perform Saṅghakamma separately from this monk— 

(4) if we do not sit in the same seating area with this monk, but sit in a seating area separately from this monk— 

(5) if we do not sit in the place for drinking congee with this monk, but sit in the place for drinking congee separately from this monk— 

(6) if we do not sit in the dining hall with this monk, but sit in the dining hall separately from this monk—'"
733:
(7) If they reside in the same dwelling under one roof, not together with this monk, but apart from him; 
(8) If they perform the duties of seniority, such as saluting, rising to greet, saluting with joined palms, and paying respect, not together with this monk, but apart from him—if they know: 'Disputes, quarrels, and contentions will arise in the presence or absence of the Saṅgha; there will be schism in the Saṅgha, or matters leading to schism; there will be dissension and separate acts in the Saṅgha'—then, O monks, those monks who care for the unity of the Saṅgha should not carry out the act of suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma) for not seeing an offense against that monk who holds the view that it is not an offense."

Thus, the Buddha preached the Dhamma on the unity of the Saṅgha. Thereafter, the Blessed One, having preached this matter to the monks who carried out the suspension, rose from his seat and went to the followers of the suspended monk (ukkittānuvattaka). Having sat on the prepared seat, he addressed the disciples and followers of that suspended monk:

"Monks, do not think that you should not make amends for an offense by reflecting, 'We have committed no offense, we have committed no offense,' even though an offense has been committed.
735:
(7) If they reside in the same dwelling under one roof, not together with me, but apart from me;
(8) If these monks perform the duties of seniority, such as saluting, rising to greet, saluting with joined palms, and paying respect, not together with me, but apart from me—
if he knows: "Disputes, quarrels, and contentions will arise in the presence or absence of the Saṅgha; there will be schism in the Saṅgha, or matters leading to schism; there will be dissension and separate acts in the Saṅgha," then, O monks, a monk who cares for the unity of the Saṅgha should confess the offense even out of faith in the other monks.'

Having preached the Dhamma on the unity of the Saṅgha, the Buddha rose from his seat and departed.

(Note: It is noteworthy here that the Suttanta-expert monk had previously honestly admitted to the Vinaya-expert monk, "If I have committed an offense, I shall confess it." Later, based on the Vinaya-expert's own earlier statement that "there is no offense if done unintentionally or through forgetfulness," he honestly believed, "I did this unintentionally and through forgetfulness; therefore, as the Vinaya-expert said, I have committed no offense." Because of this honest admission and honest belief that he was not in offense, if the Blessed One had said to the monks who carried out the suspension, "You have carried out the act of suspension against this Suttanta-expert monk without sufficient reason,"
736:
The monks who performed the act might harbor a grudge against the Blessed One, thinking, "The Blessed One is a partisan of those Suttantadhara monks," and thus increase their unwholesome states and go to a state of misery (apāya).

On the other hand, regarding the monks against whom the act was performed, the Suttantadhara monk had committed a dukkaṭa offense because he acted while knowing the matter of leaving leftover water. Despite this, his disciples claimed it was an illegal act (adhamma-kamma) only because they were biased (chandāgati) toward their teacher. Therefore, if the Blessed One had said to those monks (the Suttantadhara monk and his disciples), "Your teacher is one who has committed an offense. You are acting out of bias," then those monks might harbor a grudge against the Blessed One, thinking, "The Blessed One is a partisan of those Vinayadhara monks," and thus increase their unwholesome states and go to a state of misery.

Therefore, it should be specially noted that the Blessed One did not preach words of blame to the monks of either side, but instead preached the Dhamma of Saṅgha harmony (Saṅgha-sāmaggi) to both sides as described, and then rose from his seat and departed.

## Preaching the Two Kinds of Nānāsaṃvāsa and Two Kinds of Samānasaṃvāsa

At that time, the followers of the suspended monk performed the Uposatha and Saṅgha-kamma within the boundary (sīmā) of that very monastery. The monks who performed the suspension (ukkhepaka) went outside the boundary to perform the Uposatha and Saṅgha-kamma.

Then, a monk from the group of suspending monks approached the Blessed One, paid respectful homage, and sat in a suitable place. He addressed the Blessed One—
737:
"Venerable Sir, those followers of the suspended monk are performing the Uposatha and other formal acts of the Saṅgha within the boundary in that very monastery. We, the suspending monks, go outside the boundary to perform the Uposatha and other formal acts of the Saṅgha."

Then the Blessed One addressed that monk:

"Bhikkhu, if those followers of the suspended monk perform the Uposatha and other formal acts of the Saṅgha within the boundary in that very monastery according to the motion and proclamation (ñattikammavācā) prescribed by me, those acts performed by them will be lawful (dhammika).

Bhikkhu, if you (the suspending monks) perform the Uposatha and other formal acts of the Saṅgha within the boundary in that very monastery, those acts performed by you will also be lawful.

Why is that? It is because those followers of the suspended monk are of separate communion (nānāsaṃvāsa) from you, and you are of separate communion from those followers of the suspended monk.

## Two Ways of Being of Separate Communion (Nānāsaṃvāsaka)

Bhikkhu, there are two ways by which one becomes of separate communion: (1) One himself
738:
makes himself of separate communion; (2) A unified Saṅgha carries out the act of suspension (ukkhepaniya-kamma) against that monk for not seeing an offense, or for not making amends for an offense, or for not renouncing a wrong view. These are the two.

## Two Ways of Being of Common Communion (Samānasaṃvāsaka)

Bhikkhu, there are two ways by which one becomes of common communion: (1) One himself makes himself of common communion; (2) A unified Saṅgha, having revoked the act of suspension already carried out, performs the act of reinstatement (osāraṇā) to bring that monk back into the Saṅgha. These are the two."

Thus, he taught the two ways of being of separate communion and the two ways of being of common communion.

(In this context: "One himself makes himself of separate communion or common communion" means: when there are two factions—the proponents of Dhamma (dhammavādī) who carried out the suspension and the proponents of non-Dhamma (adhammavādī) who were suspended—if a monk, residing with either faction, listens to the views of both sides and resolves in his mind, "These suspended monks are proponents of non-Dhamma; the monks who carried out the suspension are proponents of Dhamma," then he has made himself of separate communion with the adhammavādī monks and of common communion with the dhammavādī monks. — From Samantapāsādikā, Vol. 3, p. 432).
739:
## Preaching on How to Live During a Schism in the Saṅgha

At that time, monks were engaging in disputes, quarrels, and contentious speech in the village refectory. They committed improper physical and verbal acts toward one another, and even resorted to physical violence. People criticized them, and the conscientious (lajjī) monks reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One summoned and questioned those monks, rebuked them, and preached a Dhamma suitable for the occasion, saying to the monks:

"Bhikkhus, when there is a schism in the Saṅgha and they act illegally without harmony, one should sit in a place thinking, 'At least this much will prevent us from committing improper physical and verbal acts toward one another, and from resorting to physical violence.' (This means: if there is a schism and illegal acts are being performed competitively such that harmony cannot be achieved at all, two separate rows of monks should be formed, and they should stay far enough apart—leaving the immediate vicinity (upacāra)—so that they cannot commit improper physical or verbal acts or resort to physical violence.)

Bhikkhus, even when there is a schism in the Saṅgha, if they act legally and are joyful, they should sit one seat apart."

Thus he preached on how to live during a schism in the Saṅgha.
740: ## Preaching the Dīghāvu-vatthu. At that time, the monks were engaged in quarreling, brawling, and disputing in the midst of the Saṅgha, attacking one another with the weapons of the tongue. Those monks were unable to settle that legal issue. Then, a certain monk approached the Blessed One, paid homage to the Blessed One, and after sitting in a suitable place, informed the Blessed One of this matter and requested Him to go to those monks. The Blessed One went there in person, sat on the prepared seat, and addressed those monks: "Enough, monks! Do not quarrel, do not brawl, do not contend, do not dispute." At that time, a certain unrighteous monk, a follower of one who had been expelled, who yet wished for the Blessed One's welfare, said to the Blessed One: "Wait, Blessed One, Lord of the Dhamma. Blessed One, please dwell at ease, devoted to your own happiness in this very life. We shall be known for this quarreling, brawling, contention, and dispute."
741:
For the second time, the Blessed One spoke to those monks in the same manner as before. The unrighteous monk who was a follower of the suspended monk also prohibited and addressed the Blessed One for the second time in the same way.

(In this matter: The unrighteous monk who followed the suspended monk actually wished for the Blessed One's welfare. His intention was: "These monks of both sides are burning with intense anger and will not listen to the words of the Blessed One. Let the Blessed One not weary himself by trying to admonish these monks." For this reason, he pleaded and prohibited the Blessed One twice.

The Blessed One, however, reflected and knew: "Although these monks of both sides are burning with intense anger and will not listen now, they will remember later and refrain from quarrels and disputes." Out of compassion for those monks, he preached the Dīghāvu-vatthu Jātaka, an event from the past.)

## The Story of Dīghāvu

Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Bhikkhus, in the past, there was a king of Kāsi named Brahmadatta in the city of Vārāṇasī. He was wealthy, with great possessions and wealth, and had a large army of elephants, horses, and chariots. He had a vast kingdom with full treasuries and granaries. But the king of Kosala named Dīghīti was poor, with little possessions and wealth, and had a small army of elephants, horses, and chariots. He had a small kingdom with empty treasuries and granaries.

Bhikkhus, at that time, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi prepared a large fourfold army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, and marched toward King Dīghīti of Kosala."
742:
Having prepared a great army, he marched directly towards King Dīghīti of Kosala.

## Relinquishing Pride when Powerless
Monks, when King Dīghīti of Kosala heard that news, he thought: "King Brahmadatta of Kāsi is wealthy, with great riches and possessions; he has many soldiers, elephants, horses, and chariots. He possesses a vast kingdom with overflowing treasuries and granaries. I, however, am poor, with few riches and possessions; I have few soldiers, elephants, horses, and chariots. I possess a small kingdom with treasuries and granaries that are not full. I am not able to withstand even a single attack from King Brahmadatta of Kāsi. It would be better if I were to flee from the city beforehand." Having thus considered, he took his chief queen and fled from the city beforehand.

Monks, then King Brahmadatta of Kāsi easily conquered and took possession of King Dīghīti's soldiers, elephants, horses, chariots, and the countryside, as well as the treasuries and granaries, and he reigned over them. Monks, then King Dīghīti of Kosala, together with his chief queen, set out towards the city of Vārāṇasī. In due course, having reached Vārāṇasī, he lived in disguise, wearing the clothes of a wandering ascetic (paribbājaka), in a potter's hut on the outskirts of the city.

## The Pregnancy and Cravings of Dīghāvu's Mother
Monks, thereafter, the chief queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala soon became pregnant. To that queen, (a craving arose) at sunrise to see a fourfold army in battle array...
743:
## The Great Wise and Loyal Chaplain

At that time, a friend of King Dīghīti of Kosala was serving as the chief chaplain (purohita) to King Brahmadatta of Kāsi. Bhikkhus, then King Dīghīti of Kosala went to his friend, the chief chaplain, and said: "O friend, your friend, the queen, is pregnant. These two cravings have arisen in her: (1) the desire to see a fourfold army, fully equipped in battle array, standing on level ground at sunrise; and (2) the desire to drink the water used for washing the swords." When he said this, the chaplain replied: "O Great King, if that is so, we also wish to see the queen."

Bhikkhus, then the chief queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala (according to the chaplain's wish)—
744: Monks, then the queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala went to the presence of the court chaplain. The chaplain saw the queen coming from afar, rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and with joined palms towards the queen, uttered this exclamation three times: "Friends, a King of Kosala has taken conception in the mother's womb! Friends, a King of Kosala has taken conception in the mother's womb!" Then he said: "Be joyful, O Queen! At sunrise, you shall see a fourfold army fully arrayed on level ground, and you shall drink the water from washing the swords." Monks, then the court chaplain approached King Brahmadatta of Kāsi and said: "Your Majesty, omens have appeared as I shall describe. Tomorrow at sunrise, let a fourfold army stand fully arrayed on level ground, and let the swords be washed." King Brahmadatta ordered his ministers: "Friends, do as the court chaplain has said." Monks, the queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala then saw the fourfold army at sunrise and drank the water from washing the swords (as arranged by the chaplain). Monks, then the queen of King Dīghīti of Kosala
745:
—reached the full term of her pregnancy and gave birth to a son. They named the prince "Dīghāvu."

Bhikkhus, when Prince Dīghāvu reached the age of intelligence and wisdom, a thought occurred to King Dīghīti of Kosala: "This King Brahmadatta of Kāsi has caused us much harm. He has destroyed and plundered our army, territory, treasuries, and granaries. If this king finds out about us, he will have all three of us killed. It would be better if I were to have my son Dīghāvu live outside the city (separated from us)." Having thought thus, he had his son Dīghāvu live outside the city. Bhikkhus, while living outside the city, Prince Dīghāvu soon mastered all the arts and sciences.

## The Ungrateful Barber

Bhikkhus, at that time, the former barber of King Dīghīti of Kosala was still in the service of King Brahmadatta of Kāsi. Bhikkhus, that former barber of King Dīghīti saw King Dīghīti and his queen living in disguise, wearing the clothes of wandering ascetics, in the potter's house (pottery hut) on the outskirts of Vārāṇasī. Upon seeing them, he went to King Brahmadatta of Kāsi and reported: "O Great King, King Dīghīti of Kosala and his queen are living in disguise, wearing the clothes of wandering ascetics, in the potter's house on the outskirts of this city of Vārāṇasī."
746:
Monks, then King Brahmadatta of Kāsi commanded his men, "Friends, if that is so, bring King Dīghīti of Kosala together with his queen (before me)." The men, according to King Brahmadatta's command, brought King Dīghīti of Kosala and his queen to King Brahmadatta.

Monks, then King Brahmadatta of Kāsi commanded his men, "Friends, if that is so, bind King Dīghīti and his queen tightly with their hands behind their backs with a strong rope, shave their heads with a razor, and parading them from street to street and from crossroad to crossroad while beating a harsh-sounding drum, lead them out through the south gate. To the south of the city, cut them into four pieces and throw the remains to the four directions."

Monks, those men, obeying King Brahmadatta's command, bound King Dīghīti and his queen tightly with their hands behind their backs with a strong rope, shaved their heads with a razor, and paraded them from street to street and from crossroad to crossroad (beating and striking them) while beating a harsh-sounding drum.

## The Instruction of the King of Kosala for the Cessation of Enmity

Monks, then Prince Dīghāvu thought, "It has been a long time since I have seen my mother and father. It would be good if I could see them." While entering the city of Vārāṇasī, he saw his parents being led by the king's men,
747:
bound tightly with their hands behind their backs with a strong rope, their heads shaved with a razor, being paraded from street to street and from crossroad to crossroad (being beaten and struck) while a harsh-sounding drum was beaten. Seeing this, he suppressed his grief and approached his mother and father.

Monks, King Dīghīti saw Prince Dīghāvu coming from afar. Upon seeing him, he spoke these four lines of instruction for the cessation of enmity to Prince Dīghāvu skillfully:

"Dear Dīghāvu, do not look far; do not look short.
Dear Dīghāvu, hatreds are never settled by hatred.
Dear Dīghāvu, hatreds are settled only by non-hatred."

Monks, when King Dīghīti had spoken thus, those king's men said to him:

"This King Dīghīti is mad and talking nonsense. Who is this Dīghāvu, his son? To whom is this King Dīghīti saying, 'Dear Dīghāvu, do not look far; do not look short. Dear Dīghāvu, hatreds are never settled by hatred. Dear Dīghāvu, hatreds are settled only by non-hatred'?"

Then King Dīghīti said to those men:
748:
"Friends, I am not mad or talking nonsense. Indeed, the wise will understand the meaning of my words."

Monks, for a second time, King Dīghīti spoke the same instruction referring to his son Dīghāvu, and the men spoke their misunderstanding as before, and he explained in the same way. For a third time, King Dīghīti spoke the same instruction referring to his son Dīghāvu, and the men spoke their misunderstanding as before, and he had to explain in the same way.

Monks, then those king's men paraded King Dīghīti and his queen from street to street and from crossroad to crossroad (beating and striking them), led them out through the south gate, and to the south of the city, they cut them into four pieces and threw the remains to the four directions. Having stationed a guard, they returned to the city.

## Prince Dīghāvu's Skillful Arrangement

Monks, then Prince Dīghāvu entered the city of Vārāṇasī, brought strong liquor, and gave it to the guards to drink. When the guards became intoxicated and fell down, Prince Dīghāvu gathered wood, made a pyre, placed the remains of his mother and father upon the pyre, and after cremating them,
749:
he circumambulated the pyre three times to the right with joined palms.

## King Brahmadatta's Great Terror

At that time, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, while staying in the upper story of his golden palace, saw Prince Dīghāvu circumambulating the pyre three times to the right with joined palms. He thought, "That person must surely be a relative or kinsman of King Dīghīti. Alas, that person will surely bring me harm, yet no one has come to inform me about him." Thinking thus, he was struck with great terror.

## Prince Dīghāvu Serving as an Elephant Groom

Monks, thereafter, Prince Dīghāvu went to the forest and wept as much as he desired. Then, wiping away his tears, he entered the city of Vārāṇasī, went to the elephant stable near the palace, and requested the elephant trainer, "Teacher, I wish to learn the elephant craft." The elephant trainer replied, "Young man, if you wish to learn the elephant craft, then learn it."

Monks, then Prince Dīghāvu rose early at dawn and, sitting in the elephant stable, sang with a melodious voice. He also played the lute. Monks, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, having risen early at dawn, heard the sound of the singing and the lute from the elephant stable and asked his men,
750:
"Friends, who is it that rises early at dawn and, staying in the elephant stable, sings with such a melodious voice and plays the lute?" The men replied, "Your Majesty, the one who rises early at dawn and, staying in the elephant stable, sings with a melodious voice and plays the lute is the young apprentice of the elephant trainer of such-and-such name." King Brahmadatta then commanded, "Friends, if that is so, bring that young man to me."

## Prince Dīghāvu Becoming an Inner Servant

Monks, those men replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and brought Prince Dīghāvu to King Brahmadatta. The King asked Prince Dīghāvu, "Young man, are you the one who rises early at dawn and, staying in the elephant stable, sings with a melodious voice and plays the lute?" When Prince Dīghāvu admitted it was so, the King commanded again, "Young man, if that is so, then sing and play the lute."

Monks, then Prince Dīghāvu replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and sang and played the lute with a melodious voice to the King's great satisfaction. The King was so pleased that he said, "Young man, you shall serve me." Prince Dīghāvu replied, "Very well,
751:
"Yes, your majesty," he replied. Thereafter, by serving King Brahmadatta with these five qualities: (1) rising before him, (2) going to sleep after him, (3) always waiting for orders on what should be done, (4) acting to please the king, and (5) speaking endearingly—King Brahmadatta of Kāsi soon appointed Prince Dīghāvu to the position of a trusted confidant (bodyguard).

## Prince Dīghāvu Respecting His Father's Words
Monks, then one day, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi said to Prince Dīghāvu, "Dear youth, harness the chariot; we shall go to the deer forest." Prince Dīghāvu replied, "Very well, your majesty," and having harnessed the chariot, he informed him, "Your majesty, the chariot is ready for you. Now, your majesty may go at your convenience."

Then King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, having mounted the chariot, set out for a royal hunt accompanied by his army. Prince Dīghāvu drove the chariot in such a way that the king was separated from the army. Monks, when they had reached a distant place, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi said to Prince Dīghāvu, "Dear youth, since we are far from the army, unharness the chariot. I am very tired; I shall lie down for a while." Prince Dīghāvu, following the king's command...
752:
unharnessed the chariot and sat down cross-legged on the ground. Monks, then King Brahmadatta of Kāsi laid his head on Prince Dīghāvu's lap and fell asleep. Being very exhausted, he fell into a deep sleep in a short moment.

Monks, while the King was asleep, this thought arose in Prince Dīghāvu's mind:

"This King Brahmadatta of Kāsi has done us much harm. This king destroyed and plundered our army of elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as our districts, treasuries, and granaries. This very king also killed my mother and father. Now is the time for me to take my revenge."

Thinking thus, he drew his sword from its scabbard. Monks, then another thought occurred to Prince Dīghāvu:

"My father, the King, at the time of his death, told me, 'Dear Dīghāvu, do not look far; do not look short. Dear Dīghāvu, hatreds are never settled by hatred. Dear Dīghāvu, hatreds are settled only by non-hatred.' It is not proper for me to transgress my father's words."

Having thought this, he put the sword back into its scabbard.
753:
Monks, for a second and third time, the same thought of revenge arose in him, and he drew the sword from its scabbard. Then, remembering what his father the King had instructed, he put the sword back into its scabbard.
Monks, at that time, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi woke up suddenly from his bed, trembling with fear and agitation. Monks, then Prince Dīghāvu asked King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, 'O King, why have you risen so suddenly from your bed, trembling with fear and agitation?' King Brahmadatta of Kāsi replied, 'Young man, just now in a dream, Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti Kosala, was chasing me with a sword. Therefore, I woke up suddenly, trembling with fear and agitation.'
Monks, then Prince Dīghāvu seized King Brahmadatta of Kāsi by the head with his left hand, drew his sword with his right hand, and said to King Brahmadatta, 'O King, I am that Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti Kosala. You have done us great harm. You have destroyed and plundered our army of elephants, horses, and chariots, our territories, our treasuries, and our granaries. You have also killed my mother and father. Now is the time for me to take my revenge!'
754:
Monks, then King Brahmadatta of Kāsi bowed at the feet of Prince Dīghāvu and said, 'Dear Dīghāvu, grant me my life! Dear Dīghāvu, grant me my life!' Then Prince Dīghāvu said, 'O King, how could I be able to grant you your life? It is only you, O King, who can grant me my life.' King Brahmadatta of Kāsi then said, 'Dear Dīghāvu, if that is so, then you grant me my life, and I shall grant you your life.' Monks, then King Brahmadatta of Kāsi and Prince Dīghāvu granted each other their lives. They took each other's hands and made a bond of friendship, swearing an oath not to harm one another.
Monks, after the King and the Prince had granted each other life, taken hands, and sworn an oath, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi said to Prince Dīghāvu, 'Dear Dīghāvu, if that is so, harness the chariot; let us return.' Prince Dīghāvu replied, 'Very well, O King,' and having harnessed the chariot, he said, 'O King, the chariot is ready for you. Now you know the time to depart (it is as you wish).'
755:
## Returning to the City
Monks, when King Brahmadatta of Kāsi had mounted the chariot, Prince Dīghāvu drove the chariot and soon met with the army. Monks, then King Brahmadatta of Kāsi, surrounded by his great army, entered the city of Vārāṇasī. He summoned his ministers and assembly and asked them, 'Friends, if you were to find Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti Kosala, now, what would you do?'
Some ministers said, 'O King, we would cut off his hands.' Others said, 'O King, we would cut off his feet.' Some said, 'O King, we would cut off his hands and feet.' Some said, 'O King, we would cut off his ears.' Some said, 'O King, we would cut off his nose.' Some said, 'O King, we would cut off his ears and nose.' Others said, 'O King, we would cut off his head.' Thus they spoke according to the King's perceived desire. Then King Brahmadatta of Kāsi declared:
'Friends, this is that Prince Dīghāvu, the son of King Dīghīti Kosala (pointing to the prince). Nothing more can be done to this Prince Dīghāvu. This Prince Dīghāvu has granted me my life, and I have granted this Prince Dīghāvu his life.'
756:
## Prince Dīghāvu Explaining the Dhamma of Ending Enmity
Monks, then King Brahmadatta of Kāsi asked Prince Dīghāvu:

"Dear Dīghāvu, when your father was about to die, he instructed: (1) 'Dear Dīghāvu, do not look far, (2) do not look short, (3) dear Dīghāvu, hatred is not stilled by hatred, (4) dear Dīghāvu, hatred is stilled only by non-hatred.' With what intention did your father give these instructions?"

Then Prince Dīghāvu said to King Brahmadatta:

(1) "Your majesty, when my father said 'Do not look far' at the time of his death, he meant 'Do not keep a grudge for a long time.' It was with this meaning, your majesty, that my father said 'Do not look far' before he died.

(2) "Your majesty, when my father said 'Do not look short' at the time of his death, he meant 'Do not be quick to break with friends.' It was with this meaning, your majesty, that my father said 'Do not look short' before he died."
757:
(3-4) 'O King, when my father said "Dear Dīghāvu, enmity is not stilled by revenge; Dear Dīghāvu, enmity is stilled only by non-revenge," he meant: If I, thinking that the King killed my mother and father, were to kill the King, then those who wish for the King's welfare would kill me. Then those who wish for my welfare would kill them in return. If we were to continue killing each other in revenge, that enmity would never be stilled.
But now, the King has granted me my life, and I have granted the King his life. Thus, by granting each other life and not seeking revenge, that enmity has been stilled forever. O King, it was with this meaning that my father said "Dear Dīghāvu, enmity is not stilled by revenge; Dear Dīghāvu, enmity is stilled only by non-revenge."'
Thus he preached and explained the Dhamma of ending enmity as instructed by his father.
(With this principle in mind, the wise of old left these words of advice:
1. Do not prolong the threads of enmity.
2. Do not shorten the threads of friendship.)
758:
3. Only through non-hatred is enmity destroyed.
4. If one seeks revenge, enmity only increases—
(Thus they left these words of Dhamma advice.)

## Prince Dīghāvu Regaining His Father's Royal Inheritance
Monks, when Prince Dīghāvu had thus explained the Dhamma of ending enmity, King Brahmadatta of Kāsi praised him, saying: "Friends, how wonderful! Friends, how extraordinary! This Prince Dīghāvu is indeed very wise, for he knows how to explain in detail the meaning of the words his father left in brief." He then returned to Prince Dīghāvu his father King Dīghīti's property—the soldiers, elephants, horses, chariots, and the countryside, as well as the treasuries and granaries—and also gave him his daughter, who had reached marriageable age.

## The Buddha's Admonition
Monks, if such patience and forbearance can exist even among those kings who carry sticks and swords, then monks, in this Dispensation of mine, where the Dhamma is so well-proclaimed as being good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, if you who have entered the monkhood are not patient and do not live in harmony, would such lack of patience and harmony be fitting in this Dispensation? (It would certainly not be fitting.) Having given this profound admonition, the Blessed One spoke for the third time...
759:
'Dear monks, it is not proper, it is not right. Do not engage in disputes! Do not engage in quarrels! Do not engage in offensive and contradictory speech!'
Even when he spoke for the last time, that unrighteous monk who followed the suspended one said to the Blessed One:
'Lord, let the Blessed One, the Lord of Dhamma, wait. Lord, let the Blessed One dwell at ease, devoted to the happiness of the present. We will be known by this disputing, quarreling, and offensive, contradictory speech.'
Then the Blessed One thought, 'These hollow men, who have not attained the paths or fruits and whose tasks are unfinished, are of a nature to be spiritually barren. It is not easy to make these monks understand.' Having taken this to heart, he rose from his seat and departed.
The Story of Dīghāvu ends.
(Note: This story of Dīghāvu is extracted from the Kosambaka-kkhandhaka of the Vinaya Mahāvagga. This story also appears in the Dīghīti-kosala Jātaka of the Pañcaka Nipāta and the Kosambiya Jātaka of the Navaka Nipāta in verse form; for the researcher who desires...)
760:
760
(The noble ones should also observe and note those Nipātas and Jātakas).

## The Exhortation of the Ten Verses (Gāthādasa Ovāda Desanā)

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One entered the city of Kosambī for alms. When he had finished his meal and returned from the alms-round, he put away his bedding, took up his bowl and robe himself, and while standing in the midst of the Saṅgha (just as he was about to depart), he delivered this exhortation of ten verses:

Many are the voices, like common folk;
No one thinks, "I am a fool."
Even when the Saṅgha is being divided,
They do not think of anything else (such as "The Saṅgha is divided because of me"). (1)

(This group of monks is harsh in body and speech). They have many voices and loud sounds. They are all of the same impure mind. (In that group of monks), not even one thinks or sees, "I am a fool with little wisdom." Furthermore, even when the Saṅgha is being divided and broken, they do not realize or see any other reason, such as "The Saṅgha has been divided because of me."

Forgetful, yet appearing like the wise,
They speak only of what leads to quarrels.
They open their mouths as wide as they wish;
