They do not know that they are being led by that (anger). (2)
761:
761
(These monks are harsh in body and speech). They are greatly forgetful and lack mindfulness, yet they act as if they were wise. Their speech is centered only on the object of causing quarrels. (This means they do not have the objects of meditation as their focus). Without shame or fear, they open their mouths as wide as they wish and speak words of conflict. (This means not a single monk remains silent out of respect for the Saṅgha). They do not realize that they are being led by that very anger of quarreling to a state of shamelessness. They do not see that "This is indeed a fault."

"He abused me, he struck me,
He defeated me, he robbed me."
In those who harbor such thoughts,
Hatred is never stilled. (3)

Even those who unthinkingly harbor such thoughts as: "(This person) has previously spoken words of abuse to me. (This person) has previously oppressed and ill-treated me. (This person) has previously overcome and bullied me. (This person) has previously stolen my (wealth)." By holding such thoughts in their hearts, they repeatedly bind themselves to that anger of quarreling without reconciliation. For them, hatred can never be stilled until the end of the world.
762:
762
"He abused me, he struck me,
He defeated me, he robbed me."
In those who do not harbor such thoughts,
Hatred is stilled. (4)

In those virtuous ones who do not unthinkingly harbor such thoughts as: "(This person) has previously spoken words of abuse to me. (This person) has previously oppressed and ill-treated me. (This person) has previously overcome and bullied me. (This person) has previously stolen my (wealth)." By reflecting on kamma and not letting the mind dwell on it, and by not repeatedly binding themselves to that anger of quarreling, hatred—which wishes for harm—is stilled and extinguished in those virtuous ones with clear hearts, just as a fire is extinguished when it runs out of fuel.

For hatred is never stilled by hatred
In this world at any time.
By non-hatred alone is it stilled;
This is an eternal law. (5)

In this world, hatreds that wish for harm are never stilled at any of the three times by retaliating with hatred. Just as filth cannot be washed away with filth, there is no nature of peace in it. By non-hatred alone—through the practice of patience (khantī) and loving-kindness (mettā)—is it stilled and extinguished, just as filth is washed away with clear water. This nature of stilling hatred through these two qualities of patience and loving-kindness is an ancient and eternal law.
763:
763
It is the noble path (Dhamma) trodden by the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas of the past.

Others do not realize
That we must all die here.
Those who realize this,
Their quarrels are stilled. (6)

In the midst of this large assembly of the Saṅgha, those monks who lack wisdom and engage in quarrels do not realize, "We are moving towards the presence of the King of Death at every moment," because their eye of wisdom is closed. However, those wise monks in that large assembly who possess brilliant wisdom realize clearly, with the presence of mindfulness of death (maraṇassati), that "We must go to the presence of the King of Death at every moment." Because of such realization, their quarrels and disputes are cut off and stilled through the practice of right conduct (sammā-paṭipatti).

Even those who break bones and take lives,
Who steal cattle, horses, and wealth,
Who plunder the kingdom—
Even for them, there can be reconciliation.
Why should it not be so for you? (7)

Even for those kings who break the bones of their parents, who take lives in a fit of rage, who ruthlessly plunder and take cattle, horses, wealth, and treasures, and who forcibly seize the kingdom belonging to their fathers—even for such enemies...
764:
764
...reconciliation and peace can still occur. Why then, for all of you monks, who are the beloved sons born of my Dhamma, should reconciliation and peace not be possible? It certainly should be possible.

If one finds a prudent companion,
A wise fellow-traveler of good conduct,
One should wander with them, joyful and mindful,
Overcoming all dangers. (8)

A mindful person, if they should find a companion who is a fellow-traveler in the Dhamma, who is of good conduct through the practice of the three trainings (sikkhā), who is firm and stable in concentration (samādhi), and who is a prudent person with quick and sharp wisdom—with such a fellow-traveler in the Dhamma, one should wander and practice the Dhamma with a joyful and satisfied heart, overcoming all various external dangers such as lions and tigers, and internal dangers such as greed, hatred, and delusion.

If one does not find a prudent companion,
A wise fellow-traveler of good conduct,
Like a king renouncing a conquered kingdom,
One should wander alone like a Mātaṅga elephant in the forest. (9)

(A mindful person should follow this). If one should not find a fellow-traveler in the Dhamma...
765:
765
...who is of good conduct through the practice of the three trainings, who is firm and stable in concentration, and who is a prudent person with quick and sharp wisdom—if such a companion is not found, then like King Mahājanaka or King Arindama who renounced their conquered kingdoms to become monks, or like a great elephant of the Mātaṅga breed, one should wander alone and practice the Dhamma in the deep forest away from people.

Better is the life of one wandering alone;
There is no companionship with a fool.
Let one wander alone and do no evil,
Carefree like a Mātaṅga elephant in the forest. (10)

The life of one wandering alone without a companion to practice the Dhamma is indeed praiseworthy and noble. In a fool, there is not even a trace of the group of trainings in virtue, concentration, and wisdom, which are the causes for the arising of both wisdom and faith. Just as a great elephant of the Mātaṅga breed wanders and lives carefreely in the deep forest away from people, so should one wander alone without a companion and live practicing the Dhamma. One should not commit any base or defiled evil deeds.
766:
766
The Blessed One, while still standing in the midst of the Saṅgha, preached these ten verses of Dhamma and then departed alone, without a companion, to the village of Bālakaloṇaka.
